title: Reconstruction of Dynamical Dark Energy and Gravity from latest cosmological data
text: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in non-standard late-time evolution. We investigate whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark energy density, $Ω_{\rm X}(a)$, and the gravitational response functions $μ(a)$ and $Σ(a)$. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+, and large scale structure observations, including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data, we perform reconstructions with and without a theory motivated correlation prior derived from stable Horndeski models. We find a persistent maximum in $Ω_{\rm X}$ at $z\simeq0.5$--$0.7$, corresponding to a crossing of the effective phantom divide. This feature is already present in the CMB+BAO combination and remains robust when modifications to clustering and lensing are allowed. The reconstructed gravitational response exhibits suggestive enhancements in $μ$ and $Σ$ over approximately the same redshift range, although these departures are less significant. Including LSS information instead favours a reduced lensing response, $Σ<1$, while leaving the background feature largely unchanged. An interpretation within Generalized Brans-Dicke theories illustrates how modifications to the effective gravitational coupling and a scalar-mediated fifth force may contribute to these trends. Our results indicate that current departures from $Λ$CDM are most significant in the expansion history, while leaving open the possibility of correlated modifications to gravitational dynamics that future Stage IV surveys can test.

title: Does Dark Energy Evolve $\textit{and}$ Cluster?
text: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in dynamical dark energy, and naturally raise the question of whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics. We address this question through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark-energy contribution to the expansion and the gravitational responses governing clustering and lensing, complemented by a combined covariance-mode analysis, without imposing model-specific relations between the sectors. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ supernova observations, and subsequently adding large scale structure observations including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data and other surveys, we recover a broad maximum in the effective dark-energy density near $z\simeq0.6$--$0.7$. The gravitational responses exhibit suggestive low-redshift enhancements over their GR values, approximately coincident with the background feature. Adding large scale structure information preserves the background feature but favours a mildly reduced lensing response. The combined covariance-mode analysis identifies the combinations of background and gravitational responses most tightly constrained by current observations and quantifies their departures from $Λ$CDM. The leading modes are decisively background dominated, while the gravitational sector remains less precisely constrained. Thus, present data cannot yet determine whether the suggestive low-redshift features in the two sectors share a common physical origin, a question that ongoing Stage-IV surveys will be able to address

title: Sharp nonuniqueness for the Vlasov--Navier--Stokes system
text: We consider the Vlasov--Navier--Stokes system on $\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$. For smooth data and every $p<2$, $q<\infty$, we construct infinitely many weak solutions with velocity in $L^p_tL^\infty\cap L^1_tW^{1,q}$ and bounded, renormalized distribution function; infinitely many of them violate the energy inequality. For smooth velocity data, weak solutions with velocity in $L^2_tL^\infty$ are unique, so the result is sharp at the endpoint of the Ladyzhenskaya--Prodi--Serrin scale. The fluid carries the nonuniqueness, through the convex integration scheme of Cheskidov and Luo, and the kinetic equation is solved exactly. The main new difficulty is the memory of the particles: the kinetic state at time $t$ depends on the whole past of the velocity, so a modification on a short interval changes the system at all later times. We overcome it by a causal gluing, carried out from left to right in time, which re-solves the system on every interval of regularity. This yields wild solutions that are strong outside a closed set of times of arbitrarily small Hausdorff dimension. A causal mollification extends the construction to rough data, including every finite-energy velocity datum in dimensions two and three; in two dimensions the energy class is thus exactly the borderline of uniqueness. Finally, in three dimensions we construct Leray solutions satisfying the strong energy inequality and show that they are strong outside a closed set of times of vanishing $\mathcal H^{1/2}$ measure.

title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
text: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.

title: JVT: Just Video Transformer makes pixel-space video diffusion simple
text: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.

title: Polynomial-Time Solvability of the Multi-Dimensional Slope Change Problem
text: Slope change detection seeks to identify changes in the trends of time-ordered signals. We study the problem of fitting a multidimensional time series by continuous piecewise-linear functions with a shared continuous breakpoint and unrestricted slopes. We consider both the dense setting, in which every dimension may change slope, and the sparse setting, in which at most $k$ dimensions may change slope. Although the resulting optimization problems are nonconvex mixed integer nonlinear programs and may have irrational optimal solutions even for rational data, we prove that all six variants, corresponding to the $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_\infty$ losses in both settings, are exactly solvable in polynomial time. For least-squares loss, we obtain efficient algorithms requiring $O(JT)$ operations in the dense setting and $O(J^2T\log J)$ operations in the sparse setting, where $T$ is the number of time points and $J$ is the number of dimensions. We implement these least-squares algorithms and evaluate them on simulated data and three real-world time series, namely, surface temperatures (ERA5), hand-tracking data from a mixed-reality headset (HoloAssist), and turbofan engine sensor data (NASA C-MAPSS). The dense algorithm solves instances with up to $J=10^5$ and $T=100$, that is, $10^7$ observations, in less than $0.1$ seconds on a laptop, while the sparse algorithm solves instances with about $10^3$ dimensions and up to $T=240$ in under a second. Compared with a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) formulation solved by Gurobi, our algorithms are several orders of magnitude faster (approximately $8.9 \times 10^3$ to $3.4 \times 10^6$ times) on instances where Gurobi terminates within its default optimality tolerance of $0.01\%$ optimality gap. On larger instances, Gurobi frequently reaches a 10,000-second time limit with substantial optimality gaps.

title: Modeling the Frictional Contact of Continuum Robots with Environments through Linear Complementarity Problem
text: Accurate friction modeling in continuum robots is essential for precise motion control and path planning. However, current approaches make predictions only for the mechanism's internal friction that is limited by the boundary forces of the Coulomb friction cone, which fail to characterize the static friction and motion hysteresis. In this paper, we propose a novel friction model based on complementarity constraints under the Coulomb friction assumption. This model predicts various friction effects caused by environmental interactions, including both static and sliding frictions and hysteresis behavior, as well as the corresponding robot deformation induced by these interactions, which are crucial for the practical motion planning and control of continuum robots. Additionally, real-time implementation of this model can be achieved, meeting the demand for computational efficiency in robotic applications. Experimental validations demonstrated that this model is able to reduce the maximum tip position error from 45.4 mm in the frictionless model to 5.85 mm in our friction-included model with a 287.9 mm-long tendon-driven continuum robot.

title: From smoothed analysis to backward error: The power of adaptive perturbations
text: Smoothed analysis has become a central tool in theoretical computer science, often allowing for significant improvements to worst-case running times if we settle for a solution to a small random perturbation of the problem instance. This is closely related to the classical concept of backward error in numerical analysis, which allows an algorithm to return a solution to an arbitrary perturbation of the problem. Despite the qualitative similarity of these concepts, we show that they can exhibit large quantitative differences. Notably, we prove that, while a linear system with any $n \times n$ matrix $A$ can be solved to backward error $ε$ using $O(\log(n) / ε)$ matrix-vector products with $A$, any algorithm that solves a random $ε$-sized perturbation of $A$ requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products. This means that a useful perturbation for solving a linear system in backward error must be adaptive to the input. Interestingly, however, randomness is still essential: we show that any deterministic method that attains small backward error for all linear systems provably requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products, resulting in the first separation between randomized and deterministic algorithms in a natural computational model for solving linear systems. Finally, we show that matrix structure can significantly affect backward error complexity. For example, we show a deterministic $O(1/ε)$ matrix-vector product algorithm for symmetric linear systems.

title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
text: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.

title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
text: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
text: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $π_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
text: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.

title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
text: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.

title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
text: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
text: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $κ$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $κ\rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $Θ(\logκ\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(κ, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
text: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.

title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism
text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Intercellular transfer of FOLR2 from nurse-like cells fuels chronic lymphocytic leukemia cell activation and proliferation
text: Communication with the lymphoid microenvironment is essential for the survival and proliferation of neoplastic B cells in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). While nurse-like cells (NLCs) are recognized as key components of this niche, the mechanisms and functional impact of their interactions with malignant cells remain insufficiently understood. Here, using primary patient cells, we found that NLCs express high levels of folate receptor beta (FOLR2), which correlate with increased survival of leukemic cells in vitro. Unexpectedly, we found that CLL cells acquire functional FOLR2 from NLCs via trogocytosis, enhancing their folate uptake. To further study the biological relevance of this phenomenon, we modeled lymphoid microenvironmental activation using CD40L and IL-15, which markedly increased FOLR2 transfer and induced robust NLC-dependent CLL cell activation and proliferation. These processes were closely associated, as FOLR2+ CLL cells represented the predominant population of actively cycling leukemic cells. Under the same conditions, we also observed an additional contact-independent mechanism of FOLR2 transfer, suggesting involvement of extracellular vesicles (EVs). To validate these findings in situ, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence analysis of CLL lymph nodes. This confirmed the presence of FOLR2⁺ NLCs and demonstrated their significant enrichment in more aggressive and proliferative cases. In addition, we detected FOLR2+ CLL cells in situ, supporting the occurrence of trogocytosis and possibly EVs mediated-transfer in the lymphoid microenvironment. Together, these results identify FOLR2 as a novel marker of protective NLCs and implicate trogocytosis with NLCs as an important mechanism that enhances CLL cell adaptation and promotes leukemic cell activation and proliferation.

title: KAS-CUT&Tag for direct mapping of transcription bubbles
text: Abstract Transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) generates dynamic transcription bubbles as it moves forward, but existing methods map transcriptional activity indirectly. Here we introduce KAS-CUT&Tag, a method that combines N 3 -kethoxal labeling of exposed single-stranded DNA with CUT&Tag to directly map transcription bubbles. Bubble density correlates with nascent transcription levels and varies across Pol II-bound genes at promoters, gene bodies and termination regions. Transcription bubbles are enriched at genes marked by active histone modifications H3K27ac, H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 and by chromatin-bound splicing factor U2AF2, but enrichment is highest at replication-coupled histone genes in K562 and GM12878 cells. KAS-CUT&Tag also detects co-occupancy of the histone gene transcription factor NPAT with Pol II at the histone locus body, suggesting that in these cells NPAT is juxtaposed to transcription bubbles via interaction with Pol II. Together, KAS-CUT&Tag enables direct mapping of Pol II and regulatory interactions at transcription bubbles, providing a powerful tool for precise analysis of transcriptional activity.

title: Enhancer-driven gene regulatory network of human forebrain development provides insights into autism
text: Cell differentiation is orchestrated by transcription factors binding to enhancers, shaping gene regulatory networks that drive neuronal lineage specification. Deciphering these enhancer-driven networks in human forebrain development is essential for understanding the genetic basis of neurodevelopmental disorders. Through integrative epigenomic and transcriptomic analyses of human forebrain organoids derived from 10 male individuals with autism spectrum disorder and their neurotypical fathers, we construct a comprehensive enhancer-driven gene regulatory network of early neurodevelopment. This network reveals hierarchical regulatory layers upstream of neuronal cell fate genes, experimentally validated via CRISPR interference and loss-of-function analyses. A subnetwork links autism-associated transcriptomic alterations to opposite activities of the transcription factors FOXG1, BHLHE22, EOMES, and NEUROD2, driving increased or decreased excitatory neuron specification in (respectively) macrocephalic or normocephalic individuals with autism. These findings support the association of autism with disruption of enhancer-driven regulatory networks altering neuronal cell fate decisions in the developing fetal brain. The authors construct a gene regulatory network showing the potential role of specific enhancer elements in driving lineage imbalance in autism, explaining why forebrain organoids from autism probands show heterogeneity in the generation of excitatory neurons.

title: Soil storage and growth media shape culture-based recovery of pyrophilous bacteria and fungi from burned soils
text: Increasingly frequent and severe fires worldwide underscore the need to understand how pyrophilous microbes survive, thrive, and drive post-fire ecosystem regeneration. However, characterizing their traits through omics and phenotypic assays is limited by the lack of cultured isolates. Here, we collected burned soils after a severe California shrubland wildfire and used a culturomics approach to test how culture media type and soil storage method affected the abundance and diversity of pyrophilous bacteria and fungi. Using fresh soils, we compared three media types: rich media (Lysogeny Broth [LB] for bacteria; Malt Yeast Agar [MYA] for fungi), oligotrophic Reasoner’s 2A (R2A), and a newly developed pyrogenic organic matter (PyOM) media. We also evaluated four soil storage methods using rich media: air-drying, refrigeration at 4°C, and freezing at –80°C with or without glycerol. R2A recovered the greatest richness of bacterial and fungal genera, although PyOM medium isolated several taxa not recovered on other media. For bacteria, freezing soils at –80°C without glycerol preserved the greatest genus richness, whereas freezing with glycerol preserved the greatest species richness. For fungi, freezing at –80°C without glycerol preserved the most species while maintaining genus richness comparable to fresh and refrigerated soils. These findings guided the development of a culture collection of more than 500 pyrophilous bacterial and fungal isolates. Lessons learned from media type and soil storage can also be applied to the cultivation of environmental soil microbes from many habitat types and improve culture collections of fastidious microbes.

title: Epithelium stratifies via nucleation and growth induced by foam-geometric instability
text: Epithelial stratification, the transition from a monolayer to a multilayer structure, occurs across a wide range of phenomena. Recent studies have identified several cell behaviors as triggers, including junctional tension, cell density and geometry, and topological defects. However, how these factors drive stratification throughout the entire epithelium remains poorly understood. Here, we show that epithelial stratification proceeds through a nucleation-and-growth mechanism. Combining cell culture with three-dimensional vertex modeling, we demonstrate that multilayer origins emerge in a dispersed manner and expand across the epithelium through disordered intermediate states. This transition is induced by a mechanical instability inherent in the foam-like geometry of the epithelium. Moreover, the nucleation-growth concept applies to embryonic skin development and intestinal cancer transformation. These findings conceptualize epithelial stratification as a form of structural transition governed by foam mechanics, offering a physical perspective on various epithelial developments.

title: Beyond biochemical recovery: Persistent molecular and cellular states after acute hepatotoxic injury
text: BACKGROUND: Recovery from acute hepatotoxic injury (AHTI), including drug-induced liver injury, is conventionally defined by normalization of serum biomarkers and resolution of clinical and histopathological abnormalities. However, biochemical normalization may not reflect structural and functional restitution of the hepatic microenvironment. METHODS: This hypothesis-driven narrative review brings together findings from experimental and translational evidence on molecular and cellular alterations persisting after AHTI. It distinguishes established findings from proposed mechanisms and long-term consequences, emphasizing limitations in evidence regarding clinical significance. RESULTS: Emerging studies demonstrate that molecular, cellular, and spatial alterations may persist after serum biomarkers normalize. Regeneration driven by oxidative stress, replicative demand, metabolic rewiring, and developmental pathway reactivation restores tissue mass but may reshape clonal dynamics and leave spatially restricted molecular imprints. These alterations involve hepatocytes and non-parenchymal cells, including hepatic stellate cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells. Whether persistent signatures reflect adaptive remodeling, delayed resolution, or stable scarring remains unclear. Although clinical evidence has not established whether resolved AHTI alters susceptibility to a subsequent "second hit," incomplete molecular resolution challenges definitions of hepatic resilience. Current findings derive predominately from intrinsic toxicity models and should not be extrapolated across etiologies without direct comparison. CONCLUSION: Persistent molecular scars suggest that biochemical normalization does not indicate complete hepatic recovery. Integrating spatial and single-cell modalities into toxicology frameworks may improve post-injury monitoring, identify biomarkers of resolution, and inform regulatory safety standards. Because human liver tissue is rarely accessible for these analyses, clinical translation will likely require minimally invasive approaches, including circulating biomarkers and extracellular vesicles.

title: Automated Flow Synthesis of Combinatorial Protein‐Length Polyamide Libraries
text: ABSTRACT Flow synthesis with building block mixtures permits the generation of hypervariable polyamide libraries with up to quintillions (10 18 ) of sequence‐defined compounds per pooled mixture on a timescale of < 1 h per synthesis. The semi‐automated flow platform on which we have previously developed this technique, however, lacks the efficiency required to make protein‐length polyamide chains. To facilitate the direct engraftment of variable regions into longer polyamide chains, we adapted mixture‐based library synthesis to automated flow peptide synthesis (AFPS) systems previously optimized for the production of 100‐200‐mer synthetic proteins. Using this approach, we demonstrate the single‐shot synthesis of a 101‐mer model library with empirically estimated content approaching quintillions of members composed of both L‐ and D‐amino acid building blocks. AFPS thus permits the incorporation of hypervariable polyamide libraries into synthetic protein‐length polyamide scaffolds, expanding accessible combinatorial space in protein‐length synthetic chains by orders of magnitude while retaining synthetic control for application to affinity selection‐mass spectrometry workflows.

title: BioLM-Score: Language-Prior Conditioned Probabilistic Geometric Potentials for Protein-Ligand Scoring
text: Abstract Motivation Protein-ligand scoring must address affinity prediction, pose selection, and virtual screening, but these objectives are not necessarily optimized together. Geometric likelihood models may generalize poorly when training-set structural coverage is limited. We test whether pretrained biomolecular representations improve scoring under a controlled geometric baseline. Results BioLM-Score integrates frozen protein and molecular language-model embeddings into a residue-atom distance-likelihood framework via gated graph convolutions. We evaluate geometry-only, jointly trained, and two-stage fine-tuned variants, using the jointly trained variant for the primary controlled comparisons. All three DEKOIS 2.0 screening endpoints improve over the matched geometric baseline with target-level paired support, but affinity scoring and ranking do not improve uniformly. Under a time-split protocol, scoring is significantly lower and ranking is also lower than the geometric baseline, while screening gains persist. On BDB2020+, the difference in affinity correlation between BioLM-Score and GenScore narrows after LP-PDBBind-compatible retraining. Shuffling protein embeddings at inference reduces the screening advantage. However, retrained shuffle controls recover much of the performance, so correct alignment is not established as necessary. BioLM-Score strengthens geometric scoring on screening tasks without retraining the language models. Availability and implementation Code, dataset-split identifiers, preprocessing and evaluation scripts, and language-model embedding-generation utilities are available at https://github.com/SZU-ADDG/BioLM-Score. An archival code snapshot and pretrained model weights are available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.21878818. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: A systematic review and conceptual hybrid framework for integrating blockchain and internet of medical things in secure healthcare systems
text: Abstract Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) deployments generate continuous streams of sensitive patient data, yet centralised storage remains exposed to single points of failure, unauthorised disclosure, and tampering. Blockchain offers an immutable, auditable substrate, but pairing it with resource-constrained devices raises concerns around throughput, latency, energy, and scalability. This paper presents a systematic literature review of peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025, selected under a PRISMA-aligned protocol across five databases, with all screening decisions double-rated (κ = 0.80). The review organises recurring technical gaps into a structured taxonomy, from which we derive a conceptual hybrid architecture combining an IoMT perception layer, an edge-gateway tier, a permissioned blockchain running Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) consensus, and an Interplanetary File System (IPFS) off-chain store. The device–gateway key exchange is verified in ProVerif under a Dolev-Yao adversary, establishing session-key secrecy, injective agreement, and forward secrecy over unbounded sessions. Cryptographic costs measured on constrained hardware yield 35.7–141.4 ms commit latency and 707–2,798 transactions per second across a set of 4–31 validators, with an on-chain to off-chain storage ratio near 1:20. Cryptography accounts for only 2.8–10.7% of commit latency, confirming that network delay is the binding constraint. The contribution over prior surveys is a reproducible protocol, an explicit gap analysis, a unified notation and threat model, a machine-checked proof of authentication, and an analytical committee-sizing rule.

title: From Human Inspection to Intelligent Quality Assurance: Opportunities and Limitations of AI in Electronics Manufacturing
text: Electronics manufacturing quality assurance relies on human inspection, automated equipment and electrical testing. These methods remain essential, but they face challenges involving inspection consistency, production variation, data interpretation and the identification of unfamiliar defects. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, deep learning and computer vision, offers additional ways to analyse inspection images and manufacturing data in printed circuit board (PCB) and printed circuit board assembly (PCBA) production. This focused critical narrative review examines conventional inspection methods and the potential use of AI in solder paste inspection, component-placement verification, automated optical inspection, X-ray image analysis and electrical-test data analysis. It considers reported opportunities alongside limitations involving data quality, class imbalance, domain shift, model reliability, explainability and automation bias. Published studies are discussed in their original contexts; their performance results are not treated as directly comparable across different datasets and tasks. The paper proposes a conceptual Risk-Based Human–AI Quality Assurance Framework for PCB and PCBA Manufacturing (RH-AIQA). It links product requirements and inspection risk with traceable data, AI analysis, human verification, authorised defect disposition and model monitoring. The framework has not been experimentally validated. The review concludes that AI may strengthen selected inspection activities, but dependable implementation requires task-specific validation, appropriate acceptance criteria and continuing human accountability.

title: Camera Based Reflector Degradation Detection
text: Reflectors used in the solar fields of concentrated solar thermal technologies must maintain excellent optical properties over the lifetime of the commercial projects. However, the reflector materials are prone to degradation due to environmental stresses. Measurements with portable reflectometers are the state-of-the-art technique to evaluate degradation in the field, determining the most significant optical parameter, the reflectance. Some degradation mechanisms can evolve on reflectors in early stages without compromising reflectance, until they affect a large surface. This is why alternative measurement techniques are necessary. In this work, the development of an easy-to-use field measurement procedure for the degradation of solar reflectors is presented, which was investigated at the OPAC laboratory of the CIEMAT-Plataforma Solar de Almería (PSA). An automated image processing program has been developed, to determine the degraded area of reflectors based on various image sources. The capabilities to measure different scales of defect sizes on different reflector materials, with simple commercial camera equipment and a portable microscope, were analyzed, and future development steps are presented.

title: Co-occurring Amino Acid Substitutions Reveal Shared Evolutionary Links between Mammary Gland Location and Litter Size in Mammals
text: Abstract Mammary gland patterning varies widely among mammals, ranging from thoracic-restricted glands in many singleton-bearing species to glands distributed along both the thoracic and inguinal regions in many litter-bearing species. Although this association has long been recognized, its molecular evolutionary basis remains unknown. Here, we investigated whether mammary gland patterning and litter size have evolved through shared protein sequence changes across 23 mammalian species. Using a comparative genomics pipeline, we identified fixed amino acid substitutions that distinguished species with different mammary gland patterning and litter size phenotypes. Mammary gland patterning was associated with substantially more fixed substitutions than litter size; however, proteins associated with litter size were significantly enriched among those associated with mammary gland patterning. These shared proteins contained distinct, rather than identical, fixed amino acid substitutions for the two traits, indicating repeated evolutionary modification of common molecular targets. Phylogenetic analyses using BayesTraits further identified multiple shared proteins whose evolutionary histories were significantly associated with both mammary gland patterning and litter size. Functional enrichment analyses showed that proteins harboring fixed substitutions were enriched for phosphatidylinositol metabolism, lipid transport, membrane trafficking, cytoskeletal organization, extracellular matrix remodeling, and epithelial morphogenesis, processes central to mammary gland development. Comparative analyses of domestic pig breeds differing in mammary gland number and litter size identified additional candidate proteins associated with intraspecific variation in these reproductive traits. Together, these findings provide molecular evidence that mammary gland patterning and litter-bearing strategy have undergone coordinated evolution through repeated modification of shared developmental and cellular pathways.

title: Cognitive networks reconstruct mindsets about STEM subjects and educational contexts in high-schoolers, undergraduates, experts and their digital twins
text: Attitudes toward STEM develop from the interaction of conceptual knowledge, educational experiences, and affect. Here we use cognitive network science to reconstruct group mindsets as behavioural forma mentis networks (BFMNs). In this case, nodes are cue words and free associations, edges are empirical associative links, and each concept is annotated with perceived valence. We analyse BFMNs from $$N=981$$ observations spanning high school students, university students, and early-career STEM experts, alongside LLM (GPT-OSS) “digital twins” (group-level synthetic counterparts, not individual-level copies), prompted to emulate comparable profiles. Focusing also on semantic neighbourhoods (“frames”) around key target concepts (e.g., STEM subjects or educational actors/places), we quantify frames in terms of valence auras, emotional profiles, network overlap (Jaccard similarity), and concreteness relative to null baselines. Across student groups, science and research are consistently framed positively, while their core quantitative subjects (mathematics and statistics) exhibit more negative and anxiety-related auras, amplified in higher math-anxiety subgroups, evidencing a STEM-science cognitive and emotional dissonance. High-anxiety frames are also less concrete than chance, suggesting more abstract and decontextualised representations of threatening quantitative domains. Human networks show greater overlap between mathematics and anxiety than GPT-OSS. The results highlight how BFMNs capture cognitive-affective signatures of mindsets towards the target domains and indicate that these synthetic counterparts approximate cultural attitudes but miss key context-sensitive, experience-based components of human educational anxiety.

title: Gut Dysbiosis at the Intersection of Depression and Addiction: A Microbiota–Gut–Brain–Reward Framework and Digital Precision Behavioural Health Agenda for the United Arab Emirates
text: Background The microbiota–gut–brain axis provides an emerging framework for understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. Depression and addiction, despite substantial comorbidity, are frequently investigated separately. This review examines whether gut dysbiosis contributes to vulnerability, symptom persistence and recovery through shared inflammatory, endocrine, metabolic and reward-related mechanisms. Methods A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO, supplemented by citation searching. Priority was given to systematic reviews, meta-analyses, human cohorts, randomised trials and mechanistic studies. Evidence was evaluated for methodological quality, confounding, replication, biological plausibility and clinical relevance. Results Convergent evidence implicates altered short-chain fatty acid production, intestinal barrier dysfunction, dysregulated tryptophan–kynurenine metabolism, systemic inflammation, hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal-axis disturbance and altered affective and reward signalling. Human evidence is strongest for major depressive disorder and alcohol use disorder, whereas evidence involving opioids, psychostimulants, cannabis and polysubstance use remains comparatively limited. Dietary interventions, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics and faecal microbiota transplantation demonstrate preliminary therapeutic potential. However, methodological heterogeneity, uncertain causality, limited replication and insufficient evidence of sustained benefit prevent routine clinical recommendation. Digital phenotyping, wearable technologies and artificial intelligence may facilitate integration of microbial, metabolic, behavioural and longitudinal clinical information, although prospective validation and demonstrated clinical utility remain limited. Conclusions The proposed Microbiota–Gut–Brain–Reward framework conceptualises dysbiosis as a potentially modifiable contributor rather than an independent cause of depression or addiction. Clinical translation requires longitudinal multi-omic research, harmonised methodologies, mechanistically informed trials and integration with established pharmacological, psychological and social interventions. Digitally enabled precision approaches may support personalised recovery monitoring, provided interpretability, privacy, equity and clinical governance are prioritised. The United Arab Emirates offers opportunities for culturally responsive translational research, although implementation must remain evidence-driven, ethically governed and subject to rigorous prospective evaluation before clinical adoption.

title: The Development of Neuroscience
text: Abstract Brain cells of elegant and delicate shapes, which Ramon y Cajal called las misteriosas mariposas de alma (the butterflies of the soul), hide the secrets of our mental life The study of the human brain represents a challenge for humanity, and an opportunity for societal development, from a cognitive point of view, both scientific and philosophical, and from the point of view of biomedical (new therapies for serious diseases that affect the brain) and technological (Artificial Intelligence and natural intelligence, brain-machine interfaces, robotics) applications.

title: A precision medicine approach to allergic contact dermatitis: current evidence and future opportunities
text: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a common inflammatory skin disease arising from interactions between environmental exposures and individual susceptibility. While patch testing and allergen avoidance remain cornerstones of management, advances in genetics, barrier biology and digital technologies present opportunities for more precise approaches to prediction, prevention and management. Here, we review evidence for genetic susceptibility and gene–environment interactions in ACD, including variation in epidermal barrier function, immune regulation and xenobiotic metabolism, and consider the role of genetic counselling in interpreting and communicating risk. We further examine emerging applications of artificial intelligence in patch-test interpretation, exposure assessment and predictive modelling. Finally, we propose a future framework for precision approaches to ACD, integrating genomic, phenotypic and exposomic data to characterise individual risk and disease endotypes. These insights could inform more individualised prevention, diagnosis and therapeutic selection, while supporting personalised skincare and safer topical product design. Although substantial challenges remain, convergence of these fields may shift ACD from a predominantly reactive model towards a more predictive, preventive and personalised framework.

title: MRI-based mathematical modeling to predict the response of cervical cancer patients to chemoradiation
text: Patients with locally advanced cervical cancer have a 20–30% risk of residual disease after completion of standard-of-care chemoradiation. A reliable and patient-specific method to predict treatment response is currently lacking but would be valuable for selecting therapeutic regimens with improved outcomes. We developed an MRI-based mathematical model for tumor cell movement, proliferation, and response to chemoradiation. The model was calibrated for each patient using their own MRI data before (V1) and after two weeks (V2) of chemoradiation. In the study cohort of 10 patients, the concordance correlation coefficients between the observed and predicted changes in tumor cellularity and volume from V1 to V3 (after five weeks of chemoradiation) were 0.96 and 0.78, respectively. Thus, our model can accurately predict response to chemoradiation for cervical cancer patients using each patient’s MRI data, thereby offering potential for personalizing chemoradiation regimens during treatment.

title: The CNR at the Frontier of Scientific Computing
text: Abstract Mathematical sciences play a key role in science and in a wide range of key technologies. We live in the era of mathematics; its influence and impact are profound. Yet, its role is not always well understood.

title: Adaptive dimensionality reduction for efficient deep learning on temporal video datasets
text: Abstract In the domain of computer vision and its related research fields, especially in temporal data handling, the analysis and processing of high dimensional data is a huge problem. Challenges in deep learning-based high dimension data processing often arise from their variable length sequences and their complex data patterns. As the use of high dimensional data continues to grow, the demand for dimension reduction of complex data is growing rapidly. Dimensionality reduction is the process of reducing a high-dimensional matrix of a dataset into a lower dimension. Standard approaches based on principal component analysis, independent component analysis and others, including simple padding and truncation, can lead to data loss or unwanted computational overhead. To address this issue, we introduce a VidSqeOpt method for dimensionality reduction based on feature extraction which exploits statistical approaches with reduced dimension and optimal length finding. Our method is validated on several benchmark datasets that are based on temporal data with complex dimensionality. Cross comparison with the baseline methods shows that our proposed approach adapts to diverse tasks, achieving up to 2.0% higher accuracy while reducing per-frame processing time by at least 23.7%, down to ≤0.45 seconds.

title: DPI-score: a deep learning-based metric for assessing protein-protein interfaces in cryoEM derived assemblies
text: Abstract Advances in cryoEM have led to a surge in high-resolution structures; however, model building and refinement at resolutions ( > = 3 Å) and in regions with variable local resolution remain challenging, making validation essential. CryoEM derived assemblies often contain extensive protein-protein interfaces, however, most existing validation metrics focus on density fit or overall geometry without directly assessing interface quality. To address this, we present DPI-Score, a deep learning-based metric for assessing protein-protein interfaces in cryoEM derived complexes. The method uses only raw structural coordinates of interface atoms, without requiring engineered features, and achieves 87.53% validation accuracy. DPI-Score was applied to 29,120 interfaces from 6,011 fitted entries with resolutions worse than 3 Å in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank. Here, we show that DPI-Score provides complementary information to existing validation metrics and can identify interface errors in modelled assemblies that are not detected by density-based scores alone.

title: Sex differences in the genetic basis of human recombination within 190,000 parent-child pairs
text: Meiotic recombination drives genetic diversity and chromosome segregation, yet the genetic factors governing variation in human recombination rates across studies remain poorly understood. Here, we analyze 112,144 maternal and 78,653 paternal meiosis events across four countries and identify 58 independent genomic regions (24 unique across phenotypes) associated with recombination frequency and location. These include six novel female-specific regions harboring genes linked to ovarian function and a seventh novel region linked to male recombination, with many loci demonstrating sex-dependent effects. The between-sex genetic correlation is 0.374 (0.072 SD). While DNA markers account for 30-40% of individual-level variation in recombination rate, previously known global modulators explain only 37.7% (2.7% SD) of this variation in females and 47.1% (3.8% SD) in males. We create a polygenic predictor that significantly predicts recombination rates in women and men after adjusting for age and birth year. Furthermore, female recombination correlates significantly with reproductive outcomes and aging, after adjusting for study ascertainment. In the largest meta-analysis to date of human meiotic recombination, these findings uncover novel sex-specific loci and clarify the polygenic architecture underlying meiotic variation. A meta-analysis of 190,797 human meioses across four countries maps 24 recombination loci, seven novel and mostly female-specific. Between-sex genetic correlation is 0.37, and a polygenic predictor links female recombination to reproduction and aging.

title: Governing genomic AI in the era of agentic systems
text: Genomic artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from task-specific models toward systems that can integrate genomic, molecular, and phenotypic information across increasingly complex analytical workflows. There are governance frameworks for the responsible use of genomic AI, largely developed for systems whose data use and analytical behavior are defined in advance. Agentic systems add a new governance challenge because analytical decisions, resource use, and subsequent actions may no longer be fully specified before execution. In this review, we examine how this shift changes the governance of genomic AI and suggest that oversight must extend to the behavior of the analytical system itself. Permissions, data use, provenance, validation, uncertainty, and human authority need to remain enforceable during execution. We introduce AI systems implementation at the Center for Applied Genomics (CAG) of the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), including current controls, an ongoing experiment using a restricted project-specific environment for agentic analysis, and a phased approach to broader deployment. Agentic genomic AI governance requires a shift from static review of data and models to enforceable control of system behavior during execution.

title: Binary Patterning as a Probe of Protein Language Model Representations
text: Do protein language models (pLMs) encode the physical rules that govern protein folding? The four-helix bundle provides a classic test case because binary patterning, the ordered placement of polar and nonpolar residues along an amphipathic α-helix, is sufficient to generate folded proteins with high probability. Here, we ask whether ESM2 captures the sequence grammar underlying this design strategy. Libraries of synthetic sequences constrained only by binary patterning were predicted by ESMFold to form four-helix bundles. Predicted helicity, compactness, and topological diversity changed with sequence length in the same direction as experimentally characterized libraries, although the model did not distinguish successful from unsuccessful individual designs. Principal component analysis of ESM2 embeddings revealed representations of hydrophobic patterning, helix-loop boundaries, and heptad register. Extending the analysis to all 128 heptad binary patterns produced a jellyfish-shaped manifold in which hydrophobic composition formed the dominant axis, while paired components encoded pattern phase. Manifold geometry depended on amino-acid chemistry, repeat number, and linker sequence, and collapsed when amino acids were assigned to arbitrary categories. ESM2 therefore combines general repeat recognition with protein-specific physicochemical information. More broadly, synthetic sequence libraries provide experimentally grounded probes of protein language model representations and their relationship to protein biophysics.

title: Humanized yeast ORC drives R-loop dependent transcription-replication conflicts and global gene dysregulation
text: The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) recruits Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM) hexamers to initiate eukaryotic DNA replication. While yeast ORC binds specific DNA motifs, human ORC binds sequence-agnostically nucleosome-depleted promoter regions. Here, using a mutant yeast model that recapitulates the human ORC binding landscape, we demonstrate that pervasive and unscheduled ORC binding at promoters in the compact yeast genome generates R-loop associated transcription-replication conflicts and disrupts gene expression across thousands of genes. Unexpectedly, we also uncover that substituting endogenous gene promoters with a replication origin sequence maintains robust transcription. We reveal that this intrinsic, promoter-like function relies on the ability of origins to form a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) encoded within the origin's sequence composition. However, origin-substituted loci reposition the +1 nucleosome which drives the transcription machinery to select alternative transcription start sites (TSSs). Thus, origins and promoters share an intrinsic chromatin structure-controlled ability to drive transcription initiation. Together, our results show that origin licensing in compact genomes relies on sequence-specific, coupled origin licensing to insulate transcription from the replication machinery.

title: Graph-guided flow matching enables biologically informed prediction at single-cell resolution
text: Perturb-seq enables systematic interrogation of massively parallel genetic perturbations at single-cell resolution, yet exhaustive characterization of the full perturbation space remains impractical. Here, we present Graph-guided Flow Matching (GFM), a generative framework that integrates biological knowledge graphs with latent flow matching to predict post-perturbation single-cell transcriptomes. Across multiple large-scale Perturb-seq datasets, GFM outperforms a strong linear baseline and current deep-learning models in predicting unseen single-gene perturbations, while training up to 30x faster and remaining robust with limited training data. GFM also demonstrates competitive performance in the two-gene perturbation prediction task when neither perturbed gene is observed during training. Ablation experiments show that combining flow matching with knowledge graphs enables accurate prediction of perturbation responses. Finally, GFM accurately calculates transcriptional consequences of HSP90AA1 inactivation and identifies target candidates unseen by the model in chronic myeloid leukemia. Our study establishes GFM as a biologically informed generative framework that predicts single-cell perturbation responses for prioritization of therapeutic targets.

title: In Silico Prioritization of GWAS-Derived 3′ UTR MicroRNA-Binding Variants at Colorectal Cancer Risk Loci Detected in Hispanic Patients from the All of Us Research Program
text: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic discovery has relied largely on individuals of European ancestry, leaving Hispanic individuals, who bear a disproportionate CRC burden, underrepresented and without ancestry-matched functional resources. Many CRC risk variants are non-coding, and those in 3′ untranslated regions (3′ UTRs) can alter microRNA (miRNA) binding sites and reprogram post-transcriptional gene regulation. Here, we identify allele-specific miRNA-binding variants at CRC risk loci within the Hispanic population using a discovery pipeline anchored to Hispanic-relevant resources. CRC-associated 3′ UTR variants were compiled from the GWAS Catalog, further verified in Hispanic/Latino individuals using the All of Us Research Program cohort (n = 453), expanded into proxy sets using Admixed American-specific linkage disequilibrium, annotated against Ensembl transcripts, and evaluated with TargetScan and RNAhybrid. Screening of 38 CRC-associated 3′ UTR SNPs identified 19 variants that alter miRNA binding across nine genes, with each gene represented by a variant detected in the Hispanic cohort. Three oncogenic loci, DCBLD2 (lead SNP rs11552978), GREM1 (lead SNP rs10318), and SMC1B (rs3747239, prioritized as an AMR-specific proxy in near-complete LD with lead SNP rs6007600), met all prioritization criteria. In each case, the risk allele disrupts a strong miRNA-binding site, while the gene shows increased tumor expression, weak correlation between expression and methylation, and an absence of local active transcriptional chromatin marks (cCREs/H3K27Ac). These results suggest that the variants promote gene overexpression through loss of miRNA-mediated repression rather than changes in promoter methylation. Overall, the study identifies non-coding CRC susceptibility variants in the Hispanic population and highlights DCBLD2 , GREM1 , and SMC1B as strong candidates for functional validation, and illustrate how ancestry-matched functional annotation can support more equitable genomic research.

title: Evolutionary dynamics of RNA viruses during persistent infection in Drosophila melanogaster
text: Persistent viral infections provide an extended window for viral evolution, yet their intra-host trajectories across the host lifespan remain underexplored. Here, we tracked the longitudinal evolution of three single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) viruses (Drosophila A virus [DAV], Drosophila C virus [DCV], and Nora virus) and one double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus (Bloomfield virus) during persistent infection in Drosophila melanogaster. By analyzing viral populations across early, intermediate, and late infection stages, we mapped dynamic shifts in the viral quasispecies and the emergence of adaptive mutations. These data demonstrate that long-term persistence drives viral evolution in a viral species-specific manner. DAV evolution was defined by clonal interference, driven by the continuous turnover of competing haplotypes. Nora virus exhibited prolonged evolutionary stasis punctuated by a late-stage sweep, suggesting adaptation to the senescing host environment. In contrast, standard DCV populations were locked under strong purifying selection, where no adaptive mutations were detected. However, this constraint collapsed in high-titer DCV infections, triggering extensive mutational diversification. Distinct from the ssRNA dynamics, the multi-segmented dsRNA Bloomfield virus maintained higher sequence fidelity and a stable genomic formula. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that viral evolution during persistent infection is governed by the interplay between specific host-pathogen interactions and the physiological decline of the host.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Precision Medicine: A Review from Medical Imaging and Physiological Signals to Genomics, Drug Discovery and Trustworthy Deployment
text: Precision medicine aims to fit diagnosis and treatment to the individual patient, and artificial intelligence has become one of its main tools. Deep networks now read computed tomography scans, mammograms, skin images and echocardiograms; classifiers interpret electrocardiogram and electroencephalogram signals; and learned models predict protein structures and drug–target interactions. The problem is that these advances are reported in separate literatures, each with its own data types, metrics and failure modes, and the barriers to clinical use, such as privacy, bias and security, are usually discussed apart from the models they constrain. This review brings imaging, physiological signals, clinical risk prediction, genomics and drug discovery, and trustworthy deployment into one framework. It organizes 37 studies into a five-layer taxonomy and compares their data, methods and reported results. Imaging studies report expert-level performance, including an area under the curve of 0.944 for lung cancer screening and fewer false positives and false negatives in breast screening, but also show weaker performance on darker skin tones. Signal studies report a deep network that exceeded the average cardiologist in arrhythmia detection, and automated machine learning improved cardiovascular risk prediction over the Framingham score. Genomic and drug discovery studies show that deep models can predict protein structure with near-experimental accuracy and can find new antibiotics. Deployment studies show that federated learning across 20 institutions improved average accuracy by 16% over single-site models, while privacy, security and explainability remain open. Few studies combine more than one data layer, and fairness is rarely measured. Future work should develop multimodal models trained under privacy guarantees and evaluated across diverse patient groups.

title: Salivary-based protein and RNA biomarkers as early diagnostic Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease
text: Progressive neuronal degeneration is one of the symptoms of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), which often cause cognitive and physical impairments. In order to start therapy before clinical symptoms appear and to limit the progression of diseases like Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), early screening and diagnosis are crucial. Finding new, accurate and reliable biomarkers is a key objective in recent research in order to facilitate early diagnosis and offer insights into the progression of disease. Compared with invasive, complex, and costly cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) screening methods, salivary analysis has emerged as a promising approach for identifying biomarkers and matrices relevant to assessing NDDs. Compared to other often examined biofluids, saliva collection offers a number of benefits due to its accessibility, non-invasiveness, and suitability for recurrent sampling. These characteristics facilitate early diagnosis and timely treatment of diseases. Current research indicates that β-amyloid (Aβ), tau protein, alpha synuclein (α-syn), DJ-1, and several miRNAs in saliva show potential as biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. This narrative review addresses the growing need for reliable and standardized saliva-based biomarkers by integrating evidence on biomarker performance with methodological challenges, emerging technologies, and innovative perspectives on multimarker panels, standardization, and validation to facilitate their clinical translation in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases.

title: Harnessing Nanogold in Therapeutic Cancer Vaccines
text: Abstract Cancer immunotherapy offers potential to harness one’s own immune system to eliminate existing cancer cells. Within this therapeutic umbrella, therapeutic cancer vaccines (TCVs) have been designed to train lymphocytes to recognize cancer cells as foreign invaders and eliminate them from the body. To enact this training, scientists have employed nanoscale gold constructs (nanogold) in varying ways throughout the cyclical process of antigen uptake, dendritic cell maturation, antigen presentation, T cell migration, and cancer cell elimination. In this review, we highlight the use of nanogold in TCVs, emphasizing the distinct properties that have been harnessed to improve diverse aspects of the TCV cycle. Ultimately, we discuss the challenges of utilizing nanogold in TCVs and provide our perspective on the direction of the field in upcoming years.

title: Cell-based immunotherapies for infectious diseases: current evidence and translational perspectives on cytokine induced killer (CIK) cells
text: The persistent global burden of infectious diseases, compounded by environmental challenges, emerging pathogens, and antimicrobial resistance, underscores the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antimicrobial agents. Cell based immunotherapies, which harness the body's immune system to combat pathogens, have gained increasing attention for their potential to provide targeted, durable, and adaptive responses. Recently, we demonstrated that clinically licensed cytokine-induced killer (CIK) cells, used in cancer treatment, significantly reduced Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes in vitro. This review focuses on the emerging role of CIK cells in infectious disease therapy, positioning them alongside other prominent immune effector cells such as CTLs, γδT cells, and NK cells. We explore the biology, recognition mechanisms, their potential feature, and cytotoxic functions of these cell populations, distinguishing direct findings in infection-specific CIK studies from mechanisms characterized in oncology or other cytotoxic lymphocytes. While CTLs, γδT cells, and NK cells have been extensively studied for their roles in early and adaptive immune responses, CIK cells traditionally investigated in oncology, are now being recognized for their potential in antiviral and antimicrobial immunity. Alongside with CTLs, γδT cells, and NK cells, we detail CIK cell phenotypes, activation strategies, effector functions, and the limited but growing body of evidence supporting their application in some viral infections. The available findings support further investigation of CIK cells as a candidate approach in selected infectious settings, while their broader antimicrobial applicability, comparative efficacy, target specificity, safety, and clinical benefit require further evaluation in these settings.

title: Revitalizing the Therapeutic Pipeline for C. difficile Infection through Nonantimicrobial and Host-Directed Strategies
text: Abstract Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) remains a leading cause of healthcare-associated diarrhea, arising largely from antimicrobial-induced displacement of the gut microbiota. Although antimicrobial therapy remains the clinical standard for CDI, high rates of recurrence, the spread of antimicrobial-resistant strains, and inadequate interventions for countering toxin-mediated tissue damage highlight the need for alternative strategies. In this review, we evaluate emerging nonantimicrobial approaches for CDI, focusing on microbial-derived metabolites (including short-chain fatty acids and bile acids), plant-derived phytochemicals, and host-directed therapeutics that modulate inflammatory and neuroimmune pathways. Mechanistic insights into how these strategies mitigate C. difficile pathogenesis are also examined, including roles in attenuating intestinal inflammation and preserving epithelial barrier function. Given the multifactorial nature of CDI, we propose there is a need to advance a new therapeutic framework that integrates narrow-spectrum antimicrobials with nonantimicrobial host-directed modalities. Collectively, this conceptual framework provides a rational foundation for developing next-generation interventions for CDI in an era characterized by multidrug resistance and aging populations with comorbidities that are risk factors for CDI.

title: Multi-omics signatures indicative of status and effectiveness of vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 in ferrets
text: The COVID-19 pandemic prompted one of the most rapid vaccination efforts in history in an attempt to mitigate the global health and socio-economic burden of the disease. Today, the challenge remains in maintaining vaccine efficacy given the continuous evolution of key antigenic sites in the viral Spike protein. Access to multi-omics data analysis and machine learning (ML) approaches has greatly enhanced our ability to evaluate biomarkers associated with diagnosis, prognosis, drug discovery, and therapeutics, and can be used to obtain additional insights from traditional efficacy studies. In this study, multi-omics data (transcriptomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics) were processed from 16 ferrets vaccinated with DNA vaccines based on Wuhan-Hu-1 and SynCon spike sequences. Multi-omics data was integrated into Random Forest models to identify potential biomarkers indicative of vaccination status and the development of neutralising antibody titres against six SARS-CoV-2 variants.
