Causal analysis, based on Empirical Bayes Matrix Factorisation, was used to identify biological processes occurring between vaccination and a positive immune response. Several putative transcriptomic, lipid and metabolite biomarkers associated with reducing hyper-inflammation and maintaining cell homeostasis were identified using Random Forest models incorporating the omics analyses. These were similarly found when using vaccine immune response as class labels. Additionally, causal analysis identified four and three latent factors associated with vaccination status and response, respectively. Within these, several enriched gene sets relating to cell function and regulation, including ATP-synthesis and mitochondrial related processes were identified. Other genes also included those with secondary immune functions, particularly relating to chemokine and cytokines. This study provides a holistic analysis of ferret immune response to SARS-CoV-2 by integrating multi-omics data with ML and casual analysis and potential targets for further investigation.

title: HuR coordinates cytokine translation and maturation through ER-associated RNA granules
text: Efficient biosynthesis and secretion of inflammatory mediators is indispensable for robust immune responses. This process relies on the coordination of mRNA translation and protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) govern the spatial organization of mRNA translation, yet how RBPs modulate inflammatory factor production and maturation remains poorly defined. Here, we uncover a regulatory role of the RBP HuR in inflammatory-factor mRNA translation. We find that HuR physically interacts with the ER chaperone calnexin (CANX), bringing together inflammatory factor mRNAs, the calnexin quality control complex, and the translocon in discrete ER subdomains. Mechanistically, HuR undergoes phase separation and assembles membraneless RNA granules, which are selectively enriched in inflammatory mRNAs. This allows juxtaposed calnexin to rapidly recognize their corresponding nascent polypeptides. Collectively, our findings provide molecular evidence that RBPs spatially coordinate protein translation and processing via phase separation, offering new insights into regulatory mechanisms underlying efficient inflammatory-mediator production.

title: New disease models for investigating SynGAP1-related disorder (SRD) caused by a common heterozygous nonsense SYNGAP1 mutation
text: Mutations in the SYNGAP1 gene cause SynGAP1-related disorder (SRD), a severe neurodevelopmental disorder marked by intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, autism spectrum disorder, and global developmental delay. Studies in mouse models of SRD show that restoration of SynGAP1 expression in adult animals improves memory and seizure threshold, highlighting the disorders potential for successful therapeutic intervention over the entire lifetime. We established an integrated disease-modelling pipeline centered on the recurrent SYNGAP1 c.427C>T, p.(Arg143Ter), nonsense mutation, integrating neuronal and organoid models from patient-derived human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and a humanized knock-in mouse line to investigate mutation-specific disease phenotype across complementary experimental systems. We demonstrate that the c.427C>T mutation leads to a reduction of SynGAP1 protein levels and a corresponding dysregulation of Ras/ERK signaling in human forebrain organoids as well as in the mouse model system. In vivo, mice harboring the c.427C>T mutation show a hyperactivity phenotype that corresponds well to phenotypic features seen in patients such as absence of fear, hyperactive behavior and a strong urge to investigate the immediate surroundings. Taken together, our molecular and behavioral data in the humanized mouse are in line with studies on conventional heterozygous SynGAP1 knockout models, underscoring the relevance of these new disease models for further investigations into disease pathology. Moreover, with the three models described here, we present a translational platform that enables the development and evaluation of gene therapies that target disease-causing single nucleotide variations in the SYNGAP1 coding sequence.

title: A Physically Consistent AI Framework for Predictive Design of Microfluidic Double Emulsions Toward Precision Liposome Fabrication
text: Microfluidic double emulsions offer a powerful route for templated liposome fabrication; however, precise and reproducible control over droplet architecture remains challenging due to the highly nonlinear coupling between flow dynamics and interfacial phenomena. Here, we present a physics-consistent, data-driven framework that combines artificial neural networks (ANNs) with genetic algorithms (GAs) to enable predictive inverse design and target-driven optimization of double-emulsion generation. By systematically varying lipid concentration, surfactant concentration, and flow-rate parameters within a flow-focusing microfluidic platform, the ANN model learns the underlying relationships governing droplet formation with near-unity predictive accuracy. Coupling the trained model with a GA enables precise control of droplet morphology, demonstrated here by the generation of droplets with a targeted 30 µm core diameter and 5 µm shell thickness, resulting in liposomes with diameters of approximately 30 µm after solvent extraction. Experimental results closely matched the model predictions for both the selected processing conditions and the resulting droplet properties, confirming the reliability of the proposed framework. The flow-related parameters had the greatest impact on droplet diameter and production frequency. This study demonstrates a practical, interpretable AI-guided optimization approach for complex microfluidic platforms, while offering a scalable route for the fabrication of liposomes and other structured soft-material systems.

title: The 100 most cited studies on medicinal plants in bone healing: A bibliometric analysis
text: Ethnopharmacological relevance: Botanical therapeutics are widely used in traditional medicine for osteoporosis and fracture repair.Synthesizing global research trends is essential to guide translational orthopedics.This bibliometric analysis evaluates the 100 most cited articles on medicinal plants and natural compounds in bone healing to identify key research domains, prominent plant species, active phytocompounds, and knowledge gaps.: Bibliographic data (1975 to 2024) were retrieved from Scopus on February 11, 2025 (TITLE-ABS-KEY).VOSviewer (v1.6.18) with full counting and a custom thesaurus mapped co-occurrence networks and thematic clusters.Journal of Ethnopharmacology (23) and Phytomedicine (17%) were leading publishing venues.Research was dominated by Asian institutions (China 41, India 17, South Korea 13%), with R. Maurya as top author.Nine thematic clusters were mapped, spanning preclinical models (ovariectomized rats), osteoclastogenesis inhibition, and signaling pathways (BMP/Smad, Wnt/β-catenin).Key plants included Epimedium brevicornum, Eucommia ulmoides, Cuscuta chinensis, Drynaria fortunei, and Cissus quadrangularis.Bioactive compounds (icariin, puerarin, formononetin, kaempferol) featured prominently.Conclusions: Preclinical evidence is robust, but long-term human clinical trials, standardized extraction protocols, and detailed safety studies remain scarce.African flora represents a strategic, understudied frontier for future ethnopharmacological exploration.

title: An anaerobic cell-free protein synthesis formulation for the in vitro study of oxygen sensitive proteins
text: Anaerobic microbes harbor unique enzymes and metabolic pathways with potential biotechnological applications, yet these microbes remain difficult to study and engineer. Research is limited by the labor-intensive workflows required to maintain anoxic environments and the lack of genetic tools available for non-model anaerobes. Here, we present an anaerobic cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) platform for the in vitro study of oxygen-sensitive enzymes. This study establishes two methods for conducting anaerobic CFPS, achieving an anoxic environment by (1) sparging with inert gas or (2) lyophilizing to remove oxygenated water. We show the functionality of our anaerobic CFPS formulation by producing oxygen-independent fluorescent protein reporters and a [4Fe-4S] cluster pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) with a specific activity of 5.2 ± 0.3 x 10 -4 U/µL cell-free extract. This highly modular platform will allow study of diverse oxygen-sensitive proteins and requires only minor modifications to commonly used CFPS workflows.

title: Scaling LLM Agent Tool Access: The MCP Gateway
text: LLM agents increasingly rely on tool calling to complete tasks. Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes tool calling between LLM agents and tool providers. It reduces integration cost and drives rapid growth in tool scale. In production deployments, tool access becomes difficult to scale. On the tool provider side, legacy services are not directly callable through MCP; the rapid protocol development creates ongoing compatibility cost. On the agent side, the number of mounted tools is limited by the LLM context window and inference overhead; mounting a large tool set increases token usage and inference latency and can reduce task success rate. Moreover, for stateful MCP backends with multiple replicas, preserving session affinity increases client-side complexity. We present a cloud-scale MCP Gateway system. It breaks the direct-connect model on the data plane and offloads legacy service integration, consolidating incompatible MCP variants, access control, tool recommendation, and session-aware routing at the gateway. The conversion module supports 315 OpenAPI services in the cloud and integrates MCP transport variants. Session-aware routing decouples the scalability of the gateway layer and the MCP service layer. The hybrid retrieval engine sustains $\sim$98\% Top-15 recall; it scales agent tool access to 3{,}000+ tools with improved tool selection accuracy. We also share the lessons learned from deploying the gateway system in production.

title: Artificial intelligence driven software systems for cardiovascular disease detection using physiological signals: a systematic review
text: Abstract Cardiovascular disease exacts an extraordinary global toll, with annual mortality exceeding 17.9 million lives and representing nearly one-third of all deaths worldwide. Reducing diagnostic delays, particularly in resource-limited settings, requires innovative, scalable, and cost-effective solutions. Artificial intelligence integrated with physiological signals, such as electrocardiogram (ECG), photoplethysmogram (PPG) and phonocardiogram (PCG), offers promising pathways for scalable, real-time cardiovascular assessment. Despite rapid advances, the evidence base remains fragmented, impeding identification of validated approaches and clinical translation pathways. A PRISMA-guided search across five databases (Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, Embase, IEEE Xplore) identified 35 eligible peer-reviewed studies. Quality and risk of bias were appraised using a QUADAS-2 adapted framework. Most systems utilised ECG (71.4%) with deep learning architectures, including convolutional and recurrent neural networks. Critical gaps were quantified: only 23% of studies conducted external validation, only 14% achieved clinical-scale deployment, no study integrated principled multi-signal fusion (ECG + PPG + PCG), and only one system (1/35, 2.9%) implemented a patient-facing conversational interface. Reported accuracies ranged from 70.5 to 99.9% (n = 21 reporting; unweighted mean 93.7%), but inconsistent metric reporting and limited external validation tempered translational confidence. A three-directional framework is proposed, addressing generalisability through multi-signal (ECG + PPG + PCG) models, interpretability through LLM-driven clinical narratives, and accessibility through edge-cloud deployment, to guide future research toward clinically deployable systems.

title: Institutional exit and practical autonomy: U.S. withdrawal from WHO and the option value of global health institutions
text: Abstract This paper examines when withdrawal from an international organization increases or weakens state autonomy. By using the U.S. withdrawal from the World Health Organization (WHO) as a theory-building case, it develops a function-level diagnostic framework based on two dimensions: institutional option value and autonomy cost. The framework distinguishes among option-preserving technical platforms, conditional reform functions, discretionary low-stakes activities, and autonomy-eroding commitments. Drawing on public documentary evidence, the paper identifies observed changes in U.S. institutional participation and examines four potential mechanisms through which broad withdrawal affects practical autonomy, which are information loss, rule-making vacancy, burden shifting, and credibility volatility. It distinguishes these observed changes from anticipated consequences that remain empirically uncertain. The paper also recognizes that political motivations for withdrawal differ from functional assessments and that selective participation depends on institutional rules and the feasibility of alternative arrangements. It contributes a differentiated understanding of institutional exit by showing how the same withdrawal decision expands formal discretion while potentially reducing valuable future policy options.

title: A systematic review and conceptual hybrid framework for integrating blockchain and internet of medical things in secure healthcare systems
text: Abstract Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) deployments generate continuous streams of sensitive patient data, yet centralised storage remains exposed to single points of failure, unauthorised disclosure, and tampering. Blockchain offers an immutable, auditable substrate, but pairing it with resource-constrained devices raises concerns around throughput, latency, energy, and scalability. This paper presents a systematic literature review of peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025, selected under a PRISMA-aligned protocol across five databases, with all screening decisions double-rated (κ = 0.80). The review organises recurring technical gaps into a structured taxonomy, from which we derive a conceptual hybrid architecture combining an IoMT perception layer, an edge-gateway tier, a permissioned blockchain running Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT) consensus, and an Interplanetary File System (IPFS) off-chain store. The device–gateway key exchange is verified in ProVerif under a Dolev-Yao adversary, establishing session-key secrecy, injective agreement, and forward secrecy over unbounded sessions. Cryptographic costs measured on constrained hardware yield 35.7–141.4 ms commit latency and 707–2,798 transactions per second across a set of 4–31 validators, with an on-chain to off-chain storage ratio near 1:20. Cryptography accounts for only 2.8–10.7% of commit latency, confirming that network delay is the binding constraint. The contribution over prior surveys is a reproducible protocol, an explicit gap analysis, a unified notation and threat model, a machine-checked proof of authentication, and an analytical committee-sizing rule.

title: EUBURN: The southern Europe biomass burning programme
text: Southern Europe is experiencing a shift towards a new wildfire regime, characterised by larger and more intense fires, and an extension of the fire season beyond the traditional summer months. Climate projections indicate that the occurrence and severity of fwildfires will increase faster than the global average due to an increased risk of heatwaves and droughts. These conditions are expected to reduce fuel moisture, extend the fire season and increase the likelihood of large and severe wildfires. At the same time, changes in fire regimes may alter vegetation composition and ecosystem structure, potentially favouring fire-adapted species while threatening species that are less resilient to increasingly frequent or severe fires. Addressing these emerging challenges require new tools and technologies needed to implement comprehensive fire management approaches. The community still faces challenges in predicting which wildfires may escalate into extreme events, and the environmental, climate and health impacts of the associated smoke remain poorly understood. The southern Europe biomass BURNing (EUBURN) programme was developed in response to the need to improve the prevention, monitoring and prediction of wildfire risks in southern Europe. EUBURN integrates multi-year, multi-scale field campaigns, laboratory studies, satellite remote sensing and advanced modelling to establish the research foundations for understanding the complex interactions between wildfires and the atmosphere. Based on this fundamental research, the programme aims to support fire responders, ecosystems and air quality management, while addressing specific climate research requirements by developing new or enhanced operational products, tools and services for predicting and monitoring wildfires and their associated smoke plumes. This article provides an overview of EUBURN, including its motivation and design. It also describes the measurements and modelling strategy that will be employed to fulfil the programme's scientific objectives.

title: Gut Dysbiosis at the Intersection of Depression and Addiction: A Microbiota–Gut–Brain–Reward Framework and Digital Precision Behavioural Health Agenda for the United Arab Emirates
text: Background The microbiota–gut–brain axis provides an emerging framework for understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. Depression and addiction, despite substantial comorbidity, are frequently investigated separately. This review examines whether gut dysbiosis contributes to vulnerability, symptom persistence and recovery through shared inflammatory, endocrine, metabolic and reward-related mechanisms. Methods A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO, supplemented by citation searching. Priority was given to systematic reviews, meta-analyses, human cohorts, randomised trials and mechanistic studies. Evidence was evaluated for methodological quality, confounding, replication, biological plausibility and clinical relevance. Results Convergent evidence implicates altered short-chain fatty acid production, intestinal barrier dysfunction, dysregulated tryptophan–kynurenine metabolism, systemic inflammation, hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal-axis disturbance and altered affective and reward signalling. Human evidence is strongest for major depressive disorder and alcohol use disorder, whereas evidence involving opioids, psychostimulants, cannabis and polysubstance use remains comparatively limited. Dietary interventions, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics and faecal microbiota transplantation demonstrate preliminary therapeutic potential. However, methodological heterogeneity, uncertain causality, limited replication and insufficient evidence of sustained benefit prevent routine clinical recommendation. Digital phenotyping, wearable technologies and artificial intelligence may facilitate integration of microbial, metabolic, behavioural and longitudinal clinical information, although prospective validation and demonstrated clinical utility remain limited. Conclusions The proposed Microbiota–Gut–Brain–Reward framework conceptualises dysbiosis as a potentially modifiable contributor rather than an independent cause of depression or addiction. Clinical translation requires longitudinal multi-omic research, harmonised methodologies, mechanistically informed trials and integration with established pharmacological, psychological and social interventions. Digitally enabled precision approaches may support personalised recovery monitoring, provided interpretability, privacy, equity and clinical governance are prioritised. The United Arab Emirates offers opportunities for culturally responsive translational research, although implementation must remain evidence-driven, ethically governed and subject to rigorous prospective evaluation before clinical adoption.

title: VectBox Sync: a web application for vectorcardiographic analysis of ventricular synchrony from 12-lead electrocardiograms
text: We introduce VectBox Sync, a browser-based application that implements a published vectorcardiographic (VCG) dyssynchrony index for exploratory assessment of ventricular electrical synchrony from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). Despite guideline-directed patient selection, a substantial fraction of patients who receive cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) do not obtain the expected benefit. QRS duration and morphology remain the principal electrical criteria, yet they do not capture the three-dimensional trajectory of ventricular activation. VectBox Sync prioritizes native digital ECG recordings, including matrices and common clinical and research waveform formats; optional manufacturer-PDF import and externally digitized numerical files extend access when paper-like archives are the only available source. After optional preprocessing, the user selects a QRS interval, and the application calculates the dyssynchrony index relative to a calibrated control cutoff. It also provides companion VCG descriptors (voltage and speed integrals, loop angles, and planarity), together with VCG trajectories, synchrony-field maps, and a multilingual PDF report. Labeled conditions from the same session can be overlaid for comparison, for example across successive pacing settings. VectBox Sync makes this VCG-based assessment accessible through an integrated web application, providing quantitative descriptors that complement conventional ECG criteria. The application is available at https://vectbox.com/sync for research and educational use.

title: Optimizing C-Terminal Gene Tagging Using CRISPR/Cas9 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae: From gRNA Design to Tag Incorporation.
text: Protein tags are molecular tools for dissecting protein function by enabling detection and purification. N-terminal tagging can sometimes cause protein mislocalization or compromised function. As an alternative, a protein can be tagged at the C-terminus, a procedure that also retains expression from the endogenous promoter. CRISPR/Cas9 has emerged as a powerful tool for gene manipulation, including in vivo gene tagging strategies. Traditional yeast CRISPR design tools rely on static database lookups and provide limited guidance on predicting targeting efficiency, potentially resulting in hidden design limitations that can compromise precise gene editing. We harnessed the versatility of the pML104 expression vector and combined it with a dynamic, multi-parameter scoring gRNA design tool for seamless C-terminal tagging. We observed that certain sequence features, such as an extra guanine at the 3'-end of the PAM sequence, can affect cleavage efficiency, and that under suboptimal conditions, cells can evade homology-directed repair, resulting in an increased probability of false positives. Verification that the tagged protein is expressed and fully functional is critical, and it was achieved here using Western blotting and chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP). This framework provides an efficient blueprint and comprehensive guide for streamlining C-terminal protein tagging in S. cerevisiae.

title: Protocol for CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing of murine neutrophils for in vitro and in vivo mechanistic studies.
text: Neutrophils' short lifespan and resistance to genetic manipulation have limited mechanistic interrogation of gene-specific functions in these cells. Here, we present a protocol for gene targeting in murine neutrophil-lineage cells using two complementary CRISPR-Cas9-based strategies. First, we describe steps for an ER-Hoxb8-based system for scalable gain- and loss-of-function studies. We then detail procedures for a Lineage- Sca-1+ cKit+ (LSK) progenitor cell-based hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell-targeting strategy for stable genetic perturbation of endogenous neutrophils. For complete information on the generation and use of this protocol, please refer to Bolli et al.1.

title: Nanoparticle therapeutics for infectious diseases integrating AI-guided design, crispr delivery, phage synergy, and immune modulation.
text: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

title: Spatial organization of tumor-associated macrophage states: Niche-dependent immune bottlenecks and therapy-driven adaptation.
text: Tumor-associated macrophages exhibit substantial functional heterogeneity and plasticity that cannot be adequately captured by lineage origin, individual markers, or the conventional M1/M2 framework. Advances in single-cell and spatial profiling indicate that the immunological consequences of TAM states depend on their functional programs, spatial localization, interactions with neighboring cells, and treatment context. In this review, we summarize recurrent TAM programs and examine their spatial organization within hypoxic-necrotic and lipid-rich regions, tumor-stroma interfaces, and perivascular niches, highlighting their context-dependent immunosuppressive and immune-supportive functions. We then discuss how TAM-associated mechanisms contribute to immune bottlenecks involving tumor-antigen fate, antigen-presenting cell-T-cell interactions, metabolic suppression, and restricted T-cell access. We further examine how treatment-associated changes in TAM state composition, local cell-cell interactions, and monocyte-derived replenishment may contribute to the persistence or reconstruction of suppressive niches. Against this background, we evaluate the limitations of broad TAM depletion and recruitment blockade and review emerging approaches involving myeloid checkpoint blockade, functional reprogramming, phagocytic remodeling, and macrophage engineering. Building on these findings, we explore the rationale for niche-matched combination strategies. Finally, we propose a conceptual framework integrating pretreatment and longitudinal profiling of TAM states, spatial niches, and neighboring-cell interactions to inform patient stratification based on immune barriers and their treatment-associated changes. Given current methodological and evidentiary limitations, its clinical utility requires prospective validation.

title: TAGLN2 Drives Glioma Immune Evasion by Coordinating Macrophage Recruitment and Exosome-Mediated Functional Remodeling.
text: The highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of glioblastoma (GBM) is particularly prominent in tumors exhibiting mesenchymal-like (MES-like) transcriptional programs and represents a major barrier to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we identified TAGLN2 as an immune-regulatory molecule preferentially enriched in MES-like tumor-cell states. High TAGLN2 expression correlated with increased tumor-associated macrophage infiltration and poor prognosis. Mechanistically, TAGLN2 drives immune evasion via dual pathways. Intracellularly, TAGLN2 directly interacts with HSPA8 and promotes p65 phosphorylation and NF-κB activation, with HSPA8 functioning as a downstream mediator. Intercellularly, TAGLN2 promotes ANXA2 stability and its enrichment in tumor-derived exosomes. Donor-cell ANXA2 loss-of-function experiments further showed that ANXA2 knockdown substantially attenuated the macrophage-remodeling activity, while recipient-cell analyses positioned STAT3 downstream of ANXA2, together supporting a TAGLN2-vesicular ANXA2-STAT3 signaling pathway. Direct EV intervention and donor-cell ANXA2 rescue in immunocompetent orthotopic glioma models further supported the functional involvement of this pathway in tumor progression and macrophage-associated remodeling. In an immunocompetent orthotopic glioma model, genetic TAGLN2 knockdown enhanced CD8-associated effector-marker signals and improved responsiveness to anti-PD-1 treatment. Through virtual drug screening, we identified Givinostat hydrochloride monohydrate, a histone deacetylase inhibitor prioritized by in silico prediction of central nervous system accessibility, as a candidate pharmacological modulator that directly binds TAGLN2 and modulates the TAGLN2-associated signaling network. Together, these findings support TAGLN2 as an important regulator of GBM immune remodeling and suggest a candidate combination strategy for enhancing responsiveness to PD-1 blockade.

title: [Cellular origin of DICER1 sarcoma : Universal fibroblasts as the cell of origin].
text: DICER1 syndrome predisposes children and young adults to a spectrum of neoplasms that, in some cases, share a common morphological and molecular phenotype despite arising at different anatomical sites. Their cell of origin has remained unknown. We developed a lineage-traceable genetically engineered mouse model in which a hemizygous Dicer1 RNase IIIb mutation is activated in a temporally controlled manner in Hic1-positive mesenchymal stromal cells. The resulting renal tumors faithfully recapitulated the histological and molecular continuum of human DICER1-associated mesenchymal neoplasms. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses identified a Pdgfra+/Dpt+/Pi16+ fibroblastic progenitor population that can either undergo rhabdomyoblastic differentiation or transition into proliferative sarcomatous cell states. Chromosomal alterations, loss of p53, and MAPK pathway activation were associated with the proliferative state. Analogous cell states and developmental trajectories were also identified in human DICER1-associated tumors. These findings establish a universal fibroblast as the putative cell of origin of DICER1 sarcoma and suggest that the morphological continuum of these tumors reflects a shared developmental hierarchy. Das DICER1-Syndrom prädisponiert Kinder und junge Erwachsene zu einem Spektrum von Neoplasien, die in einigen Fällen trotz unterschiedlicher anatomischer Lokalisation einen gemeinsamen morphologischen und molekularen Phänotyp aufweisen können. Ihre Ursprungszelle war bislang unbekannt. Wir haben ein linienverfolgbares, genetisch modifiziertes Mausmodell entwickelt, in dem eine hemizygote Dicer1-RNase-IIIb-Mutation zeitlich kontrolliert in Hic1-positiven mesenchymalen Stromazellen aktiviert wird. Die resultierenden Nierentumoren bildeten das histologische und molekulare Kontinuum humaner DICER1-assoziierter mesenchymaler Neoplasien getreu ab. Einzelzellanalysen und räumliche Transkriptomanalysen identifizierten eine Pdgfra+/Dpt+/Pi16+ fibroblastäre Vorläuferpopulation, die entweder rhabdomyoblastär differenzieren oder in proliferative sarkomatöse Zellzustände übergehen kann. Chromosomale Alterationen, Verlust von p53 und Aktivierung des MAPK-Signalwegs waren mit dem proliferativen Zustand assoziiert. Analoge Zellzustände und Entwicklungswege fanden sich auch in humanen DICER1-assoziierten Tumoren. Die Ergebnisse unserer Forschungsarbeit legen einen universellen Fibroblasten als putative Ursprungszelle des DICER1-Sarkoms nahe, und das morphologische Kontinuum dieser Tumoren dürfte, unabhängig von der Tumorlokalisation, eine gemeinsame Entwicklungshierarchie widerspiegeln.

title: CosMxScope: scalable reconstruction and digital pathology integration of imaging-based CosMx spatial transcriptomics data.
text: Spatial transcriptomics technologies have transformed the capacity to quantify gene expression from human tissues, simultaneously capturing both the cell functional state and spatial organization at cellular and subcellular resolution. The CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager (SMI) is one of the leading platforms at single-cell spatial multi-modal omics profiling, capable of measuring thousands of RNA or protein targets at single-cell and subcellular resolution across whole slide sections. Exported data include field-of-view (FOV) image tiles, subcellular transcript coordinates, and cell segmentation polygons, outputs that are rich in spatial information but not directly compatible with widely used digital pathology tools. Here we present CosMxScope, a lightweight open-source Python framework designed for data exported from the CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager through the AtoMx platform, bridging CosMx spatial outputs with histopathology visualization environments. CosMxScope provides functions for stitching FOV image tiles into reconstructed whole-slide images, converting cell segmentation polygons and transcript coordinates into GeoJSON objects for downstream visualization and assessment within QuPath, and generating spatial visualization plots of cell types, transcript locations, and gene expression patterns. The framework is designed for practical use in translational research settings, enabling interactive exploration of spatial transcriptomic data alongside cell morphology. CosMxScope has been applied in multiple ongoing research projects involving CosMx profiling of human and mouse tissues, supporting pathology-based spatial analysis workflows. This open-source software is available at https://github.com/AivaraX-AI/CosMxScope.

title: From QSAR-guided fragment design to 500 ns dynamics: multiscale mechanistic dissection of novel MNK2 inhibitors.
text: MNK2 is a promising anticancer therapeutic target, yet currently reported MNK2 inhibitors suffer from insufficient subtype selectivity and unsatisfactory druggability, which restricts their further clinical translation. Rational computer-aided drug design provides an effective route for discovering novel MNK2 inhibitors. In this contribution, we constructed reliable HQSAR and Topomer CoMFA QSAR models to extract key substituent modification principles for potency improvement, aiming to discover new MNK2 lead candidates with favorable pharmacokinetic profiles. Fifteen novel MNK2 derivatives were designed via fragment-based screening, molecular docking, ADMET profiling, and MM/PBSA calculation, with N4, N8, and N9 identified as leads. A progressive extension strategy was applied: 100 ns simulations first verified short-term binding stability, and the same three complexes were then extended to 500 ns production simulations for long-timescale binding-mechanism analysis. The native ligand was only subjected to 100 ns MD simulation as a structural reference, and it failed to form sustained stable hydrogen bonds with the binding pocket throughout the trajectory. RMSD, RMSF, Rg, SASA, hydrogen bond and FEL analyses confirmed stable binding of all three complexes without conformational drift or ligand dissociation. N8 showed the most robust binding, featuring persistent hydrogen bonding with LYS A:113 and full hydrophobic enclosure. van der Waals interactions dominated binding free energy, while the LYS A:113-centered hydrogen bond network contributed to ligand anchoring and kinetic stability. All compounds adopted an ATP-competitive binding mode. This study provides clear SAR guidelines and privileged scaffolds for selective MNK2 inhibitor development, pending experimental validation.

title: Targeted siRNA-lactobionic lipid nanoparticles with novel ionizable lipid inhibit antithrombin III expression in hepatocytes.
text: Targeted reduction of hepatic antithrombin (AT) via siRNA offers a promising strategy to enhance thrombin (TMB) generation in bleeding disorders, though efficient hepatocyte delivery remains challenging. This study developed and evaluated a targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation incorporating a novel morpholine-based ionizable lipid (MIL) and a lactobionic-octadecylamine conjugate (LBN) for hepatocyte-specific delivery of AT-siRNA (siAT). Following synthesis of MIL and LBN, siAT-loaded LNP (siAT LNP LBN) were prepared using microfluidics and characterized for size, morphology, zeta potential, polydispersity index, and encapsulation efficiency (EE). Functional assays on HepG2 cells assessed cellular uptake, protein knockdown, and AT activity. The optimized formulation exhibited uniform particles (124 nm, PDI 0.125, zeta potential - 8.9 mV) and high EE (90%). Cytotoxicity assays confirmed safety up to 65 pmol siRNA. LBN-decorated LNP significantly enhanced hepatocyte uptake compared to non-targeted LNP and naked siRNA. Optimal AT mRNA suppression occurred at ~ 65 pmol siRNA and 16 h, with protein knockdown confirmed at 48 h. Functionally, siAT LNP LBN reduced AT activity to 48.1 ± 5.5%, substantially outperforming non-targeted LNP (64.1%) and naked siRNA (86.6%). The developed siAT-LNP-LBN platform demonstrated efficient hepatocyte uptake, robust AT knockdown, and low cytotoxicity in vitro, providing preliminary evidence for its potential as a hepatocyte-targeted siRNA delivery platform. Further in vivo studies are warranted to evaluate its biodistribution, liver-targeting efficiency, pharmacodynamic effects, therapeutic efficacy, and biosafety.

title: Hybridization-Mediated Reversible sgRNA Caging Enables Tumor-Selective Gene Editing for Potentiating Antitumor Immunity via cGAS Demethylation.
text: Spatiotemporal precision remains a critical challenge against the gene editing technology used for disease treatment. We herein developed a tumor cell-selective CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system by introducing a complementary single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) containing apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) sites (AP-ssDNA) along the target region of single-guided RNA (sgRNA). The engineered hybrid (AP-ssDNA/sgRNA) could tracelessly release the native sgRNA in tumor cells due to cleavage of AP-ssDNA by the overexpressed apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1), thus enabling tumor-selective gene editing. Subsequently, a biodegradable lipid nanoparticle based on dynamic covalent bonding was developed to codeliver Cas9-encoding mRNA (mCas9) with AP-ssDNA/sgRNA targeting the SUV39H1 gene, which mediated silence of cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) methylation to activate stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and enhanced antitumor immunity. As thus, when coupled with radiotherapy, the gene editing platform provoked robust antitumor efficacy in B16F10 xenograft tumor-bearing mice. This study provides a versatile paradigm for conditionally controlled gene editing and highlights the therapeutic potential of cGAS demethylation in reactivating cGAS-STING pathway for antitumor immunotherapy.

title: The mRNA-Based Therapeutic Vaccine NTX250 Induces Potent Antitumor Immunity in HPV-Driven Cancers.
text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) plays a pivotal role in various malignancies, including cervical, anogenital, head, and neck cancers. Despite the availability of highly effective prophylactic vaccines, many individuals remain susceptible to HPV-driven cancers because of barriers such as limited vaccine access, lack of awareness, or personal preferences. Current treatments primarily target lesions without eradicating persistent HPV infections, leading to an increased risk of subsequent HPV-associated cancers. This scenario underscores an urgent need for innovative treatment modalities aimed at eliminating persistent HPV infections. In this study, we developed NTX250, a messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutic platform engineered to deliver HPV type 16 (HPV16) E6 and E7 antigens, in conjunction with the immunomodulators interleukin (IL) 12 and LIGHT. A lipid and ionizable peptoid nanoparticle system facilitated precise intralesional delivery of NTX250. Localized NTX250 administration in HPV16-transformed tumor-bearing models led to complete tumor regression and established durable, antigen-specific immune memory. Replacing the HPV antigens with a construct comprising colorectal cancer cell-specific neoepitopes enabled stimulated antitumor immunity and suppressed tumor growth, supporting the generalizability of the approach. Overall, NTX250 represents a promising nonsurgical immunotherapy platform that is capable of eliciting robust and targeted antitumor immune responses across diverse malignancies. This adaptable mRNA nanoparticle approach enables the codelivery of tumor-specific antigens and immunomodulators, with the potential to target tumor-associated antigens beyond HPV. NTX250 is an mRNA-based therapeutic platform that offers a noninvasive approach to eradicate persistent HPV infections and induce strong antitumor immune responses, fulfilling a critical need in HPV-related cancer treatment.

title: Current perspectives on the design of functional fermented food systems: Substrate valorization, microbial community engineering and intelligent control.
text: Fermentation has evolved from a conventional food preservation process into a versatile biotechnological platform to produce functional foods and value-added bioactive compounds. Recent advances increasingly recognize fermented food systems as dynamic microbial ecosystems in which substrate composition, microbial interactions, environmental conditions, and process interventions jointly determine functionality, safety, and product quality. However, advances in substrate engineering, microbial community design, metabolite optimization, sensing technologies, and artificial intelligence have progressed faster than their integration into reproducible and scalable fermentation processes. The central bottleneck is therefore not the lack of individual enabling technologies, but the limited ability to translate biologically variable fermentation states into standardized and interoperable data, transferable predictive models, and effective process-control strategies across different substrates, microbial systems, and production scales. This review adopts this process-integration challenge as its organizing perspective and critically evaluates why individual technological advances, although necessary, remain insufficient when developed in isolation. The transition from spontaneous fermentation toward defined microbial consortia, together with the emergence of precision fermentation platforms, is evaluated with particular emphasis on microbial succession, metabolic cross-feeding, ecological interactions, and omics-guided starter selection. Conventional and emerging substrates, including agro-industrial by-products, plant-derived materials, and food processing side streams, are assessed as functional feedstocks within circular bioeconomy strategies. Bioactive metabolites and postbiotics are examined together with the role of fermented food matrices as natural delivery systems and their technological and health-related functions. Multi-omics approaches, biosensors, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things platforms, and digital twins are further evaluated as tools for predictive monitoring and adaptive process control. Attention is given to biological variability, limited data standardization and interoperability, insufficient cross-scale validation, and poor transferability of predictive models across fermentation systems. Finally, a systems-level framework is proposed that connects substrate design, microbial ecology, metabolic functionality, real-time sensing, data integration, predictive modeling, and process control with measurable food performance. This perspective argues that progress toward reproducible, scalable, functional, and sustainable fermentation will depend less on technological sophistication alone than on establishing transferable links between biological state, measurement, prediction, and process control.

title: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources and Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Integration for Health Data Interoperability in Belgium: Mixed Methods Study.
text: Managing health information is one of the greatest challenges in modern health care. In Belgium, decentralization and fragmentation further complicate interoperability. Primary data, collected through electronic health records, and secondary data, used for research and policy, require distinct approaches. Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) enables real-time clinical data exchange, while the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) model standardizes heterogeneous datasets for large-scale analysis. The goal of this study was to assess the strengths, weaknesses, and feasibility of using FHIR and OMOP together in the context of Belgian health care to identify barriers and opportunities for their combined use. To answer the research questions, a mixed methods approach was used (using both qualitative and quantitative methods). This included an analysis of FHIR and OMOP technical documentation and technical literature as well as semistructured interviews with 8 research experts drawn from 3 professional backgrounds, including health data governance, clinical practice, and biomedical research. Findings show that primary data use is facilitated by FHIR by improved electronic health record interoperability, public health surveillance, and clinical decision support. However, adoption is hindered by constant updates, economic constraints, and fragmented regulation. OMOP demonstrates great potential for secondary data, facilitating harmonized epidemiological studies, pharmacovigilance, and global collaboration. Integration with legacy systems, high costs, and low granularity are major obstacles. Experts identified clinicians as essential for ensuring data quality and highlighted their importance in preventing administrative burden and encouraging uptake by training and designing user-friendly tools. FHIR and OMOP complement one another in addressing disparate but connected sides of the reuse of health information. Both together can enhance interoperability, streamline clinical workflows, and expand the ability to perform research. Achieving this requires targeted investment, regulatory alignment, and clinician engagement, placing Belgium at the forefront of digital health innovation in Europe.

title: Digital health infrastructure and research priorities across neonatal intensive care units in Germany: A nationwide cross-sectional survey.
text: Digital infrastructure increasingly determines whether clinical data can be reused for quality improvement, federated research, and population-level health surveillance, yet the digital maturity of neonatal intensive care has not been characterized at national scale. Neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) generate dense, continuous data for an extremely vulnerable population, a high-stakes exemplar of data-rich, high-acuity care. We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional online survey of NICUs in Germany to map digital infrastructure and to capture respondents' attitudes, perceived barriers, and research priorities. Of 340 invited units, 136 (40%) began the questionnaire and 124 (36%) submitted analyzable unit-level responses between June and September 2025. Respondents were almost exclusively senior physicians, with no nurses or biomedical engineers, and responding centers were larger and more often university-affiliated than non-responders. Digitization was highly uneven: laboratory and imaging data were predominantly digital, whereas vital-sign, physician-note, medication, and nutrition documentation remained largely paper-based. A composite digitization score was apparently bimodal, suggesting a possible digital divide; only 33% of units operated a dedicated patient data management system at the bedside. Most respondents (83%) wanted further digitization, and demand was strongest in the least-digitized units (Spearman ρ = - 0.39, p < 0.001), although ceiling effects and common-method variance may contribute to this association. The dominant perceived barriers were shortages of information-technology personnel and the cost of software and hardware. These findings identify bedside documentation as the principal modernization priority and provide an exploratory indicator and baseline for tracking digital maturity over time. Mandated interoperability standards and targeted structural investment may be warranted to close the divide and to support more equitable and collaborative use of neonatal data across regions and health systems.

title: Evolution of Automated Insulin Delivery Devices in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Narrative Review.
text: Insulin delivery has evolved through distinct technological phases, each improving the usability and dosing control and accuracy. This review traces the historical evolution of insulin delivery devices through distinct eras, beginning with the early use of insulin syringes for manual administration, followed by the introduction of insulin pens that improved portability and dosing precision. Subsequently, the emergence of continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII), sensor-augmented pump (SAP) therapy, and finally, the automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, have created a significant breakthrough in the evolution of modern diabetes care. Safety-oriented automation, including low-glucose suspend (LGS) and predictive low-glucose suspend (PLGS), marked the first steps toward closed-loop control. The commercialization of hybrid closed-loop (HCL) systems represented a paradigm shift, enabling real-time, algorithm-driven basal insulin modulation and significantly improving glycemic outcomes, including increased time in range (TIR) and reduced hypoglycemia. Advanced hybrid closed-loop (AHCL) systems have since introduced customizable targets, automated correction boluses, and interoperability standards, creating flexible ecosystems for personalized diabetes management. Fully closed-loop systems have entered clinical trials offering automated insulin delivery independent of meal announcements. Despite these advances, adoption remains limited by suboptimal user-friendliness, intensive training requirements, and high costs leading to inequitable access, with an ongoing need for user engagement, alarm management, and periodic troubleshooting in real-world settings. Looking ahead, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and neural network-based algorithms is expected to drive the next wave of innovation, enabling more adaptive, autonomous, and patient-centered diabetes care.

title: Advancing FAIR sharing for epidemiological, clinical and public health study data: the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI4Health).
text: Access to high-quality, FAIR health data is essential for advancing epidemiological, public health and clinical research. NFDI4Health, one of the consortia of Germany's National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI), was established in 2020 to address this need by improving data FAIRness for the scientific community. During the initial funding phase, NFDI4Health developed key infrastructure components and services focusing on interoperability, data sharing and research support. Our approach was guided by user needs and real-world use cases in alignment with (inter)national FAIR standards and infrastructures. We advanced findability of health data by establishing a central Health Study Hub and connecting it to local infrastructures, e.g., through the Local Data Hub software, to facilitate transfer of metadata from the local infrastructures to the Health Study Hub. Accessibility was improved by expanding the German Research Data Portal for Health (FDPG) to provide central access to study data and by providing tools to support anonymisation and synthetic data generation. We also developed an interoperable metadata schema for publishing study data and implemented it in the Health Study Hub. To further improve interoperability, a NFDI4Health FAIR sharing collection and AI support for metadata annotation and harmonisation workflows were established. To enhance reusability, data quality assessment tools were further developed, and two frameworks for federated analysis of sensitive health data were piloted. Intensive engagement with our communities through training, advisory services, and collaborative development ensured user relevance. NFDI4Health has established a scalable, interoperable, and user-centred infrastructure to support FAIR data sharing in health research. Future work will focus on further developing and consolidating the infrastructure, expanding cross-domain data integration, fostering broader adoption within our research community, and strengthening national and international collaboration.

title: A Machine Learning Model Based on Ultrasound Radiomics and Multi-modal Clinical Features for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma in the Setting of Hashimoto's Thyroiditis.
text: To investigate the value of multi-modal features (ultrasound characteristics, BRAF V600E mutation, and TPO-Ab) in predicting lymph node metastasis (LNM) of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in the context of Hashimoto's thyroiditis (HT), and to construct machine learning models for individualized risk assessment. A retrospective cohort of 377 patients with pathologically confirmed PTC and concurrent HT was enrolled and divided into LNM n=186 and non-LNM n=191 groups. Preoperative ultrasound features (e.g., Minimum Tumor-to-Capsule Distance (DTC_min), calcification type and ratio, lesion location, nodule morphology), serological and pathological indicators were collected. Random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost and XGB), logistic regression (LR), and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) were used to build prediction models. Feature importance was assessed, and model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and calibration curves. Univariate analysis showed that calcification type, nodule diameter, DTC_min, and aspect ratio were significantly associated with LNM, with nodule diameter contributing the most. Overall, the integration of multi‑omics features significantly improved the accuracy of lymph node metastasis prediction. Radiomics features contributed the largest share (81.5%), followed by morphological features (M1: DTC_min/Size/Calcification, 12.7%), while molecular markers and genetic biomarkers provided supplementary information (M2: TPO‑Ab, 3.8%; M3: BRAF V600E, 2.0%). Notably, the optimal XGBoost model achieved a stable accuracy of 0.879 in an independent external cohort (n = 107), confirming its robust generalizability for clinical risk assessment. In the HT setting, machine learning models based on multi-omics feature fusion enable effective individualized risk stratification for PTC LNM, offering precise support for clinical decision-making.

title: Multichannel Deep Learning Radiomics for Predicting Chemoimmunotherapy Response in Gastric Cancer: Multicenter Validation and Chemotherapy-alone Specificity Assessment.
text: To develop and validate a computed tomography-based model integrating multichannel deep learning and radiomics for predicting pathologic significant response (PSR) to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) in locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC), and to assess whether the model specifically captures immunotherapy-related phenotypes by testing it on a chemotherapy-alone cohort. This multicenter study included 455 patients with LAGC: 411 receiving NACI (split into training, internal validation, and external test set 1) and 44 receiving chemotherapy alone (test set 2). From three-dimensional (3D) segmentations, the largest axial, coronal, and sagittal slices were stacked as three-channel input for a pretrained ResNet50 to extract deep features; radiomic features were extracted from the 3D volume. Features were fused, reduced by the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator, and modeled with a support vector machine to construct a deep learning radiomics (DLR) signature. A combined model further incorporated mismatch repair status, programmed death-ligand 1 combined positive score, and tumor grade. Model performance was evaluated by area under the curve (AUC), calibration, and decision curve analysis, with SHAP for interpretability. The multichannel model outperformed single-plane models (AUCs: 0.783, 0.749, 0.706). The DLR model achieved the highest AUCs (0.827, 0.802, 0.776), surpassing radiomics-only (0.756, 0.712, 0.691) and multichannel deep models. Critically, its AUC dropped to 0.597 in the chemotherapy-alone cohort. SHAP provided global and individual feature attributions. The multichannel DLR model accurately predicts PSR to NACI in LAGC. The substantial performance decline in the chemotherapy-alone cohort suggests that the captured imaging phenotypes may be more closely associated with immunotherapy-related response, rather than with general chemosensitivity, potentially offering a noninvasive, interpretable tool for pretreatment stratification.

title: Structure-based phenotypes of knee and hip osteoarthritis display clinical and genetic differences with potential implications for stratified treatment.
text: Osteoarthritis is a heterogeneous disease, with diverse structural patterns likely reflecting distinct pathomechanisms. However, scalable imaging-driven approaches to define clinically meaningful phenotypes are limited. This study aimed to identify structure-based osteoarthritis phenotypes incorporating demographic features at population scale and evaluate their clinical and genetic profiles. Machine learning models were applied to knee and hip DXA scans from UK Biobank to quantify osteophyte area, minimum joint space width, and B-scoresDXA. Imaging and demographic features were clustered using k-means to classify individuals with at least one osteoarthritis feature. Associations with joint pain and total joint replacement (TJR) were evaluated relative to structurally normal controls. Genetic correlations and polygenic risk scores were analysed to characterise shared and differing genetic architecture across phenotypes. Among 59,539 participants, a nine-phenotype clustering solution was derived in 28,953 participants with structural features of osteoarthritis, spanning joint-specific and multi-joint patterns. Across the nine phenotypes, prolonged knee pain ranged from 12.2% (95% CI 11.5-13.0) to 61.2% (52.7-69.0), and during follow-up knee replacement from 0.37% (0.25-0.55) to 14.9% (9.9-21.9), with the lowest proportions in the narrower joint space phenotype and highest in knee end-stage. The adjusted odds ratio for knee replacement in knee end-stage versus structurally normal controls was 98.8 (95% CI 55.5-175.9). Hip replacement ranged from 0.21% (0.12-0.35) in narrower joint space to 13.6% (10.7-17.1) in left hip end-stage (adjusted OR versus controls 72.9 [95% CI 50.3-105.6]). Genetic differences included an inverse genetic correlation between wider and narrower joint space phenotypes (rg -0.46 [95% CI -0.91, -0.01]). End-stage phenotypes demonstrated the highest joint-specific polygenic risk scores. Population-scale imaging identifies structure-based osteoarthritis phenotypes, encompassing variation in demographics, structural components and severity, with distinct clinical outcomes and genetic profiles. This provides a scalable framework for stratifying osteoarthritis patients. Whether these phenotypes predict treatment response or inform treatment selection remains to be established and further investigation is required.

title: Machine learning for small-molecule antibiotics - discovery to pre-clinical optimization.
text: The rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health crisis, with 4.71 million associated deaths and 1.14 million attributable deaths in 2021. By 2050, these tolls are forecasted to rise to 8.22 million associated deaths and 1.91 million attributable deaths annually. Despite this growing burden, the antibacterial pipeline is alarmingly lean, with few candidates exhibiting truly novel mechanisms of action (MOA). This innovation gap is worsened by the lack of economic incentives for large pharmaceutical companies to develop new antibiotics, placing increasing pressure on academic laboratories and small biotechnology companies. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising, albeit unproven, toolset to accelerate and reduce the cost of antibiotic discovery and development. To review a cross-section of ML methods and their applications across the preclinical antibiotic discovery and development pipeline. Google Scholar and PubMed were searched through June 2026, combining terms for machine learning, deep learning, and artificial intelligence with antibiotic discovery and development, virtual screening, generative molecular design, and ADMET prediction. Primary research articles were prioritized, with preprints from arXiv and bioRxiv included where no peer-reviewed version was available. Reference lists of retrieved articles and WHO antibacterial pipeline reports were also screened. ML approaches enable more efficient exploration of vast chemical spaces in silico, facilitating the discovery of structurally novel antibacterial compounds in phenotype- and target-based applications. Both discriminative and generative models have demonstrated success in discovering new scaffolds and in multi-property optimization tasks. In target-based discovery, ML-guided docking strategies have improved scalability relative to more computationally demanding physics-based methods. ML-guided methods can improve the efficiency, scalability, and success rate of antibiotic discovery and development programs. However, the implementation of these models will require high-quality training data and rigorous experimental validation prior to end-to-end integration.
