title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
text: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $ρ= -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $φ= 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
text: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).

title: Non-Invasive Bioelectronic Analytics
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] Biomarkers can be evaluated to provide information about disease presence or intensity and treatment efficacy. By recording these biomarkers through noninvasive clinical techniques, it is possible to gain information about the autonomic nervous system (ANS), which involuntarily regulates and adapts organ systems in the body. Machine learning and signal processing methods have made it possible to quantify the behavior of the ANS by statistically analyzing recorded signals. This work will aim to systematically measure ANS function by multiple modalities and use decoding algorithms to derive an index that reflects overall ANS function and/or balance in healthy able-bodied individuals. Additionally, this study will determine how transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS), a noninvasive method of stimulating the vagus nerve without surgery, affects the ANS function. Data from this research will enable the possibility of detecting early and significant changes in ANS from "normal" homeostasis to diagnose disease onset and assess severity to improve treatment protocols.

title: Evaluating Continuous Pressure Monitoring in the Community
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] There are many situations where an individual will spend prolonged periods in their bed or chair, often observed in community settings where individuals may have impaired mobility. In many cases, individuals, carers and care providers are not alerted to periods of prolonged immobility. This results in poor self-management and limits access to care support to promote movement. A potential consequence of these prolonged periods of sitting or lying are pressure ulcers, often termed bed sores, which can develop into wounds which are painful and can take a long time to heal. This has a significant impact on the quality of life for the individual affected and is a risk to patient safety and poorer quality of care. The investigators represent a team of scientists, clinicians, care providers and industry collaborators who have been working with technologies to monitor individuals whilst lying and sitting. Over the last seven years the investingating team have successfully used commercial continuous pressure monitors in community and hospital healthcare settings to evaluate movement patterns over prolonged periods. Through monitoring pressures between the individual and their cushion or mattress they have been able to effectively communicate when they have been less mobile. The technology has also been used to improve the type of cushion or mattress they use to support their health. This has helped individuals understand the risks of being less mobile and supported them to self-manage through regular repositioning and cooperation in care. The investigators have co-developed improvements to the sensing system and display which is purposefully designed for people living in the community at high risk of pressure ulcers. This was achieved through the principles of co-production, which means working together with patients and the public, service providers and industry partners on a 'fit for purpose solution'. The project has been designed to maximise the input from those who will be using the technology, where innovation must fit around the end user. Through monitoring of posture and mobility we aim to promote self-management through prompts and alerts. Data will also be shared with care service providers, so timely interventions can be made to prevent illness or injury which may otherwise have resulted in hospitalisation. It is necessary to consider the user experiences (UX) of patients, carers and health and social care professionals when exploring the use of medical devices such as continuous pressure monitors. Ergonomic design principles can also reduce the cost of medical device production. This study will help the investigators determine whether the continuous pressure monitor is acceptable for use in community settings such as the person's own home or a care home. This will mean exploring the views of patients, carers and health and social care professionals who will be using the technology as part of an assessment for the risk of pressure ulcers. The investigator team will work with clinicians to provide training (in person and online videos) and manuals for the use of the continuous pressure monitor and ask nurses to implement the technology in community settings (care homes, nursing home and private homes). This will be used with individuals either at risk of getting a pressure ulcer or who currently have a pressure ulcer. The investigators will then explore how easy the technology was to use and explore any barriers and facilitators for its use in practice. During the study investigators will use interviews, surveys and the data from the continuous pressure monitoring device to assess this. The data will be used to explore how feasible it is to recruit 60 individuals from the community and 20 of their carers and health and social care professionals supporting them. title: Using Machine Learning to Model Early-onset Neonatal Sepsis Risk in Uganda and Zimbabwe
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] The goal of this observational study is to develop a risk prediction model for early-onset neonatal sepsis in term and late preterm neonates in Uganda and Zimbabwe. The main questions it aims to answer are: * What are the risk factors for early-onset neonatal sepsis in low-resource settings? * How can these be combined into a risk prediction model? Mother-baby pairs will be recruited in Uganda. They will have extensive data taken on their medical and obstetric histories and lifestyles, and their newborns will have a blood sample taken just after birth for culture. Machine learning techniques will be used to create the risk prediction model, which will then be validated in a second population in Zimbabwe.

title: Investigating Subcellular Skeletal Muscle Adaptations to 10 Weeks of Lower-Body Resistance Training
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The goal of this clinical trial is to learn how a 10-week, lower-body strength-training program changes the structure of a large thigh muscle called the vastus lateralis. Researchers want to know when these changes start, how large they are, and which processes inside the muscle cause them. They are also interested in how quickly new proteins are made in the muscle during training. Healthy adults of any sex will take part in the study. One leg will begin training right away, and the other leg will start one week later. This staggered start lets researchers compare muscle changes at different points without taking too many muscle samples from one leg. Training sessions will be supervised and will use two common gym machines (leg press and leg extension) three times per week for 10 weeks. At the end of the program, participants will repeat the baseline tests to see how much they have improved. Before training begins, participants will complete a series of tests, including a body-composition scan (to measure body fat and muscle mass), an ultrasound scan of the thigh muscle (to measure muscle thickness), and a strength test to find the maximum weight the leg can lift. Participants will also drink a special type of water called "heavy water." Heavy water looks and tastes like normal water but contains a form of hydrogen that lets researchers measure how fast new muscle proteins are made. The total amount of heavy water is very small. Participants drink a body-weight-based amount on the first day, split into three small doses, and then a much smaller dose every day for the rest of the study. To monitor the heavy water in their bodies, participants will provide saliva and blood samples at the beginning of the study and at each biopsy visit. During the 10-week program participants will: * Train three times per week on the leg press and leg extension machines under supervision. * Drink a small amount of heavy water daily as explained above. * Wear a Fitbit activity tracker for one week at the start, one week at the middle, and one week at the end of the study to record daily steps and sleep. * Provide muscle samples (biopsies) from each thigh: once before and once after a workout in week 2, and once after weeks 3, 7, and 10. A brief ultrasound scan of the thigh muscle will be done at each biopsy visit to track changes in muscle thickness. After training is completed, participants will repeat the body-composition scan, ultrasound, and strength test. The muscle samples will be analyzed in a laboratory to count the number of tiny fibres (myofibrils) inside each muscle cell, measure their size, and determine how new proteins were made using the heavy-water tracer. The researchers will also look at markers of muscle growth and repair. By comparing results from the trained and delayed legs and by looking at changes over time, the study aims to provide a detailed picture of how human muscle adapts to resistance training. This information could help health professionals design better exercise programs for building strength, preventing muscle loss, and aiding recovery from injury.

title: Prospective Multicentre Validation of a Landmark Machine Learning Model for ICU Mortality in Neurocritical Care
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Mortality prediction in neurocritical care relies on scores computed at admission, which cannot update as the clinical course evolves. We previously developed a landmark-based machine learning model that converts hourly physiological data, including intracranial pressure, into an updating risk of death. The model was developed in a large public database and validated retrospectively in a second, independent one. This prospective multicentre study will test the model in consecutive patients at participating hospitals in Fujian Province, China. Physiological data will be collected as part of routine care. The model will generate risk estimates that are recorded for analysis but not shown to treating clinicians, and no treatment decision will be influenced by the study. The primary analysis will assess discrimination and calibration of the model for death during the intensive care stay. Secondary analyses will compare the model with severity scores in routine use and examine performance by aetiology.

title: Impact of Positive Airway Pressure Therapy on Clinical Outcomes in Older Veterans With Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Comorbid Obstructive Sleep Apnea (Overlap Syndrome)
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: RECRUITING] Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) are highly prevalent chronic respiratory diseases in the Veteran population. OSA co-occurring with COPD, known as Overlap Syndrome (OVS), is a complex chronic medical condition associated with grave consequences. OVS is highly prevalent in Veterans. Veterans with OVS may be at increased risk for cognitive deficits, poor sleep quality as well as a reduced quality of life (QoL). The overall objective is to study the effects of positive airway pressure therapy on clinical outcomes in patients with OVS.

title: Evaluation and Treatment of Patients With Connective Tissue Disease
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] This study offers evaluation and treatment of patients with a suspected connective tissue disorder. The protocol is not designed to test new treatments; rather, patients receive standard care. The study is designed to: 1) allow NICHD's staff to learn more about connective tissue disorders, 2) train physicians in the evaluation and treatment of these disorders; and 3) establish a pool of patients who may be eligible for other NICHD protocols for connective tissue disorders. (Participants in this protocol will not be required to join another study; the decision will be voluntary.) Patients of all ages with a suspected connective tissue disorder and their unaffected family members may be eligible for this study. Participants undergo diagnostic procedures that may include a medical history, physical examination, X-ray studies, eye examinations, and blood drawing, as well as other specialized tests, when needed. Additional tests may include: * Blood test for DNA genetic analysis * Skin biopsy: Removal of a small piece of tissue for microscopic examination. The area of skin selected for the biopsy is numbed and a small circle of skin, usually from the upper arm, is removed with a surgical cookie cutter-like instrument. * Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): This test uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to show structural and chemical changes in tissues. The patient lies on a table that slides into a narrow cylinder containing a magnetic field. Ear plugs are worn to muffle loud knocking and thumping sounds that occur with electrical switching of the magnetic fields. * Computed tomography (CT) scans: This test allows the doctor to view the organs inside the body in small sections. The patient lies in a doughnut-like machine. Scanning can be done from different angles, allowing a three dimensional picture of the part of the body being studied. It may be done with or without injection of a contrast material. * Referral to appropriate sub-specialists when potential complications are found.

title: Physiology-directed Epinephrine Dosing in Pediatric Cardiac Arrest
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] This is a prospective, observational, multi-center cohort study of pediatric cardiac arrests. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the physiologic response to epinephrine as an outcome discriminator in pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). In addition, the investigators will determine optimal epinephrine dosing strategies based on the initial physiologic response to epinephrine, and to develop machine learning (ML) algorithms to guide intra-arrest therapy.

title: Functional Loss of Invasion Quantified in a CRISPR Knockout Hydrogel Model.
text: Genetic screens have transformed functional genomics but remain poorly suited for interrogating invasion phenotypes in defined three-dimensional (3D) microenvironments due to low nucleofection efficiencies and the lack of high-content, quantifiable invasion assays. Here we present a chemically defined hyaluronan-based hydrogel platform that enables quantitative, single-cell-resolved measurement of cell invasion and is compatible with arrayed CRISPR-Cas9 perturbation. Specifically, hyaluronan-oxime (HAox) was used to study the invasion of multiple patient-derived cell lines, modelling the invasive properties in two diseases - glioblastoma and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Efficient CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of 93 genes allowed identification of potential invasion-suppressing targets, including effects detectable only at single-cell resolution. This framework expands functional genetic screening to complex invasion behaviours in controlled 3D microenvironments and may be broadly applicable to other heterogeneous disease models. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Cellular invasion in cancer drives tumour recurrence and metastasis. Identification of target genes which correspond to a quantitative functional loss of invasion is challenging due to the lack of physiologically relevant microenvironments to model cell invasion in vitro, and robust nucleofection protocols to efficiently knock out target genes. We report HAox, a hyaluronan-based hydrogel platform, designed based on components enriched in the diseased cell microenvironment. HAox can robustly identify invasiveness of diseased cells compared to healthy controls in two model diseases characterized by diffuse cellular invasion. HAox, coupled with efficient electroporation protocols to perform targeted gene knockout, enabled efficient knockout of 93 genes and quantification of cellular invasion, providing a platform for researchers to perform high-content screening against invasion phenotypes.

title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.
text: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.

title: A Cas9D10A nickase mouse line for precise genome editing.
text: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing involves DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) whose repair can generate unintended on- and off-target mutations. Here, we report a transgenic mouse line ubiquitously expressing Cas9D10A nickase, which creates targeted single-strand breaks (SSBs) to stimulate precise gene editing while substantially reducing the undesired editing products associated with Cas9 nuclease. We demonstrate the versatility of this resource in primary T cells, B cells, and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), achieving efficient (5%-50%) high-fidelity reporter integration and introduction of cancer-relevant mutations at the Cd79b and Notch1 loci. By enabling precise, low-mutation-burden gene editing directly in primary cells, the Cas9D10A nickase mouse line provides a resource for inserting mutations relevant for hematopoietic disorders and malignancies and may be utilized more broadly for precision genome engineering across primary cell types.

title: CRISPR/Cas for diatom gene editing: pitfalls, solutions, and emerging tools.
text: Diatoms are ecologically important unicellular photosynthetic microalgae that are of increasing interest in biotechnology. Remarkably, probably due to their complex evolutionary history, diatoms hold many species-specific genes, most of which have an unknown function. The development of CRISPR/Cas-based genome editing techniques offers a unique opportunity to elucidate the function of these genes and to introduce novel traits of interest. Just as Arabidopsis thaliana serves as the reference model for higher plant genetics, Phaeodactylum tricornutum has emerged as the principal model for diatom genome editing. Its CRISPR/Cas toolkit comprises Cas9, Cas12a, CRISPR interference, and genome-wide screens. However, progress remains uneven. Methods optimized for P. tricornutum are not readily transferable to other diatoms, which often require species-specific adjustments. In this review, we discuss the current state of CRISPR/Cas-mediated editing in diatoms and, where relevant, compare it with the more well-established field of plant genome editing. We argue that extending these tools is essential to understand diatom biology and realize their full biotechnological potential.

title: CRISPR-Mediated PABPC1 Upregulation via ELF5 Binding Disruption Enhances Milk Protein and Lipid Biosynthesis in Goat Mammary Epithelial Cells.
text: Post-transcriptional control of milk protein and lipid production in goats remains poorly understood. Here we combined ONT full-length transcriptome sequencing with RNA pull-down coupled to LC-MS/MS to identify RNA-binding proteins associated with milk protein mRNAs, and uncovered poly(A)-binding protein cytoplasmic 1 (PABPC1) as a central regulator. PABPC1 bound the 3'UTRs of casein and lipid-related transcripts such as CSN2, CSN3, LALBA, and FASN, stabilizing these mRNAs and promoting their translation, while dose-dependently modulating alternative polyadenylation (APA) site selection to reshape 3'UTR isoform usage. ELF5 directly bound the PABPC1 promoter, repressing its transcription. CRISPR/Cas9 editing of this binding motif relieved this repression, elevating PABPC1 levels and increasing casein accumulation and triglyceride synthesis in goat mammary epithelial cells. Our findings define an ELF5-PABPC1-APA regulatory module and nominate a tractable target for molecular breeding to enhance goat milk protein and lipid content.

title: Killers by Design: How Innovative Gene-Engineering Fine-Tunes NK Cells as Next Generation Immunotherapies.
text: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as promising candidates for adoptive immunotherapies. Their natural cytotoxic capabilities and low incidence of side-effects such as cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity, render NK cells a favorable alternative to T cells. Incorporation of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) has been shown to greatly enhance NK cell's antitumor capacity. Nevertheless, CAR-NK cell therapies still face several challenges, such as low in vivo persistence, low tumor homing of the transfused cells and the effects of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Genetic modifications of key cellular mediators show great potential to overcome these hurdles. While well-established viral engineering strategies are currently the most commonly used techniques, biosafety concerns, high costs, and labour-intensive protocols have encouraged innovation toward nonviral strategies. In this review, we describe recently established viral and nonviral technologies used for NK cell engineering, focusing on their respective advantages and disadvantages. In addition, we highlight the most important functional refinements and mechanistic characterizations of NK cells and genetically optimized NK cells in the context of the TME and how these advances can be progressed toward therapeutic translation.

title: Fitness costs and effects on the peritrophic matrix associated with chitin synthase 2 gene knockout in Vip3Aa-resistant Helicoverpa zea.
text: Genetically engineered crops producing insecticidal Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) proteins are used globally to manage key insect pests, including Helicoverpa zea (Lepidoptera: Noctuidae). In the United States, H. zea has evolved practical resistance to Bt corn and cotton producing crystalline Bt proteins and early warning of resistance to the vegetative insecticidal protein Vip3Aa has been reported. CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing that introduced disruptive mutations in the H. zea chitin synthase 2 (CHS2) gene facilitated creation of a strain (CHS2-KO) with 29 000-fold resistance to Vip3Aa relative to its parental susceptible strain, LAB-S. However, quantitative information about fitness costs associated with CHS2-mediated resistance remains limited. Here, we tested whether CHS2-KO exhibited costs affecting survival, development time, and pupal mass on diet without Vip3Aa, and examined direct effects on the peritrophic matrix (PM). Relative to LAB-S, fitness costs in CHS2-KO were 27.8% for neonate to adult survival, 23.2% for neonate to adult development time, and 17.8% for pupal mass. An intact PM was evident in LAB-S and F1 larvae, but not in CHS2-KO larvae. Mutations disrupting the CHS2 gene in the CHS2-KO strain of H. zea were associated with large fitness costs affecting survival, development time, and pupal mass when reared on diet under laboratory conditions. Also, no intact PM was evident in CHS2-KO. These results suggest that costs could oppose the spread of knockout alleles in the absence of Vip3Aa, although their magnitude on host plants and applicability to less disruptive CHS2 resistance alleles remain to be determined. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry. This article has been contributed to by U.S. Government employees and their work is in the public domain in the USA.

title: Emerging gene and stem cell therapies for hereditary hearing loss: from molecular correction to regenerative reconstruction.
text: Hearing loss is among the most common sensory impairments globally and remains a significant unmet clinical challenge. Current rehabilitative approaches, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, provide partial functional compensation but fail to restore the structural and physiological integrity of the cochlea. This review summarizes progress in therapeutic development targeting key deafness-associated genes, including OTOF, GJB2, and SLC26A4, highlighting the rationale, current clinical evidence, and major translational challenges. We further discuss the potential of combining gene therapy with stem cell-based approaches to promote inner ear regeneration and restore sensorineural function. Emerging technologies such as CRISPR/Cas, adeno-associated virus, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived otic progenitors have opened new avenues for causal correction and tissue reconstruction. Integrated therapeutic models that combine gene or stem cell therapy with cochlear implants are reshaping the treatment paradigm from symptom management to biological repair. Advances in gene editing, gene delivery, and stem cell technologies are establishing these approaches as promising treatments for hereditary hearing loss, with ongoing progress expected to accelerate clinical translation despite remaining challenges in delivery efficiency, immune responses, ethics, and long-term efficacy. Collectively, these advances mark a pivotal step toward personalized and regenerative interventions for hereditary hearing loss.

title: Analysis of single-cell sequencing data reveals metabolic reprogramming characterized by high PDK4 expression in non-inflammatory myocardial fibrosis.
text: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a metabolic disorder that poses a notable threat to human health, with post-MI heart failure (HF) markedly affecting patient prognosis. The overactivation of inflammation and fibrosis serves an important role in the progression of post-MI HF; however, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. The present study aimed to investigate the associations among metabolic reprogramming, inflammation and fibrosis after MI. By integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics data from MI and dilated cardiomyopathy, a common metabolic feature, glycolysis, was identified. This feature was shared by cardiomyocytes and monocytes in myocardial infarction and was specifically localized to the peri-infarct region. Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 4 was identified as a core gene linking metabolic reprogramming to fibrosis. A mouse model of MI was established by permanent ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. PDK4 knockout was applied to evaluate its role in post-infarction fibrotic remodeling. Furthermore, the results of the present study revealed a cross-cellular metabolic reprogramming process mediating chronic inflammatory cell interactions. In conclusion, the findings of the present study suggested that targeting metabolic reprogramming may offer a promising strategy for preventing inflammation and fibrosis to mitigate post-MI HF.

title: Androgen deprivation drives prostate cancer cells into a glycolysis-coupled senescence-like state.
text: The cellular origin, clinical significance, and metabolic features of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) in prostate cancer remain poorly resolved. We integrated bulk transcriptomes from TCGA-PRAD (primary, n = 495) and SU2C (mCRPC, n = 208), two single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, seven Visium sections, and one Xenium prostate adenocarcinoma section, together with immunoblotting in LNCaP and castration-adapted C4-2 cells treated with charcoal-stripped serum (CSS), enzalutamide (ENZ), and dihydrotestosterone (DHT). SASP formed a smooth, continuous gradient across bulk tumors rather than discrete subtypes. In Xenium, 4,657 of 25,517 tumor cells (18.3%) were positive for a senescence surrogate driven predominantly by p21 (CDKN1A) transcript detection; the local fraction of these cells correlated with a bin-level matrix-remodeling SASP program and glycolysis, but not with inflammatory SASP. The single-cell atlas revealed expansion of AR-low, stasis/senescence-like states in advanced disease. Within the adenocarcinoma compartment of one CRPC section, senescence-like hotspots showed higher glycolysis scores without a concomitant rise in proliferation. In vitro, CSS and ENZ increased p21/p16 and glycolytic proteins (GLUT1, LDHA, HK2), and treatment with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) or the LDHA inhibitor FX-11 was associated with lower p21/p16 abundance. Androgen deprivation is associated with a prostate cancer senescence-like state and a glycolysis-related program; LDHA is a candidate metabolic node for further investigation; the present data do not establish therapeutic selectivity or efficacy. These spatial associations do not establish the cellular source of the SASP-related transcripts or paracrine signaling.

title: TIMP1 and CLDN23 may contribute to adenoma-to-colorectal cancer progression and nominate ruxolitinib for repurposing.
text: Colorectal cancer (CRC) may develop through the conventional adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence or alternative routes of carcinogenesis, accompanied by changes in epithelial cell states and remodeling of the tumor microenvironment, yet its core driving mechanisms and therapeutic options remain unclear. This study integrated single-cell, bulk transcriptomic, and spatial transcriptomic datasets for comprehensive bioinformatics analyses, followed by validation in CRC cells and clinical samples using immunohistochemistry. Epithelial cells showed the most pronounced transcriptional and cell-communication remodeling during adenoma-to-carcinoma progression, with marked expansion of tumor-related subpopulations including tumor epithelial cells, stem-like tumor cells, and proliferating tumor cells. Multi-omics integration identified tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 (TIMP1) and claudin-23 (CLDN23) as core genes closely linked to inflammatory, immune, and metabolic pathways. Ruxolitinib was predicted to target the TIMP1/CLDN23 regulatory network, and in vitro experiments confirmed that it downregulated TIMP1, upregulated CLDN23, and suppressed CRC cell proliferation. Functional assays further showed that TIMP1 promoted while CLDN23 inhibited CRC cell proliferation and migration, and that the two genes may act cooperatively through their shared downstream molecule selenium-binding protein 1 (SELENBP1). These findings suggest an epithelial-centered mechanism of adenoma-to-CRC progression, identify TIMP1 and CLDN23 as molecules with diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic potential, and provide preliminary support for repurposing Ruxolitinib in CRC.

title: Artificial intelligence in basic and translational cardiovascular research.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in cardiovascular research where conventional analysis struggles with scale, heterogeneity, and multimodal integration. Its contribution differs across imaging, computational omics, mechanistic simulation, and drug discovery. This narrative review examines substantive applications of machine learning and deep learning while distinguishing them from routine bioinformatics and purely biophysical modeling. We assess independent biological units, validation strategies, and strength of inference in representative studies. Deep-learning imaging systems can provide reproducible quantitative phenotypes, but workflow performance alone does not establish mechanism. In single-cell and spatial studies, clustering, integration, trajectory inference, and network reconstruction generally yield associations or hypotheses unless experimentally supported. Mechanistic interpretation is bounded by the specific effect established through targeted perturbation or rescue with functional testing; lineage tracing and orthogonal readouts provide complementary support, not standalone proof of causation. Hybrid AI-biophysical models may accelerate personalized simulation, whereas heart-on-chip, engineered tissue, and organoid systems without learned components are validation platforms rather than AI methods. In drug discovery, active learning and molecular redesign can prioritize candidates, but predicted reductions in ion-channel liability do not demonstrate biological safety or reduced proarrhythmic risk. Major limitations include pseudoreplication, data leakage, domain shift, batch effects, uncertain labels, few independent hearts, demographic imbalance, incomplete calibration, and limited transfer among animal, iPSC-derived, and adult human systems. AI is most valuable when it produces robust phenotypes or experimentally testable hypotheses within a transparent validation framework, rather than when predictive accuracy is treated as mechanistic evidence.

title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts promote thyroid cancer progression and reduce radioiodide uptake via lactylation.
text: Radioiodine (RAI) therapy is a cornerstone of thyroid cancer management, but impaired iodide uptake limits its efficacy. How distinct cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) populations alter tumor-cell iodide handling remains incompletely understood. We investigated a complement factor D-positive (CFD+) CAF population and the associated lactate-dependent paracrine signaling pathway. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics sequencing (ST-seq) were used to characterize CAF heterogeneity. Histone H3 lysine 27 lactylation (H3K27la) CUT&Tag and ChIP-qPCR analyses were integrated with molecular and functional experiments. Thyroid cancer cells were evaluated in CAF co-culture systems, and xenografts were used to examine tumor growth and NIS expression. Cellular radioiodide-handling capacity was assessed by a sodium/iodide symporter (NIS)-inhibitable 125 I uptake assay. CFD + CAF exhibited enhanced glycolytic activity and lactate production, accompanied by increased AARS1-associated H3K27la. H3K27la enrichment at PDGFA and PDGFB regulatory regions was associated with increased expression of these ligands. CAF-tumor-cell signaling implicated the PDGF/PDGFR-RAS/MAPK pathway in NIS downregulation and reduced iodide uptake. Sorafenib attenuated tumor growth and was associated with increased NIS expression and cellular 125 I uptake. A lactate-AARS1-H3K27la-PDGF signaling program in CFD + CAFs is associated with thyroid cancer progression and impaired NIS-dependent iodide uptake. These data support investigation of stromal PDGF signaling and sorafenib-mediated redifferentiation strategies; restoration of in vivo RAI treatment sensitivity remains to be demonstrated.

title: Integrating morphology and spatial omics in gastric cancer: bridging classical mucin phenotypes and molecular stemness.
text: Gastric cancer has been described through successive frameworks, each capturing a different dimension of the same heterogeneous tumor. The Lauren, World Health Organization, and Japanese Gastric Cancer Association report histological morphology; mucin phenotyping reports gastric versus intestinal lineage differentiation; and the The Cancer Genome Atlas and Asian Cancer Research Group classifications report molecular state. These systems correspond to one another only in part, and none fully represents the coexistence of distinct differentiation states within a single tumor. Bulk profiling averages across tissue compartments, and single-cell approaches, while resolving cellular diversity, discard the coordinates that link molecular state to tissue architecture. Spatial transcriptomics restores those coordinates. In this review, we revisit mucin phenotyping as an early attempt to read tumor cell differentiation from morphology and protein expression, reconstruct it from the standpoint of gastric epithelial stem cell biology and metaplastic lineage plasticity, and consider how spatially resolved expression may refine our understanding of differentiation and stemness within gastric cancer. Nuclear factor I X is presented as an example of a candidate molecule identified from a spatially defined stem-like compartment. Stemness and spatial niches are discussed as potential axes for future classification.

title: Multicenter CT-Based Deep Learning for Preoperative Nodal Risk Stratification in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma.
text: Accurate preoperative risk stratification for lymph node metastasis (LNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains difficult. We developed and validated ThyLNT, a Transformer-based 2.5D deep learning model using preoperative computed tomography (CT), and explored related biological features in multi-omics analyses. A total of 1560 patients with PTC from six hospitals were retrospectively included. The Tongji Hospital cohort was divided into training and internal validation sets, and five external cohorts were used for independent testing. Seven 2.5D tumor slices were extracted per patient, encoded with a DenseNet201 backbone, and fused by a Transformer. Model performance was compared with radiomics, ensemble learning, and multi-instance learning using AUC, calibration, decision curve, and precision-recall analyses. Bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics were used to explore related biological features. ThyLNT achieved an AUC of 0.882 (CI, 0.858-0.905) in the training cohort, 0.787 (CI, 0.738-0.835) in the internal validation cohort, and 0.772 (CI, 0.662-0.878) to 0.827 (CI, 0.763-0.885) across the five external cohorts. It showed multicenter discrimination, whereas calibration and threshold-dependent operating characteristics varied across cohorts. Multi-omics analyses provided exploratory biological context, including candidate associations with vascular endothelial growth factor A-related signaling and lipid metabolism. ThyLNT demonstrated multicenter performance for preoperative LNM prediction in PTC and may support risk stratification, although calibration, threshold use, and clinical utility require prospective validation.

title: Editorial Focus on PG-00296-2025R2.
text: Parturition involves coordinated endocrine, inflammatory, extracellular matrix, and mechanical processes that are regulated differently across reproductive tissues. Here, we discuss the study by Davila Ruiz et al., which investigated tissue-specific responses to prepartum estradiol (E2) exposure in pregnant ewes using transcriptomic and protein analyses. The cervix exhibited the most pronounced transcriptional response, particularly in pathways associated with extracellular matrix organization, steroid metabolism, prostaglandin synthesis, and immune signaling, whereas the myometrium and placental membranes showed comparatively limited changes. Reduced myometrial progesterone receptor expression further supports the role of functional progesterone withdrawal in preparing for labor. These findings highlight the cervix as an active molecular target of endocrine signaling rather than merely a passive structural component. Future studies integrating single-cell and spatial transcriptomics should clarify the cellular mechanisms underlying cervical remodeling and determine whether these pathways are conserved in humans, with potential implications for understanding preterm birth and cervical insufficiency.

title: Spatially Resolved Functional Heterogeneity of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures Combined with Basal-Squamous Epithelial States Predicts Prognosis and Immunotherapy Response in Upper Tract Urothelial Carcinoma.
text: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) exhibits poor outcomes and modest immunotherapy response. While tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) orchestrate anti-tumor immunity, their spatial functional heterogeneity and interaction with neoplastic epithelium in UTUC remain poorly characterized. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (n=4) with Xenium-based spatial transcriptomics (n=20) to delineate TLS functional states. A 17-gene, four-module TLS functional signature trained in The Cancer Genome Atlas–Bladder Urothelial Carcinoma (TCGA-BLCA) was combined with a four-gene basal-squamous signature to construct a dual-dimensional risk framework, validated in IMvigor210 (n=348) with GSE32894 (n=224) as a cross-platform sensitivity cohort. We identified a functional maturation continuum across TLS zones (core, edge, peri-TLS), with enhanced antigen presentation and cytotoxic activity in TLS-positive microenvironments. Spatial analysis revealed that basal-squamous epithelial cells co-localized with TLS but established immunosuppressive niches via SPP1/FN1-mediated fibrosis and checkpoint upregulation. The dual-dimensional model significantly stratified survival in both TCGA-BLCA and IMvigor210 cohorts (log-rank p<0.05) and was associated with immunotherapy response in IMvigor210. Notably, patients with TLS-positive/basal-high tumors (Q3) exhibited paradoxically poor outcomes comparable to immune-desert phenotypes, suggesting basal-squamous features compromise TLS-mediated immunity. This study establishes a spatially resolved functional taxonomy of TLS in UTUC, revealing antagonistic interplay between TLS-mediated immunity and basal-squamous epithelial immune evasion. The dual-dimensional framework provides a biologically grounded tool with modest prognostic discrimination in urothelial carcinoma.

title: Discovery and Preliminary Mechanistic Investigation of 5-Aminoquinoline Hydrazone Derivatives as Antifungal Leads against Sclerotinia sclerotiorum.
text: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum is a destructive necrotrophic pathogen that causes severe yield losses in economically important crops. In this study, a series of 5-aminoquinoline-based hydrazone derivatives were designed and synthesized, and their antifungal activity was evaluated. Compound A16 exhibited superior activity against S. sclerotiorum (EC50 = 2.42 μg/mL) and Phomopsis sp. (EC50 = 5.32 μg/mL), outperforming the commercial fungicide oxine-copper. In-vivo tests demonstrated that A16 possessed excellent curative (94.5%) and protective (72.9%) efficacies. Preliminary mechanistic studies showed that A16 inhibited succinate dehydrogenase activity, perturbed membrane-associated physiological processes, and promoted the accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species accumulation, indicating substantial disruption of fungal energy and redox homeostasis. Moreover, A16 exhibited relatively low toxicity toward zebrafish under the tested conditions. These results suggest that A16 is a promising lead compound worthy of further optimization for the development of fungicidal agents for the management of Sclerotinia diseases.

title: Rational Design of Novel Piperine Derivatives Bearing an N-Sulfonylpiperazine Moiety as Selectively Potent OfChtII Inhibitors.
text: OfChtII, an indispensable enzyme whose expression precedes other chitinases in the chitin metabolic system of Ostrinia furnacalis, becomes a promising target for green pest control. In this work, a series of novel piperine derivatives bearing an N-sulfonylpiperazine moiety were rationally designed and synthesized based on the binding cavity characteristics of OfChtII. Among them, compound I-H15 (Ki = 0.88 μM) exhibited superior inhibitory potency against OfChtII over piperine (Ki = 50.06 μM). In vivo bioassays demonstrated that I-H15 displayed high insecticidal efficacy and prominent growth-inhibitory effects on O. furnacalis at 500 μg/mL. Molecular mechanism demonstrated that I-H15 deeply occupies the previously unexploited subsite -2 of OfChtII and forms critical interactions through hydrogen bonding, π-π stacking, and π-cation with key residues Trp1951 and Phe1889 in OfChtII, as shown by molecular simulations. This study validates a subsite-targeted optimization strategy by discovering novel piperine derivatives and offers a promising lead for developing eco-friendly Chitinase inhibitors against O. furnacalis.

title: Machine-Learning-Driven Inverse Design of NURBS-Parameterized Auxetic Piezoelectric Energy Harvesters for Self-Powered Wireless Sensing.
text: Low-frequency vibration energy is abundant in infrastructure, transportation, and industrial equipment, but piezoelectric harvesters face a power-stress-concentration trade-off: the large strain required for high output can intensify localized peak stress. In this paper, we develop a machine-learning-assisted inverse-design framework for NURBS-parameterized auxetic piezoelectric energy harvesters. NURBS control variables define a compact and continuous design space for curved re-entrant lattices, expanding deformation and load-transfer pathways beyond straight-wall geometries. A finite-element dataset generated by Latin hypercube sampling trains a neural-network surrogate to predict maximum average output power and peak von Mises stress from geometric parameters. Coupling this surrogate with NSGA-II enables co-optimization of electrical output and stress concentration. The optimized geometry increases effective biaxial stress/strain in the piezoelectric layer while redistributing localized stress. Under 0.5 g excitation at resonance, the optimized harvester delivers 7.56 mW maximum average output power and a normalized power density of 2.84 × 10 - 3 mW / ( mm 3 · g 2 · Hz ) . Integrated with a self-powered LoRa sensing node, the device transmits temperature data over 150 m . This work offers a surrogate-assisted route to high-power, stress-aware energy harvesters and energy-autonomous IoT sensing.

title: AI-powered virtual cells, digital twins and agentic AI are reshaping multi-omics, spatial biology and drug discovery.
text: Predicting individual disease trajectories and treatment responses remains challenging in drug discovery. Molecular profiling provides static snapshots that miss cellular dynamics, spatial context and adaptive responses. The convergence of single-cell and spatial omics with generative AI is driving a paradigm shift toward AI-powered virtual cells that model cellular states, interactions and treatment responses. This review introduces a nested framework of six capabilities for AI-powered virtual cells, spanning population-derived models, digital twins and agentic twins. Virtual cells generate synthetic cellular states and predict responses from population data. Digital twins link models to specific biological counterparts, enabling longitudinal updating and prospective prediction. Agentic twins add spatial context, biologically constrained interactions and actions, and environmental feedback, enabling personalized, dynamic and interactive representations of cellular ecosystems. This narrative review is based on literature acquired from PubMed, Web of Science, bioRxiv and arXiv searches up to October 2026. AI-powered virtual cells could support drug discovery as foundation models that transfer biological knowledge across tasks, including data-limited settings. Their value depends on faithful extrapolation beyond training data and prospective validation against biological observations. Coupling these models to repeatedly measured experimental systems could enable personalized prediction, iterative updating and prioritization of perturbations, targets and therapeutic strategies.

title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.
text: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.

title: A single-dose membrane-anchored F1/LcrV mRNA vaccine confers protection against pneumonic plague: a preclinical study.
text: The success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms has prompted significant interest in their application against bacterial pathogens. However, adapting these platforms requires optimising host-expressed antigen structure to ensure robust immunogenicity. While membrane anchoring enhances the efficacy of viral mRNA vaccines, its application in bacterial mRNA platforms remains largely unexplored. Plague, caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Yersinia pestis, has been one of the most devastating diseases throughout human history. Despite extensive studies, there are no licenced vaccines available. We developed a bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine against Y. pestis, utilising the major antigens F1 and LcrV (5 μg of each mRNA). We evaluated glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored and transmembrane (TM) variants alongside secreted native and hFc-conjugated formats to assess immunological profiles and determine protective efficacy in a murine model of pneumonic plague. Membrane-tethering of F1 and LcrV antigens improved overall immunogenicity. Whereas secreted native and hFc-conjugated variants elicited predominantly cell-mediated and serological immune responses, respectively, the membrane-anchored bivalent mRNA vaccine generated a robust, protective immune response. This dual humoural and cellular immunity facilitated robust (87.5%, 7/8 mice) protection following a single-dose vaccination. By progressing towards the single-dose biodefense benchmark prioritised by the World Health Organisation Target Product Profile, this membrane-anchored construct emerges as a promising translational candidate for a rapid-response plague vaccine. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that extending established antigen-tethering strategies to bacterial targets may be a highly effective approach for generating the potent immunity required to overcome complex bacterial infections. This research was supported by the Israeli Science Foundation (grants 2012/20, 842/25), the Lewis Trust and the Shmunis Family Trust.

title: Mechanistic insights into benzoxaborole activity against Cryptosporidium parvum: CPSF3 targeting genetically validated for AN3661, with implications for resistance.
text: Cryptosporidiosis is a major enteric disease affecting humans and animals worldwide, with severe consequences in young children and neonatal livestock, yet treatment options remain extremely limited. Benzoxaboroles have emerged as promising broad-spectrum antiparasitic compounds, but their mechanisms of action, molecular targets, and resistance pathways in Cryptosporidium spp. remain incompletely understood, limiting their optimal therapeutic deployment. We previously showed that the benzoxaborole AN3661 inhibits the endonuclease Cleavage and Polyadenylation Specificity Factor 3 (CPSF3) in Cryptosporidium hominis, likely by disrupting pre-mRNA processing and restricting parasite growth. Here, we further investigated the mode of action of AN3661 and compared it with two additional benzoxaboroles, AN13762 and AN7973. Cell culture assays combined with imaging-based quantification were used to assess drug activity and determine the impact of treatment on parasite growth and development. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was used to introduce a point mutation into Cryptosporidium parvum CPSF3 and evaluate resistance to benzoxaboroles in vitro and in vivo. Nanopore sequencing was performed to examine the effects of drug exposure on parasite mRNA processing. We identified a single mutation in C. parvum CPSF3 (Y385N) that conferred strong resistance to AN3661. In contrast, this mutation did not reduce sensitivity to AN13762 or AN7973, which are also suspected to target CPSF3. All three benzoxaboroles impaired mRNA processing, a process mediated by the CPSF machinery, and exhibited parasiticidal activity, with pronounced effects during late-stage maturation of first-generation meronts, including inhibition of parasite egress; two compounds also affected gametogenesis. Notably, AN7973 controlled severe infection in susceptible mice challenged with the AN3661-resistant C. parvum CPSF3 Y385N mutant. In Toxoplasma gondii, AN7973 remained active against strains resistant to AN3661 and AN13762, supporting a distinct mechanism of action. Finally, AN3661 and AN7973 were active against Eimeria tenella, and AN3661 against Giardia duodenalis. Together, these results identify a resistance mechanism affecting AN3661 in Cryptosporidium, and highlight AN7973 as a promising alternative compound with broad antiparasitic activity and efficacy against AN3661-resistant parasites.

title: Engineered Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) as Carriers for CRISPR/Cas9 Therapeutics: Recent Advances in Cargo Loading and Targeted Delivery.
text: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

title: Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models.
text: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non-invasive delivery of mRNA-encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood-brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA-LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age-related and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: An Integrated DNA Origami-Based RNA Degrader for Targeted Degradation of Oncogenic Mutant KRAS mRNA.
text: Targeting mutant KRAS represents a critical yet unmet therapeutic challenge across multiple malignancies, as the structural diversity of oncogenic variants and absence of druggable pockets have impeded the development of effective small-molecule inhibitors. Here, we report an integrated RNA degrader system constructed on a six-helix bundle DNA origami (6HB) scaffold that enables efficient and targeted degradation of mutant KRAS mRNA. The system coassembles two modular functional units: an enzyme activity control module comprising an engineered barnase variant and a programmable recognition strand for direct, endogenous-machinery-independent RNA cleavage, and a cell-penetrating module featuring TAT peptides for cytosolic delivery. This integrated architecture eliminates spatiotemporal barriers between delivery and catalysis, achieving robust KRAS mRNA degradation within 16 h while maintaining sufficient specificity for mutant transcripts with minimal impact on wild-type forms. This study demonstrates a proof-of-concept nanoscale platform that integrates targeting, delivery, and catalytic functions for RNA degradation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Precision Nutrition: From Multi-Omics Integration to Personalized Dietary Interventions.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated as a tool for precision nutrition because it can analyse heterogeneous dietary, clinical, physiological, behavioural, and molecular data. This narrative review critically examines how machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, explainable AI, continuous glucose monitoring, wearable technologies, and multi-omics approaches may support individualized nutritional assessment and decision-making. Particular attention is given to the distinction between predictive research, digital personalized nutrition, AI-enabled clinical interventions, and commercial nutrition platforms. Current evidence shows that personalized digital nutrition can improve selected dietary behaviours, while observational AI and multi-omics studies can predict substantial inter-individual variation in metabolic responses. Importantly, evidence that an AI-enabled intervention improves clinical outcomes is still limited and is concentrated in selected settings, including a multicentre randomized trial of an AI-based dietary management platform in adults with type 2 diabetes. Emerging technologies such as large language models, digital twins, federated learning, and adaptive algorithms remain promising but require prospective clinical validation. Major barriers include data quality, algorithmic bias, privacy, interoperability, model transparency, regulatory uncertainty, and limited external validation. Future research should prioritize pragmatic multicentre randomized trials, transparent reporting of model performance, independent validation, health-economic evaluation, and clinically meaningful outcomes. AI should therefore be considered an adjunct to evidence-based nutritional care rather than a replacement for professional clinical judgement. The review differs from technology-centred and methodology-focused reviews by explicitly linking AI modalities and multi-omics data with evidence maturity, clinical trial findings, implementation barriers, and the level of inference justified for each technology.

title: Higher county-level need is associated with greater naloxone distribution from U.S. syringe services programs in 2023: A cross-sectional study.
text: To assess whether U.S. syringe services programs (SSPs) in counties with higher levels of need in 2022 had greater financial resources and larger-scale delivery of overdose prevention interventions in 2023. This study utilized a cross-sectional design. As a measure of underlying, community-level need, our primary exposure was 2022 county-level opioid overdose fatalities, categorized as low (1-33), moderate (34-198), or high (199-1923). Outcomes included annual SSP budget, number of naloxone recipients from the SSP, naloxone doses distributed by the SSP, and buprenorphine availability at the SSP. Using weighted generalized estimating equations with exchangeable correlation structures to account for clustering of SSPs within Census divisions, we used gamma, negative binomial, and logit specifications as appropriate for each outcome. SSPs reported a median budget of $141,842; 596 naloxone recipients; 2001 naloxone doses distributed; and 44% had integrated buprenorphine. Compared to SSPs in low overdose fatality counties, SSPs in moderate- and high overdose fatality counties had significantly larger budgets, greater number of naloxone recipients and greater number of naloxone doses distributed. SSPs in higher need counties were not significantly more likely to have buprenorphine available (aOR=1.40; 95% CI:0.72-2.75; p = 0.321). Our findings showed that higher levels of need were positively associated with greater financial resources for and naloxone distribution from SSPs in 2023 but was not associated with greater buprenorphine availability. Aligning higher levels of naloxone distribution with higher need maximizes potential for population health impact. Focused infrastructure and implementation support for buprenorphine integration at SSPs likely remain.

title: Advancing patient-centered outcomes research data capacity and infrastructure through policy and demonstration projects.
text: Robust data capacity and infrastructure are needed to leverage electronic health data and health information technology (IT) for patient-centered outcomes research (PCOR). The objectives of this article are to identify PCOR needs, steps taken by Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) PCOR projects, and remaining work. Leveraging health IT and electronic health data for PCOR requires enhancements in (1) policy (ie, consent, governance, privacy and security, auditing), (2) data (ie, access, quality, completeness, bias, and methodological), (3) infrastructure (ie, linkage, interoperability, patient-reported outcome [PRO] data integration, and PRO capture and extraction), and (4) implementation (ie, interface, training, workflow, and continuous improvement). Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology PCOR projects addressed needs spanning all 4 areas, particularly data and infrastructure needs with a focus on standards development. Future work should reduce burden associated with PCOR data needs through improved automation and engage stakeholders in the codevelopment of PCOR data, infrastructure, and policy.

title: Scaling PROMs Implementation Across Clinical Pathways: Lessons from Hospital Moinhos de Vento's Experience with ICHOM Standard Sets.
text: This case study presents the 7-year experience of Hospital Moinhos de Vento (HMV), a leading private hospital in Brazil, in implementing patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) through the International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement (ICHOM) standard sets. The primary objective was to share practical insights into how PROMs were operationalized across multiple departments and conditions, highlighting implementation strategies, scalability, and challenges. Between 2017 and 2024, PROMs were embedded in clinical workflows across nine health conditions, including stroke, heart failure, breast cancer, and prostate cancer. Results showed improved adherence to data collection and enhanced patient-clinician communication. The authors retrospectively applied the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to map barriers and enablers. Although substantial clinical improvements were observed, they present these as contextual trends within a broader quality improvement ecosystem rather than establishing direct causal attribution to PROMs alone. Key factors for successful scaling included strong institutional leadership, the establishment of a Clinical Practice Office (CPO), shared digital infrastructure, and continuous process improvement. The case underscores that effective PROMs implementation requires deliberate planning, cultural change, and investment in interoperable systems. By detailing the who, how, and when of implementation, this article serves as a practical guide for health care organizations aiming to integrate patient-centered outcomes into routine care.

title: Mixed-methods process evaluation of a digitally supported, needs-adapted and risk-adapted complex intervention in the BETTER-CARE breast cancer aftercare programme.
text: With breast cancer being the most common cancer among women in Germany, there is a need for structured, needs-based aftercare. The BETTER-CARE (BrEasT cancer afTERcare) study is a cluster-randomised controlled trial in Germany implementing a digitally supported needs-adapted and risk-adapted complex intervention for breast cancer patients after primary therapy. Here, we report the process evaluation of the implementation of the BETTER-CARE intervention by focusing on reach, fidelity, feasibility and contextual factors. In parallel with the cluster-randomised intervention study, a process evaluation was conducted using mixed methods. Data sources included administrative records such as screening protocols, dropout lists and monitoring reports; semistructured interviews with patients and healthcare professionals and a cross-sectional online survey of staff at the intervention centres. The data were analysed descriptively and qualitatively using content analysis. In addition, intervention fidelity was assessed for each intervention component. Patients after treatment of primary breast cancer were recruited at 15 intervention centres and 15 control centres in Germany between March 2023 and June 2024. They were followed up for 1 year during aftercare. Between March 2024 and February 2025, a total of 12 patients and 11 healthcare professionals took part in semistructured interviews. In addition, 11 staff members completed the online survey in June and July 2025. The intervention included a multidisciplinary care network, regular telephone-based needs assessments, a shared electronic patient record (myoncare) and two digital applications: the PIA Health app for self-reporting well-being and communicating with the breast cancer centre and the 10-week ACTonCancer intervention programme for patients with high psychological distress. Patients valued personal contact, structured symptom assessments and the facilitation of access to specialists via the network. The PIA Health application was generally usable as it supported self-reflection and engagement, although patients wished for more personalised and dynamic content. The ACTonCancer programme was rarely used. The varying digital literacy of patients may have led to different levels of usage of the digital applications. Challenges in the implementation of the electronic patient record included technical difficulties, a high documentation workload for healthcare professionals and limited integration with outpatient providers. Most components of the BETTER-CARE intervention were generally feasible, demonstrating its potential to improve coordination, patient engagement and continuity of care. However, differences between intervention centres existed. Further developments of the programme should focus on reducing the administrative burden, improving interoperability between digital systems and tailoring digital content to individual preferences and levels of digital literacy. German Clinical Trial Register DRKS00028840. Registered in April 2022.
