title: Engineering GFPuv Reporters for Visual Screening across Filamentous Fungi to Enable CRISPR Genome Editing in Aspergillus pseudoterreus.
text: GFPuv is a UV-excitable fluorescent reporter that enables rapid monitoring of gene expression, particularly in microbial systems. However, its application in filamentous fungi remains limited. Here, we evaluated GFPuv variants and identified one that performs robustly across Aspergillus species and the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica. Under UV illumination, transformed green fluorescent colonies can be visualized without colony dissection or microscopy, significantly simplifying screening. CRISPR-based genome editing has not been previously established in Aspergillus pseudoterreus. By integrating the optimized GFPuv reporter into a transformation and selection system, we established, to our knowledge, the first CRISPR knockout platform in this species. Targeted disruption of the genes pyrG, CAD, and PrID505606 validated the platform. PCR and Sanger sequencing confirmed that GFPuv-positive colonies were true mutants, while loss-of-function phenotypes of pyrG and CAD further supported platform reliability. This work establishes GFPuv as a rapid, microscopy-independent screening tool in select fungi and provides a foundational CRISPR framework for engineering A. pseudoterreus.

title: An EFHD1-associated ADSC niche modulates treatment response in experimental models of ER-positive breast cancer.
text: Adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) modulate the breast cancer (BC) microenvironment, but their role in endocrine therapy resistance and clinical outcomes remains ill-defined. By integrating single-cell and multi-cohort bulk RNA-seq data from ER⁺ BC patients, we built an ADSC-derived prognostic model via a four-dimensional filtering strategy and 10 machine-learning algorithms. Spatial transcriptomics, co-culture assays, and orthotopic mammary fat-pad model validated the hub gene's function and mechanism. ADSCs were enriched in non-responders and exhibited elevated stemness. A 17-gene Ridge regression model stratified patient risk across five cohorts, with high-risk tumors showing TP53 mutations and immunosuppression. EFHD1 emerged as the key hub gene spatially co-localized with ADSCs. Mechanistically, co-culture with ER⁺ BC cells upregulated EFHD1 in ADSCs by ∼2.0-fold, which triggered NF-κB/p65 nuclear translocation and a ∼1.5-fold increase in FN1 protein levels. Functionally, EFHD1-overexpressing ADSCs promoted BC proliferation and invasion. In an orthotopic xenograft model, tumors co-injected with control ADSCs reached ∼500 mm³ by day 30 and maintained robust growth under letrozole + ribociclib (∼350 mm³), compared with BC cells alone (∼300 mm³). In contrast, EFHD1 knockdown in ADSCs reduced tumor volume to ∼200 mm³ and further sensitized tumors to letrozole + ribociclib (∼150 mm³, a ∼40% reduction relative to the drug-only group), with Ki-67 positivity decreasing from ∼4.0% to ∼1.5%. We established a robust ADSC-based prognostic model and uncovered a novel stromal EFHD1/NF-κB/FN1 axis driving ER⁺ BC progression and endocrine therapy resistance, identifying stromal EFHD1 as a candidate target whose pharmacological validation remains to be established.

title: Subclonal evolution can shape the transition toward a sarcomatoid phenotype in pleural mesothelioma.
text: A better understanding of intratumor heterogeneity in pleural mesothelioma (PM) is crucial to implementing precision medicine for this deadly cancer. Using single-cell RNA sequencing approaches on tumor samples and derived primary cell lines, we defined four phenotypic cell types, related to overall survival in larger bulk cohorts: epithelioid, sarcomatoid, intermediate, and nondifferentiated. Some tumor samples showed intratumor phenotypic heterogeneity, associated with subclonal evolution, in which sarcomatoid cells can emerge from parental cells with an intermediate phenotype following the acquisition of copy number variations. Subclones were conserved in cell lines and retained their specific phenotypes, suggesting high phenotypic heritability. Spatial transcriptomics illustrated the link between phenotypic and subclonal evolution, showing that subclonal cells were colocalized and exhibited specific morphologies within the tumor tissue. Our study provides a comprehensive single-cell profiling of PM tumor cells and reveals a link between phenotypic evolution, clonal architecture, and tumor spatial organization.

title: Targeting Neutrophil Extracellular Traps to Inhibit Colon Cancer Tumor Necrosis and Metastasis.
text: Tumor necrosis is associated with poor prognosis in colorectal cancer (CRC) yet is generally viewed as a passive consequence of tumor growth rather than a therapeutic target. We demonstrate that necrosis correlates with metastatic disease in human CRC independently of tumor size. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of primary CRC and colorectal liver metastases revealed that peri-necrotic programs are associated with metastatic progression. Patients with CRC exhibited increased circulating neutrophils, including NET-primed and CD177-low neutrophils with reduced extravasation capacity. Consistent with these findings, intravascular NET aggregates localized adjacent to necrotic regions in human CRC specimens. In a mismatch repair-proficient mouse model of CRC, neutrophil infiltration and NET formation increased during tumor progression, whereas genetic and pharmacologic NET inhibition reduced tumor necrosis, decreased metastasis, and enhanced chemotherapy efficacy. Together, these findings identify NET-driven tumor necrosis as an active promoter of CRC metastasis and support NET inhibition as a therapeutic strategy.

title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc.
text: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

title: Sjögren's Disease Salivary Gland Fibroblast Subsets are Interferon Enriched and Aberrantly Promote Pain.
text: Fibroblasts are emerging as critical mediators in the pathogenesis of Sjögren's Disease (SjD) onset and progression. This study aimed to define fibroblast subpopulations within salivary glands (SG) and elucidate their functional contributions to SjD pathogenesis. We analyzed 3' single-cell RNA sequencing data from minor SG biopsies of individuals with SjD (n = 17; 58,205 cells) and controls (n = 19; 33,584 cells). Data processing and analysis employed Cell Ranger, Seurat, Harmony, DESeq2, ENRICHR, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis, and CellPhoneDB. Key findings were validated using immunofluorescence microscopy of human SG tissue, primary human fibroblasts, mouse dorsal root ganglion cells, in vivo mouse models, and spatial transcriptomics. Salivary glands from SjD patients exhibited an expanded fibroblast compartment enriched for interferon (IFN)-responsive gene expression. Subclustering identified six distinct fibroblast populations. Among these, FMO2+ fibroblasts demonstrated the strongest IFN signature and engaged in disease-specific ligand-receptor interactions with myeloid cells, which spatially co-localized in SjD tissue. A distinct NEGR1 (aka: KILON)+ fibroblast population uniquely expressed nerve- and axon-associated transcripts. Functional studies revealed Kilon treatment sensitized mouse dorsal root ganglia sensory neurons in vitro (p≤0.01) and increased pain sensitivity in vivo (p≤0.01). This study defines previously unrecognized fibroblast heterogeneity in SjD. FMO2+ fibroblasts exhibit an IFN-enriched transcriptional profile and might communicate with myeloid cells. In contrast, KILON+ fibroblasts represent a novel neuro-associated subset possibly capable of modulating pain. Together, these findings highlight distinct and pathogenic roles for fibroblast subsets in SjD and identify new avenues for therapeutic intervention.

title: Kidney fibrosis mechanisms in the single‑cell era: From cellular heterogeneity to therapeutic opportunities (Review).
text: Chronic kidney disease affects >13% of adults worldwide, yet no approved antifibrotic therapy is available. Recent advances in single‑cell and spatial transcriptomics have transformed the understanding of renal fibrosis. These technologies have unmasked unexpected heterogeneity among myofibroblasts and macrophages, identified scar‑associated macrophage subsets and resolved the long‑standing debate over myofibroblast origins by confirming resident fibroblasts as the principal source. Spatial transcriptomics has further defined functional communities and pathologically distinct niches, including maladaptive repair niches centred on SOX9+ epithelial cells, profibrotic microenvironments enriched in tenascin‑C and immune‑activation niches where macrophages and fibroblasts co‑localize. Intercellular crosstalk networks involving TGF‑β, NOTCH and paracrine signals from injured tubules have been systematically mapped. These insights are now being translated into targeted strategies, such as surface marker‑directed agents against CD248 and fibroblast activation protein, epigenetic modulators including HDAC6 inhibitors and advanced 3D bioprinted human models. The present review synthesized these single‑cell and spatial discoveries to provide a conceptual framework for developing precision antifibrotic therapies for progressive kidney disease.

title: Space-map: 3D single-cell atlas reconstruction from serial sections.
text: High-resolution three-dimensional (3D) tissue atlases promise to link cellular architecture to tissue function, but assembling them from serial sections containing millions of cells remains challenging. Here we present Space-map, an accurate and efficient method for reconstructing 3D tissue models from high-content spatial molecular profiles. Space-map combines multiscale feature matching with large deformation diffeomorphic metric mapping to automate global alignment across serial sections while preserving local microanatomy. We generate spatial transcriptomics (Xenium; ~2.7 million cells) and proteomics (CODEX; ~4.8 million cells) datasets from serial sections to build 3D models of a colon polyp and healthy intestinal tissues. These models reveal cell-type heterogeneity in the polyp and preserved crypt and glandular architecture and mucosal-cavity continuity in healthy intestines. Benchmarking on our own and publicly available datasets demonstrates that Space-map achieves substantially higher registration accuracy and up to a tenfold speedup over existing methods, supporting its use as a robust framework for constructing 3D human tissue atlases at single-cell resolution.

title: Small Molecule-Protein Target Validation Strategies From Biophysical Binding Analysis to AI-Assisted Mechanistic Discovery.
text: The rapid development of phenotypic screening, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven drug discovery has accelerated the identification of bioactive small molecules and potential therapeutic targets. However, establishing reliable relationships between small molecules and their functional protein targets remains a major challenge in modern drug discovery. Precise characterization of small molecule-protein interactions is essential for elucidating mechanisms of action, optimizing lead compounds, improving target selectivity, and minimizing off-target effects. Nevertheless, phenotypic responses or individual binding assays alone are often insufficient to confirm bona fide pharmacological targets and define their functional consequences. This review summarizes current strategies for small molecule-protein target validation, including quantitative biophysical binding analysis, cellular target engagement assessment, stability- and affinity-based target identification, chemical proteomics, and structural characterization of ligand binding sites and key residues. We discuss how complementary approaches, such as surface plasmon resonance, biolayer interferometry, isothermal titration calorimetry, microscale thermophoresis, nuclear magnetic resonance, cellular thermal shift assay, and proteome-based technologies, provide distinct layers of evidence for defining molecular recognition, intracellular target engagement, and functional regulation. In addition, emerging applications of AI-assisted approaches in protein structure prediction, binding pocket identification, virtual screening, affinity prediction, and rational compound optimization are highlighted. We propose that reliable mechanism of action elucidation requires an integrated evidence framework combining computational prediction, biochemical validation, cellular evaluation, structural analysis, mutational studies, and functional confirmation. Such multidisciplinary strategies will strengthen target validation, reduce mechanistic uncertainty, facilitate rational drug optimization, and accelerate the development of safer and more effective therapeutics.

title: Targeting FSP1 to induce ferroptosis: advances in small-molecule inhibitors, degraders and their structure-activity relationships.
text: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death characterized by excessive lipid peroxidation. Ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), a critical glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4)-independent ferroptosis suppressor, regenerates reduced coenzyme Q and vitamin K via its membrane-associated oxidoreductase activity, rendering it an attractive therapeutic target for pharmacological modulation of ferroptosis. Since its identification as a ferroptosis suppressor, substantial efforts have been devoted to the discovery and optimization of FSP1-targeting small molecules. Early studies validated the pharmacological tractability of FSP1 and identified multiple chemically distinct inhibitor scaffolds. Structural studies, particularly the FSP1-FSEN1 co-crystal structure, have elucidated key structure-activity relationships for inhibitor binding. Meanwhile, AI-augmented virtual screening, targeted protein degradation, and clinically used FSP1 modulators have broadened the landscape of FSP1-directed interventions. This review summarizes recent advances in FSP1-targeted drug discovery from a medicinal chemistry perspective, and discusses current challenges and future opportunities in improving selectivity, drug-like properties, and in vivo efficacy.

title: A Machine-Learning Framework Integrating Frequency-Domain Spectral Features for Ligand Classification and Candidate Prioritization.
text: AI-assisted drug discovery (AIDD) combines molecular modeling with machine learning to support lead identification and candidate prioritization. Conventional molecular descriptors principally encode static chemical structures, leaving frequency-domain behavior as an additional source of molecular information. We therefore developed the terahertz fusion descriptor (THz-FD), a feature-fusion framework that integrates terahertz (THz) frequency-domain features for Na+/K+-ATPase ligand classification and retrospective ranking. Extra Trees (ET), Random Forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM) classifiers were evaluated under repeated-stratified, Molecule_Key-grouped, and scaffold-grouped cross-validation. In repeated-stratified validation, the combined representation achieved mean macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.8538, 0.8423, and 0.8480 for ET, RF, and SVM models, respectively. Adding the model-derived fragment integral spectrum descriptor (FISD) features and protein-reference context features produced absolute macro-AUC changes of -0.0014, -0.0011, and +0.0016 for ET, RF, and SVM, respectively, and absolute macro-F1 changes of +0.0017, +0.0049, and +0.0090. None of the 27 paired comparisons reached statistical significance after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Molecular docking and quantum-chemical calculations provided auxiliary structural and vibrational context for the selected ligands. These findings establish THz-FD as a traceable framework for integrating frequency-domain information with conventional descriptors in ligand-activity modeling and target-specific drug screening.

title: FusionGDB 3.0: integrating breakpoints, generating personalized sequences, and inferring tumorigenic scenarios for human fusion genes.
text: FusionGDB has served diverse biological, health, and clinical research communities as a unique functional annotation knowledgebase of human fusion genes. In this study, we report an updated resource of human fusion gene annotation (FusionGDB 3.0), available at https://compbio.uth.edu/FusionGDB/. FusionGDB 3.0 includes substantial content updates: 156K up-to-date human fusion genes established by integrating 216K RNA-seq-based and 100K WGS-based breakpoint events, comprehensive open reading frame annotations, protein domain retention searches, and 1.13 million personalized fusion protein sequences reflecting individual nsSNVs from TCGA and CCLE, as well as N- and C-truncated protein sequences alongside canonical in-frame products. Furthermore, it incorporates 18K potential tumorigenic scenarios, supported by evidence from the literature, spanning drug-targetable gene group fusions, the epigenomic architecture around breakpoint junctions, and therapeutic prioritization scoring. FusionGDB 3.0 establishes a systematic framework for the functional annotation of coding structural variants. FusionGDB 3.0 serves as a pivotal reference knowledgebase for the genomics, oncology, and precision pharmacology communities, while also functioning as a foundational benchmark dataset for training and validating machine learning models, structural biology platforms, and AI-driven therapeutic discovery pipelines.

title: A Small Molecule Inhibitor of the Staphylococcus aureus agr Quorum Sensing System with Low-Nanomolar Potency.
text: The accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum sensing system regulates virulence in certain common Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus. Small molecules that block agr have been reported, but most have modest potencies and warrant further mechanistic characterization. Herein, we report a structure-function study on CP-20, a compound recently shown to inhibit agr in S. aureus by targeting the histidine kinase AgrC. We designed a robust new synthetic route to the CP-20 scaffold, generated a collection of CP-20 analogues, and evaluated their activities in cell-based agr reporter and phenotypic assays. These investigations led to the discovery of a compound, CP-20t, which inhibits agr in S. aureus with low-nanomolar potency and acts on AgrC. CP-20t represents, to our knowledge, the most potent small molecule inhibitor of agr known-bridging the almost 1000-fold potency gap between peptide- and small molecule-based inhibitors-and is a powerful tool to study quorum sensing in S. aureus.

title: PEG-free tunable poly(2-oxazoline) lipids modulate mRNA-LNP biodistribution and expression in vivo.
text: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed drug delivery, enabling the stabilization and efficient intracellular delivery of nucleic acids. Current LNP platforms, including those used in clinical COVID-19 vaccines, rely on polyethylene glycol (PEG) to stabilize the nanoparticle. However, anti-PEG antibodies are ubiquitous in the population and are a major cause of anaphylaxis and reduced therapeutic efficacy by accelerating the blood clearance of PEGylated products. Here, we report the development of poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) lipids as alternatives. POx polymers are poorly immunogenic and mitigate accelerated blood clearance. Upon varying polymer hydrophilicity and molecular weight, we screened transfection efficiency in multiple cell lines and evaluated top candidates in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that POx-lipids incorporating short hydrophilic oxazoline chains enhance target transfection while mitigating liver expression. These POx-lipids boost expression in key extrahepatic tissues, including lymph nodes and spleen. This marks a notable advancement toward replacing PEG in LNP therapies and provides a clear path to optimizing POx-lipids for targeted vaccine and therapeutic applications.

title: Influenza virus and coronavirus: evolution, epidemiology, antiviral drugs and vaccine development.
text: Influenza viruses and coronaviruses are enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses that pose persistent and pandemic threats to global public health. Despite belonging to distinct viral families, they share remarkable parallels in modes of transmission, clinical manifestations, and socioeconomic impacts, yet diverge fundamentally in evolutionary mechanisms and epidemiological trajectories. This review compares the history, spread, treatments, and vaccines for these two types of viruses. Influenza viruses possess a segmented genome, which enables antigenic shift and reassortment. In contrast, coronaviruses have large, nonsegmented genomes and rely on recombination, mutation accumulation, and insertions to achieve host switching and immune evasion. Both spread to humans through wildlife (intermediate hosts), live animal markets, intensive agriculture, and global travel. Antiviral strategies have evolved from M2 and neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs) for influenza to polymerase inhibitors and protease inhibitors for coronavirus, yet drug resistance remains a common challenge. Vaccine platforms, including inactivated, live-attenuated, recombinant, mRNA, and viral vector technologies, have been deployed against both viruses. This review concludes that integrated, platform-based preparedness, encompassing broad-spectrum antivirals, universal vaccines, and proactive ecological surveillance, is essential for building pandemic-resilient public health systems capable of responding to both influenza and coronavirus threats, as well as future emerging respiratory viruses.

title: Biofoundry Data Interoperability Requires Community Action.
text: Biofoundries are automated laboratory platforms that execute design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycles at scale, generating vast experimental datasets with the potential to accelerate biological discovery and grow the bioeconomy. Independent development across institutions has produced incompatible data formats and no agreed schema linking experimental metadata across cycles or between facilities, preventing aggregation for cross-institutional validation, machine learning, and reproducibility. Neither the international consortium nor the formal standards body with the mandate to act has done so, leaving an organizational gap that no technical solution has yet resolved. Closing the gap will necessitate three sequential steps: a community-driven working group to establish minimum data standards and schema, a funded international pilot cohort to test and refine them, and downstream formalization through established standards bodies. Community consensus must run ahead of, not concurrently with, formal standardization. Both the Bermuda Principles and the Protein Data Bank demonstrate that global scientific communities can establish binding data norms without a mandate, through collective agreement or through incentive structures that make compliance desirable.

title: Exploratory comparison of DVH and dosiomic feature spaces for machine-learning-based prediction of radiation-induced xerostomia in head-and-neck cancer.
text: Normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) modeling for radiation-induced xerostomia in head-and-neck cancer (HNC) radiotherapy traditionally relies on dose-volume histogram (DVH) metrics that summarize dose distributions but discard spatial heterogeneity. Although 3-dimensional dosiomic descriptors have been proposed, their added potential utility remains unclear. To perform an exploratory comparison of DVH-based, dosiomic, and clinical feature frameworks for predicting early severe xerostomia using a reproducible machine-learning pipeline. This retrospective single-institution study included 60 HNC patients treated with helical tomotherapy. The endpoint was severe xerostomia at 3 months (University of Michigan Xerostomia Questionnaire [UMXQ] score ≥ 60; 16/60 cases, 27%). Six feature frameworks were evaluated alongside 2 baselines (mean parotid dose logistic regression; clinical-only model). Feature selection used analysis of variance (ANOVA) F-tests within each training fold (top 15 features). Random Forest and radial basis function support vector machine (RBF-SVM) classifiers were trained under stratified 5-fold cross-validation with 3 imbalance-handling strategies (original data, synthetic minority oversampling [SMOTE], class-weighted learning). Both baselines showed near-chance discrimination (clinical-only area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] ≈ 0.49; mean parotid dose logistic regression AUC ≈ 0.50). Dosiomic-enriched frameworks yielded numerically higher AUCs; the DVH + dosiomics Random Forest configuration achieved the best observed performance (mean AUC ≈ 0.60). However, confidence intervals were wide and overlapping, and no statistically significant differences were detected. In this exploratory single-cohort analysis, dosiomic-based models showed only modest, nonsignificant performance differences relative to DVH-based models. These findings do not establish superiority of either feature space but support further investigation in larger, multi-institutional datasets.

title: Two-sample machine-learning estimation of rifampicin exposure in tuberculosis: an external validation study.
text: Subtherapeutic rifampicin exposure drives treatment failure and acquired resistance in tuberculosis. We aimed to develop and externally validate a concentration-driven machine learning (ML) model predicting rifampicin systemic exposure (AUC0-24h) from sparse clinical sampling, addressing the structural biases and limited generalizability of conventional Bayesian precision dosing. Twenty-six published population pharmacokinetic models were benchmarked against real-world TDM data from a French cohort; the five externally compatible models were used to simulate a training cohort of 4,500 virtual patients. An XGBoost regression model was trained to predict AUC0-24h from a two-point sampling strategy and evaluated against Maximum A Posteriori Bayesian Estimation (MAP-BE) and dynamic Model Averaging (MA). External validation was performed on two completely independent datasets: a US cohort of healthy volunteers and a Brazilian cohort of inpatient tuberculosis cases, including HIV-coinfected patients. A sampling strategy at 2 and 8 hours post-dose provided optimal accuracy. Across the combined cross-continental validation cohorts (n = 40), the concentration-driven ML model showed consistent external predictive performance. It achieved 75.0% of predictions within ±20% of the reference exposure, significantly outperforming the dynamic MA strategy (42.5%, P < 0.001) and all five individual MAP-BE priors (0-60.0%, P < 0.01). Furthermore, the ML approach yielded substantially lower overall imprecision (relative root mean square error: 26.2% vs. 52.6% for MA) and systematic bias (17.5% vs. 38.1%). By integrating mechanistic pharmacology with data-driven inference, this framework enables covariate-free estimation of rifampicin exposure from two plasma samples. External evaluation in two independent cohorts supports its further prospective assessment as a scalable TDM decision-support approach.

title: MultiNSDE: treatment-aware neural SDEs for generative modeling of real and counterfactual patient trajectories.
text: Synthetic patient data may facilitate biomedical research, trial planning, and the construction of synthetic control arms, but there is a lack of methods that enable the realistic generation of mixed-type longitudinal clinical trial data while accounting for treatment effects. We developed MultiNSDE, a neural stochastic differential equation framework for modeling high-dimensional static and longitudinal clinical study data, including continuous, categorical, and time-to-event outcomes. The model separates treatment- and placebo-associated dynamics, enabling treatment-aware individual trajectory simulation and counterfactual treatment assignment. MultiNSDE was evaluated on three neurodegenerative disease trial datasets: A4 in Alzheimer's disease, PRO-ACT in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and DATATOP in Parkinson's disease. The model reproduced static and longitudinal data distributions, extrapolated clinically plausible trajectories, and generated coherent counterfactual outcomes under treatment-to-placebo and placebo-to-treatment shifts. Synthetic data generated by MultiNSDE preserved average treatment effect estimates observed in the real datasets. MultiNSDE provides a proof-of-concept for the generation of realistic mixed-type longitudinal clinical trial data while preserving clinically meaningful treatment-associated differences in outcomes. It may support disease modeling, counterfactual simulation, and synthetic control generation in neurodegenerative disease research.

title: From attribution to causation: A probability-sampled methodological audit of SHAP implementation and explanation validation in published clinical oncology machine learning.
text: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) feature attributions can explain oncology prediction models, but technical reporting, empirical explanation evaluation and causal interpretation require separate assessment. To audit explanation implementation, validation and inferential claims in clinical oncology research. We re-audited an original 500-record probability sample from 2,792 candidates. The observed cohort comprised 227 eligible articles; 167 records lacked full text and had unknown eligibility. Design-weighted estimates retained the original 30 strata, weights and finite-population corrections. Missing-text identification regions and source-uncertainty sensitivities were calculated. Empirical SHAP explanation-evaluation procedures were documented in 3/227 articles (weighted 1.33 %; 95 % confidence interval (CI) [0.47 %, 3.67 %]); two further stability assertions remained unclear. External-cohort prediction evaluation was confirmed in 83/227 (36.72 %; [31.30 %, 42.50 %]); 10 reports remained unclear. Five-item reporting was complete in 2/227 (0.88 %; [0.25 %, 3.06 %]). Dedicated implementations were named in 63 articles; 20 reported version strings and 18 identifiable releases. Workflow A/B/C/D/E counts were 5/49/22/24/127. One article made a strict unsupported causal claim. Weighted missing-text explanation-validation bounds were [0.76 %, 43.15 %]. This probability-sampled oncology audit reveals a marked descriptive gap between independent-cohort prediction evaluation and empirical testing of SHAP explanations. Predictive performance evidence cannot substitute for attribution reliability or causal validity. Sparse explanation events and wide missing-text bounds limit population-wide inference. MINIMUM proposes priorities for reporting and testing, not a validated guideline.

text: Adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) modulate the breast cancer (BC) microenvironment, but their role in endocrine therapy resistance and clinical outcomes remains ill-defined. Functionally, EFHD1-overexpressing ADSCs promoted BC proliferation and invasion. In an orthotopic xenograft model, tumors co-injected with control ADSCs reached ∼500 mm³ by day 30 and maintained robust growth under letrozole + ribociclib (∼350 mm³), compared with BC cells alone (∼300 mm³). In contrast, EFHD1 knockdown in ADSCs reduced tumor volume to ∼200 mm³ and further sensitized tumors to letrozole + ribociclib (∼150 mm³, a ∼40% reduction relative to the drug-only group), with Ki-67 positivity decreasing from ∼4.0% to ∼1.5%. We established a robust ADSC-based prognostic model and uncovered a novel stromal EFHD1/NF-κB/FN1 axis driving ER⁺ BC progression and endocrine therapy resistance, identifying stromal EFHD1 as a candidate target whose pharmacological validation remains to be established.

title: Reliability-aware QSAR prioritization of donafenib analogues for hepatocellular carcinoma.
text: Reliable prioritization of Donafenib-inspired kinase inhibitors requires consideration of chemical diversity, predictive reliability, and developability. We evaluated 2000 CyberAIDD-generated structures using structural quality control, five kinase-specific QSAR datasets, distribution-shift-aware machine learning, uncertainty assessment, applicability-domain (AD) filtering, ADMET prediction, and VEGFR2 structural analyses. Of the initial structures, 1901 passed isotope and structural qualification, representing 584 unique BemisMurcko scaffolds. Of the five kinase-specific QSAR targets initially evaluated, three-RAF1, PDGFRB, and KDR-were retained for applicability-domain-restricted prospective screening based on their relative predictive performance, yielding 893 compounds eligible for three-target consensus prioritization. Developability criteria reduced this set to 35 compounds for ADMET evaluation, followed by selection of 11 analogues alongside Donafenib as a benchmark. The selected models yielded unrestricted cluster-held-out R² values of 0.538 for RAF1, 0.262 for PDGFRB, and -0.408 for KDR, highlighting target-dependent differences in predictive generalization under chemical distribution shifts. Applicability-domain restrictions defined prospective prediction eligibility, whereas the corresponding AD-gated performance estimates were treated as selection-conditioned rather than independent validation results. RAF1 contributed the largest individual consensus weight (41.2%). A RAF1-only ranking sensitivity analysis showed moderate concordance with the three-target consensus (Kendall's τ-b = 0.522), highlighting the influence of secondary kinase predictions and the need for cautious interpretation of consensus ranks. Four analogues underwent VEGFR2 docking and 500-ns molecular dynamics simulations. P859AM424933 and P859AM405047 showed comparatively restrained conformational behavior and persistent binding-site contacts, whereas structural uncertainty limited interpretation of P859AM630255. Predicted solubility, transporter, metabolic, and liver-injury liabilities remained substantial across the series. The workflow provides chemically informed, reliability-conscious candidate prioritization rather than evidence of experimentally improved potency, safety, or efficacy.

title: Chinese Pathologists' Adoption of Large Language Models: Cross-Sectional Survey on Influencing Factors.
text: The growing demand for pathology services and the shortage of pathologists in China have created an urgent need for innovative tools to improve diagnostic efficiency and support professional practice. Large language models (LLMs) may assist pathologists in clinical practice, scientific research, and medical education, but their implementation depends on many factors, such as pathologists' awareness and willingness to adopt these technologies. This study aimed to assess Chinese pathologists' awareness, practical experience, perceptions, ethical concerns regarding LLMs; their willingness to adopt LLMs; and factors associated with willingness to use LLMs in pathology. A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among certified pathologists practicing in mainland China. The survey assessed participants' demographic and professional characteristics; LLM awareness, use, and perceived performance in clinical practice, scientific research, and medical education; ethical concerns; and suggestions for future improvement. Questionnaire reliability and validity were assessed using Cronbach α, Guttman Lambda 6, and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure. Group differences in perceived performance were examined using Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment. Factors associated with willingness to use LLMs in pathology were measured as the summed score of three 5-point Likert items and analyzed using ordinal logistic regression. Of 339 eligible pathologists, 248 (73.2%) had heard of LLMs, and 64 of these (25.8%) had used them. ChatGPT was the most recognized and most commonly used model. Compared with nonusers, LLM users rated clinical applications more cautiously, particularly for analyzing patient data, organizing medical history, and supporting the understanding of disease mechanisms and treatments; these differences were significant after domain-specific FDR adjustment (adjusted P=.02) but borderline after overall correction across all performance items (adjusted P=.05). Perceptions of research and educational applications did not differ significantly between users and nonusers. A higher education level, attending physicians (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.39, 95% CI 1.09-5.22; P=.029), chief physicians (aOR 4.64, 95% CI 1.57-13.69; P=.005), and more than 43 weekly working hours (aOR 2.33, 95% CI 1.40-3.89; P=.001) were associated with greater willingness to use LLMs, whereas working in fourth- or lower-tier cities (aOR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22-0.79; P=.007) and reading 1001-3000 slides annually (aOR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20-0.94; P=.034) were associated with less willingness. Major ethical concerns included model transparency, sensitive data security, and academic misuse. Chinese pathologists show high awareness of LLMs and generally favorable attitudes toward their potential application in pathology, but actual use is limited. The gap between awareness and use highlights the need for improved accessibility, targeted training, pathology-specific validation, workflow integration, and ethical governance. Future implementation should emphasize locally adapted models, data security, and equitable access, particularly for pathologists in lower-tier cities and resource-limited settings.

title: AI-Based Monitoring Devices for the Identification of Circadian Parameters as Digital Predictive Biomarkers of Neurodegenerative Diseases in Older Adults: Systematic Review.
text: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and related dementias are a growing health burden among older adults. Circadian disruption is increasingly recognized as both a consequence and a potential early marker of neurodegenerative progression. Wearable sensing combined with AI enables continuous, noninvasive, and ecologically valid monitoring of circadian parameters as potential digital biomarkers. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on AI-enhanced wearable and objective sensing devices used to monitor circadian parameters in older and cognitively vulnerable adults and evaluates their potential as digital predictive biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines, an original search of PubMed, Scopus, and JMIR journals (June 2025) yielded 12 studies, 7 of which met updated eligibility criteria on rescreening. A complementary search of PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library (March 24, 2026) added 3 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references (excluded records retained to delimit the corpus boundary). Two reviewers (JMH-Z and JM-R) independently assessed risk of bias with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Heterogeneous end points precluded meta-analysis; the narrative synthesis covered 4 prespecified domains: device class, circadian construct, AI and machine learning (ML) method family, and population and neurocognitive context. The final corpus comprised 13 records (10 eligible studies and 3 sensitivity references) published from 2015 to 2025. Wrist actigraphy predominated, and samples ranged from community-dwelling older adults to nursing home residents with advanced dementia (n=16-7297). Circadian parameters included interdaily stability, intradaily variability, relative amplitude, midline estimating statistic of rhythm, acrophase, and circadian stimulus. AI/ML methods included supervised learning (random forests, gradient boosting, and regression models), unsupervised clustering, and algorithm development or validation; 7 studies applied deterministic algorithms without fitting a predictive model. Circadian fragmentation was associated with functional decline, dementia risk, and cognitive performance. Most studies were descriptive or observational with small, nondiverse samples; no AI model was externally validated, and no study followed an AI-specific reporting guideline. AI-enhanced wearable devices show meaningful potential for noninvasive measurement of circadian disruption in older and cognitively vulnerable populations. Evidence certainty is moderate for actigraphy-derived fragmentation-function associations in institutional settings and low for predictive biomarker claims in community populations. From 6 recurring challenges along the sensing-to-biomarker pipeline, we propose a 4-layer reference architecture (sensing and acquisition, circadian parameter extraction, AI/ML inference, and a clinical and validation interface) with a layered validation pathway. Longitudinal, multisite validation studies using standardized circadian metrics, diverse populations, and explainable AI remain necessary before clinical deployment as neurodegenerative biomarkers.

title: Predicting early treatment termination in opioid use disorder: a machine learning model for risk stratification.
text: Background: Half of patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) discontinue opioid agonist treatment within the first year. Identifying premature termination risk at intake could enable targeted clinical responses.Objectives: To develop and externally validate a machine learning model predicting premature treatment termination in OUD; to derive a clinical risk stratification system; and to identify variables most associated with predicted probability.Methods: Retrospective data from the Information System of the Andalusian (South Spain) Plan on Drugs and Addictions (SiPASDA) covered 11,475 patients (86.2% male) admitted to 121 public outpatient centers between 2015 and 2023 (90.8% termination rate). A CatBoost classifier was developed (n = 10,328) and externally validated (n = 1147). Predicted probabilities were discretized into low, moderate- and high‑risk strata. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis quantified global and stratum-specific predictor contributions.Results: CRIBOOST achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.652 ± 0.018 in cross-validation and 0.646 externally. Termination rates rose monotonically across strata: 34.6% (low); 69.6% (moderate); 80.8% (high). Housing instability was the strongest positive predictor (SHAP= +0.569; +0.601 in high‑risk). Judicial referral was most protective (SHAP = -0.412), attenuating from low (-0.553) to high (-0.254); employment showed a similar gradient. Mood disorder (SHAP = +0.470) and benzodiazepine use disorder contributed positively, escalating with risk.Conclusions: CRIBOOST stratifies OUD patients into risk groups at admission using routine intake data, enabling clinicians to target retention-focused interventions where most needed and supporting efficient resource allocation. Stratum-specific SHAP contributions reveal which factors drive risk within each group, informing intervention design.

title: Integrating distributed lag non-linear models and deep learning reveals meteorological drivers of influenza A and B positivity in a 6-year subtropical surveillance study.
text: Subtropical influenza forecasting is complicated by non-linear meteorological dynamics and surveillance bias stemming from pandemic-era testing fluctuations. Existing approaches either characterize lagged environmental associations without forecasting capacity or apply deep learning without epidemiological interpretability. We analyzed multisite influenza surveillance data from Putian, southeastern China (2018-2023); test positivity was the primary outcome to mitigate testing-related bias. Distributed lag nonlinear models estimated type-specific associations between eight meteorological variables and positivity over a 15-day lag window. A Bayesian-optimized long short-term memory (LSTM) network incorporating meteorological, autoregressive, and socio-behavioral covariates was benchmarked against covariate-matched multivariate autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models. For influenza A, the temperature-associated relative risk (RR) peaked at 15°C (3.01; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.03-8.78), and positivity was associated with narrow diurnal temperature ranges. Influenza B positivity was associated with colder conditions (8°C; RR = 26.12, 95% CI: 7.79-87.61), higher humidity (91%; RR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.00-2.29), and lower solar radiation. The LSTM had lower mean absolute error for influenza A (0.009 vs 0.136 for ARIMA and 0.138 for XGBoost) and B (0.002 vs 0.049 and 0.070); symmetric mean absolute percentage error was 0.521 vs 1.212 and 1.081 for A and 0.484 vs 0.810 and 0.737 for B. Covariate ablation and Shapley additive explanations analyses suggested that historical positivity and testing-related variables contributed to forecast stability. External validation in Sanming provided preliminary evidence of regional portability. This framework combines interpretable meteorological associations with short-horizon forecasting under variable surveillance conditions.

title: AMY-SA-XGBoost: A Machine Learning Model to Predict Amylase Specific Activity.
text: Amylase is an important enzyme preparation, and its enzyme activity directly determines its catalytic efficiency in starch hydrolysis. However, current experimental methods for determining amylase specific activity are time-consuming and costly, and experimentally measured specific activity data are sparse and noisy, with limited experimental data currently available. We developed AMY-SA-XGBoost, a machine learning-based approach for predicting amylase specific activity. We systematically constructed a high-quality dataset comprising 178 samples suitable for studying amylase catalytic efficiency by collecting and screening amylase activity data from enzyme databases and literature. The XGBoost-based model exhibited strong predictive performance for amylase activity, with an R2 of 0.9378 and an RMSE of 0.4329. The AMY-SA-XGBoost can capture specific activity changes in mutated enzymes and identify amino acid residues with substantial impact on specific activity. In addition, we screened 14 amylase mutants with the highest predicted increases in specific activity and experimentally validated each mutant. Experimental results confirm that AMY-SA-XGBoost accurately predicts the specific activity of amylase mutants based on their amino acid sequences, successfully identifying variants with higher activity. Among the tested mutants, S359N demonstrated the most significant improvement, achieving a specific activity of 9573 ± 21.30 U/mg. This work provides both theoretical foundation and practical insights for enhancing the catalytic efficiency of amylase in pharmaceutical and food industry applications.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Predicting Risk Factors for Chronic Postsurgical Pain After Cesarean Delivery: A Prospective Cohort Study.
text: Chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) after cesarean delivery can severely impair the mother's quality of life and her ability to care for the infant. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a high-performance, interpretable, machine learning-based prediction model to identify high-risk factors for chronic incisional pain at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively and chronic non-incisional pain at 12 months postoperatively. A total of 678 patients who underwent elective cesarean delivery at our hospital were included in the prospective study. A total of 38 preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative variables, including demographic characteristics, psychological scale scores, and anesthesia/analgesia regimens, were collected. We combined the Boruta algorithm, recursive feature elimination, and the Mantel test for feature selection and constructed a high-performance machine learning-based prediction model (MLPM-CPSP-CD). The incidence of chronic incisional pain at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively was 12.39%, 9.73%, and 7.96%, respectively, whereas the incidence of chronic non-incisional pain was 24.04%. The MLPM-CPSP-CD model demonstrated excellent predictive performance. The core high-risk factors for postoperative chronic incisional pain were SQ-6 (history of dysmenorrhea), SH-5 (patient-controlled analgesia [PCA] pump pressing frequency), and SH-6 (PCA opioid consumption). This study provides an important foundation for developing and optimizing perioperative pain management strategies.

title: FusionGDB 3.0: integrating breakpoints, generating personalized sequences, and inferring tumorigenic scenarios for human fusion genes.
text: FusionGDB has served diverse biological, health, and clinical research communities as a unique functional annotation knowledgebase of human fusion genes. In this study, we report an updated resource of human fusion gene annotation (FusionGDB 3.0), available at https://compbio.uth.edu/FusionGDB/. FusionGDB 3.0 includes substantial content updates: 156K up-to-date human fusion genes established by integrating 216K RNA-seq-based and 100K WGS-based breakpoint events, comprehensive open reading frame annotations, protein domain retention searches, and 1.13 million personalized fusion protein sequences reflecting individual nsSNVs from TCGA and CCLE, as well as N- and C-truncated protein sequences alongside canonical in-frame products. Furthermore, it incorporates 18K potential tumorigenic scenarios, supported by evidence from the literature, spanning drug-targetable gene group fusions, the epigenomic architecture around breakpoint junctions, and therapeutic prioritization scoring. FusionGDB 3.0 establishes a systematic framework for the functional annotation of coding structural variants. FusionGDB 3.0 serves as a pivotal reference knowledgebase for the genomics, oncology, and precision pharmacology communities, while also functioning as a foundational benchmark dataset for training and validating machine learning models, structural biology platforms, and AI-driven therapeutic discovery pipelines.

title: DriverDBv5: a multi-omics integration database for cancer driver gene research.
text: Cancer is driven by alterations across multiple molecular layers, but whether multi-omics drivers carry prognostic weight has received little systematic attention. DriverDBv5 (https://driverdb.bioinfomics.org/) extends DriverDB from driver identification to prognostic evaluation. It has been expanded to 187 cohorts, 43 862 patients, and 129 655 samples, with 154 cohorts from non-TCGA (The Cancer Genome Atlas) repositories reconciled by a generalized multi-omics barcode. Driver genes can be evaluated with Cox and mixture cure models, with machine learning on the full multi-omics feature matrix, and for the joint prognostic effect of alterations in two omics layers. The Customized Analysis module has grown from 4 to 10 tools for user-defined gene sets, subgroups, and covariates, and a human body map offers an anatomical entry point. DriverDBv5 thus reveals not only which alterations drive a tumor, but also which of them relate to patient outcome.

title: Machine learning prediction of cyclosporine nephrotoxicity in pediatric patients using therapeutic drug monitoring and clinical data.
text: Cyclosporine A (CsA) nephrotoxicity is a dose-limiting toxicity in pediatric immunosuppression, and early identification of children at risk of CsA-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) remains an unmet clinical need. In retrospective cohorts of CsA-treated inpatients undergoing therapeutic drug monitoring (352 children; 342 adults), a regularized logistic-regression model was compared with six machine-learning classifiers under five feature-selection schemes, three small-sample strategies were evaluated, and adult-child transferability was assessed on 95 aligned features. A 14-variable model was externally validated in an independent pediatric cohort (n = 257). Regularized logistic regression achieved the best discrimination in children (hold-out AUC 0.800) and adults (hold-out AUC 0.956), with complex models overfitting. Adult and pediatric risk architectures differed fundamentally, with transfer AUCs near chance (≈0.6). The 14-variable model retained discrimination on external validation (AUC 0.784, 95% CI 0.656-0.912). On small clinical datasets, regularization rather than complexity determines predictive performance. We provide an interpretable, TDM-integrated pediatric CsA-AKI model, deployed as an online calculator, supporting early risk stratification in pediatric CsA therapy.

title: Sleep Variability From Routine Nursing Observation and Wearable Actigraphy and Post-Enrollment Length of Stay in Acute Psychiatric Inpatients: Prospective Observational Study
text: BackgroundLength of stay (LOS) in acute psychiatric inpatient settings is clinically and operationally important, but practical early markers for identifying patients at risk for prolonged hospitalization remain limited. ObjectiveTo evaluate whether sleep instability measured during the early inpatient observation period was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization in acute psychiatric inpatients. MethodsThis observational study included 94 consecutive patients admitted to an acute psychiatric inpatient unit. Monitoring began after study enrollment, and participants contributed 5 to 7 available nightly observations from wrist actigraphy and routine nursing observation; observations were not required to occur on consecutive calendar days. The primary exposure was intraindividual sleep variability (IISV), defined as the within-subject standard deviation of nightly total sleep time across available post-enrollment observations. The primary outcome was prolonged post-enrollment length of stay, defined using the 75th percentile of the cohort distribution. Age- and sex-adjusted logistic regression models evaluated associations, discrimination, calibration, and risk stratification. Total length of stay from admission was examined as a temporally distinct sensitivity estimand. ResultsParticipants were enrolled a median of 4 days after admission (IQR 2-7) and contributed 5 to 7 available nightly observations, which accumulated over a median of 8 calendar days (IQR 7-10); 39 of 94 observation series (41.5%) fell on consecutive calendar days. Prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization was defined as more than 24.0 days, yielding 23 events among 94 participants. Greater actigraphy-derived IISV was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 2.30 per 1-hour increase; 95% CI, 1.08-4.93; P=.03), with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.756 (95% CI, 0.626-0.852; optimism-corrected, 0.725) compared with 0.692 for a model containing age and sex alone. Nursing-derived IISV showed an association of similar direction (adjusted OR, 3.10; 95% CI, 1.15-8.39; P=.03; AUC, 0.723; 95% CI, 0.571-0.837; optimism-corrected, 0.690). A combined model containing both measures did not improve discrimination over actigraphy alone (AUC, 0.751). ConclusionsSleep instability measured during the early inpatient observation period, derived independently from wearable actigraphy and from routine nursing sleep documentation, was associated with prolonged post-enrollment hospitalization. Because the outcome interval overlaps the period during which the sleep observations were accumulated, these findings describe an association across the early inpatient course rather than a prediction made at enrollment. The results support further evaluation of repeated sleep variability as a longitudinal inpatient measure; the variable observation schedule, single-center sample, and absence of external validation mean that clinical implementation remains premature.

title: Systematic Benchmarking and Optimization of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Clinical Phenotyping: A Type II Diabetes Case Study in an ICD-Screened Cohort
text: Traditional EHR phenotyping methods can require substantial disease-specific development and long-term maintenance. While integrating large language models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising, the impact of RAG configurations remains underexplored. We systematically evaluated these design choices for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) phenotyping in an ICD-screened cohort. Using GPT-4o, we processed 170,678 clinical notes from 275 patients. We evaluated seven embedding models and three prompt strategies (baseline, improved zero-shot, and few-shot). Using the improved zero-shot prompt, we tested 350 embedding model-chunk size-retrieval depth combinations on the training set and selected eight optimized configurations for test-set evaluation. Combined with three prompts, these yielded 24 prompt-configuration combinations for comparison with ICD codes and the institutional PheNorm method. RAG achieved a mean sensitivity of 0.9019 (95% CI: 0.8866-0.9172), specificity of 0.7907 (0.7749-0.8066), PPV of 0.9405 (0.9365-0.9445), NPV of 0.6967 (0.6653-0.7281), and F1-score of 0.9204 (0.9124-0.9283). All combinations achieved higher PPV than ICD codes (0.7838). Compared with PheNorm, sensitivity was significantly higher (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), while specificity differences were not significant. Paired bootstrap analyses showed higher NPV and F1-score, with no significant PPV difference. General-purpose embeddings showed higher sensitivity, whereas biomedical embeddings exhibited higher specificity and PPV. Few-shot prompting increased specificity and PPV but reduced sensitivity. Token usage varied substantially across embedding models. These findings suggest the importance of aligning RAG design with task-specific clinical priorities and token efficiency.

title: Genetic Determinants of Disease Trajectory in Sarcoidosis
text: BackgroundSarcoidosis is a complex granulomatous, systemic inflammatory condition of unknown origin, characterized by diverse clinical profiles, most notably Lofgrens syndrome (LS) and non-LS sarcoidosis. We investigated the genetic underpinnings of disease trajectory defined by chronic and nonchronic phenotypes. MethodsTwo pulmonologists assessed sarcoidosis disease trajectory over two years and classified patients as chronic or nonchronic. We conducted genetic analyses of disease trajectory in a Swedish cohort comprising 1,484 sarcoidosis cases (775 chronic and 709 nonchronic) and 5,817 controls, for a total of 7,301 individuals. We further stratified genetic analyses by LS and non-LS and performed SNP-heritability analyses, gene-based analyses, eQTL enrichment, and pathway analyses to assess the biological significance of the identified genomic loci. ResultsGenetic associations with chronic and nonchronic sarcoidosis identified distinct loci. In chronic sarcoidosis, the lead signal was rs3135387 (OR = 1.659, 95% CI 1.436 - 1.916) near HLA-DRA. In nonchronic sarcoidosis, the strongest signal resided within TSBP1 rs2849018 (OR = 3.70, 95% CI 3.14 - 4.37). Notable clinical-subtype signals included rs2849018 in LS nonchronic sarcoidosis (OR = 5.90, 95% CI 4.83-7.22), rs3117224 in non-LS chronic sarcoidosis (OR = 1.683, 95% CI 1.439 - 1.968), and rs59344869 in non-LS nonchronic sarcoidosis (OR = 2.424, 95% CI 1.738 - 3.380). SNP heritability was 32.8% (95% CI 23.9-41.7%) for chronic and 47.5% (95% CI 37.5-57.6%) for nonchronic sarcoidosis. ConclusionsThis study highlights the distinct genomic features that differentiate disease trajectories across sarcoidosis clinical phenotypes, underscoring the critical involvement of immune-related genes and regulatory networks. These findings pave the way for further molecular studies and patient stratification based on genetic profiles.

title: Competing event regression on the relative subdistribution and cumulative-incidence scales
text: In competing risks settings, covariate effects and group comparisons are usually assessed one event at a time, through log-rank or Cox tests on the cause-specific hazards, or Grays test or Fine-Gray regression on a cumulative incidence function (CIF). This can obscure a clinically important quantity: the ratio between the event of interest and the competing event, since groups may differ little on the individual events yet differ sharply in their ratio. The generalized competing event (GCE) framework makes this ratio the object of inference; on the cause-specific scale the hazard ratio{omega} +(t) ={lambda} 1(t)/{lambda}2(t) is estimated efficiently from a single stacked (Lunn-McNeil) model. We extend the framework to two scales that describe realized incidence. The subdistribution hazard ratio [Formula] is estimated by a stacked, risk-set-weighted extension of the Lunn-McNeil construction; the cumulative-incidence ratio {rho}(t) = F1(t)/F2(t) by a stacked per-cause pseudo-observation regression of the Aalen-Johansen estimator. We relate the three contrasts:{rho} equals{omega} + exactly under proportional cause-specific hazards, and equals [Formula] only in the small-time limit under proportional subdistribution hazards, drifting toward 1 thereafter. The orthogonality that makes{omega} + efficient is lost on both cumulative-incidence scales: [Formula] through overlapping weighted risk sets and shared censoring weights, and{rho} through the shared survivor. Each carries a covariance term that must be handled and bounds efficiency relative to the hazard-scale test. We derive the corresponding variances, study operating characteristics by simulation, illustrate on hypothetical clinical cohorts, and provide an implementation in the gcemod R package.

title: Diversification without convergence: national childhood respiratory pathogen spectra diverge as they diversify, 1990-2023
text: BackgroundNational childhood respiratory pathogen spectra are diversifying nearly everywhere -- within-country diversity rose in 203 of 204 countries between 1990 and 2023 -- yet whether countries are diversifying toward a common spectrum or along divergent paths is unknown. We quantified between-country compositional distance of national pathogen spectra over the same period. MethodsWe built national pathogen share vectors from Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 lower respiratory infection etiologic attributions (26 pathogens, 204 countries, ages 0-19 years) at five timepoints spanning 1990-2023. Between-country distance was measured as all pairwise Jensen-Shannon divergences (JSD; primary) and Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, with Baselga and Jaccard decompositions; robustness was assessed across metrics, pathogen panels, low-count thresholds and a balanced panel of 107 countries. ResultsMean pairwise JSD rose from 0.0084 in 1990 to 0.0283 in 2023 (+238%; trend p = 0.030), peaking in 2021 (+283%) with a partial 2023 pullback. Bray-Curtis dissimilarity rose +120% and the balanced panel +423%. Divergence was entirely balanced variation (share reallocation), with spectrum richness rising from 18.5 to 21.1 of 26 pathogens. Dispersion rose fastest for influenza (coefficient of variation 0.03 to 0.55) and respiratory syncytial virus (0.08 to 0.48). Within-region distance rose in every computable GBD super-region (five of seven): divergence occurs within regions, not between blocs. A country-level bootstrap confirmed the increase (+238%, 95% CI +165 to +331), and segmented trend analysis found no supported breakpoint, with divergence proceeding steadily at +4.1% per year (95% CI 2.0-6.3) rather than in stages. ConclusionsNational spectra are re-sorting along country-specific axes as vaccine-preventable dominance recedes at different speeds. Diversification is universal, but convergence is absent: the transition at the etiologic-spectrum level is asynchronous and path-dependent, with implications for empirical treatment policy and pathogen surveillance. Summary boxO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSO_LIEpidemiological transition theory and the global health convergence agenda imply that national cause-of-death structures become more alike as mortality declines, but this expectation has been tested mainly at the level of mortality rates and broad cause groups, not etiologic spectra. C_LIO_LIWithin-country (alpha) diversity of the childhood respiratory pathogen spectrum rose in 203 of 204 countries between 1990 and 2023. C_LI What this study addsO_LIBetween-country (beta) compositional distance roughly tripled over the same period (mean pairwise Jensen-Shannon divergence +238%, 1990 to 2023), robust to distance metric, pathogen panel, COVID-19 exclusion, low-count threshold, and a fixed balanced panel. C_LIO_LIDivergence is driven entirely by reallocation of pathogen shares (balanced variation), is fastest for viral pathogens, and occurs within every GBD super-region, indicating that countries diversify along country-specific paths rather than toward a common spectrum. C_LIO_LIA non-parametric bootstrap puts a 95% confidence interval of +165% to +331% on the tripling of between-country distance between 1990 and 2023, and BIC-selected joinpoint models identify no breakpoint -- divergence is steady (+4.1% per year), not staged.
