We propose a two-step framework that decouples geometric representation from learning the physics response, to enable shape-informed surrogate modeling under data-scarce conditions. First, a shape model learns a compact latent representation of left ventricular geometries. The learned latent space effectively encodes anatomies and enables synthetic geometries generation for data augmentation. Second, a neural field-based surrogate model, conditioned on this geometric encoding, is trained to predict ventricular displacement under external loading. The proposed architecture performs positional encoding by using universal ventricular coordinates, which improves generalization across diverse anatomies. Geometric variability is encoded using two alternative strategies, which are systematically compared: a PCA-based approach suitable for working with point cloud representations of geometries, and a DeepSDF-based implicit neural representation learned directly from point clouds. Overall, our results, obtained on idealized and patient-specific datasets, show that the proposed approaches allow for accurate predictions and generalization to unseen geometries, and robustness to noisy or sparsely sampled inputs.

title: Stimulus-driven leakage in naturalistic neuroimaging
text: This article elucidates a methodological pitfall of cross-validation for evaluating predictive models applied to naturalistic neuroimaging data—namely, “stimulus-driven leakage.” While this problem is well known as “leakage in training examples” in machine learning, it may be difficult to detect in practice due to conventions in neuroscience. Stimulus-driven leakage can occur when predictive modeling is applied to data from a conventional neuroscientific design, characterized by a limited set of stimuli repeated across trials and/or participants. It results in spurious predictive performance due to overfitting to repeated signals, even in the presence of independent noise. Through comprehensive simulations and real-world examples, following a theoretical formulation, the article underscores how such data leakage can occur and how severely it can compromise results and conclusions when combined with widespread informal reverse inference. The article concludes with practical recommendations for researchers to avoid stimulus-driven leakage in their experimental design and analysis.

title: Radiographic assessment of bone maturation as a tool for age estimation in common dolphins (Delphinus delphis)
text: We present the first radiographic ageing framework for common dolphins ( Delphinus delphis ), based on ossification and epiphyseal fusion patterns in the pectoral flipper, demonstrating higher reliability for chronological age estimation than currently available epigenetic approaches for this species. Using individuals of known dental age ( n = 120), we calibrated two modelling approaches to predict dental age from radiographic bone scores: (1) a univariate polynomial regression using a total bone score (sum of 16 scores across all assessed flipper bones), and (2) a multivariate canonical analysis of principal coordinates (CAP) incorporating 16 individual bone-score variables. Both approaches successfully predicted dental age from skeletal ossification patterns. For an age range of 0 to 24 years, polynomial regression demonstrated high predictive accuracy with median absolute errors (MAEs) of 1.25 years in females (Spearman’s ρ = 0.93, R² = 0.90) and 1.08 years in males (ρ = 0.95, R² = 0.86). The CAP model yielded MAEs of 1.35 years in females (ρ = 0.90, R² = 0.85) and 1.80 years in males (ρ = 0.94, R² = 0.84). Prediction accuracy declined in individuals with dental ages above 20 years, likely as a consequence of subtle age-related variation in skeletal changes in this species. Nevertheless, both radiographic bone ageing models achieved equal or lower median absolute errors and higher coefficients of determination than a recently developed epigenetic clock for common dolphins derived from the same population (MAE = 1.80, Pearson’s correlation ( r ) = 0.91, R² = 0.82). When applying the bone ageing models to individuals of unknown dental age, both models produced age estimates consistent with expected life-history stages (foetus, neonate, juvenile, subadult, adult), showing that radiographic ageing provides an accurate non-invasive tool for demographic assessment to support conservation management of common dolphins.

title: Microkinetically informed library generation for modeling effective rate laws from kinetic data
text: A profound methodological divide separates top-down macroscopic rate law identification from bottom-up, first-principles microkinetic modeling. While top-down macroscopic models often oversimplify underlying chemistry and fail to capture localized kinetic variations, bottom-up microkinetic simulations provide an exceptionally detailed look at elementary reaction pathways. However, these complex microscopic networks are frequently bottlenecked by uncertainties in both their kinetic parameters and topologies and remain too computationally demanding for full-scale reactor engineering. To bridge this gap, we present a methodology that leverages first-principles simulations for automated library generation, circumventing the bottleneck of scarce experimental data. Central to this pipeline is the novel Linearized Ensemble Motif Operator Network framework, which extracts the underlying effective kinetic information by filtering key kinetic motifs from symbolic expressions, effectively distilling intricate microkinetic networks down to simple, chemically interpretable macroscopic rate laws. This pre-compiled motif library is integrated into a sparse model identification architecture with derivative ensembles (SMIDE). To robustly handle experimental noise, SMIDE generates an ensemble of splines from heteroscedastic noise realizations to capture derivative uncertainty. Through multi-objective optimization, the framework maps out a comprehensive Pareto front of candidate models. This approach transforms rate law discovery from a simple curve-fitting exercise into a rigorous statistical analysis of the kinetic mechanisms supported by the physical system, eliminating the need for manually predefined structural libraries.

title: A safety-constrained AI framework for CAR-T design in solid tumors
text: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, but its translation to solid tumors remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, poor tumor infiltration, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, and on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Here, we present a safety-constrained artificial intelligence framework for rational CAR-T design in solid tumors. The workflow integrates four linked stages: CD-antigen prioritization, safety-by-design CAR architecture mapping, constrained large language model (LLM)–assisted reasoning, and statistical feature-structure analysis. Curated CD-antigen functional annotations and tumor-associated expression descriptors were encoded into a multi-criteria scoring system that stratified targets into high-confidence, conditional, and unsafe classes. Across the analyzed CD-antigen space, 38% of markers were classified as high-confidence candidates, 34% as conditional targets requiring logic-gated or controllable architectures, and 28% as unsafe targets because of predicted off-tumor risk. External benchmark analysis using MSLN, HER2/ERBB2, EGFR/EGFRvIII, CEA/CEACAM5, GD2, B7-H3/CD276, and CD47 supported the framework’s ability to distinguish direct targets from safety-constrained or unsuitable candidates. An updated four-model LLM benchmark, including GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.5, Grok 4.5, and Claude Sonnet 5, showed convergence toward dual-antigen logic-gated, trafficking-enhanced, and armored CAR designs, while revealing model-dependent differences in safety awareness, traceability, and hallucination risk. Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol showed the strongest safety-oriented performance, whereas Grok 4.5 required greater expert oversight. Correlation and clustering analyses further identified redundant safety-liability features and candidate antigen combinations for logic-gated CAR design. This study provides a reproducible, human-in-the-loop decision-support framework for generating safety-aware CAR-T hypotheses. The framework is computational and hypothesis-generating and does not constitute experimental validation of CAR-T efficacy or safety.

title: CLaRe: A General Evaluation Framework for Selecting Compact Near-lossless Latent Representations of High-Dimensional Object Data
text: Latent feature representation methods play an important role in dimension reduction and statistical modeling of high-dimensional complex data objects. However, existing approaches to evaluate these methods have two main drawbacks: they often rely on aggregate measures of information loss, such as average or total loss, which can mask variation across observations, and they typically do so using training rather than generalization error. CLaRe (Compact near-lossless Latent Representations) addresses these issues by estimating the distribution of individual generalization errors via cross-validation and controlling the worst-case error, or a tail quantile of the error distribution. CLaRe can assess any latent feature representation method with an encoder-decoder structure, including classical statistical methods and modern machine learning approaches. The framework is implemented in GLaRe Citation1 (Graphical Analysis of Latent Representations), an open-source R package. We demonstrate CLaRe in three case studies using high-dimensional datasets from diverse application areas, selecting among principal components, wavelets, and autoencoder representations for each dataset. The results show that the optimal representation depends on dataset characteristics, highlighting the need for a flexible evaluation framework. A simulation study in distributional data analysis additionally shows that, compared with conventional approaches based on total in-sample variance explained, selecting a representation using CLaRe can preserve individual-level characteristics that are important for valid downstream statistical modeling. R code scripts and data to reproduce the analysis are available at GitHub Citation2 .

title: Generative AI for high-dimensional biological data under HDLSS constraints: a critical review and comparative study
text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models have become central to modern Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems and analysis in high-dimensional, low-sample-size (HDLSS) biological domains. This article presents a critical review and comparative analysis of major Gen-AI families—including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), diffusion-based probabilis-tic models, and energy-based models—with emphasis on their behavior, stability, and generative fidelity under data-scarce conditions. We survey the literature from 2015–2025, organize the field through a taxonomy of current generative paradigms, and analyze how these models are adapted to omics settings such as 1 scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, metabolomics, and related molecular data. A recurring finding across the literature is that most models rely on aggressive preprocessing, such as highly variable gene selection, principal component analysis, or the latent space structure of an encoder-decoder network , effectively replacing the original HDLSS problem with a lower-dimensional proxy. These models are typically applied to moderate to medium-sized data sets and currently lack validation in biological applications where sample size is significantly small, e.g., fewer than 10 replicates. We further identify the absence of embedded sparsity-aware feature selection as a major methodological gap. To complement the survey, we experimentally compare representative VAE-, GAN-, and diffusion-based models on benchmark biological datasets in the HDLSS regime. The results show that VAEs remain comparatively stable in low-sample settings, whereas GANs and diffusion models improve substantially as sample size increases. Overall, this review provides a structured perspective on genera-tive modeling under HDLSS biological constraints and highlights open directions in data-efficient, interpretable, and reproducible Gen-AI for biological discovery.

title: Startup sustainability forecasting through natural language processing of business plans
text: Recent surveys show that only 1 in 400 startups secure funding and achieve post-fund sustainability. Startup assessment is becoming increasingly complicated due to the evolving entrepreneurial landscape, which is affected by too many factors, compelling venture capital firms to harness state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI). Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a promising approach for startup assessment, by analyzing documents that summarize key factors of long-term success. Although startup sustainability research is active, modern NLP for assessing business plans has received limited attention. Specifically, the majority of previous works consider only short text descriptions of startups instead of complete business plans, and do not offer adaptability to the varying investment criteria of different investors. In this paper, we propose ForeStart, a startup sustainability forecasting system powered by a transformer-based language model that offers seamless adaptability to the particular needs of users. The proposed system can analyze business plans of unlimited length, including also startup-related content such as pitch deck presentations and company websites. ForeStart is based on a hierarchical Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers–Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (DistilBERT–BiLSTM) architecture trained using both unsupervised domain adaptation and supervised learning, effectively leveraging both unlabeled and labeled business plans. In addition, the proposed system addresses issues arising from privacy concerns and low-resource settings of the startup environment. Our experiments on actual business plans achieve 79% $$F_{1}$$ score in forecasting startup sustainability, even with a limited number of labeled business plans as training data. As an assisting screening tool for analysts, ForeStart can significantly reduce the time required for startup assessments, providing value to Venture Capital (VC) organizations. Moreover, startup founders can also use ForeStart for self-assessment.

title: Comparative genomics of Mycobacterium wolinskyi: phylogenomic relationships, pan-genome structure, and clinically relevant genomic features
text: Introduction Rapidly growing nontuberculous mycobacteria can cause post-procedural skin and soft-tissue infections, yet rare species such as Mycobacterium wolinskyi remain challenging in culture-based identification and poorly characterized at the genomic level. Methods In this study, we reported a clinical M. wolinskyi isolate (SYF4192) recovered from a post-liposuction infection using culture, probe-capture metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). We further performed comparative genomic analyses, including genome-based species delineation, phylogenomics, pan-genome analysis, mobile genetic element characterization, virulence-associated gene profiling, and resistome analysis. Results Based on the AST results, the patient was treated with susceptible antimicrobial agents and obtained a favorable outcome. The 7,257,454 bp genome assembly of SYF4192 comprised a 7,102,780 bp circular chromosome and a putative 154,674 bp circular extrachromosomal replicon. Comparative genomic analyses revealed close genetic relatedness between SYF4192 and publicly available M. wolinskyi genomes, although ANI and dDDH estimates showed discrepancies in species delineation. The seven-genome dataset contained 9,881 gene clusters, including 5,654 core and 4,227 accessory clusters, and was consistent with an open pan-genome in this limited dataset. SYF4192 harbored 608 gene clusters not detected in the other six genome assemblies, representing the largest isolate-specific gene repertoire in the dataset. Additionally, a predicted 51.9 kb prophage-like region and putative homologs of mce2A–E , mce8 -associated genes, and ESX-5 components were identified. Resistome analysis revealed multiple putative resistance-associated determinants, while phenotypic susceptibility testing demonstrated clarithromycin resistance and an elevated tobramycin MIC, highlighting the importance of integrating genomic predictions with phenotypic susceptibility data. Discussion This study expands the limited genomic resources available for M. wolinskyi and provides preliminary insights into its genomic diversity, mobile genetic elements, and resistance-associated features. Further investigations involving larger, geographically and clinically diverse isolate collections, together with functional validation, are warranted.

title: PEG-free tunable poly(2-oxazoline) lipids modulate mRNA-LNP biodistribution and expression in vivo
text: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed drug delivery, enabling the stabilization and efficient intracellular delivery of nucleic acids. Current LNP platforms, including those used in clinical COVID-19 vaccines, rely on polyethylene glycol (PEG) to stabilize the nanoparticle. However, anti-PEG antibodies are ubiquitous in the population and are a major cause of anaphylaxis and reduced therapeutic efficacy by accelerating the blood clearance of PEGylated products. Here, we report the development of poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) lipids as alternatives. POx polymers are poorly immunogenic and mitigate accelerated blood clearance. Upon varying polymer hydrophilicity and molecular weight, we screened transfection efficiency in multiple cell lines and evaluated top candidates in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that POx-lipids incorporating short hydrophilic oxazoline chains enhance target transfection while mitigating liver expression. These POx-lipids boost expression in key extrahepatic tissues, including lymph nodes and spleen. This marks a notable advancement toward replacing PEG in LNP therapies and provides a clear path to optimizing POx-lipids for targeted vaccine and therapeutic applications.

title: Lung‐Targeting Interleukin‐10 mRNA Sulfonium Lipid Nanoparticles Ameliorate Acute Lung Injury
text: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most severe manifestation of acute lung injury (ALI), characterized by diffuse pulmonary inflammation, impaired gas exchange, and high morbidity and mortality. Despite the clinical significance of ARDS, no effective pharmacological therapies are currently available. In this study, we developed a lung-targeted mRNA-sulfonium lipid nanoparticle (mRNA/sLNP) delivery system for the treatment of ALI/ARDS in a mouse model. We first examined different heads and tails to optimize sulfonium lipid structure, leading to the identification of a top-performing HOSEH formulation. HOSEH sLNP was comprehensively characterized and subsequently loaded with interleukin-10 (IL-10) mRNA, an immunomodulatory cytokine with potent anti-inflammatory activity. As a proof-of-concept, in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced ALI mouse model, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP demonstrated both prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, significantly attenuating pulmonary and systemic inflammation, restoring alveolar-capillary barrier integrity, and reducing lung tissue damage. These findings highlight the potential of lung-targeted mRNA therapeutics in inflammatory lung diseases. With further development, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of ALI and ARDS.

title: Identification of Proteomic Subtypes with Differential Responses to Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Cutaneous Melanoma
text: PURPOSE: Predictive biomarkers for combined PD-1/CTLA-4 blockade in metastatic melanoma remain limited. We analyzed pretreatment proteogenomic data to define response and resistance biology. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: We profiled 208 pretreatment FFPE specimens from patients with metastatic cutaneous melanoma treated across 12 institutions, including 164 receiving dual PD-1+CTLA-4 blockade (Discovery, n=97; Validation 1, n=67) and 44 receiving PD-1 monotherapy. Tumors underwent TMT-based proteomics, RNA sequencing, and targeted/low-pass whole-genome sequencing. Pathway clustering, survival modeling, deconvolution, and machine-learning classification defined and validated subtype signatures. RESULTS: Proteomic pathway clustering identified three reproducible ICI subtypes: immune-enriched ICI-sensitive, ribosome-high, and EMT-like/stromal-enriched. Subtypes stratified progression-free survival after dual ICI in the Discovery (P=0.01) and Validation 1 cohorts (P=0.02). The ICI-sensitive subtype had the highest responder fraction (74% and 73%), compared with ribosome-high (67% and 60%) and EMT-like tumors (44% and 43%) in the Discovery and Validation 1 cohorts, respectively. Subtype-outcome associations were consistent with previous immunotherapy datasets, with pooled hazard ratios ≈0.5-0.8 for immune-enriched tumors. Subtypes plus clinical variables predicted 3-year progression/death better than clinical variables alone in Validation 1 (AUC 0.80 vs 0.64). A 127-protein classifier recapitulated subtype membership in Validation 1 (AUC 0.89-0.97) and predicted 3-year progression/death with AUC 0.79. Subtypes reflected distinct immune, translational, and stromal/ECM programs and nominated POLR3A-associated biology as a candidate resistance axis. CONCLUSIONS: Proteomic pathway states define reproducible, biologically interpretable melanoma subtypes associated with differential benefit from dual PD-1/CTLA-4 blockade. A clinically tractable 127-protein classifier provides a foundation for prospective biomarker-driven combination immunotherapy trials.

title: Exogenous Calcium Silicate‐Primed Mitochondria Reverse Diabetic Wound Chronicity via Dual Proteolytic Regulation and Metabolic Reprogramming
text: Impaired diabetic wound healing is characterized by chronic inflammation, severe bioenergetic deficits, and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation driven by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). Here, a cell-free therapeutic strategy is developed utilizing exogenous calcium silicate-primed mitochondria (CSMito) embedded within a collagen hydrogel to overcome these pathological barriers. Multi-omics analyses reveal that silicate conditioning activates intracellular signaling cascades, shifting mitochondrial dynamics toward fusion and enriching CSMito with critical therapeutic cargos: UQCRC1 (respiratory Complex III) and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 1 (TIMP-1). Upon transplantation, CSMito orchestrates a distinct dual-action mechanism. Extracellularly, surface-associated TIMP-1, confirmed via nano-flow cytometry, acts as a molecular shield to sequester host-secreted MMPs prior to cellular internalization, thereby preventing scaffold degradation. Intracellularly, following endocytosis, the UQCRC1-fortified respiratory chain rapidly restores oxidative phosphorylation capacity in recipient cells. This bioenergetic rescue mitigates oxidative stress and metabolically reprograms inflammatory macrophages toward a pro-resolving phenotype. Targeted loss-of-function studies using TIMP-1 depletion and Complex III pharmacological blockade confirm that both proteolytic shielding and metabolic reprogramming are essential for tissue resolution. In a diabetic rabbit full-thickness wound model, CSMito accelerates macroscopic closure, orchestrates dense collagen deposition, and stimulates robust angiogenesis. Ultimately, this work establishes inorganic ion-engineered mitochondria as advanced, dual-functional therapeutics to reverse diabetic wound chronicity.

title: Cross-Modal Attention Fusion for Clinical Risk Prediction: Integrating EHR Data with Dual-Attribution Explain ability
text: Clinical prediction models have historically relied on structured electronic health record data, leaving the rich prognostic signal embedded in free-text clinical documentation systematically underutilized. The proposed Clinical Multimodal Adaptive Clinical Prediction (CMACP) architecture — a dual-pathway prediction system integrating structured EHR features through gradient-boosted tree processing with unstructured clinical note embeddings through Clinical BERT encoding, unified by a cross-modal attention mechanism that weighs each modality's contribution by predictive confidence. The architecture is designed for geriatric acute care settings where clinical notes capture disease severity, symptom trajectory, and functional context unavailable from structured data alone. A federated fine-tuning protocol enables privacypreserving multi-institutional model development across health systems with different EHR platforms and patient populations. An attribution framework combining SHAP-based structured feature importance with Integrated Gradients note concept attribution provides role-differentiated clinical explanations, with a concordance quality badge signalling modality alignment. A governance framework specifies deployment standards, post-market performance monitoring, and equity evaluation protocols calibrated to multi-site clinical NLP systems. The CMACP framework addresses the technical and governance requirements for safe deployment of multimodal clinical AI in settings where older adult patients are most vulnerable to prediction errors. External validation across multiple health system types, equity stratification by race and documentation quality environment, and prospective evaluation of attribution quality are identified as priority research requirements.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Health: Integrated SPAR-4 Systematic Literature Review and Bibliometric Analysis
text: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming multiple sectors, including public health. Recent years have witnessed a substantial increase in research on integrating AI into public health systems, reflecting a growing interest in its potential to improve surveillance, diagnostics, policy development, and health outcomes. Objective: This study aims to identify how AI has been applied in public health, examine its impact on the field, and determine future research directions at the intersection of AI and public health. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted to analyze existing scholarly research on AI applications in public health. Relevant studies were collected, screened, and categorized to identify dominant research themes and gaps in the literature. Results: The analysis revealed five primary thematic clusters within the literature: (1) AI model development and performance, (2) public health threats and outbreak management, (3) systematic reviews and evidence synthesis, (4) social and ethical issues in public health, and (5) governance, policy, and innovation. The review also identified underexplored areas and inconsistencies across studies, highlighting significant research gaps. Conclusions: AI has demonstrated substantial potential to enhance public health practice and research. However, further investigation is needed to address ethical, governance, and implementation challenges. Future research should focus on strengthening policy frameworks, improving transparency and accountability in AI systems, and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the responsible and equitable integration of AI into public health.

title: Data Sharing in Autism Research: Case Studies From the United States and the United Kingdom and Recommendations for Practice
text: Data sharing has become common in Autism research. In the context of a history of eugenics, additional risks are present, including re-identification, misinterpretation and deficit-framing of Autism. We, a group of community members and researchers, aimed to (a) describe our ‘opt-in’ data-sharing approach in two Community-Based Participatory Research studies based in the United States (AASPIRE Outcomes Project) and the United Kingdom (Autism from Menstruation to Menopause; AM2M), (b) report on how many people opted to data share and (c) co-develop recommendations for ethical data sharing in Autism research. In the AASPIRE Outcomes Project, 680 of 870 (78.2%) participants opted to share quantitative survey data, with no differences by demographic, disability, or health characteristics. In AM2M, 36 of 100 (36.0%) participants opted to share longitudinal qualitative data, with significant variation when controlling for family-wise error rate by menopause status ( p = .007). We provide recommendations for ethical data sharing in Autism research, directed at governments, policy makers, research funders, data repositories, ethics boards and researchers. We favour approaches that centre autonomy and dignity, including, ‘opt-in’ data-sharing consent models and Autistic community participation. We hope that these recommendations will balance data-sharing benefits with strong protections for Autistic research participants. Lay Abstract Data sharing is when people’s information from a study are anonymised (names taken out) and shared in an online library. Other researchers can use this data to answer new research questions at reduced cost. Some funders say researchers must share data. However, some Autistic people worry this could be bad for Autistic people. One solution is letting research participants decide if they want to share their answers. This is called ‘opt-in’ data sharing. We are a neurodiverse group of Autism researchers and community members. We had three goals: 1. Share how we handled data sharing in studies in the United States and the United Kingdom; 2. Say how many people agreed to data share 3. Make recommendations for ethical data sharing in Autism research. We had concerns about data sharing, including not keeping participants’ identities private and researchers doing studies that were dehumanising or used deficit views of Autism. For this reason, the U.S. study decided not to share interview data, and both studies used separate data-sharing information and consent forms after people had decided to take part in the study. In our U.S.-based survey study, most people (680 of 870 or 78%) decided to data share their survey data. There were not many differences between people who did or did not decide to share their data. In our U.K.-based interview study, one third (36.0%) of 100 participants decided to share their interview data. Menopausal participants shared less often. We developed best-practice recommendations for Autism research data sharing. We make suggestions for governments, research funders, data repositories, ethics boards and researchers. We recommend using ‘opt-in’ consent for data sharing. We also think Autistic adults should be involved in deciding if new research that uses shared data is good for the Autistic community. We hope these recommendations will provide stronger protections for Autistic research participants.

title: Integrated Digital Sustainability Framework for Inclusive Growth and Social Development
text: Digital transformation is becoming an integral mechanism to facilitate sustainability, inclusive development, and social progress. Availability of digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things, cloud computing, digital platforms, mobile applications, and data-driven services provides new avenues for enhancing access to education, health care, job opportunities, financial services, governance, and environmental management. But digital transformation does not ensure that such initiatives will be sustainable or inclusive. Access asymmetry to connectivity, digital skills, devices, funding, and services can strengthen social and economic disparities. Increasing reliance on digital systems poses new environmental, institutional, privacy, cybersecurity, and governance issues. In this paper, we create a conceptual framework for understanding the relationship between digital sustainability and inclusive growth and social development. We consider the following four dimensions of sustainability: economic, social, environmental, and institutional. These dimensions are enabled by the following components: digital infrastructure, digital skills, governance, and innovation. The article highlights the limitations of current literature on digital sustainability, digital inclusion, sustainable development, and socially enabling technologies. It outlines how digital technologies could support inclusive education, health care access, livelihoods, financial inclusion, smart governance, and green digitization through various paths. A plan for implementation has been outlined, highlighting the role of each stakeholder such as the government, business, community, educational institutes, and technology companies. Sustainability metrics have been proposed to assess the outcomes for economy, society, environment, and institutions. The paper focuses on the fact that responsible governance, access to technology, digital literacy, and assessment are prerequisites for a digital transformation to result in sustainable development.

title: AI-Enabled Decision Support Systems for Improving Public Administration Effectiveness
text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming one of the sources for transforming public administration through introducing new techniques in information processing, policy analysis, service provision, resource management, and decision-making. Public organizations work in an information-intensive environment in which administrators have to analyze large amounts of structured and unstructured data, taking into account changes in the socio-economic, environmental, and technological environment. Traditional decision-making techniques can be restricted by fragmented information systems, manual information processing, limited analytic capacity, time delays in information processing, and difficulties in finding complex interrelations in large datasets. Integration of artificial intelligence techniques with databases, analytic models, visualization techniques, and current e-governance technologies in AI-enabled Decision Support Systems (DSS) creates an opportunity to overcome these limitations and provide administrators with information, predictions, recommendations, and scenarios for decision-making based on evidence. This paper analyzes the role of AI-enabled DSS in enhancing the efficiency of public administration through a conceptual and literature review approach. The study will focus on the evolution of DSS, application of AI in public administration, decision-making theories, technological, organizational, and governance issues. Conceptual framework is generated through the integration of decision-support concepts into the Technology–Organization–Environment framework. The use cases under discussion include applications in the development of policies, delivery of services to citizens, resource allocation, fraud detection, urban planning, healthcare, education, social services, and disaster response. Challenges associated with data accuracy, privacy issues, cybersecurity, biases of algorithms, explainability of decisions, legal aspects, digital divide, skills of personnel, and organizational barriers are discussed as well. The analysis shows that the utilization of AI technologies within decision support systems may increase the effectiveness, analytical capabilities, timeliness, forecasting abilities, monitoring and resource planning if there is relevant data and proper organizational and governance mechanisms. Nonetheless, the application of AI needs to be limited to a decision-support tool rather than a substitute for the human decision-making in public organizations.

title: A multimodal foundation model for molecular and morphologic data in oncology
What is the Role of Small Models in the LLM Era: A Survey
text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in various reasoning tasks, which leads to the development of increasingly large models. However, scaling up model sizes results in significantly higher computational costs and energy consumption, which makes these models impractical for academic researchers and businesses with limited resources. At the same time, Small Models (SMs) are frequently used in practical settings, although their significance is currently underestimated. This raises important questions about the role of SMs in the era of LLMs, a topic that has received limited attention in prior surveys. In this work, we systematically examine the relationship between LLMs and SMs from two key perspectives: Collaboration and Competition ( or Complementarity ). We hope this survey provides valuable insights for practitioners, fostering a deeper understanding of the contribution of small models and promoting more efficient use of computational resources. Code and additional resources for this survey are available at: https://github.com/tigerchen52/awesome_role_of_small_models.

title: A Primer on the Analysis of Randomized Experiments and a Survey of Some Recent Advances
text: The past two decades have witnessed a surge of new research in the analysis of randomized experiments. The emergence of this literature may seem surprising given the widespread use and long history of experiments as the "gold standard" in program evaluation, but this body of work has revealed many subtle aspects of randomized experiments that may have been previously unappreciated. This article provides an overview of some of these topics, primarily focused on stratification, regression adjustment, and cluster randomization.

title: Leveraging transfer learning for predicting acute graft- versus -host disease in stem cell transplantation
text: Acute graft- versus -host disease (aGvHD) is a major complication after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), occurring when transplanted donor immune cells attack the recipient’s tissues. Despite advances in HSCT, no reliable clinical method currently exists to predict which patients will develop aGvHD. Early identification of high-risk individuals could improve donor selection and guide preventive strategies. Although machine learning techniques have demonstrated promising predictive performance, their practical deployment is limited by data privacy regulations, heterogeneity in healthcare records, and the scarcity of labeled samples across institutions. We propose a machine learning framework for aGvHD prediction that avoids raw-data sharing and addresses these limitations in decentralized data environments. The framework leverages three publicly available datasets and applies a transfer learning strategy. A source model is trained locally using only shared attributes, and its learned representations are transferred to enhance a target model trained on a different dataset. This approach enables knowledge integration across institutions without sharing sensitive patient-level data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms baseline models, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) greater than 0.7 on the three datasets. Statistical significance was assessed using Dunnett’s test and bootstrap confidence interval test, revealing significant improvements in AUROC compared to the majority of baselines ( p < 0.01). A post-hoc explainability analysis further identifies key factors associated with aGvHD development. The findings of this study demonstrate that this strategy yields noteworthy outcomes, especially in terms of AUROC, despite the differences in the diagnoses, donor types, and graft manipulation between the datasets.

title: Opinion: When should medical school start?
text: STAT readers weigh in on shortening medical school, fixing pediatric emergency care, and more.

title: DNA barcoding and cellular senescence in atherosclerosis: Vascular smooth muscle cell lineage tracing and potential for future Senotherapeutics.
text: Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and substantial risk persists even with optimal preventive therapy. Cellular senescence is a state of growth arrest accompanied by a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and has emerged as a candidate driver of vascular disease states. Recently, vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) have moved from passive bystanders in vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, to pivotal cells integral to many facets of plaque biology. Within the lesion microenvironment, VSMCs undergo phenotypic switching and de-differentiation into macrophage-like, osteogenic, fibromyocyte, and senescent states, frequently extinguishing canonical lineage markers. However, defining the independent contribution of senescent VSMCs is complicated by two converging problems: the absence of a universal, specific senescence marker, and the loss of identity that accompanies VSMC trans-differentiation. We argue that DNA barcoding, a high-resolution, marker-independent lineage-tracing strategy matured in hematology and oncology, can address both obstacles. Building on the established foundation of multicolor reporters, we contrast static high-diversity libraries with evolving CRISPR-Cas9 recorders and human-translatable retrospective approaches, emphasizing that barcoding reports clonal lineage and must be paired with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to position the senescent state on a reconstructed clonal tree. We further appraise emerging senotherapeutics, whose inconsistent and occasionally harmful in vivo results reflect a failure to identify the target cell rather than a failure of pharmacology. This distinction argues for lineage-restricted targeting. Integrating clonal barcoding, spatial multi-omics, and senescence atlases may help resolve the role of VSMC senescence in atherogenesis and enable cell-state-specific therapy.

title: Integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses identify an SFRP2 + fibroblast state associated with gastric cancer perineural invasion.
text: Perineural invasion (PNI) marks aggressive gastric cancer, yet the stromal states associated with nerve-invasive disease remain poorly resolved. Here, we integrated bulk transcriptomic cohorts with single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data to define the stromal cell states associated with PNI in gastric cancer and determine their cellular, spatial and regulatory context. We integrated bulk transcriptomic cohorts with single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data, employing phenotype projection, deconvolution, trajectory analysis, metabolic and regulon analysis, and multiplex immunofluorescence to identify key cell types, regulons, and functional heterogeneity among cells. A 13-gene stromal PNI-associated signature (S-PNIS) was enriched in PNI-positive tumors and associated with advanced disease and adverse outcome. Cross-modal analyses localized S-PNIS and an independently derived NMF-PNIS program to SFRP2 + myofibroblastic cancer-associated fibroblasts (myCAFs) near nerve-rich niches. Multiplex immunofluorescence demonstrated the enrichment of SFRP2 + PDPN + cells near TUBB3 + neural structures in PNI-positive gastric cancer tissues. SFRP2 + myCAFs showed retinoid-associated transcription and increased PBX1 regulon activity. SFRP2 + myCAFs define a stromal state associated with gastric cancer PNI and nominate coordinated ALDH1A3-linked retinoid metabolism and PBX1 activity as a testable framework for stromal-neural interactions in the perineural niche.

title: Discovery of thiol-reactive Staphylococcus aureus sortase A inhibitors from natural products by machine learning and thiocholine mass-shift profiling.
text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) remains a major clinical challenge, and Sortase A (SrtA), a cysteine transpeptidase involved in surface-protein anchoring and biofilm formation, represents an attractive anti-virulence target. In this study, we developed an integrated analytical workflow combining machine-learning (ML)-guided taxon prioritisation, affinity magnetic capture, mass-shift profiling, and biochemical target-engagement assays to identify natural-product SrtA inhibitors from complex botanical extracts. A random-forest classifier trained on ChEMBL SrtA bioactivity data was applied to the LOTUS natural-product database to prioritise Michael-acceptor-containing botanical sources, leading to the selection of Piper retrofractum for constituent-level analysis. Subsequent chemical profiling and affinity-capture experiments identified piperlongumine as a thiol-reactive constituent preferentially associated with active SrtA. Piperlongumine inhibited SrtA transpeptidase activity with an IC50 of 27.83 ± 1.04 μmol/L and showed a higher TCI-adduct response and stronger SrtA inhibition than the structurally related alkaloid piperine. Time-dependent enzyme inhibition, competitive 5-FAM-LPETG bead imaging, and mPEG-maleimide thiol-occupancy analysis further supported thiol-dependent SrtA engagement under the assay conditions. Piperlongumine also inhibited biofilm formation across multiple S. aureus strains while exerting limited effects on planktonic growth at corresponding concentrations. These findings demonstrate an analytical strategy that links computational prioritisation, crude-extract chemical profiling, affinity capture, and target-engagement validation for the discovery of thiol-reactive natural products targeting SrtA.

title: Discovery of a Potent and Selective First-In-Class Antagonist of GPR15 With In Vivo Anti-Obesity Activity.
text: GPR15 (G Protein-coupled Receptor 15), an atypical chemokine receptor, is implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple diseases, yet small-molecule GPR15 antagonists remain undeveloped. Herein, we identify and characterize YL410, the first-in-class potent and selective GPR15 antagonist. In the cAMP-GloSensor assay, YL410 inhibits GPR15 with an IC50 of 0.027 ± 0.005 µM, and displays high selectivity against a panel of related GPCRs and kinases. It suppresses GPR15L-induced Jurkat T-cell migration, and exhibits favorable pharmacokinetics and acceptable safety. Molecular docking, replicated molecular dynamics simulations, quantitative contact analyses, and mutagenesis experiments support a plausible orthosteric binding model for YL410, maintained by a reproducible network of polar and hydrophobic contacts, which rationalizes its potent antagonism and observed structure-activity relationships (SAR). Complementary AI-based structure predictions (AlphaFold3, Chai-1, and Boltz) recapitulated the energetically accessible orthosteric poses but not the dynamically stable pose selected by the MD simulations, underscoring the importance of kinetic-stability validation in antagonist pose selection. Notably, in a diet-induced obesity (DIO) mouse model, YL410 administration induced significant weight loss and exerted blood glucose-lowering effects. Collectively, this study presents the first potent, selective, and in vivo efficacious GPR15 antagonist, providing new insights into the development of therapeutics for the treatment of obesity.

title: High-Throughput Technologies for Targeted Covalent Drug Discovery: Recent Advances and Perspectives.
text: Covalent drugs have attracted increasing attention in modern drug discovery because of their prolonged target engagement, enhanced pharmacological efficacy, and potential to address traditionally challenging protein targets. The rapid development of electrophilic warhead chemistry, chemical biology methods, and high-throughput screening technologies has shifted covalent drug discovery from serendipitous identification to target-oriented and rational design. In recent years, phage display, mRNA display, and DNA-encoded library technologies have enabled the efficient de novo discovery of covalent peptides and small molecules, expanding the accessible chemical space for targeting cysteine, lysine, tyrosine, serine, and other reactive residues. Meanwhile, artificial intelligence has further accelerated covalent drug research by supporting covalent database construction, binding-site prediction, virtual screening, molecular generation, and structure-based ligand optimization. This article reviews recent advances in high-throughput strategies for targeted covalent drug discovery, with a focus on phage display, mRNA display, DNA-encoded libraries, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches. We further discuss current challenges and future opportunities in the field and provide our perspectives on emerging directions for next-generation covalent ligand discovery.

title: Structure-Guided Design of Calcium-Dependent Protein Kinase 1 Inhibitors for Cryptosporidiosis.
text: Calcium-dependent protein kinase 1 (CDPK1) has emerged as a protozoan-specific target for the treatment of cryptosporidiosis. A previous study identified pyridopyrimidinones as new Cryptosporidium parvum CDPK1 (CpCDPK1) inhibitors with potent growth inhibition against C. parvum and Cryptosporidium hominis. Docking analyses suggested the unique positioning of the kinase's αC-helix could present refinement opportunities. Compounds designed to optimize the pyridopyrimidinones focused on the back-pocket region predicted to be proximal to the αC-helix, the solvent-exposed region, and the ATP ribose-binding site. Designed derivatives were synthesized and assessed for CpCDPK1 and Src kinase inhibition and for Cryptosporidium spp growth inhibition in mammalian cells. AMP/Mg+2 and 3 inhibitors were cocrystalized with CpCDPK1, and 2 inhibitors were profiled for kinase selectivity. WIN 4-88 was identified with CpCDPK1 (half maximum inhibitory concentration [IC50] = 0.056 μM), and growth inhibition of zoonotic C. parvum NLuc (half maximum effective concentration [EC50] = 0.042 μM), anthroponotic C. parvum Tu114 (EC50 = 0.030 μM), and C. hominis Tu502 (EC50 = 0.062 μM), as well as enhanced kinome selectivity. The crystal structures confirmed the predicted binding mode, indicating key interactions with hinge residue Y155, similar orientations of the solvent-expose moieties, occupancy of the back pocket near the αC-helix, and for 1 inhibitor containing a solubilizing hydroxyethyl attached to the central heterocycle extension into the ATP ribose-binding site. The expanded structure-activity relationship and structural insights will potentially be applicable to other chemotypes with similar binding modes and will enhance development of CpCDPK1 inhibitors for the treatment of cryptosporidiosis.

title: Dysregulation of the kynurenine pathway in Parkinson's disease: a review of systems biology and multi-omics.
text: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss and widespread cellular dysfunction. The kynurenine pathway (KP), the major route of tryptophan metabolism, produces neuroactive metabolites, including quinolinic acid, 3-hydroxykynurenine and kynurenic acid. Although KP alterations have been implicated in PD, their causal contribution remains uncertain. This review critically evaluates genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, lipidomic and network-modeling evidence linking KP dysregulation to PD. It examines therapeutic approaches targeting indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1), tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2) and kynurenine 3-monooxygenase (KMO), including enzyme inhibition, targeted protein degradation, drug repurposing and central nervous system delivery strategies. Emerging applications of single-cell and spatial omics, digital-twin modeling and gut-brain-KP interactions are discussed. The literature search was updated to September 2026. SSystems-level KP investigation may identify disease-modifying therapeutic opportunities in PD. However, small heterogeneous cohorts, non-standardized metabolite measurements and insufficient evidence of human brain target engagement remain major limitations. Future translational studies must establish therapeutic selectivity, brain exposure, target engagement, safety and clinical efficacy before KP-targeted interventions can advance toward clinical application.

title: Harnessing mucosal and systemic immunity against respiratory viruses: vaccine platforms, delivery strategies, and adjuvants.
text: Long-lasting immunity against respiratory viruses, including influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus, remains a challenge. Effective vaccines and vaccination strategies that confer durable protection against these viruses require the induction of both systemic and mucosal immunity. This review covers the latest trends in respiratory viral vaccine platforms, including modified virus-like particles and mRNA-based vaccines, as well as adjuvants, and new vaccination strategies that induce systemic and mucosal immunity and generate lung-resident memory cells. A better understanding of innate immune responses to vaccination is critical for improving vaccine efficacy and safety and for identifying early predictive correlates. This article outlines recent advances and approaches to developing next-generation respiratory viral vaccines and new vaccination strategies to induce systemic and mucosal immunity. It also discusses the gap between preclinical and clinical outcomes of mucosal vaccination.

title: Squalenoyl siRNA nanoparticles biodistribution enable non-invasive gene silencing in the central nervous system via intravenous and intranasal delivery.
text: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) remains a major obstacle to the delivery of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to the central nervous system (CNS), limiting the development of RNA-based therapies for neurological disorders. Squalenoyl nanoparticles (SQ NPs) represent a promising delivery platform due to their self-assembling properties and ability to protect nucleic acids. Here, we evaluated the ability of siRNA-SQ nanoparticles to achieve functional gene silencing in the CNS following intravenous (IV) and intranasal (IN) administration in the PLP-eGFP reporter mouse model. We observed significant reductions in GFP mRNA and protein levels across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord, indicating that the delivered siRNA retained biological activity in the CNS. Pharmacokinetic analyses revealed rapid brain-associated siRNA exposure (Tmax ≈ 5 min), followed by a marked decline and a slower terminal phase (apparent half-life ≈ 80 h) after IV administration. Additionally, systemic administration in two non-human primates (NHPs) resulted in measurable brain-associated antisense siRNA signals, with regional and interindividual variability. These findings suggest that SQ NPs enable functional siRNA delivery to the CNS via both IV and IN routes. The observed mRNA and protein-level silencing supports the potential of this platform for RNA-based therapies targeting neurological disorders, though further studies are needed to elucidate the mechanisms of delivery and optimize translational applications.

title: Targeted Gene Delivery with Enhanced Efficacy through Heterochiral Coassembly of Peptides.
text: The development of gene-based therapeutics faces substantial delivery challenges. To address this, we report a strategy involving heterochiral peptide coassembly to create an efficient peptidyl delivery platform. Our experimental results reveal that equimolar mixture of l-KH-CCR and d-KH-CCR peptides exhibit significantly enhanced gene condensation efficiency, improved structural stability, and more effective endosomal membrane disruption compared to their pure enantiomeric counterparts. These superior properties facilitate increased cellular internalization and efficient endosomal escape, ultimately leading to optimized delivery of various gene therapeutics, particularly mRNA and siRNA. Building upon these findings, we engineered a four-component system that integrates a targeting peptide and PEG-conjugated anti-adhesion peptides within the heterochiral peptide system, which was evaluated for pulmonary mRNA delivery and expression in an orthotopic A549 lung tumor model. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these peptides can effectively bind to mRNA through a combination of electrostatic, hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions, leading to the self-assembly of nanoparticles with accessible targeting and anti-adhesion motifs. In this model, the targeting-peptide-containing heterochiral formulation produced higher lung reporter expression than the corresponding homochiral formulations. These findings underscore the pivotal influence of chirality in optimizing the performance of peptidyl nanocarriers for targeted gene delivery applications.

title: Predicting the naturalistic course of obsessive-compulsive disorder during two-year follow-up in adolescence.
text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) during adolescence follows heterogeneous trajectories, from remission to persistence. Early identification of these patterns is crucial for optimizing clinical management. This study examined whether behavior symptoms or neuroimaging data could predict the persistence of OCD diagnosis at two-year follow-up. 492 children between 9-10 years old with OCD were selected from Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. They were classified as persisters or remitters by clinical status at two year follow-up. Baseline Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) item scores and multimodality MRI measures were used to examine behavioral and neuroimaging differences associated with follow-up OCD diagnostic status. We further applied machine learning models to predict individual symptom persistence using CBCL scores alone, MRI features alone from single modality or multimodal data, and combined CBCL and MRI features. Group-level CBCL and neuroimaging analyses identified significant behavioral, structural and functional brain differences at baseline between persisters and remitters. The best-performing CBCL model demonstrated limited discriminative ability (AUCbest = 0.638). In comparison, the best MRI-derived model, utilizing resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) features, performed slightly above chance (AUCbest = 0.577). Integrating rsfMRI features with CBCL improved performance only marginally and non-significantly (AUCbest = 0.665). Integrating rsfMRI features with CBCL did not significantly outperform the CBCL-only model, although the performance was numerically higher (AUCbest = 0.665). Feature-importance analyses suggested that the most clinically informative signals were compulsive behavior and functional connectivity linking large scale networks with widely distributed subcortical regions. These findings suggest that OCD persistence follow-up OCD outcome is related to distinct clinical symptoms and brain measures. However, the accuracy to predict diagnosis is limited, indicating that OCD persistence naturalistic course is difficult to predict from clinical and neuroimaging data evaluated here.

title: Machine learning and cheminformatics-driven identification of potential histone deacetylase 1 inhibitor candidates.
text: Histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) is an important epigenetic regulatory enzyme and plays a key role in cancer development. This highlights the need for novel inhibitors targeting the HDAC1 isoform of the histone deacetylase family of proteins. Traditional high-throughput screening requires a lot of resources, and current clinical inhibitors often have poor pharmacokinetics and off-target side effects. In this study, we introduce a machine learning-driven screening pipeline that can identify novel scaffolds from large chemical libraries that are structurally viable potential HDAC1 inhibitor candidates. After comprehensive testing of machine learning models with multiple input training features, an XGBoost model combined with high-resolution ECFP6 topological fingerprints was found to be the best option for inhibitor identification. SHAP analysis revealed a strong statistical correlation between the model's highest-weighted predictive ECFP6 bits and the established Cap-Linker-ZBG pharmacophore. This understanding allowed for successful scaffold hopping by the ML model, leading to a new carboxylate-based lead (CX-2) and hydroxamate-based (HX-1 and HX-2) compounds as potential inhibitor candidates. Further molecular docking and 200 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations showed that these compounds perform comparably to existing HDAC1 inhibitors (Vorinostat and Valproic acid). MM-PBSA energy approximations showed a potential (pharmacophoric compensation) profile for the carboxylate-based CX-2, where favorable Van der Waals interactions from its cap and linker regions theoretically compensate for a weaker zinc-binding group to maintain comparable estimated binding free energies. Furthermore, in-silico ADME profiling indicated that the prioritized candidates comply with Lipinski's rule of five and exhibit favorable predicted physicochemical properties. This integrated ML and cheminformatics workflow successfully identified novel in-silico candidate scaffolds against HDAC1, demonstrating an efficient computational pipeline to accelerate the discovery and prioritization of epigenetic inhibitor candidates.

title: Predicting long-term tumor response to Gamma Knife radiosurgery in vestibular schwannoma: an integrated model of auto-segmentation, MRI radiomics, and dosimetric parameters.
text: Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is a common benign intracranial tumor for which Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) is an important treatment option. However, post-treatment changes in tumor volume vary considerably and can complicate follow-up and response assessment. This study developed a framework that uses deep learning-based segmentation and MRI radiomics to predict long-term treatment response to GKRS for VS. We developed an nnU-Net model to automate VS segmentation on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI. Patients with long-term follow-up after GKRS were classified into four response patterns: direct regression, delayed regression, stable disease, and growth. A two-stage machine-learning framework was then constructed. Stage 1 distinguishes regression from non-regression, while Stage 2 differentiates direct from delayed regression. Pretreatment MRI radiomics features were combined with clinical and dose-related variables and used to train multiple machine-learning models. The models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation, and SHAP analysis was used to interpret the results. The nnU-Net model achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 91.16 ± 0.47% on the external test dataset. Among the 155 patients, 53 showed direct regression, 83 delayed regression, 9 stable disease, and 10 tumor growths. In Stage 1, the Balanced Random Forest algorithm achieved accuracy of 74.19 ± 7.21%, an AUROC of 72.43 ± 10.18%, and AUPRC of 93.08 ± 4.27%. In Stage 2, the Support Vector Machine achieved accuracy of 64.05 ± 4.16%, an AUROC of 66.70 ± 6.21%, and AUPRC of 57.10 ± 7.30%. SHAP analysis identified radiomics and dose-related features as important predictors. Deep learning-based segmentation combined with pretreatment MRI radiomics, clinical variables, and dose-related parameters may provide useful information for predicting long-term response after GKRS for VS. This framework could support more individualized follow-up planning and help clinicians distinguish delayed regression from treatment failure.

title: Basophil Activation Testing: From Diagnostic Adjunct to Precision Allergy Management.
text: Basophils are rare circulating granulocytes that trigger immediate hypersensitivity reactions through IgE-mediated degranulation and also contribute to innate immunity. The basophil activation test (BAT) is a flow cytometry-based functional assay that quantifies basophil reactivity and sensitivity following allergen stimulation, offering a safe, blood-based alternative to in vivo provocation testing. This review summarizes the immunological basis of the BAT, its technical requirements, and its expanding clinical applications across food, respiratory, drug, and hymenoptera venom allergies, autoimmune chronic spontaneous urticaria, and vaccine hypersensitivity. Beyond diagnosis, the BAT increasingly supports monitoring of allergen immunotherapy and biologic treatments, prediction of reaction severity and treatment response, and personalized management decisions. Its performance varies by allergen and clinical context, and wider adoption is constrained by the absence of standardized protocols, validated cut-offs, and reference materials, as well as by basophil non-releasers and dependence on fresh viable blood. Passive BAT and mast cell activation test formats extend testing to patients in whom the conventional BAT is uninterpretable. Automated, data-driven analysis and machine learning-assisted, label-free platforms offer promising routes toward more objective, scalable interpretation. With continued standardization, harmonization, and prospective validation, the BAT is positioned not only as a diagnostic adjunct but as a platform for precision-based allergy management.

title: Machine learning-based prediction of 30-, 60-, and 90-day postoperative mortality and major complications: an 11-year population-based cohort study in Hong Kong.
text: Existing surgical risk prediction tools are often limited by short-term outcomes. Our study aimed to develop and validate perioperative models and preoperative models for predicting mortality and major complications using surgical data from Hong Kong. This population-based retrospective cohort study analysed 11 years of surgical data (July 2014-June 2024) collected from 17 public hospitals in Hong Kong. Of 124 clinically relevant candidate predictors, 67 predictors were retained for the perioperative full models. To improve clinical usability and facilitate preoperative risk assessment, reduced preoperative models were trained using 13 predictors. Separate models were developed for emergency and elective surgery. Primary outcomes were 30-day, 60-day, and 90-day all-cause mortality in emergency and elective surgery cohorts. Secondary outcomes included 30-day major surgical-related and medical-related complications. Multiple risk prediction models were evaluated using training data from 2014 to 2021 with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, while temporal external validation was performed using data from 2022 to 2024. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), Brier score, calibration intercept and slope, integrated calibration index (ICI), E50, and E90. SHAP was used for model interpretation. Models showing poor calibration underwent logistic recalibration using five-fold out-of-fold development predictions. 43,601 subjects were included in the training set and 16,143 in the external validation set for emergency surgeries, whereas 151,016 subjects were used for training and 37,586 for external validation for elective surgeries. In temporal validation, the perioperative full models achieved AUROCs of 0.89, 0.89, and 0.89 for 30-day, 60-day, and 90-day mortality after emergency surgery and 0.91, 0.90, and 0.90 after elective surgery. Corresponding AUPRCs were 0.27, 0.36, and 0.41 for emergency surgery and 0.05, 0.10, and 0.13 for elective surgery. AUROCs for medical- and surgery-related complications were 0.88 and 0.78 in emergency surgery and 0.87 and 0.80 in elective surgery. The 13-predictor preoperative models retained useful discrimination, although performance was lower than that of the perioperative full models. Calibration assessment indicated variable agreement between predicted and observed risks, supporting the need for recalibration before clinical implementation. Eight complication-specific models showed validation AUROCs ranging from 0.75 to 0.94. SHAP analysis revealed clinically plausible risk factors, such as higher ASA status, abnormal laboratory results (such as renal dysfunction and low albumin), and surgical complexity. Logistic recalibration improved Brier scores and calibration indices across all full and reduced models without changing AUROC or AUPRC. We have developed and validated comprehensive surgical risk prediction models with excellent discrimination and robust performance using 11 years of population-based data from Hong Kong. The identified predictors were clinically interpretable, which can serve as a data-driven tool to assist clinicians and patients for surgical risk assessments.
