title: Artificial Intelligence-Guided Precision Nanomedicine: Bridging Delivery Barriers, Controlled Release, and Clinical Translation.
text: Targeted drug delivery aims to enhance therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity, yet its clinical translation remains limited by the unpredictable in vivo behaviour of nanocarriers. Although a broad range of nanocarrier platforms-including lipid-, polymer-, protein-, inorganic- and biomimetic-based systems-can improve drug solubility, pharmacokinetics, lesion-site accumulation and controlled release, their performance is frequently constrained by heterogeneous disease biology, insufficient tissue penetration, premature clearance, immune recognition and manufacturing variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a powerful strategy to address these multidimensional challenges. Machine learning, deep learning and computational modelling can support prediction of formulation-property relationships, release kinetics, nano- bio interactions, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, toxicity and patient-specific therapeutic responses. In this Review, we propose an integrated, AI-guided framework that connects rational nanocarrier design, biological-fate prediction, controlled-release engineering and clinical translation within a single development pipeline. We further articulate a "translation-by-design" principle and the concept of minimum sufficient complexity, which together distinguish this Review from earlier surveys that address these stages separately. Finally, we examine key translational barriers-including data standardization, model interpretability, scalable manufacturing, safety assessment, regulatory uncertainty and the gap between preclinical efficacy and clinical outcomes-and propose that future targeted nanomedicine should move beyond increasingly complex carrier architectures toward predictive, interpretable and clinically validated AI-integrated development pipelines. Despite these capabilities, most reported models are validated on internal or closely related data; independent external and prospective validation-the evidence required before a prediction can reliably influence formulation, manufacturing or patient-level decisions-remains the principal gap in the field.

title: Machine Learning Models Using Routine Clinical Data versus Conventional Clinical Scores for Survival Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Single-Center Study.
text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has a poor prognosis, and conventional clinical scores have limited accuracy in predicting individualized survival. We aimed to determine whether machine learning (ML) models using routine clinical data discriminate survival better than established clinical scores in HCC and to compare the prognostic profiles of MASLD- and HBV-associated HCC. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 233 patients with HCC diagnosed between 2010 and 2026. Patients with valid survival data and ≤20% missingness across 29 pre-specified predictor variables were included. During a median follow-up of 15 months, 143 patients died. Random Survival Forest, XGBoost, a Hybrid ensemble model, and penalized Cox regression were trained using 5-fold cross-validation. Model discrimination was assessed using Harrell's C-index and the fixed-horizon AUROC. The score-excluded V2 analysis removed clinical scores from ML inputs. SHAP values quantified feature contributions. The best-performing ML model (Hybrid) achieved a C-index of 0.797, higher than BCLC stage (0.735), Child-Pugh class, and ALBI grade, but only modestly higher than penalized Cox regression with the same variables (0.773). In the score-excluded sensitivity analysis, the Random Survival Forest maintained a strong performance (C-index 0.784). The best fixed-horizon 12-month AUROC was 0.878. SHAP analysis identified AFP, ECOG performance status, albumin, tumor diameter, and total bilirubin as the most influential predictors. Among 57 patients with MASLD-associated HCC, the median survival was 23.0 months vs 54.0 months in 116 patients with HBV-associated HCC (p=0.0328); this difference was not explained by age, comorbidities, tumor characteristics, or treatment. In this single-center cohort, models using routinely available variables discriminated survival in HCC better than conventional clinical scores by combining more information.

title: The gut microbiome and incident atherosclerotic cardiovascular events: Prospective analyses in three Swedish cohorts
text: BackgroundVariation in the gut microbiome composition has been associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in case-control designs. We aimed to investigate associations with incident ASCVD events applying a prospective design to reduce the impact of reverse causality. MethodsWe assessed associations between gut microbiome features measured by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and incident total ASCVD, ischemic heart disease (IHD) and ischemic stroke, including fatal and non-fatal events as defined by registry follow-up in 17,216 participants from three Swedish population-based cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS). Results from Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for demographic, and lifestyle factors, medication, and prevalent diabetes were combined across cohorts using a fixed-effect meta-analysis accounting for multiple testing. Associations were tested for replication in HUNT and FINRISK. ResultsDuring a median of 6-8 y follow-up, 769 incident ASCVD events occurred. Species diversity was inversely associated with ASCVD and IHD, with a hazard ratio for IHD of 0.86 per SD increase in species richness (95% CI: 0.79-0.95). Sixty-eight common species (i.e., present in [≥]30% individuals) were associated with incident IHD after adjusting for sex and birth country, but only eight remained in fully adjusted models, including Ruminococcus_B gnavus. Among others, inverse associations were observed for SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 from Christensenellales, an order in which butyrate production has been reported. Streptococcus mutans and Limosilactobacillus fermentum, oral-associated species previously associated with coronary atherosclerosis, were associated with a higher risk of incident IHD, which remained after adjustment for dental health. Replication analysis in the HUNT study supported the finding for S. mutans. No associations were observed with ischemic stroke. ConclusionsGut species diversity and specific species abundance were associated with incident IHD, providing evidence supporting a protective role of two Christensenellales species and an adverse role of oral species and R. gnavus in the development of IHD.

title: Gut microbiome associations with incident cardiovascular disease in Nordic populations
text: BackgroundThe gut microbiome is an emerging risk factor for cardiovascular disease. However, there is a lack of large-scale metagenomic studies with replication that identify gut microbial features associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD). MethodsWe tested for gut microbiome associations with CVD using metagenomes from stool samples in a discovery-replication framework across four large prospective Nordic cohorts with 635 incident CVD in 11,604 participants in the discovery cohort and 2,309 incident CVD in 20,965 participants combined across three replication cohorts. ResultsHigher Shannon diversity index and species richness were consistently associated with a lower risk of incident CVD. In addition, the relative abundance of nine species and eleven bacterial functional modules showed reproducible associations with incident CVD in the discovery cohort and in a meta-analysis of the three replication cohorts. We identified a female-specific gut microbiota-related pathway involving the prevalent oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, enriched among denture users, thus serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health. Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal effect of denture use on increased relative abundance of Rothia mucilaginosa_A. This pathway was linked to increased CVD risk through altered gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating imidazole propionate levels, and increased levels of systemic inflammation biomarkers. The second pathway involved both -diversity metrics and the remaining eight species, all of which were strongly associated with multiple markers of metabolic syndrome and with bacterial pathways related to purine metabolism, microbial stress responses, altered redox balance, ascorbic acid degradation, and branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis. ConclusionsThese findings demonstrate that gut microbiota diversity, specific taxa, and functional pathways provide new insights into the underlying biology of CVD. Furthermore, these findings suggest that the link between poor oral health and cardiovascular disease may, at least partly, operate through altered gut microbiota.

title: Aging, Structural, and Neighborhood-Environmental Correlates of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Factor Burden Across U.S. Census Tracts
text: BackgroundThe American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023. Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling. It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions. MethodsWe built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020. In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging x environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning. The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcomes BRFSS source; a second added them. Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates. ResultsAgreement with NHANES was modest. Burden clustered spatially (Morans I = 0.657) and highest in the South. Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing. Each percentage-point increase in adults [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts. LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile. Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses. The primary models residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both. ConclusionsCKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South. LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts. These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIAcross 69,530 US census tracts, a combined cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic burden index built from CDC PLACES was clustered in space and highest across the South. C_LIO_LIEach 1-percentage-point higher share of adults aged [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (crude prevalence, not age-standardized). C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LITract-level burden maps can help health systems and public health agencies direct cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic screening and prevention to high-burden areas, including the South, as area-level needs assessment rather than individual risk prediction. title: Optimizing dosing strategies for children with leprosy: A weight-banded dosing approach
text: BackgroundDosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. MethodologyA pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to 10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80-125% of adult area under the concentration-time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. ResultsProposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10-14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25-39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6-24.9 kg. ConclusionsA harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed. Author SummaryLeprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available. In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care. This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.

title: Stroboscopic Light Stimulation in Adults Reporting Depressive Symptoms: Safety, Tolerability, Feasibility, and Active-Comparator Development in a Staged Early-Phase Study
text: Stroboscopic light stimulation (SLS) is a candidate non-pharmacological intervention that induces transient visual and affective experiences, with potential application in depression. Before efficacy testing, clinical development requires safety, tolerability, and feasibility data. We report a staged, single-site programme in adults reporting depressive symptoms. Study 1 tested 11 SLS parameter sets for safety and tolerability. Study 2 assessed whether an active comparator reduced subjective visual effects while preserving session context. Study 3 randomised 84 participants to four weekly supervised 31-minute sessions of strobe-emphasis or wash-emphasis SLS. In Study 1, 31 participants were analysed; no severe adverse reactions occurred, mean discomfort was low (0.49/10), and the highest session-level upper 80% confidence limit was 1.13/10, well below the prespecified threshold. Study 2 supported within-participant experiential separation between the two SLS configurations in healthy adults. In Study 3, endpoint data were available for 70/84 randomised participants (83.3%): 39/42 assigned to strobe-emphasis and 31/42 assigned to wash-emphasis. Discomfort remained low, with no serious SLS-attributable adverse events. Both configurations produced visual phenomenology in the Study 3 target sample, and the phenomenological separation observed during Study 2 was not reproduced between groups in Study 3. The comparison estimates differences between two active SLS configurations, rather than SLS versus no stimulation. Exploratory depressive-symptom estimates were imprecise, limited by differential endpoint availability, and should inform endpoint selection and subsequent trial design rather than efficacy. Overall, the programme supports further controlled evaluation of supervised SLS while identifying experiential separation, retention, masking, and endpoint selection as priorities for the next trial.

title: Population-based reference equations and Z-scores for blood biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases
text: BackgroundBlood biomarkers are increasingly used to support the diagnosis and monitoring of neurodegenerative diseases. However, their interpretation is complicated by physiological determinants, including age, sex, body-mass index, and renal function, and by differences in absolute concentrations between analytical methods. We aimed to develop population-based reference equations allowing individualized interpretation of selected blood biomarkers blood biomarkers used in neurology. MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, we analysed plasma samples from cognitively unimpaired participants selected from the French CONSTANCES and Three-City population-based cohorts. Generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape were used to model neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), phosphorylated tau 181 (p-tau181), amyloid-{beta}40, amyloid-{beta}42, and their ratios according to age, sex, body-mass index, and renal function. The resulting equations provided individualized expected concentrations, percentiles, and Z-scores. Previously established disease-specific concentrations were converted into Z-score. Cross-calibration equations were developed for NfL measurements across analytical methods and sample matrices. FindingsThe final reference populations comprised 5123 participants for amyloid biomarkers and p-tau181 and 5122 for NfL and GFAP; median age was 52.3 years and 49.7% were women. Between ages 40 and 80 years, expected NfL and GFAP concentrations increased by an average of 2.6% and 2.2% per year, respectively. Renal function, body-mass index, and sex had additional biomarker-specific effects. Application of the equations to clinical cohorts preserved distinct disease-associated profiles: NfL Z-scores were increased across disorders characterized by neuroaxonal injury, whereas p-tau181 and GFAP showed its greatest increase in Alzheimer disease. NfL cross-calibration equations showed excellent agreement between methods and matrices, with intraclass correlation coefficients greater than 0.90. InterpretationThis population-based multibiomarker framework enables blood biomarker concentrations to be interpreted relative to individuals with similar physiological characteristics. Publicly available equations, reference curves, and standardized Z-scores could improve individualized interpretation and comparability across biomarkers, laboratories, and clinical populations.

title: A multicountry trial-based and model-based economic evaluation of youth mental health interventions: a protocol for assessing the short- and long-term societal impacts of YOUTHreach interventions
text: BackgroundMental health problems among young people impose a burden extending beyond healthcare, including impaired health-related quality of life and high societal costs from disrupted education, lost productivity, and informal care. Youth-friendly interventions may reduce this burden by providing early support and preventing escalation. However, their broader societal economic impact remains insufficiently explored. Evaluations incorporating consequences beyond healthcare and longer time horizons can better capture their societal value. MethodsThis protocol outlines harmonised trial-based and model-based economic evaluations of YEAH, SELFIE, and MOST, three mental health interventions for young people aged 12-25. Each intervention will be compared separately against care as usual over 12 months, with longer-term costs and outcomes projected at 2, 3, 5, and 10 years. Multicountry participant data will be pooled, using a prespecified reference country for base-case costing and methodological guidance. A harmonised, context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument was developed to capture healthcare and broader societal resource use consistently across participating countries and to support evaluation of the economic impact of youth mental health interventions from a multicountry perspective. Uncertainty will be assessed through sensitivity and scenario analyses. DiscussionThe proposed harmonised methodological framework will support consistent estimation of the short- and long-term cost-effectiveness of three youth-friendly mental health interventions. It will enable comparison of intervention-specific results generated using different trial designs and support consistent estimation of costs and outcomes across the three interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument will further support consistent measurement of healthcare utilisation, productivity losses, and informal care across the economic evaluations. ConclusionBy integrating trial-based evidence with long-term modelling and standardised measurement of resource use, this study aims to generate robust, policy-relevant evidence to inform health technology assessment and decision-making for youth mental health interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument is also intended to support future economic evaluations of mental health interventions conducted across multiple countries.

title: A framework for guiding integrated disease control measures through multipathogen surveillance
text: Global health programs have traditionally focused on single diseases. There is potential for synergy through integrated intervention delivery, particularly in areas with overlapping geographic disease burden, but there is limited methodology developed to guide integration. Here, we propose a framework to translate multipathogen surveillance data into summary indices that can guide integrated program delivery to target multiple pathogens at once. We considered several measures of diversity to quantify multipathogen infection or undervaccination across three large-scale surveys: subregions in Bangladesh (90 clusters, n = 7,187) and Kenya (89 clusters, n = 9,077), and a national survey in Cambodia (100 clusters, n = 2,150). We found that strategies guided by a measure of diversity, Raos quadratic index, consistently identified more efficient integrated strategies than other multipathogen indices across a range of intervention combinations. We then identified case studies in each setting that used immunization as the backbone for integration and found that incorporating information from co-occurring pathogens led to only modest reductions in efficiency for vaccine-preventable diseases, while affording potentially large gains for other pathogens. Compared with a strategy that prioritized a single vaccine-preventable disease, prioritization using a multipathogen index required targeting 4% (95% CI: 0-12%) fewer spatial clusters in Bangladesh to target four additional pathogens, 10% fewer clusters in Kenya (95% CI: 3-17%), and 11% (95% CI: 5-22%) fewer clusters in Cambodia to reach 80% of all potential intervention beneficiaries across diseases. In all settings, we observed geographic clustering of multiple pathogens, with moderate to high spatial autocorrelation in Bangladesh (Morans I = 0.58), Kenya (I = 0.56), and Cambodia (I = 0.26), indicating potential for more efficient, spatially concentrated integrated interventions. We also found that a multipathogen index was significantly associated with a multidimensional poverty index in Bangladesh (Spearmans {rho} = 0.25), Kenya ({rho} = 0.51), and Cambodia ({rho} = 0.59), suggesting that multipathogen-guided strategies may effectively target impoverished populations with the highest public health need. The framework provides a systematic approach to guide integrated program delivery, offering potential for greater efficiency in disease control.

title: Hard to Halt: Automation Bias in Agent-Driven Sequencing Prior Authorization Workflows
text: PurposePrior authorization (PA) for exome or genome sequencing (ES/GS) is a time-consuming process that impedes timely rare disease diagnosis. Large language model (LLM)-based browser agents offer potential for automating these workflows, but their clinical reliability remains uncharacterized. MethodsWe built a sandbox with a simulated ES/GS payer portal and a synthetic electronic health record (EHR) of 836 patient profiles, including compliant profiles and deficient profiles with designed issues. Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, and Claude Opus 4.5 were evaluated on task completion, form accuracy, and appropriate withholding. Two replication experiments were run on 100 profiles to assess run-to-run variability of agent performance. ResultsGemini 3 Pro (95.5%) and Claude Opus 4.5 (93.7%) completed far more tasks than Gemini 3 Flash (56.1%), consistently across runs. In the first run, all models rarely withheld deficient profiles for the correct reason (Gemini 3 Pro 0%, Gemini 3 Flash 17.3%, Claude Opus 4.5 5.2%). Replication revealed substantial variability: Gemini 3 Pros correct withholding rose to 28.8-36.8%, and only 18.0-48.0% of tasks yielded identical outcomes across all three runs. Without agentic scaffolding, Gemini 3 Pro flagged designed issues in 91.3% of deficient profiles but also halted on all compliant profiles. ConclusionCurrent LLM-based browser agents show a systematic bias toward form submission. A modular, multi-agent architecture with human supervision may be warranted for safe clinical deployment.

title: Facial Emotion Processing and GABAergic Modulation in Individuals at Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis
text: Deficits in social cognition, including facial emotion recognition (FER), are present in individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P). Altered GABAergic and glutamatergic signalling within corticolimbic circuitry has been proposed to underlie FER deficits in psychosis. We investigated FER performance and brain activation in CHR-P individuals, and whether pharmacological enhancement of GABAergic signalling with diazepam modulates these processes. In Study 1, 24 antipsychotic-naive CHR-P individuals and 24 healthy controls underwent fMRI while performing the Penn Emotion Recognition Task. In Study 2, 24 antipsychotic-naive CHR-P individuals participated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study of 5mg diazepam versus placebo. Threat-related FER performance and neural activation were compared between groups and drug conditions. In Study 1, CHR-P individuals showed longer reaction times across emotions (n=22 vs n=23, p=0.01) and greater amygdala (pFWE=0.01) and hippocampal (pFWE=0.04) activation for neutral>fixation. Lower amygdala activation for threat>neutral (pFWE=0.03) and non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.01), and lower hippocampal activation for non-threat>neutral (pFWE=0.04) may reflect this elevated response to neutral faces. Follow-up analyses showed lower insula (pFWE=0.01) and medial prefrontal cortex activation (pFWE=0.02) for threat>fixation. In Study 2, no significant drug effect on sensitivity was observed in the full sample (n=23), although secondary reduced-sample analyses, excluding one participant identified as influential, suggested improved overall sensitivity under diazepam (n=22; p=0.0499). After adjusting for global cerebral blood flow, diazepam reduced midcingulate cortex activation during neutral>fixation (pFWE=0.04). These findings highlight altered neural processing of neutral expressions in individuals at CHR-P, and suggest that aspects of emotion processing may be sensitive to GABAergic modulation.

title: From "Tech Fear" to Digital Self-Efficacy: A COM-B and TDF Analysis of Tele-Exercise Engagement in Older Adults at Risk of Falls
text: BackgroundTele-exercise offers an alternative approach to physical activity for older adults, however remote delivery introduces distinctive challenges. ObjectivesNested within a 3-month randomised controlled trial (RCT), this qualitative study explored the experiences of community-dwelling older adults at risk of falls who completed synchronous tele-exercise, mapping findings to the COM-B model, Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF), and Behaviour Change Techniques (BCTs) to inform intervention design. MethodsSemi-structured interviews and delivery format preference queries were conducted with 25 purposively sampled older adults following the intervention. Data were analysed using hybrid thematic analysis integrated with COM-B, TDF, and the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW). ResultsDespite baseline digital literacy barriers, participants engaged successfully across six themes: Technological Skills, Access & Support; Coach Support & Exercise Adaptability; Health Motivation & Goal Achievement; Emotional Journey with Technology; Home Environment & Accessibility; and Social Interaction Dynamics. Core BCTs addressing low digital literacy and physical limitations included practical social support (in-home onboarding), environmental restructuring (hardware setup), graded tasks, and social reward. These techniques facilitated an emotional transition from initial apprehension to pride, fostering digital self-efficacy. Notably, an implementation paradox emerged: while over half preferred face-to-face (f2f) delivery, they demonstrated high adherence in tele -exercise programme, indicating that delivery preference does not preclude digital capability. ConclusionTele-exercise is feasible and acceptable for older adults at risk of falls, challenging assumptions that low digital literacy precludes digital health adoption. Embedding targeted BCTs within a scaffolded framework addresses structural and psychological barriers, reinforcing digital self-efficacy to sustain remote participation. Key PointsO_LITele-exercise is feasible when behaviour techniques shift participants from digital anxiety to self-efficacy. C_LIO_LIRemote delivery removes transport barriers but requires personalized home-safety checks to address domestic hazards. C_LIO_LISocial connectedness, peer modelling, and instructor feedback transform isolated routines into engaging communal experiences. C_LIO_LIClinicians should prescribe structured tele-exercise with standardized onboarding and targeted techniques to reduce fall risks. title: Adrenergic nerve fibers are depleted in adenomyosis myometrium
text: Structured AbstractO_ST_ABSObjectiveC_ST_ABSUterine dyscontractility in adenomyosis and endometriosis is at the heart of pain symptoms and disease pathogenesis. To elucidate possible causes of dyscontractility, we examined the distribution of smooth muscle, blood vessel, collagen and nerve fibers in full-thickness, serosa-to-endometrium myometrium of adenomyosis patients versus control. DesignRetrospective study. SubjectsUterine biopsies from patients who underwent hysterectomy for adenomyosis (n = 26) or other non-adenomyosis indications (n=22, mostly myomas). Main Outcome MeasuresDensity profiles along the serosa-to-endometrium axis of smooth muscle (SMA), endothelium (PECAM), general innervation (PGP9.5) and adrenergic innervation (TH) obtained by immunofluorescence, mosaic epifluorescence imaging and machine-learning assisted segmentation. Fibrous collagen type I&III was quantified by second-harmonic generation microscopy (SHG). ResultsThe density profiles of smooth muscle, endothelium, collagen and PGP9.5 were similar between both patient groups. Sympathetic adrenergic nerve fiber density radiated from the serosa inwards, with a continuously decreasing density from the outer to the inner myometrium. Adrenergic inhibitory nerve fibers were 4 times less dense in the inner myometrium of adenomyosis uteri compared to controls. ConclusionThe enrichment of inhibitory adrenergic nerve fibers in the outer vs inner myometrium provides a neuro-muscular mechanism by which contractions are restricted to the inner myometrium outside of pregnancy. The depletion of TH fibers in adenomyosis implies that a higher thickness of myometrium is involved in uterine contractions, thus explaining junctional zone thickening and dyscontractility in this pathology. This depletion may be due to defective post-pregnancy adrenergic re-innervation of the myometrium.

title: Psychometric analysis of the Evaluation of Multidimensional Functioning and Risks in Aging (EMFRA) scale: reliability, structural validity, and concurrent validity.
text: Background: EMFRA is a brief scale developed to assess physical, cognitive, emotional, and social functioning in older adults. This study examined its initial psychometric properties. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 201 older adults aged [≥]65 years without a diagnosis of dementia, recruited from the community, day-care and nursing centres from Madrid. Dimensional structure was examined through bootstrap parallel analysis (PA), bootstrap exploratory graph analysis (EGA), and factor analysis (FA), followed by progressive item refinement. Internal consistency, test-retest reliability in a subsample (n = 22), SEM, MDC95, floor and ceiling effects, and associations with SPPB, MoCA, Barthel Index, and HADS were assessed. Results: The 21-item version did not reproduce the four hypothesized domains, yielding a three- dimensional solution with limited stability. A nine-item version comprised two factors, Autonomy and Psychological Distress, although FA fit was limited (TLI = 0.80; RMSEA = 0.13). A low hierarchical omega (0.409) did not support a total score, whereas factor reliability was adequate ({omega} = 0.840 and 0.785). Test-retest ICCs were 0.82 and 0.78, with wide 95% CIs. No floor or ceiling effects were observed. Autonomy correlated with SPPB (r = 0.751), MoCA (r = 0.697), and Barthel (r = 0.56), and Psychological Distress with HADS (r = 0.625). Conclusions: The nine-item EMFRA shows preliminary evidence of a two-factor structure whose factors should be scored separately. Its temporal reliability and measurement error remain uncertain, and external validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Attitudes and Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots in the Peer Review of Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine Research: A Large-Scale, International Cross-Sectional Survey
text: BackgroundGenerative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are being explored for their potential to support the peer review process by improving efficiency and analytical capacity. While early applications show promise, concerns regarding ethics, privacy, and research integrity remain, and their use within traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine (TCIM) remains underexplored. This study examines TCIM researchers attitudes and perceptions regarding the use of GenAI chatbots in peer review through a large-scale international survey. MethodsCorresponding authors of TCIM-related publications indexed in Ovid MEDLINE were invited to participate in an online, anonymous, international cross-sectional survey distributed via SurveyMonkey. The questionnaire collected data on demographic characteristics, the perceived importance of GenAI in peer review, the likelihood of adoption, and the perceived benefits and concerns. ResultsA total of 889 eligible respondents participated. Overall, 40.25% (n=285/708) reported a positive perception of GenAI in peer review, and 41.67% (n=295/708) considered it important to the field. 34.24% researchers reported being likely (n=253/739) or 18.27% (135/739) very likely (totaling 52.51%) to use GenAI in peer review, highlighting a gap between perceived importance and intended adoption. Identified benefits included improved efficiency (50.72%, n=350/690), reduced reviewer workload (51.16%, n=353/690), and generation of constructive feedback (46.30%, n=319/689), reflecting respondents selecting "agree." Concerns included bias (49.85%, n=333/668), lack of transparency (42.86%, n=285/665), inaccuracies (49.40%, n=329/666), accountability challenges (45.20%, n=301/666), and data privacy risks (36.05%, n=239/663). Most respondents believed that peer reviewers require either some training (43.91%, n=310/706) or a lot of training (40.93%, n=289/706) to use GenAI chatbots effectively in peer review. ConclusionRespondents reported perceived benefits of GenAI in peer review, alongside notable concerns regarding its use. While opinions were mixed, findings suggest both perceived utility and apprehension about potential risks. Further work is needed to understand these perspectives better and to explore how GenAI can be responsibly integrated into peer-review processes.

title: Digital cytometry of immune cell types from dried blood microsamples
text: Enumeration of circulating immune cells is an established clinical practice implemented across a plethora of indications. While flow cytometry is the gold standard for this task, cellular deconvolution algorithms provide a robust computational alternative using molecular data. These digital cytometry pipelines typically rely on millilitre-scale venous blood samples. Here, we evaluated the potential of capillary blood microsampling as a patient-centric and minimally invasive approach for the digital cytometry of major lymphocyte populations (T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells; TBNK). In a cohort of 200 participants, we compared RNA sequencing based deconvolution performance between matched PAXgene-stabilised venous blood and Mitra capillary blood microsamples. While venous transcriptomes enabled highly accurate TBNK estimation, patient-matched capillary microsamples exhibited a significant reduction in deconvolution accuracy. Computational adaptations, including the integration of capillary-specific single-cell reference profiles, yielded only limited improvements. Instead, our analyses revealed that the performance deficit was primarily driven by the decreased transcriptome complexity of the capillary microsample libraries. This study highlights the critical role of transcript diversity for cellular deconvolution and reveals the current pre-analytical challenges that must be overcome to harness transcriptomics based digital cytometry using dried blood microsamples.

title: Intraoperative arterial blood pressure waveform morphology variability is associated with acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery
text: PurposePostoperative acute kidney injury (post-AKI) remains common after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Conventional blood pressure (BP)-related measures may overlook hemodynamic information contained in the arterial blood pressure waveform (ABP). We hypothesize that intraoperative ABP morphology variability, quantified by VarM, captures the hemodynamic impact of CPB beyond its duration and may improve intraoperative post-AKI prediction. MethodsWe conducted a prospective observational cohort study at a tertiary medical center enrolling adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery with CPB between November 2019 and November 2022. VarM was calculated from the intraoperative ABP using an unsupervised manifold-learning algorithm. Post-AKI occurring within two weeks was defined according to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) serum creatinine criteria. Logistic regression evaluated VarMs predictive value, its complementarity to CPB duration, and the performance of a combined model for post-AKI prediction. ResultsOf 101 patients enrolled, 18 were excluded for preoperative end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis. Subjects developing post-AKI had lower VarM and slower recovery after CPB. Post-CPB VarM was inversely associated with postoperative creatinine (Spearman correlation coefficient, -0.387[-0.597,-0.152], P=0.0029). VarM achieved an area-under-curve (AUC) of 0.747 for post-AKI prediction, outperforming eGFR (0.624) and EuroSCOPE (0.623), and similar to CPB duration (0.756). A combined VarM-CPB duration model achieved an AUC of 0.817, significantly outperforming either variable alone (P=0.0025). ConclusionPost-CPB VarM was associated with post-AKI, and provided complementary information to CPB duration. Combining both measures may improve intraoperative post-AKI prediction.

title: Population-level indirect effects of HPV vaccination in high-income settings: a Bayesian modelling study
text: BackgroundHuman papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination provides direct protection to vaccinated individuals, but also indirectly protects unvaccinated individuals through reduced HPV transmission. Mechanistic transmission models that predict the magnitude of such effects have been crucial to informing vaccination strategies. However, nearly two decades of post-vaccination experience in high-income countries now allow us to empirically characterise how population-level indirect effects vary with vaccine coverage, time since vaccine introduction, and age. MethodsWe synthesised studies reporting HPV16/18 prevalence before and after vaccine introduction in high-income settings between 2007 and 2025. Indirect effects were estimated as the observed reduction in HPV16/18 prevalence after accounting for expected direct vaccine protection. We used a Bayesian hierarchical model to examine associations with vaccine coverage, time since vaccine introduction, and age at effect assessment across routine, catch-up, and non-targeted vaccination groups. XGBoost was used as a complementary, non-parametric approach. FindingsData from 11 high-income settings were included. Indirect effects increased during the first five to eight years after vaccine introduction and then remained relatively stable. Indirect effects generally decreased with increasing vaccine coverage. Patterns with age differed across vaccination groups. In the routine group, indirect effects increased during adolescence and remained positive at older observed ages. In the catch-up group, indirect effects decreased with age and approached zero or became negative after approximately age 25 years. XGBoost identified similar non-linear patterns. InterpretationIndirect protection against HPV16/18 develops gradually after vaccine introduction and varies with vaccine coverage, age, and vaccination group. This empirical approach can complement transmission models by using real-world evidence to characterise population-level indirect protection. However, making predictions outside the populations and ranges represented in the data should be done cautiously. FundingThis study received no specific funding. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed for studies published up to Oct 26, 2026. The search terms were ("HPV vaccin" [All Fields] OR "human papillomavirus vaccin" [All Fields]) AND ("herd immunity" [All Fields] OR "herd effect" [All Fields] OR "indirect effect" [All Fields] OR "indirect protection" [All Fields] OR "herd protection" [All Fields]). We included systematic reviews, meta-analyses, observational studies, and modelling studies that assessed the indirect effects of HPV vaccination on HPV infection or HPV-related outcomes. We excluded studies that focused exclusively on direct vaccine protection or economic evaluations that included herd immunity without separately estimating or reporting indirect effects. We identified 301 articles, of which 77 met the inclusion criteria: 52 observational studies, 22 modelling studies, and three systematic reviews or meta-analyses. From those studies, two systematic reviews by Drolet and colleagues (2015 and 2019) synthesised evidence from 14 high-income countries and provided evidence of herd protection following vaccine introduction. A meta-analysis of results from 16 transmission dynamic models by Brisson and colleagues (2016) projected substantial herd effects under different vaccination coverage levels. More recently, an observational study by Meglic and colleagues (2026) used nationwide registry data from Sweden and found age-varying herd effects, with lower incidence of high-grade cervical lesions among unvaccinated women in cohorts exposed to school-based vaccination. Despite growing real-world evidence from high-income countries over nearly two decades, few studies have examined how indirect protection varies with vaccination coverage, time since programme introduction, and age across settings. title: Wastewater sequence data reveal national and cross-border virus transmission dynamics
text: Spatial epidemic models estimate disease transmission counts between populations using human mobility data, but location-to-location transmission is rarely observed directly. To address this gap, we develop mutation-counting methods to infer transmission structure from viral genetic variation measured in wastewater. In epidemic simulations with known transmission networks, our primary estimator robustly recovers spatial structure under realistic mutation-detection limits. Applied to spatiotemporal SARS-CoV-2 wastewater data from Austria, the method reveals strong seasonal reorganization, with inferred transmission becoming more geographically localized in winter and more dispersed in summer. We further identify locations with systematically higher or lower connectivity than expected from commuting, with temporal changes coinciding with regional restrictions, reopening and tourism. We then test whether such inference remains possible across national borders, recovering coherent spatial structure and temporal variation in connectivity between Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. These results establish wastewater sequence data as a promising complement to mobility data for monitoring spatial transmission and detecting changes in epidemic spread associated with seasonality and interventions.

title: Evaluation of out-of-hospital management of asthma attacks prior to consultation at the paediatric emergency department in Martinique
text: BackgroundAsthma is a chronic, multifactorial disease that progresses in episodes and requires effective coordination of care between healthcare professionals and patients. ObjectiveTo describe and evaluate pre-hospital therapeutic management of asthma attacks. MethodsCross-sectional, prospective, single-centre, observational and descriptive study of patients consulting for asthma attacks at the Fort de France paediatric emergency department between July and November 2024. All patients included were children between the ages of 1 and 18 who had already been diagnosed with asthma by a doctor and who presented to the emergency department for an asthma attack. Several other parameters were assessed, such as the parents perception of the emergency situation, the childs asthma control in the month prior to the attack, the childs usual medical follow-up, and their usual treatment. Results175 patients were included in the study. Eight patients were excluded from the study because their questionnaire had a response rate of less than 50%. Of the 175 patients included, only 6.7% received perfect pre-hospital care, 29.3% received good quality care, 36% received moderate quality care, and 10.3% received poor quality care before arriving at the emergency department. (17.7% did not complete all the items necessary to calculate the score). 11.6% of children did not receive treatment before consulting the emergency department. Among the 88.9% who took short-acting {beta}2 agonists, only 52% received at least 3 series and 66.2% were given doses appropriate for their weight. 21.6% received oral corticosteroids before arriving at the emergency department. ConclusionsThe management of asthma attacks outside of hospital settings is not optimal for a large proportion of patients in the study. Several areas for improvement have been identified and require joint action by healthcare professionals.

title: Bipolar Disorder and Education: Deciphering a Complex Relationship using Genetic and Sibling Differences in a Multi-cohort Study
text: BackgroundWhile bipolar disorder has a positive genetic correlation (r[~]0.3) with educational attainment (EA), individuals with bipolar disorder diagnoses have lower EA in adulthood. To clarify this paradox, we hypothesise that bipolar disorder and educational outcomes share a positive genetic association, reflected in high academic performance earlier in life, but that emerging bipolar disorder symptoms disrupt academic trajectories, leading to the observed poor long-term educational outcomes. MethodsWe employed a sibling comparison design across four population-based cohorts (Ntotal = 1,145,795 siblings). First, we tested the association between bipolar disorder polygenic scores (PGS) and educational outcomes (EA and academic performance) in the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and UK Biobank (UKB). Second, we examined associations between academic performance at ages 10, 12, 13, and 14 and subsequent bipolar disorder diagnosis using registry data from Statistics Netherlands and Statistics Norway (with the Norwegian Control and Payment of Health Reimbursements Databases). FindingsSiblings with higher bipolar disorder PGS had significantly higher EA ({beta}W = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.05], N=16,746) as well as higher academic performance at age 10 (0.03 [0.01, 0.05], N=17,677) in MoBa. Secondly, individuals with bipolar disorder had better overall academic performance than their unaffected sibling at ages 10 (HRW = 1.12 [1.02, 1.22], N=343,898) and 12 (1.59 [1.16, 2.19], N=619,796). However, individuals with bipolar disorder experienced a decline in academic performance at ages 13 (0.84 [0.73, 0.96], N=320,342) and 14 (0.72 [0.61, 0.85], N=299,039). InterpretationBipolar disorder shares a positive genetic association with educational outcomes, reflected in early academic advantage. This is followed by an academic decline in mid-adolescence, highlighting the period of educational disruption associated with bipolar disorder. FundingThe Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Sciences, European Research Council, The Research Council of Norway, The Swedish Research Council

title: Chatbot as an intervention on physical activity: A systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression
text: BackgroundChatbots offer scalable, accessible, and personalized support for physical activity (PA). This review synthesized evidence on their efficacy and examined potential moderators. MethodsEleven databases were searched for English-language published through January 27, 2026. Eligibility was assessed using the PICOS framework. Data extraction was guided by research questions, mERA checklist, and PRISMA 2020. Risk of bias was evaluated using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and the NIH Quality Assessment Tool. Meta-analyses reported Hedges g. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots, Eggers regression, and trim-and-fill analyses. Potential moderators were examined through subgroup analyses and meta-regression. ResultsA total of 12,481 records were identified, of which 43 studies were included in the systematic review and 27 in the meta-analysis. Most studies included in the meta-analysis had some risk-of-bias concerns (16/27). Chatbot interventions produced a significant small-to-moderate post-intervention effect on PA (g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.19, 0.44]; n = 24), whereas the follow-up effect was small and non-significant (g = 0.11, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.22]; n = 4). Effects varied across PA outcomes (g = 0.08-0.44), and several subgroup differences helped explain the significant heterogeneity. For daily steps, significant subgroup differences were observed by clinical status, while intervention duration (QM = 6.09, p = 0.048) and clinical status (QM = 5.69, p = 0.017) were significant moderators. ConclusionsChatbot interventions showed small-to-moderate post-intervention effects but limited follow-up effects. Few significant moderators were identified, underscoring the need for more rigorous RCTs.

title: ASSESSMENT OF KNOWLEDGE AND DISPOSAL PRACTICES OF SPENT AND BROKEN ENERGY-SAVING BULBS AMONG HOUSEHOLDS IN MTENDERE COMPOUND LUSAKA ZAMBIA
text: The widespread adoption of energy-saving bulbs like light-emitting diodes and compact fluorescent lamps in Zambia has raised significant environmental and public health issues because some of these bulbs contain dangerous materials like mercury. This study sought to evaluate households understanding and disposal practices of used and damaged energy-saving bulbs in Lusaka, Zambias Mtendere Compound. A cross-sectional design was used, with structured questionnaires distributed to a randomly chosen sample of households. The research showed that, although most participants were aware of the energy efficiency advantages of these bulbs, they had little understanding of their possible health risks and safe disposal procedures. The majority of households reported throwing away broken and used bulbs with their regular household trash, while only a small percentage followed the suggested disposal procedures. Environmental contamination and heightened health risks are exacerbated by a lack of awareness and inadequate municipal waste management systems for hazardous household waste. The research advocates for improved public education initiatives, the creation of specific collection sites for dangerous waste, and the formulation of explicit national regulations and policies for the handling of discarded and damaged energy-saving bulbs. In rapidly urbanizing areas like Mtendere, tackling these issues is essential for protecting public health and advancing environmental sustainability.

title: Cluster Editing in Subexponential Fixed-Parameter Time
text: Cluster Editing asks whether at most $k$ edge additions and deletions turn a given $n$-vertex graph into a disjoint union of cliques. For more than a decade, the fastest algorithm for it was the golden-ratio algorithm of Böcker with running time $O(1.62^k+n^{O(1)})$. Cao and Chen had conjectured that the subexponential running time $2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$ is possible, but this contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). Recently, the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT of OpenAI and Anthropic refuted ETH itself. Our main result transfers running times from 3-SAT to Cluster Editing. If 3-SAT on formulas with $m$ clauses can be decided in time $T(m)$, then there is an algorithm that, given a graph with $n$ vertices and integers $k$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le k^{1/3}$, decides Cluster Editing in time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot T(2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$. Combined with the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT, this proves Cao and Chen's conjecture, as it solves Cluster Editing in time $2^{O(k\cdot(\log\log\log k)^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log k})}\cdot n^{O(1)}=2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$. The key ingredient is a sparsification theorem for Cluster Editing, the counterpart of the Sparsification Lemma for satisfiability: In time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$, it reduces a given instance to $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}$ weighted instances with $O(rk)$ vertices and degree $O(r)$, each of which is equivalent to a 3-SAT formula with $2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k$ clauses. Conversely, by a known reduction with linear blow-up, every saving in the exponent for Cluster Editing is, up to constant factors, a saving for 3-SAT.

title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
text: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.

title: AnimalFarm: Auditing the Generation and Detection of Hateful Images Featuring Anthropomorphic Characters
text: Anthropomorphic non-human characters have long been used to convey hateful messages targeting human groups, from Nazi-era propaganda to recent AI-generated imagery on social media. However, the safety risks posed by such imagery remain largely unexplored. We thus conduct the first systematic study of hateful image generation and detection involving anthropomorphic non-human characters. We construct a benchmark from conservatively screened source scenes, covering five character types and three image generation tasks: text-to-image generation, image editing, and conversational image generation. Across 14,250 scheduled queries, image generation systems produce images for 92.1\% of queries, of which 95.9\% contain hateful content. We further collect 4,370 hateful images and evaluate five popular hateful-content detectors. Even the strongest detector, GPT-5.5, identifies only 73.9\% of hateful images, while most detect fewer than 58\%. Our analysis reveals that existing detectors often misclassify hateful images as benign when their main subjects are non-human characters. We explore two effective mitigation approaches: a training-free pipeline that maps non-human characters back to human representations before classification and a detector fine-tuned for this type of hateful content. These approaches achieve F1 scores of 0.962 and 0.979, respectively. Our findings expose significant safety gaps in both image generation and hateful-content detection. Disclaimer: This paper contains hateful text and imagery.

title: From Gist to Verbatim: The Controllable Path of One Image Through a Diffusion Prior
text: Modern generative models are typically studied for their ability to generalize, while memorization is treated as a failure mode. We invert this perspective and ask how a generative model can recall a single datum. We frame memorization as a control problem: a learned conditioning signal steers a frozen diffusion model toward a target image, and we follow the formation of this memory throughout training. Before converging to exact reproduction (verbatim), memory passes through a regime of abstraction: samples preserve the target's semantic content (gist) while remaining diverse in appearance, leaving predictable detail to the generative prior. This semantic organization emerges despite the absence of labels, captions, or any explicit semantic objective. In the abstraction regime, the learned memory approaches ordinary text conditioning and supports editing, one-shot recognition, and retrieval more effectively than in the near-perfect reconstruction regime. These results suggest that memorization can serve as a probe of the relevance structure encoded by a generative model: what must be stored about a datum, what can be reconstructed from prior knowledge, and how learned memories interpolate between reconstructive recall and literal data storage.

title: Refrain: Learning Multi-Shot Consistency from Inconsistent References for A$^2$O Video Generation
text: A comic-book character, a photorealistic cityscape, an oil-painted coffee cup -- such stylistically diverse references provide visual guidance across shots and frames, yet generating a coherent multi-shot video that unifies their visual styles while preserving subject identities and scene content remains challenging. Existing methods maintain cross-shot continuity through additional attention control or memory processing. However, they struggle to resolve disparate per-shot styles or handle reference-target duration mismatches within a single framework. We introduce Refrain, a unified model that learns cross-shot consistency through a self-supervised reconstruction task. Reference clips from the same original video are deliberately perturbed with distinct visual edits, and the model recovers the unedited source footage under a shared style prompt. The resulting pipeline yields DurMix-300K, which pairs independently edited references of varying durations with their original videos. Operating on the A$^2$O principle (Any Reference, Any Duration, One Timeline), Refrain maps image and video references onto a shared temporal canvas without auxiliary conditioning modules. For evaluation, experiments show that standard CLIP or DINO metrics frequently overlook stylistic clashes or misinterpret intended narrative cuts as inconsistency. We propose Shot-Debiased Consistency (SDC), which uses an extensive real-video bank to establish a baseline for style variation associated with content changes within shots. By discounting this baseline divergence, SDC evaluates cross-shot style shifts against real-world distributions, where smaller residual differences indicate higher stylistic continuity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Refrain achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-shot consistency, while excelling at shot timing, reference adherence, and text alignment.

title: Abstract What Varies, Reuse Longer Patterns: Efficient Offline Chain-of-Thought Compression
text: Offline chain-of-thought (CoT) compression creates shorter supervision for efficient reasoning, but per-example compressors repeatedly process similar expressions across traces, wasting compressor budget. Methods that reuse identical text across examples miss longer shared expressions when names, numbers, or formulas change from one question to another. We introduce CRAFT, which abstracts problem-specific details into slots to uncover partially lexicalized expression templates (PLETs) and clusters wording variants into families. Compressing each family representative once yields shared deletion or rewriting edits, which are applied with each occurrence's own details to construct compact, ordinary-text training targets. Compared with per-example rewriting, CRAFT Rewrite reduces weighted compressor budgets by a median 90.7% with a median accuracy loss of 1.21 percentage points, while generating shorter reasoning. Against cross-sample encoding, it shortens reasoning across all eight model-dataset settings by 25.3% on average and improves accuracy in five.

title: Sketch2TikZ: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Converting Hand-Drawn Sketches to Executable TikZ
text: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

title: Edge transport mechanisms in small-ELM and type-I ELM regimes at JET using global gyrokinetic simulations
text: To explore tokamak operating regimes that combine high energy confinement with edge dynamics relevant for ITER, new regimes with small edge-localized modes (ELMs), referred to as baseline small-ELM (BSE), have been obtained at JET with the Be wall and W divertor. In this work, the edge transport mechanisms in a selected BSE discharge are compared with those in a standard H-mode with type-I ELMs using radially global gyrokinetic simulations with the GENE code. The simulations use experimental input profiles and include kinetic electrons and deuterium ions, electromagnetic (EM) effects, and the radially varying equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. At low toroidal mode number $n$, the type-I ELM pedestal is found to be unstable to kinetic-ballooning modes (KBMs), with radial mode structures covering the full pedestal. In the BSE regime, no KBM branch is found, and the same spectral range is dominated by hybrid ITG--TEM modes. The modifications of the linear modes by finite$-β$ effects are discussed in details. In nonlinear simulations of the type-I ELM regime, KBM-driven turbulence produces high transport levels that are resilient to the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. By contrast, in the BSE regime, EM effects moderately increase transport, which is strongly regulated by the equilibrium $E\times B$ flow. The two regimes also differ in their radial turbulence organization and in the amplitude and persistence of the zonal shearing rate. These results identify the interplay between EM effects and equilibrium $E\times B$ flow as a key element of edge transport regulation.

title: Can Language Models See the Circuit in Pixelated RFIC Passives?
text: The emergence of inverse-designed, pixelated passives for microwave and millimeter-wave applications has been a major development in the field of RFIC design. These devices, which appear to be QR-code-like in structure, exist in a generalizable, high-dimensional design space that includes conventional passive topologies. However, these structures are naturally unintuitive for designers, and failures or deviations in performance are difficult to debug. In this work, we ask whether a frontier language model can understand, predict, and edit the responses and layout structure of pixelated passives. The agent, run with all tools disabled, is first asked to read layouts on 18x18 and 27x27 tile grids and, in a single reply, predict the input impedance and loss of the structure from 20-100 GHz. On eight GA-synthesized layouts and five random fills, the predicted Smith-chart locus follows full-wave simulation results closely, with a systematic shift that places features about 16% lower in frequency than EM. On multipath loop structures it identifies notches successfully but shows a smaller frequency bias, about half that of an ideal transmission-line model that ignores bends. The agent is then asked to debug seven designs that fail their specification, and given a budget of five EM simulations and at most twelve changed tiles, it is able to improve all seven and bring five designs within specification. These experiments suggest language models can serve as an interpretability and debugging tool for traditionally non-intuitive inverse-designed passives.

title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition
text: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions. Cecilia-OMR predicts this representation through metadata and measure-bounded music segments from shared visual memory. A learned count head determines the number of output segments. Across paired complete scores under a common tokeniser, the ratio of mean MusicXML to Cecilia sequence lengths is 27.73. Cecilia-OMR outperforms Legato 2 on Camera String Quartets and both Lieder conditions, with a four-condition OpenScore macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998. Separate evaluations of lyrics, notation trees and rendered layout reveal complementary aspects of reconstruction and quantify the contribution of layout instructions. Training-stage, reward and candidate-selection studies further examine how recognition changes across model adaptation and decoding.

title: Convergence of a finite element Chorin projection method for the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations
text: We analyze a fully discrete finite element projection method for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and multiplicative noise. We show solvability and uniform moment estimates for the intermediate and the corrected velocity approximations under the assumption that the initial data is square-integrable and divergence free, and that the deterministic forcing term is bounded in $L^{q}(0,T;H^{-1}(D))$ for a sufficiently large $q$. Under standard stability and approximation assumptions on the finite element spaces and a coupling condition on the spatial and temporal discretization parameters, we prove convergence of a subsequence to a martingale solution of the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations. The analysis combines the complementary spatial and temporal estimates of the predicted and the corrected velocity approximations and uses the numerical dissipation to identify their common limit. We establish tightness of the piecewise constant temporal interpolations of the velocity field approximations using Aldous' criterion combined with the uniform discrete moment estimates. The convergence result holds in two and three space dimensions as it does not rely on any additional regularity of the limiting martingale solution beyond the one naturally available from the energy inequality. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the scheme in numerical experiments in two space dimensions for smooth and vortex sheet initial data.

title: Differential Transmutations and First-Passage Expansions for Monomial Brownian Boundaries
text: Let $P_t=\exp(t\partial_x^2/2)$ be the heat semigroup and let $F(t)=ρt^p$, where $p\ge2$ is an integer. title: Atmospheric parameters and chemical abundances of young stars with APOGEE -- II. Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen, and Sulphur abundances in Orion
text: We derived the abundances of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur, and iron in young G-, K-, and M-type stars (effective temperatures of 3500--5900 K) using APOGEE-2 infrared spectra. Our final sample comprises 195 slow rotators ($v\sin i$ $\leq$ 30 km~s$^{-1}$) in the Orion complex (Orion A, B, OB1, and $λ$~Ori). The abundances were determined using MARCS model atmospheres, atmospheric parameters derived with \tona, and the \bacc\ code. We obtained median abundances of $ε$(C) = 8.37$\pm$0.10, $ε$(N) = 7.35$\pm$0.16, $ε$(O) = 8.63$\pm$0.08, $ε$(S) = 7.19$\pm$0.18, and $ε$(Fe) = 7.45$\pm$0.05.
