title: Recent advances in multi-agent human trajectory prediction: A comprehensive review
text: With the emergence of powerful data-driven methods in human trajectory prediction (HTP), gaining a finer understanding of multi-agent interactions lies within hand’s reach, with important implications in areas such as social robot navigation, autonomous driving, and crowd modeling. This survey reviews some of the most recent advancements in deep learning-based multi-agent trajectory prediction, focusing on studies published between 2020 and 2025. We categorize the existing methods based on their architectural design, their input representations, and their overall prediction strategies. Furthermore, we highlight key challenges and future research directions in multi-agent HTP.

title: Single-cell dissection of immune-state architecture across diverse human population cohorts
text: The extension of human lifespan is accompanied by a growing burden of chronic disease and multimorbidity. The immune system, whose functional state is continuously remodelled by ageing, environmental exposures, infection history and disease, is pivotal to respond to these challenges. However, how these factors jointly influence immune variation, regulatory mechanisms and disease susceptibility across populations remains poorly understood. Here we present an outline and first results of the CARDINAL (Cellular Architecture of immune-state Regulation, Disease, and Immune Networks across the Adult Lifecourse) project. We generated a new population-scale single-cell atlas of peripheral blood comprising almost 10 million immune cells from 6,003 individuals across two UK cohorts with integrated genomic and longitudinal electronic health record data: the UK Biobank (predominantly European ancestry British) and Genes & Health (British Bangladeshi and British Pakistani). We identify immune-state architectures, shared across cohorts, associated with ageing, chronic viral exposure, inflammatory activation and premalignant conditions. We show that demographic and lifestyle factors induce largely conserved immune programmes, while chronic cardiometabolic diseases are associated with cohort-dominant cellular programmes and transcriptional states. Disentangling of genetic and clinical influences reveals coordinated regulatory programmes associated with metabolic, inflammatory and infectious remodelling. These programmes are observed in specific disease contexts and immune states, such as those induced by chronic viral exposure, often independently of genetic differences. Together, our findings support a model of immune-state architecture shaped by ageing, environment, disease history and genetic variation, which can be read from population-specific regulatory landscapes.

title: scPACE: A Personalized Autoencoder for Cell Evolution in Single-Cell Transcriptomics
text: Single-cell studies increasingly profile large cohorts of individuals, measuring thousands of cells in each donor. These datasets contain information at two levels: variation among individual cells and among donors. Analyzing both levels requires methods that can learn cellular representations, infer cell and donor states, and account for cell types that may be missing in some donors. Existing methods partially address these tasks. We introduce scPACE, a hierarchical personalized variational autoencoder handling these tasks. scPACE learns a cell representation, a cell state, and then aggregates cells within each type of cell to infer a donor state. It also imputes missing cell types with confidence estimates. Across simulated cohorts and a developing mouse visual-cortex dataset, scPACE recovered held-out cell and donor states accurately while achieving efficient cell-type imputation and representation. scPACE provides a unified framework for learning phenotypes across cellular and donor scales in cohort-scale single-cell transcriptomics.

title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
text: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 ~50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region ≥10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

title: Comprehensive variant effect map of parkin-mediated mitophagy in Parkinson’s disease
text: The development of Parkinson's disease has a substantial genetic basis. Variants in the PRKN gene account for roughly half of autosomal-recessive Parkinson's disease cases, yet most remain classified as variants of uncertain significance. PRKN encodes the E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase Parkin, which plays a key role in mitochondrial quality control by initiating mitophagy. In this work, we introduce a multiplexed mitophagy assay and measure the activity of more than 99% of all possible single amino acid substitution and nonsense variants of Parkin. The obtained activity landscape closely reflects known structural and functional aspects of Parkin, while also revealing new insights into specific functional effects across the protein. This dataset near-perfectly distinguishes pathogenic from benign variants and surpasses both computational predictors and abundance-based metrics in pathogenicity assessment. Finally, the data pinpoint hypomorphic variants that could be amenable to rescue in future personalized therapeutic approaches for Parkinson's disease.

title: Dysregulated ASH1L-MUC1-CD133 axis promotes lung metastasis and reprograms the metastatic niche in SPOP-deficient prostate cancer
text: Metastasis remains the leading cause of mortality in prostate cancer (PCa). Loss-of-function mutations in SPOP, commonly observed in metastatic PCa, have undefined roles in the metastatic niche. Histone methyltransferase ASH1L plays a crucial role in leukemogenesis and is overexpressed in various solid tumors. However, its post-translational regulation and protein homeostasis in cancer remain poorly understood. Here, we report that SPOP mutations promote PCa lung metastasis and induce infiltration of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) in graft models. We identified that the CUL3-SPOP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex is a key regulator of ASH1L protein, mediating its polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. PCa-associated SPOP mutations cause aberrant stabilization of ASH1L, thereby epigenetically activating the oncogenic glycoprotein MUC1. Dysregulation of the ASH1L-MUC1 axis augmented CD133-associated cancer stemness and TAM recruitment in the metastatic niche. In preclinical models, genetic knockdown of ASH1L or pharmacological inhibition of MUC1 significantly suppressed lung metastasis driven by SPOP mutations. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized SPOP-ASH1L-MUC1-CD133 regulatory axis linking genetic alterations to metastatic niche remodeling and reveal actionable vulnerabilities in metastatic PCa. It uncovers novel post-translational regulation of pro-metastatic epigenetic factor ASH1L and informs biomarker-guided MUC1-targeted therapy for metastatic PCa.

title: Expanding flavonoid production in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 from lignin-derived aromatics
text: Background Flavonoids are valuable plant secondary metabolites with broad applications in the food, nutraceutical, cosmetic, and pharmaceutical industries. While microbial biosynthesis offers a renewable alternative for chemical synthesis and plant extraction, most production platforms rely on lengthy biosynthesis pathways from sugars, requiring extensive pathway engineering and often focusing on individual products. Lignin-derived aromatics (LDAs) offer attractive precursors for flavonoid biosynthesis, but their utilization requires a host capable of aromatic substrate tolerance and metabolism. Results We engineered Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 for the conversion of LDAs into multiple flavonoid products. We identified a novel heterologous enzyme combination CHS–CHI (CHS from Stenoloma chusanum and CHI from Medicago sativa ) that supported flavonoid biosynthesis, namely 3.4 mg/L homoeriodictyol from ferulate and 24.2 mg/L eriodictyol from caffeate in flask cultivations after 24 h. The engineered strain produced a different flavonoid from each tested substrate in flask cultivations, enabling product switching through feedstock selection without further genetic engineering. In fed-batch bioreactors fed with a mixture of ferulate, caffeate, and p -coumarate, the strain produced three flavonoids (homoeriodictyol, eriodictyol, and naringenin). Finally, flavonoid production was demonstrated directly from alkaline-pretreated liquors (APLs) derived from wheat straw and organosolv lignin. Ferulate and p -coumarate were detected in both liquors, yielding homoeriodictyol and naringenin, confirming the compatibility of the platform with complex lignin-derived feedstocks. Conclusions This work establishes A. baylyi ADP1 as a promising platform for the production of multiple flavonoids from LDAs, including directly from APLs. By leveraging native aromatic catabolism, the strain bypasses the need for extensive precursor biosynthesis and enables substrate-driven product diversification. These results provide a proof of concept for converting LDAs into structurally different flavonoids in a single microbial host.

title: AI Policy Research: A New Inquiry
text: AI policy is proliferating in universities worldwide, yet AI policy research remains heavily descriptive, cataloguing institutional responses without examining the capacities required to make policy well. This Element argues that the missing capacity is AI policy literacy, the institutional capability to interrogate AI policy as text, discourse, and practice, and to attend to how authority, inequality, and time shape what governance can achieve. Drawing on policy sciences, applied linguistics, and decolonial thought, it develops a six-dimension framework for AI policy literacy. It also demonstrates that AI policies are simultaneously language policies, and that the absence of AI policy research in language education is creating deeper digital divides and knowledge injustices. Treating AI as cognitive infrastructure rather than a tool to be regulated, this Element proposes technodiversity as the orienting principle for governance aligned with universities' educational and social purposes. This title is also available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.

title: Multiancestry genome-wide association and integrative multiomics analyses implicate key pathways in endometriosis
text: Endometriosis is a painful and heterogeneous condition that affects up to one in ten women. Its genetic underpinnings remain partially unknown, and its precise disease mechanisms are yet to be elucidated. Here we report a genome-wide study of endometriosis as part of the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative representing over 1 million participants (32% non-European ancestry). We detected 58 genomic regions (27 previously unreported) across diverse ancestry groups and new procedure-confirmed case identification algorithms. These include loci unique to African and admixed American populations. A search for genetically driven comorbidities revealed dozens of associations with known and previously uncharacterized risk factors. Then, within prioritized cellular contexts, we found numerous examples of gene expression affected by endometriosis status. Including further multiomic analyses, we implicated a total of 314 genes, suggesting multiple targets for therapeutic intervention. Our findings span molecular, cellular and phenotypic scales, highlighting interconnected pathways that underscore the multifaceted etiology of endometriosis.

title: B-CONCORD: a scalable Bayesian high-dimensional precision matrix estimation procedure
Geraniol exerts hormetic effects on proteostasis through SKN-1/Nrf2 and DAF-16/FOXO activation in neurodegeneration models
text: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are fundamentally linked to proteostasis failure and the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates. Identifying compounds capable of activating endogenous defense systems represents a critical therapeutic priority. In this study, we demonstrate that geraniol, a natural monoterpene, exerts hormetic effects with potent protective outcomes in Caenorhabditis elegans models of Parkinson’s disease (PD). Geraniol treatment significantly mitigated locomotor deficits, reduced α-synuclein-associated fluorescence, and preserved the structural and functional integrity of dopaminergic neurons. Mechanistically, we show that geraniol enhances cellular responsiveness to autophagy-inducing stimuli, suggesting a “priming” effect that facilitates the efficient clearance of misfolded proteins. In parallel, genetic analyses reveal that these beneficial effects are dependent on the conserved transcription factors SKN-1/Nrf2 and DAF-16/FOXO, key regulators of the cellular stress response. Importantly, we found that the effects of geraniol extend beyond PD, also mitigating proteotoxicity in C. elegans muscle models of β-amyloid and polyglutamine aggregation. However, geraniol produces dose- and model-dependent effects, with beneficial effects at lower concentrations and toxicity at higher concentrations, particularly in the β-amyloid and polyglutamine models. These findings support a hormetic response in which the biological outcome of geraniol exposure depends on both concentration and proteotoxic context. Overall, our results provide evidence that geraniol may modulate proteostasis through the hormetic activation of endogenous stress-response pathways, contributing to its beneficial effects in models of protein aggregation.

title: STAT+: New biotech aims to develop next generation CAR-T for multiple myeloma
text: Relapse in multiple myeloma is common. A new type of CAR-T aims to avoid that by adding a target to evade the tumor.

title: Opinion: If the AI bubble bursts, it could create a serious problem for health care
text: “A health AI company's market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things,” writes David Adler.

title: STAT+: A string of wins with cancer drugs sets Genmab up for its next chapter
text: The Danish biotech Genmab in on a roll with cancer drugs, with success in three late-stage clinical trials over the course of a month.

title: Opinion: A Chinese research entity FOIA’d my scientific work. I had to give it to them
text: A $25 fee and simple online FOIA request gave a Chinese “consultant” access to this writer’s scientific research.

title: As diabetes association’s turmoil continues, what does it mean for patients?
text: The American Diabetes Association has made concrete differences in patient care in the past. Its disarray has experts worried about the future.

title: Artificial intelligence-guided open-source CRISPR tools for designer crops.
text: AI-guided protein design enables rational optimization of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR) components. Das et al. harnessed the AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 to create a suite of tools for plant gene editing. Their open-source platform, PlantOpenCRISPR-1, targets academic and translational use and could offer a more accessible option for researchers facing licensing barriers, highlighting open-source CRISPR's future potential.

title: Gene Therapy for Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type I: Current Advances, Clinical Translation, and Future Perspectives.
text: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) is a group of rare autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiencies characterized by impaired leukocyte migration resulting from defective expression or function of adhesion molecules. The most common and severe form, LAD-I, is caused by biallelic mutations in Integrin Subunit Beta 2 (ITGB2), which encodes the β2-integrin subunit CD18, leading to recurrent life-threatening infections and impaired wound healing. LAD-II arises from mutations in the fucose-metabolism gene SLC35C1, and LAD-III from mutations in FERMT3, which disrupt integrin activation through kindlin-3. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has historically been the only established curative treatment for severe LAD-I, but donor availability, conditioning toxicity, and graft-versus-host disease limit its use and have motivated the development of autologous approaches. Autologous gene therapy using self-inactivating lentiviral vectors to introduce functional ITGB2 into patient-derived hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells has shown promising clinical results, including restored CD18 expression, improved leukocyte function, and fewer severe infections. In March 2026, the FDA granted accelerated approval to marnetegragene autotemcel (Kresladi; RP-L201), making it the first approved gene therapy for severe LAD-I in the United States. CRISPR/Cas9, base editing, and prime editing are also being investigated as alternative approaches for correcting ITGB2 mutations, although their application in LAD-I remains preclinical. These methods could allow correction of pathogenic ITGB2 variants without relying on integrating viral vectors, but their efficacy and long-term safety in LAD-I have yet to be established. However, conditioning-related toxicity, the need for long-term safety monitoring, and the complexity and cost of manufacturing remain important limitations to wider clinical use. This review examines the molecular basis of LAD, preclinical and clinical studies of gene therapy for LAD-I, and the challenges that remain in translating genome-editing approaches into clinical practice.

title: Problem-Driven Innovation in Genome Editing: From Programmable Nucleases to DSB-Free Precision Editors and the Path to Clinical Translation.
text: Precise, heritable modification of living genomes is among the most consequential advances in modern biology, offering the prospect of correcting molecular lesions underlying monogenic diseases. Realizing this potential has required successive rounds of innovation, in which each generation of tools addressed limitations while revealing new constraints. This Review traces that trajectory through a problem-driven lens, from programmable nucleases to RNA-guided systems and double-strand break (DSB)-avoiding precision editors. Zinc-finger nucleases and TALENs established programmable DSB induction, whereas CRISPR-Cas9 simplified retargeting through an RNA guide but retained DSB-associated risks, including stochastic indels, large deletions, and chromosomal rearrangements. Base and prime editors avoid programmed DSBs but are not consequence-free: Most base editors use Cas9 nickase and can generate bystander editing, off-target deamination, and low-frequency indels, whereas prime editing also uses nicked intermediates and remains sensitive to endogenous repair, editor architecture, and locus-specific efficiency. Clinical programs likewise use distinct mechanisms. Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) is an ex vivo SpCas9-ribonucleoprotein therapy in autologous HSPCs that disrupts the BCL11A erythroid enhancer through nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ)-dominated DSB repair; NTLA-2001 is an in vivo liver-directed lipid nanoparticle (LNP) therapy that codelivers Cas9 mRNA and a TTR-targeting guide RNA for NHEJ-mediated gene disruption; and VERVE programs deliver adenine base editor mRNA with a PCSK9-targeting guide RNA in LNPs for targeted base conversion. Translational constraints now include efficient and safe delivery, particularly beyond the liver and ex vivo-accessible cell populations, immunogenicity, long-term genomic safety, manufacturing scalability, and equitable access. Resolving these challenges will determine the ultimate clinical impact of genome editing on human health.

title: AAV-mediated XIST deletion in female human hepatocytes with skewed X-inactivation induces limited reactivation of the X-linked OTC gene in vivo.
text: Reactivation of silenced wild-type alleles on the inactive X chromosome (Xi) offers a promising therapeutic avenue for X-linked disorders affecting females. The long non-coding RNA XIST is central to Xi silencing, yet its complete loss risks chromosome-wide dosage imbalance. To explore reactivation in a translational context, we employed chimeric mouse-human FRG livers repopulated with primary hepatocytes from a female patient with ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency exhibiting highly skewed X-inactivation. Adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 delivery was used to disrupt XIST in vivo to assess effects on chromatin landscape and OTC expression. Despite differential XIST promoter methylation, the Xi remained accessible to CRISPR-Cas9, with editing frequencies comparable to those of the active X chromosome. XIST deletion induced limited reactivation of the wild-type OTC allele and was accompanied by broader epigenetic effects. CUT&RUN profiling distinguished effects of vector delivery and XIST deletion, including global H3K4me3 reduction after AAV transduction, X chromosome-restricted H3K27me3 reduction after XIST deletion, and broader H3K27ac reduction in edited hepatocytes. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of manipulating the human Xi in vivo while revealing distinct Xi-specific and broader chromatin effects. Together, they highlight the need for precise, locus-specific strategies to achieve therapeutic gene reactivation while preserving chromosome-wide epigenetic regulation.

title: Engineering Theranostic Nanomedicines for Clinical Translation: Nano-Bio Interactions, Responsive Design, Multimodal Function, and Scale-Up.
text: Theranostic nanomedicines are engineered multifunctional systems that integrate diagnostic sensing, imaging, and therapeutic delivery within a single nanoscale platform. Their performance depends not only on material composition but also on controllable nano-bio interactions, transport, targeting, stimulus responsiveness, and manufacturability. This review examines the bioengineering principles underlying next-generation theranostic nanomedicines, including lipid, polymeric, mesoporous silica, inorganic, extracellular-vesicle-derived, and cell-membrane-camouflaged platforms. Particular emphasis is placed on how physicochemical design governs protein-corona formation, circulation, biodistribution, cellular uptake, and clearance, and how endogenous or externally applied stimuli can be engineered for spatiotemporally controlled cargo release and imaging feedback. We further discuss the integration of multimodal imaging with nucleic-acid delivery, CRISPR/Cas gene editing, immunotherapy, ferroptosis, sonodynamic therapy, and photothermal therapy, together with emerging uses of artificial intelligence and machine learning for formulation optimization, image analysis, toxicity prediction, and treatment-response modeling. Despite rapid technological progress, clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous biological behavior, limited targeting efficiency, long-term safety uncertainties, complex manufacturing, batch-to-batch variability, and regulatory challenges. Future development should shift from increasingly complex multifunctional constructs toward platforms with measurable design-function relationships, scalable Good Manufacturing Practice-compatible production, standardized characterization, and clinically relevant validation. Such an engineering-focused approach could help advance theranostic nanomedicine from predominantly preclinical multifunctional systems toward reproducible technologies for precision diagnosis and therapy.

title: Targeting MS4A4A Enhances Intratumoral Temozolomide Concentration and Treatment Response in Aged Glioblastoma Models.
text: Aging is associated with poor temozolomide (TMZ) response in glioblastoma, but whether age-related vascular and matrix changes limit intratumoral TMZ concentration remains unclear. We therefore examined the effects of aging on the myeloid-vascular interface and intratumoral TMZ concentration, and the effects of CD68 promoter-directed Ms4a4a knockdown on vascular structure, intratumoral TMZ concentration, and treatment response in aged glioblastoma. We integrated clinical analysis, young and aged orthotopic GL261 models, single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, CD68 promoter-directed Ms4a4a knockdown, and macrophage-endothelial co-culture assays. Older age was associated with shorter survival. In aged mouse tumors, perivascular collagen IV deposition and matrix expansion were greater, vascular markers were altered, and tracer signals were lower despite a larger CD31-positive area. Single-cell profiling further identified an age-associated MS4A4A-positive myeloid state, and human and mouse tissues showed higher MS4A4A in older tumors. Consistently, preimplantation Ms4a4a knockdown reduced perivascular collagen IV, improved junction-protein and pericyte coverage, increased intratumoral TMZ concentration 4 hours after dosing, and prolonged survival during TMZ treatment. In vitro, MS4A4A silencing reduced macrophage VEGF secretion and endothelial tube formation, and BMDM assays linked Ms4a4a knockdown to attenuated AKT/STAT3 phosphorylation. These findings associate an age-associated MS4A4A-positive myeloid state with perivascular matrix remodeling and lower intratumoral TMZ concentration measured 4 h after dosing, and show that preimplantation Ms4a4a knockdown improves vascular markers, intratumoral TMZ concentration, and survival in aged GL261 models.

title: Leishmania cytochrome bc1 complex inhibition has potential for shortening leishmaniasis treatment duration.
text: Leishmaniasis affects approximately 1 million people annually with visceral infections resulting in death if left untreated and the cutaneous disease leading to disfiguring skin lesions. Leishmaniasis is caused by the Leishmania spp. parasites and is difficult to treat as existing drugs are far from optimal. Despite increased efforts to identify better drugs for leishmaniasis, there are few new chemical entities that have entered clinical development, thus highlighting the persistent need for such compounds. Here we describe GNF5885, an orally available and parasite-selective inhibitor of Leishmania cytochrome bc1 complex. GNF5885 was derived through phenotypic optimization of buparvaquone. GNF5885 exhibits unparalleled efficacy in vivo and can efficiently clear parasites from mice in models of visceral and cutaneous infections. Furthermore, its ability to clear parasites rapidly with short treatment regimens makes it particularly desirable for treating patients residing in regions endemic to leishmaniasis. Cryo-EM structure of the Leishmania cytochrome bc1 complex with GNF5885 at 2.8 Å resolution revealed that the inhibitor binds in the Qi ubiquinone-binding pocket. Our data provide validation of the Leishmania cytochrome bc1 complex as a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of leishmaniasis and underscore the possibility of developing a short-course oral treatment for this neglected disease. In addition, the availability of the cytochrome bc1 complex costructure with GNF5885 opens an opportunity to rationally design new cytochrome bc1 complex inhibitors suitable for clinical development.

title: Multitarget docking and toxicity-guided prioritisation of phytochemicals from Bangladeshi medicinal plants against wheat fungal pathogens.
text: The rising issue of fungicide resistance, along with environmental concerns related to synthetic fungicides, highlights the need for safer and more sustainable antifungal agents. In this computational study, we screened nineteen phytochemicals from locally available medicinal plants in Bangladesh against three fungal protein targets associated with major wheat diseases: class I sesquiterpene synthase (PDB ID: 8H4P) and trichothecene 3-O-acetyltransferase (TRI101; PDB ID: 3B2S) from Fusarium graminearum, and the AvrSr50 effector protein (PDB ID: 7MQQ) from Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. Blind docking was performed using AutoDock Vina (with an exhaustiveness setting of 16) and evaluated for reliability through consensus docking with CB-Dock2. We analyzed protein-ligand interactions using BIOVIA Discovery Studio, and the top-ranked compounds were further assessed for toxicity and ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) properties with ProTox-3 and ADMETlab 3.0. Thevetin B, Thevetin A, and Uscharin were computationally prioritized as candidate multitarget binders. Notably, Thevetin B formed extensive hydrogen-bond and hydrophobic interaction networks across all three proteins and showed comparatively strong predicted binding affinities. However, ProTox-3 predicted high acute oral toxicity for Thevetin B (LD₅₀ = 4 mg/kg, Class I) and Thevetin A (LD₅₀ = 8 mg/kg, Class II), while Uscharin had a substantially higher predicted LD₅₀ (2000 mg/kg, Class IV). The ADMET analysis revealed shared liabilities such as mutagenicity and nephrotoxicity, along with limited absorption, but also highlighted compound-specific differences in physicochemical properties and environmental toxicity. These findings indicate an efficacy-safety trade-off among the computationally prioritized candidates and support their further evaluation as testable hypotheses rather than establishing a definitive efficacy-safety hierarchy. This study provides a structured computational prioritization of locally available phytochemicals and emphasizes that any claims of practical antifungal utility must be supported by experimental validation of both efficacy and safety.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Aligning Structure-Based Molecular Generation toward Make-on-Demand Chemical Spaces.
text: Generative models for structure-based drug design have strong potential to accelerate early-stage drug discovery by enabling the conditional generation of target-specific molecules. However, a major bottleneck is that generated compounds are frequently difficult or impossible to synthesize, limiting their direct experimental validation and utility. We address this by optimizing for membership in make-on-demand chemical libraries, ensuring that generated molecules can be directly purchased and tested. To this end, we apply reinforcement learning to a pocket-conditioned generative molecular model, steering generated molecules toward two large make-on-demand spaces: Enamine REAL and Freedom 4.0. We compare an offline, preference-based strategy (direct preference optimization, DPO) and an online RL strategy (DiffusionNFT) across single-target and multi-target settings. In single-target optimization for KRAS, the fraction of unique purchasable candidates rises from 10.0% to 25.5% for Enamine REAL and from 4.3% to 12.1% for Freedom 4.0, while drug-likeness and docking-based affinity proxies are preserved. In multi-target optimization, DPO achieves consistent improvements across diverse protein targets, including a 23-fold increase for the challenging CDK4 pocket. These results demonstrate that RL alignment can substantially improve the experimental accessibility of SBDD candidates without sacrificing structural or chemical quality.

title: A synthetic, small-molecule, allosteric inhibitor of human factor XIa for thrombosis.
text: Only a handful of anticoagulants have reached the clinic to treat and prevent thrombotic episodes in the millions of patients with cardiovascular, cancer, viral (COVID-19), and metabolic diseases. In this study, we report the discovery, chemical synthesis, mechanistic biochemistry, pharmacology, and toxicology of SB-01, a novel, allosteric, activated human factor XIa (hFXIa) inhibitor that displays potent antithrombotic activity in preclinical models. SB-01 is a synthetic, highly sulfated, aromatic agent that binds in both anion-binding exosites of hFXIa to induce inhibition of FIX activation. SB-01 inhibited rodent arterial and venous thrombosis at doses of 6 and 3 mg/kg, respectively. In addition, a twice-a-day regimen of 6 mg/kg SB-01 was significantly more effective (P< .001) in preventing deep vein thrombosis in animals with lung cancer. Michaelis-Menten kinetics and competition with unfractionated heparin and polyphosphate revealed SB-01 to be an allosteric inhibitor. Critically, at the effective dose of 6 mg/kg, SB-01 did not significantly increase mouse tail bleeding time or blood loss. Furthermore, SB-01's anticoagulation could be readily reversed with protamine sulfate, the US Food and Drug Administration-approved antidote for heparin. Finally, SB-01 showed no major adverse effects across multiple toxicological assays including gross, cardiac, metabolic, hematological, and clinical chemistry. Overall, this study presents a structurally and functionally unique, allosteric small molecule as a highly promising candidate for safer anticoagulation.

title: When does personalization matter? An evidence-to-action beyond smart devices demonstrating the added clinical value of personalization in precision MedTech.
text: Precision medicine (PM) seeks to improve prevention, diagnosis, and treatment by incorporating biologic, clinical, environmental, and behavioral variation rather than relying exclusively on population averages. Medical technology (MedTech) provides a practical interface through which this approach can be translated into continuous sensing, decision support, and individualized intervention. We use the term personalized/precision medical devices (PMDs) for a conceptual class of devices that combine person-specific inputs with analytics and device-level configuration or adaptation. PMDs overlap with smart devices, connected health, and digital therapeutics, but are distinguished by their explicit coupling of individualized data to clinically meaningful device behavior. This perspective uses a structured narrative literature approach. The literature survey was extended through targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and major regulatory/standards sources for publications addressing precision or personalized medicine, biosensing, wearable and implantable devices, point-of-care diagnostics, automated drug delivery, digital therapeutics, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), interoperability, regulation, cybersecurity, and health equity [Oct. 2025-Oct. 2026]. Preference was given to peer-reviewed clinical studies, systematic reviews, authoritative regulatory guidance, and international standards. Evidence was synthesized narratively around a device lifecycle framework linking individual profile, sensing, data infrastructure, analytics, actuation, clinical workflow, evidence generation, and governance. Clinical evidence demonstrates that some components of the PMD concept are already established. In a randomized trial, automated insulin delivery increased time in the target glucose range by 14% points versus sensor-augmented pump therapy at 24 weeks. Remote pulmonary-artery pressure monitoring reduced heart-failure hospitalization by 28% in a prespecified analysis of patients with reduced ejection fraction. In the Apple Heart Study, 419,297 participants were enrolled; 0.52% received an irregular-pulse notification, and atrial fibrillation was identified in 34% of participants who returned an analyzable electrocardiographic patch. Digital therapeutics and adaptive neurostimulation further illustrate how software and implantable systems can individualize treatment, although clinical generalizability and long-term evidence remain uneven. PMDs should be viewed as an engineering and clinical integration paradigm, not as a new regulatory category. Their value depends less on novelty of individual components than on reliable linkage among person-specific data, clinically validated algorithms, device actuation, and longitudinal feedback. Translation therefore requires evidence generation, interoperability, cybersecurity, lifecycle regulation, accountable AI, and equity-by-design. The next phase of precision MedTech will be defined by selective deployment of these capabilities where individualized sensing and adaptation demonstrably improve clinical outcomes or care efficiency.

title: Meeting Report: Interoperability of Diabetes Device Data into the Electronic Health Record.
text: Diabetes Technology Society hosted the Interoperability of Diabetes Device Data into the Electronic Health Record (EHR) meeting on June 4 to 5, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. Meeting topics included (1) the importance of interoperability of diabetes devices, (2) security and privacy for diabetes devices and enterprise information systems, (3) computerized insulin delivery in the hospital, (4) current and emerging wearable devices for diabetes, (5) the benefits of a diabetes management platform from pediatric endocrinologist, adult endocrinologist, and educator/practice management perspectives, (6) billing for remote continuous glucose monitor data interpretation, (7) a clinician panel discussion on the advantages and disadvantages of current EHR interoperability, and (8) the future of interoperability.

title: Predicting Ischemic and Bleeding Risk in Patients on DAPT After PCI: A Machine Learning Model.
text: Dual antiplatelet therapy after coronary stenting prevents ischemic complications but increases bleeding risk. Individualized assessment of these combined risks may inform treatment strategies. This study sought to develop a machine learning algorithm for clinical outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with potential to support clinical decisions around antiplatelet therapy. Data from 11 clinical trials encompassing 19,106 patients who underwent PCI with everolimus-eluting stents were randomly split 3:1 to train and validate 2 separate machine learning algorithms for ischemic (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or stent thrombosis) and bleeding (Bleeding Academic Research Consortium type 3 or 5) risk prediction at 1 year. The Boruta algorithm was used to select the top 11 variables (providing >80% of predictive information) for final model development. An independent cohort of 10,696 patients undergoing PCI at a tertiary-care center (Mount Sinai Hospital) was used for external validation. There were 594 (4.1%) ischemic and 448 (3.1%) bleeding events in the training data set. Random survival forest was selected as the best-performing model (mean time-dependent area under the curve of 0.76 for ischemic events and 0.81 for bleeding). Internal and external validation yielded a mean time-dependent area under the curve of 0.72 and 0.70 for ischemic events and 0.72 and 0.71 for bleeding, respectively. The 2 models met the prespecified performance goal in both validation cohorts. A machine learning-based tool exhibited good discriminative ability for the prediction of ischemic and bleeding events at 1 year post-PCI and warrants prospective evaluation in clinical decisions surrounding antithrombotic therapies.

title: [Predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Lewy body disease: machine learning models using multimodal neuroimaging data].
text: Isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) is a well-established prodromal marker of α-synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. However, the time to phenoconversion and the resulting clinical phenotype vary considerably among individuals. This review summarizes current neuroimaging biomarker research in iRBD and provides an overview of machine learning-based prediction models for phenoconversion, with a focus on their methodology, performance, and clinical applicability. Structural MRI studies have consistently identified gray matter volume reduction in subcortical structures and cortical thinning across frontal, temporal, and parieto-occipital regions, with several Cox regression analyses demonstrating their utility in phenoconversion risk stratification. Resting-state functional MRI has revealed disrupted connectivity within basal ganglia, cortico-striatal, and cortico-cortical networks, some of which correlate with cognitive and motor impairments. Notably, functional connectivity alterations are detectable even at early stages when structural changes remain subtle. Nuclear medicine studies, particularly dopamine transporter SPECT and cardiac metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy, provide complementary information on dopaminergic and autonomic denervation. Recent studies have applied machine learning algorithms to integrate these multimodal data, with preliminary evidence suggesting higher predictive performance than single-modality approaches. Machine learning models using clinical, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging features have demonstrated promising accuracy in predicting both the timing and subtype of phenoconversion. Nevertheless, several challenges must be addressed before clinical implementation: ensuring model explainability, elucidating patient heterogeneity through data-driven subtyping approaches, and validating models in prospective longitudinal cohorts. The clinical significance of prodromal prediction research is expected to grow in parallel with the development of disease-modifying therapies.

title: Spatial tumor-stromal-immune architectures predict immunotherapy outcomes in recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
text: Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) benefits fewer than 20% of patients with recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (RM-HNSCC), and the spatial determinants of response remain undefined. Here, using spatial transcriptomics on 28 biopsies from 20 ICB-naive RM-HNSCC patients, we demonstrate that immunotherapy sensitivity is encoded in spatially organized tumor-stroma-immune interactions rather than tumor genetics alone. Transcriptionally distinct malignant clusters share a conserved copy-number backbone, revealing microenvironment-driven plasticity as the basis of intratumoral heterogeneity. Cycling malignant compartments function as dominant signaling hubs directing cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) engagement and checkpoint signaling; reduced myofibroblastic CAF signaling tracks with clinical response. Spatial contexture, beyond cellular composition alone, stratifies immune-permissive from immune-constrained tumors with differential progression-free survival and ICB response. A spatially informed transcriptional signature retains predictive value across 1,936 ICB-treated patients from 26 cohorts spanning seven cancer types, establishing spatial tumor microenvironment architecture as a pan-cancer determinant of ICB sensitivity. (The clinical trials have been registered at ClinicalTrials.gov [NCT02644369 and NCT04606940]).

title: Predicting expert-adjudicated appropriateness of postoperative antibiotic prescriptions from routine demographic, diagnostic and laboratory data: development and internal validation of machine learning models.
text: Prospective review of antibiotic prescriptions by antimicrobial stewardship teams is effective but labour-intensive. We examined whether routinely available structured data can predict an expert committee's judgement that a postoperative antibiotic prescription is appropriate. This retrospective single-centre study analysed 11,651 postoperative systemic antibiotic prescriptions adjudicated by an infectious diseases committee (88.5% approved). Predictors were age, sex, diagnostic category and eleven routine laboratory values. Because 19.3% of records were exact duplicates, data were split into development (80%) and test (20%) sets with group-aware stratified sampling. Logistic regression, random forest, extremely randomised trees and gradient boosting were compared by cross-validation and evaluated on the test set for discrimination, calibration, clinical utility and permutation importance, following TRIPOD+AI. Random forest had the highest cross-validated ROC-AUC (0.78) and test ROC-AUC (0.80; 95% CI 0.77-0.82), followed by gradient boosting (0.77), extremely randomised trees (0.75) and logistic regression (0.71); average precision was 0.95-0.97 against a no-skill baseline of 0.885. The class-weighted random forest systematically underestimated the probability of approval (calibration slope 1.75; Brier score 0.097 versus 0.102 for a non-informative model), whereas unweighted gradient boosting was well calibrated (slope 0.87; Brier 0.091). At a 0.50 threshold, random forest identified 22 of 268 rejected prescriptions (specificity 0.082). Its net benefit exceeded that of approving all prescriptions only at thresholds of 0.80 or higher, where gradient boosting provided greater net benefit despite lower discrimination. Age was the dominant predictor, and discrimination was lower in patients aged 65 years or older (0.73 versus 0.83). Routine structured data moderately predicted committee-adjudicated appropriateness but cannot determine whether an individual prescription is appropriate. Class weighting improved ranking at the cost of calibration and clinical utility. The findings support further evaluation of such models only as tools for prioritising prescriptions for expert review, after external validation and recalibration.

title: Development and Evaluation of Embeddings for Representing Injuries in Patients With Traumatic Injuries: Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Patients with traumatic injuries present with heterogeneous injury patterns that are difficult to represent in statistical models. Common approaches either retain individual injury codes in high-dimensional sparse representations, such as one-hot encoding, or aggregate injuries into summary scores, reducing dimensionality at the cost of patient-specific detail. This study aimed to develop low-dimensional data-driven ICD-10 embeddings for traumatic injuries and compare their downstream discriminatory performance with one-hot encoding of the same injury codes. We conducted a retrospective study using National Trauma Data Bank (NTDB) records from 2018 and 2019. International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification diagnoses were mapped to World Health Organization ICD-10 codes, retaining traumatic-injury codes S00-S99 and T15-T34. A denoising autoencoder was developed on 2018 data and temporally evaluated on 2019 data. Representations with 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 dimensions were compared with one-hot encoding across 16 downstream tasks using logistic regression and LightGBM. Performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for binary tasks and macro one-vs-rest AUC for multiclass tasks. Models were trained and evaluated within individual hospitals and separately on the full NTDB. Hospitals were stratified into volume categories, from small (≤500) to major (2500 patients/year). CIs were obtained from 1000 nonparametric bootstrap samples. The development cohort included 1,041,021 eligible patients from 2018, and the temporal evaluation cohort included 1,094,933 patients from 2019. At the hospital level, embeddings outperformed one-hot encoding. With LightGBM at 16 dimensions, the mean paired AUC difference across tasks was 0.054 (95% CI 0.048-0.060) in small hospitals (n=120) vs 0.023 (95% CI 0.020-0.025) in major hospitals (n=99). With logistic regression, differences were 0.056 (95% CI 0.050-0.063) and 0.041 (95% CI 0.039-0.043), respectively. In the full NTDB, 803-indicator one-hot encoding outperformed embeddings. Mean differences were -0.004 (95% CI -0.004 to -0.003) with LightGBM and -0.030 (95% CI -0.030 to -0.029) with logistic regression. At 64 dimensions, these differences narrowed to -0.001 and -0.016, respectively. Embeddings with as few as 8 dimensions achieved predictive performance comparable to or better than one-hot encoding, with up to a 100-fold reduction in dimensionality. Compared to one-hot encoding, embeddings improved performance in models trained at individual hospitals, particularly lower-volume hospitals. These gains may reflect reduced dimensionality, parameter sharing across codes, and representation of codes absent from hospital-specific training data, enabled by embeddings learned from the larger development cohort. In models trained on the full registry, one-hot encoding achieved higher mean AUC with both estimators, although the differences were minor (<0.005 AUC difference) for LightGBM with 16- to 64-dimensional embeddings. The embeddings and software are openly available.

title: Classifying brain metastases by primary tumor etiology on MRI: Addressing limitations and lesion multiplicity.
text: Brain metastases (BM) are the most common adult brain malignancies. In a subset of patients, the primary tumor is unknown upon BM diagnosis, creating a potential role for non-invasive, imaging-based prediction of tumor origin. We investigated a machine-learning framework utilizing MRI radiomics, clinical, and qualitative imaging features for primary tumor classification on a lesion-level and a patient-level. We retrieved a total number of 228 patients with 933 metastases originating from six primary tumor sites. Magnetic resonance imaging with both contrast-enhanced T1-weighted (T1CE) and T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences were analyzed. Contrast-enhancing lesions on T1CE and associated FLAIR hyperintensities were manually segmented in three dimensions and radiomic features were then extracted from both masks. XGBoost classification was performed at the lesion level and, after feature aggregation across multiple metastases, at the patient level. The additional value of clinical and qualitative imaging features was then evaluated. Classification performance was evaluated using cross-validated analysis of One-Vs-Rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Cross-validated class-wise AUC ranged from 0.52 (non-small cell lung cancer) to 0.69 (gastrointestinal cancer) for radiomics-based lesion-level classification. Melanoma classification improved from 0.55 (lesion-level) to 0.65 (patient-level) after radiomic feature aggregation. Overall, integration of clinical and qualitative imaging features showed little additional benefit for classification performance. For breast cancer, combined radiomics and clinical features achieved an AUC of 0.62 on a patient-level. Melanoma classification modestly improved from 0.65 (radiomics only) to 0.70 after addition of clinical and qualitative imaging features. Our study highlights the challenging nature of primary tumor site prediction using radiomic features, even with supplementary qualitative and clinical information. Reliable diagnosis might require the addition of further advanced imaging techniques.

title: Machine learning-assisted fusion of urinary Raman and fluorescence spectra for detection of urothelial carcinoma.
text: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) diagnosis still relies on invasive procedures such as cystoscopy, motivating the development of non-invasive urine-based alternatives. Here, we investigate a multimodal spectroscopic approach combining Raman with UV-excited and VIS-excited fluorescence measurements for UC detection from unprocessed urine using fibre-optic probes. A cohort of 285 patients was analyzed, including 120 UC cases and 165 controls. Spectral analysis revealed consistent biochemical differences between groups, associated with variations in key urinary constituents such as NADH, flavins, porphyrins, urea, and amino acids, supporting the diagnostic potential of urine composition. Two machine learning strategies were evaluated. A PCA-LDA classifier integrating multimodal features achieved moderately low performance (∼64% accuracy), highlighting both the feasibility of spectral data fusion and the limitations of linear methods for complex datasets. In contrast, an artificial neural network (ANN) applied to full spectral data significantly improved classification performance, reaching accuracies above 90% when combined with data augmentation. These results demonstrate that the multimodal spectroscopy approach, particularly when coupled with advanced machine learning strategies, can enable effective non-invasive detection of UC. Despite limitations related to fibre-probe measurements and bulk urine variability, the proposed approach represents a promising step toward rapid and cost-effective bladder cancer screening.

title: Predictive Modeling of Sarcopenia Using Machine Learning: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
text: Sarcopenia is an age-related syndrome characterized by muscle loss and functional decline, increasing fall risks. Early identification is crucial, yet convenient and accurate screening tools remain limited in routine practice. Machine learning (ML) models show promise for early sarcopenia detection, but their diagnostic performance and methodological quality have not been systematically quantified. This review aimed to quantitatively evaluate the diagnostic performance of ML models for sarcopenia prediction, compare performance across ML algorithms, and identify key sources of heterogeneity and methodological limitations. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched from inception to April 15, 2026. Eligible studies developed or validated at least one ML model for sarcopenia and provided sufficient data to reconstruct a 2×2 contingency table. Risk of bias was assessed using PROBAST (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool) developed by Moons et al. The primary analysis used a bivariate random‑effects (Reitsma) model to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values were pooled using a univariate random‑effects model with the Hartung‑Knapp‑Sidik‑Jonkman (HKSJ) method, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were estimated. A secondary analysis incorporated all models using cluster-robust variance estimation (RVE). Subgroup analyses and meta‑regression explored heterogeneity. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Twenty studies (20 prespecified index models) were included. The pooled AUROC was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82-0.93; 95% PI 0.54-0.98), with pooled sensitivity of 0.77 (95% CI 0.68-0.83; 95% PI 0.37-0.95) and specificity of 0.88 (95% CI 0.83-0.91; 95% PI 0.62-0.97). Gradient boosting had the highest pooled AUROC (0.92), but CIs overlapped across algorithms. Externally validated models had a pooled AUROC of 0.85, lower than that of internal ones (0.91). The secondary analysis of all 115 models yielded consistent results. Meta‑regression identified no significant covariates. PROBAST assessment revealed that half of the studies were at high risk of bias. This review provides the first quantitative synthesis of ML‑based sarcopenia prediction models, with several innovations: (1) it provides algorithm‑stratified pooled estimates of diagnostic accuracy, (2) it formally quantifies performance across algorithms and addresses the unit‑of‑analysis issue through a 2‑tier approach, and (3) it quantifies the performance gap between externally and internally validated models. By identifying specific weaknesses-insufficient external validation, poor calibration reporting, and high risk of bias-this review offers a roadmap for improving future studies. Practically, these models may serve as cost‑effective prescreening tools. However, GRADE certainty was very low, with substantial heterogeneity, insufficient external validation, and high risk of bias, indicating that current models are not yet ready for routine deployment. Future research should prioritize rigorous external validation, transparent reporting, calibration assessment, and clinically implementable design. PROSPERO CRD420251267598; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251267598.

title: Beyond PSA: a narrative review of novel biomarkers for prostate cancer screening and early detection.
text: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening reduces prostate cancer (PCa) mortality but is limited by poor specificity, unnecessary biopsies, and overdiagnosis. This review summarizes current evidence for blood-, urine-, and genetics-based biomarkers that refine risk prediction before magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or biopsy. Blood-based biomarkers (Prostate Health Index, 4Kscore, Stockholm3 (incorporating SNP-based genomic risk), and IsoPSA) and urine biomarkers (PCA3, MyProstateScore, SelectMDx, and ExoDx) generally improve risk stratification for clinically significant PCa (csPCa) compared with PSA alone and reduce unnecessary biopsies in men with elevated PSA, while missing 1-13% of csPCa. Stockholm3 has randomized screening-trial validation; 4Kscore has been evaluated as a post-PSA reflex test within screening trials; and ExoDx has randomized evidence in the diagnostic setting. The polygenic risk score, an investigational PSA-independent screening strategy, has shown promising results and is currently being evaluated in the ongoing TRANSFORM trial. Further emerging biomarkers, including PSA glycoforms, proteomic profiles, DNA methylation, cell-free DNA fragmentomics, microRNAs, mRNA profiling (PROSTest), and metabolomic profiles (volatile organic compounds), remain investigational. A new generation of molecular biomarkers holds promise to reshape PCa early detection by complementing PSA with individualized risk assessment. Clinical implementation requires prospective comparative studies, validation in diverse populations, cost-effectiveness analyses, and machine learning algorithms combining biomarkers, imaging, and clinical data.

title: Whole-Brain Dynamics and Cognitive Flexibility in Level 1 ASD: An HMM-Based Approach.
text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by differences in cognitive flexibility, which are closely associated with restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). However, the dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural correlates of cognitive flexibility difficulties in ASD by analyzing dynamic brain network features and explored their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. We applied hidden Markov models (HMMs) to resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to characterize dynamic brain network states in children with ASD (n = 69) and typically developing (TD) children (n = 50). Cognitive flexibility was assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF). An independent ABIDE II dataset was used for external validation. Machine learning models evaluated the diagnostic utility of behavioral and neuroimaging markers. Children with ASD showed atypical brain network dynamics, specifically a reduced brain state switching rate (p < 0.01) and asymmetric activation of the frontoparietal network (FPN). These alterations were significantly associated with cognitive flexibility difficulties and RRB severity in the ASD group (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q < 0.05) and generalized to the independent sample. Combining cognitive flexibility scores with brain state switching rates yielded high diagnostic accuracy (internal AUC: 0.897 (95% CI 0.812-0.963); external AUC: 0.869 (95% CI 0.781-0.943)). This study provides novel insights into the dynamic neural mechanisms underlying cognitive flexibility differences in ASD. The findings support combined behavioral and neuroimaging biomarkers for improving ASD diagnosis and lay the groundwork for individualized intervention research.

title: Artificial intelligence in epilepsy care: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical applications in diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical decision-making.
text: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, with disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where access to specialized care remains limited. Despite advances in neuroimaging and electrophysiology, accurate diagnosis, etiological classification, and timely identification of surgical candidates remain major clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to integrate multimodal data and support clinical decision-making across the epilepsy care continuum. To systematically assess and meta-analytically quantify the evidence on AI applications for diagnosis, etiological classification, outcome prediction, surgical candidate selection, and workflow optimization in epilepsy. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251117939). Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, and SciELO for studies published between January 2014 and March 2026. Eligible studies included original research in human subjects with epilepsy applying AI or machine learning models and reporting at least one quantitative performance metric with internal or external validation. Study quality was assessed using PROBAST. Pooled estimates of Area Under the Curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity were derived using DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models across four clinical task groups: diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical referral. From 423 identified records, 102 studies met inclusion criteria. Research output increased markedly after 2018, peaking in 2021 and 2024, with geographic concentration in China (n = 31) and the United States (n = 11). Electroencephalography and MRI were the dominant input modalities, and Support Vector Machines (n = 41) and Convolutional Neural Networks (n = 22) were the most frequently employed algorithms. Most studies relied exclusively on internal validation, and external validation remained scarce across all domains. PROBAST assessment revealed high risk of bias in the majority of studies, particularly in the participant and analysis domains. Meta-analysis demonstrated strong discriminative performance across all groups: the classification group achieved the highest pooled AUC (0.929; 95% CI: 0.837-0.971), followed by diagnosis (0.899; 95% CI: 0.859-0.929), surgical referral (0.895; 95% CI: 0.870-0.916), and outcome prediction (0.807; 95% CI: 0.740-0.861). Sensitivity was highest in the diagnosis group (0.885; 95% CI: 0.840-0.918) and lowest in surgical referral (0.729; 95% CI: 0.681-0.771), a clinically relevant asymmetry given the high cost of missing true surgical candidates in drug-resistant epilepsy. Substantial variability was observed across studies, reflecting differences in data modalities, AI architectures, and sample sizes, and indicating that pooled estimates should be interpreted with caution rather than as fixed, generalizable performance figures. AI demonstrates robust and clinically meaningful performance across the spectrum of epilepsy care, particularly for diagnosis and surgical planning. However, uniformly high between-study heterogeneity, predominant reliance on internal validation, variable study quality, and underrepresentation of low- and middle-income country contexts limit the generalizability of current evidence and hinder clinical translation. Prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, and context-adapted implementation strategies are essential to realize the full clinical potential that this body of evidence consistently demonstrates.

title: Network toxicology and single-cell transcriptomics identify acrylamide- and glycidamide-related candidate biomarkers in diabetic ulcers.
text: Diabetic ulcers (DU) are severe complications of diabetes, and environmental contaminants such as acrylamide (AA) and its metabolite glycidamide (GA) have been associated with metabolic disturbances relevant to diabetes. In this study, public transcriptomic datasets, network toxicology, protein interaction analysis, and machine learning were integrated to identify plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers overlapping with predicted AA or GA targets. Functional enrichment, immune infiltration analysis, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and single-cell RNA sequencing were further applied to characterize their biological roles and cellular distribution. Eight candidate genes were identified from the intersection of differentially expressed genes and predicted toxicant targets, and PNP and CTSB were ultimately identified as plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers. These genes were associated with proteasome function, DNA damage and repair, immune dysregulation, and altered cell communication. Single-cell analysis highlighted macrophages and T cells as major cell populations with dynamic plausible candidate biomarker expression. ELISA in streptozotocin induced diabetic ulcer mice further confirmed significantly increased CTSB and PNP protein levels, providing preliminary protein-level support for their association with DU. However, the overlap of PNP and CTSB with predicted AA/GA targets represents hypothesis-generating computational evidence only and does not establish that AA/GA exposure modulates these genes in vivo. These findings support PNP and CTSB as plausible candidate DU-associated biomarkers, while the predicted AA/GA-related associations require direct exposure-based experimental validation.

title: Subphenotyping and precision medicine approaches to ARDS.
text: Sixty years after its initial description, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains defined by bilateral radiographic opacities and impaired oxygenation rather than by its underlying biology. This syndromic definition encompasses considerable clinical and biological heterogeneity, which may contribute to the ineffectiveness of pharmacotherapy trials to date. Subphenotyping aims to address this heterogeneity by identifying more homogeneous patient groups that differ in prognosis and/or treatment response. In this narrative review, framed by the research questions outlined in the 2023 European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines, we synthesize current approaches to ARDS subphenotyping across complementary domains: clinical (etiology, rapidly improving ARDS), physiological (gas exchange, recruitability, elastance, and ventilatory ratio), morphological (focal versus non-focal radiological patterns), and biological (individual injury biomarkers and the hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory subphenotypes). We examine their pathobiological basis, temporal dynamics, and retrospective evidence for heterogeneity of treatment effect, and consider how parsimonious biomarker panels, machine-learning classifiers, and adaptive basket trial designs may support clinical implementation. Prospective validation across diverse populations, including resource-limited settings, remains a key priority.

title: Large-Scale and Systematic Prediction of ADMET Properties through Heterogeneous Network and Kernel-Based Deep Learning.
text: Accurately predicting absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) properties remains a major challenge in accelerating drug discovery, especially for underexplored natural products (NPs). Herein, we present a unified multitask learning framework that integrated heterogeneous network (HN) embeddings and a modified kernel-based deep neural network (DNN) to simultaneously predict all ADMET properties. Our model named as hdADMET captures complex molecular interactions through HNs that incorporated compound-drug relationships, experimental validated ADMET features, and the interrelationships among ADMET properties to transform the embedding representations into a kernel-based DNN for boosting the learning ability of the prediction model. Hold-out cross-validation on benchmark data sets, including ChEMBL, BindingDB, CTRPandGDSC, and NPASS, demonstrated improved and robust accuracy through data integration. Compared with the state-of-the-art multitask models, the hdADMET model achieved competitive performance with a significantly lower computational cost. Its practical utility was further demonstrated by accurately predicting the ADMET profiles of newly identified NPs mined from the literature studies. The promising candidate with high anticancer activity, low toxicity, and favorable metabolic properties was identified for further experimental validation. The hdADMET model offered an alternative way to prioritize leading compounds for clinical translation through HN embeddings and deep learning.

title: HyperDFI: Cross-View Hypergraph-Graph Contrastive Learning for Drug-Food Interaction Prediction.
text: Drug-food interactions (DFIs) are one of the major factors that trigger adverse drug events and have important research and clinical application value. However, experimental identification of DFIs remains costly and limited in scalability, leading to insufficient coverage of known interactions. Existing computational methods often treat DFI prediction as a variant of drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction and primarily focus on drug-food constituent relationships, which restrict their ability to directly model drug-food interactions. In this study, we propose a cross-view hypergraph-graph contrastive learning framework named HyperDFI for predicting interactions between drug and food (food constituents). We first construct four benchmark data sets by integrating information from DrugBank and PubMed, covering both drug-food and drug-food constituent interactions. Based on these data sets, heterogeneous bipartite graphs were established. HyperDFI jointly captures local topological structures and global high-order semantic relationships by combining graph neural networks (GNNs) and dynamic hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs). Furthermore, a cross-view contrastive learning strategy is introduced to align representations at different structural scales, thereby enhancing their consistency and discriminability. Extensive experiments on four benchmark data sets demonstrate that HyperDFI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. In addition, case studies on grapefruit further validate its ability to uncover novel DFIs.
