title: What Australian Health Practitioner Tribunals Decide, and What Automated Analysis Misses: 3,586 Decisions, 1999 to February 2026
text: Published tribunal decisions are the public record of the most serious health practitioner discipline in Australia, but they have not been analysed at scale. This study assembled 3,586 tribunal decisions (December 1999 to February 2026) from all eight jurisdictions. The author coded a random sample of 160 decisions, stratified by period and weighted to the corpus, blind to any machine output; these codes give the primary estimates. An independent second coder recoded 60 of them: agreement was substantial or better for disciplinary status (kappa 0.79) and most other fields, but moderate for dishonesty or fraud (0.59) and professional conduct (0.60). Among disciplinary decisions, breaches of professional conduct were found in 68.7% (95% CI 58.9-77.5), dishonesty or fraud in 41.6% (29.7-53.1), clinical competence failures in 38.6% (27.5-50.3), and boundary violations in 36.3% (24.8-48.0). Professional misconduct was found in 83.0%, and registration was cancelled in 30.6%. Across the ten professions regulated since 2010, disciplinary decisions rose from 1.25 to 2.36 per 10,000 registrants between 2011-2013 and 2023-2025. A text classifier, trained on a separate gold standard and applied to the whole corpus, identified disciplinary decisions accurately (accuracy 0.98) but missed almost half of dishonesty matters, and it detected them more often in later decisions, so its rising fraud trend partly reflects changing classifier error. Automated corpus-wide trends need checking against representative human coding across time.

title: Virtual brain twins guide personalized treatment decision in schizophrenia
text: Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder whose pathophysiology spans multiple spatial and temporal scales. Structural and functional neuroimaging studies have identified a broad range of disease-associated markers encompassing cortical atrophy, white matter disruptions, and aberrant functional connectivity patterns. Their application to personalized diagnosis and treatment selection has remained elusive. Here, we introduce the first Virtual Brain Twin (VBT) pipeline that integrates individual connectome-based network models with multimodal neuroimaging data, incorporating patient-specific structural connectivity, cortical thickness, and resting-state fMRI features to construct personalised whole-brain dynamical models. Dopaminergic and serotonergic signaling pathways are embedded within a mean-field framework, and simulation-based inference (SBI) is used to recover key pathophysiological parameters from individual patient data. The validity of this inference is first established using synthetic patients with known ground truth parameters, confirming that the pipeline can accurately identify underlying neurochemical states from simulated functional data. Applied to a cohort of 53 subjects in three clinical centers, the framework identifies personalized pathophysiological parameter regimes consistent with current neurobiological hypotheses of schizophrenia. Simulated pharmacological interventions within the VBT generate individualized medication effect trajectories that align retrospectively with known treatment outcomes, demonstrating the frameworks capacity to capture patient-specific pharmacological responses. These results establish a principled and extensible computational foundation for neuroimaging-guided personalized medicine in psychiatry, with direct implications for two prospective clinical trials conducted in Marseille and Munich as part of the Virtual Brain Twin project, designed to evaluate VBT-guided individualised antipsychotic treatment selection.

title: Research Involvement and Partnership Outcomes Among Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Partners
text: Importance: Meaningful patient and community involvement is increasingly emphasized in health research. Still, little is known about how such research involvement relates to the quality of patient and community partnerships. Objective: To examine the associations of patient and community involvement in research with partnership outcomes. The associations of patient involvement in specific research phases (e.g., grant writing, recruitment, and data collection) with these metrics were examined as a secondary objective. Design: This cross-sectional observational study used baseline data from a national cohort study across the United States collected from September to December 2024. Setting: This national study was conducted online with recruitment occurring over multiple channels. Participants: Participants included patient and community research partners aged 18 years and older and were recruited in a convenience sample. Exposures: The extent to which participants have contributed to prior research studies were calculated by adding binary indicators representing their involvement in phases of the research process. These indicators were examined individually as secondary exposures. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Primary outcomes included partnership quality and research engagement, with trust in medical researchers and partnership recommendation as secondary and tertiary outcomes. Multivariable linear and modified Poisson regressions were utilized to estimate regression coefficients and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs). Results: Among 330 participants (mean age = 36.5 years, SD = 9.7), 56.1% were male, and 37.3% and 31.8% were White or Black, respectively. Involvement in patient-centered outcomes research was associated with partnership quality ({beta}, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.30-1.42, P=0.003), research engagement ({beta}, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.01-0.06, P=0.006), trust in medical researchers ({beta}, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.31-1.07, P<0.001), and greater willingness to recommend becoming a research partner (aPR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.05-1.14, P<0.001). Conclusions and Relevance: Patient-centered outcomes research may provide patient and community research partners with a sense of shared ownership, improving partnership quality. While the causal links require further investigation, these associations may be driven by inclusion in recruitment, grant writing, data collection, and shared governance.

title: Old lineages, new threat: the re-emergence of pneumococcal serotype 14 in adults in Catalonia, Spain (2023-2025).
text: IntroductionThe introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines resulted in a decline in invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD). Nevertheless, recent studies report a re-emergence of vaccine-included serotypes. AimTo describe the recent re-emergence of serotype 14 IPD among adults in Catalonia and to investigate the factors underlying its resurgence. MethodsWe analysed two collections of adult IPD isolates: a historical series from Hospital Universitari de Bellvitge (1996-2025) and a multicentre series from seven tertiary hospitals in Catalonia (2023-2025). Isolates were serotyped (Quellung) and genotyped by PFGE/MLST (1996-2022) or Illumina sequencing (2023-2025). Clinical data were retrospectively collected. ResultsThe historical series showed that, after peaking in 2009, serotype 14 frequency gradually declined, with only 0-4 cases reported annually between 2016 and 2020. However, the number of serotype 14 isolates increased again in 2025, reaching 11.0% of all isolates at HUB and 10.8% across Catalonia. Genomic data showed that this increase involved multiple previously circulating lineages (GPSC6, GPSC18, GPSC16 and GPSC39), with no dominant clone. Analysis of the capsular locus revealed substantial genetic diversity, with no association between capsular variants and either lineage or year of isolation. A substantial proportion of patients (56.3%) had multiple comorbidities and only 18.8% were appropriately vaccinated. DiscussionThe re-emergence of serotype 14 was not associated with a novel lineage or capsular variant. Instead, it may reflect a combination of post-pandemic transmission changes, higher-valency paediatric vaccines, and natural fluctuations in serotype circulation. These findings highlight the limits of herd protection and underscore the need to strengthen adult vaccination, particularly among at-risk populations.

title: B-cell involvement supports anti-CD20 therapy in paediatric rheumatic heart disease: Proof of concept and initial safety
text: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, yet no therapy targets its underlying autoimmune mechanisms.[1],[2] We combined transcriptomic analyses of rheumatic mitral valves tissues with a translational approach. Using a panel of 750 mRNAs, we found a marked upregulation of B-cell-related pathways, including CD20-associated and multiple immunoglobulin genes, supporting a pathogenic role of B cells in RHD. We therefore evaluated an anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody (Rituximab), in a feasibility study in children with RHD, in Dakar, Senegal. Treatment was well tolerated, and in the following RCT first year preliminary safety analysis asked by the ethical committee, children who received rituximab showed a decrease in anti-streptolysin O titers and clinical improvement compared to controls. This proof-of-concept reveals B cells as a therapeutic target and suggests that an anti-CD20 agent may represent a potential disease-modifying therapy for RHD.

title: Cardiorespiratory Limits Exist in HFpEF Independent of Age and BMI
text: BackgroundHeart-failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome marked by exercise intolerance associated with impairments in cardiac and respiratory performance. HFpEF is associated with age and weight; however, it remains unclear whether cardiorespiratory limitations exist independent of these comorbidities. HypothesisIndependent of age and BMI, there are cardiorespiratory limitations inherent to the HFpEF syndrome that have yet to be fully elicited. MethodsA patient cohort with a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF (HFpEF; N = 38) and counterparts without identifiable cardiopulmonary disease (control; N = 21) underwent phenotyping with echocardiography and cardiopulmonary exercise testing with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. ResultsStudy cohorts were similar in age, BMI and height (p=NS for all metrics). Body-surface area (BSA) (2.1 m2 v 1.9 m2, p < 0.05), atrial fibrillation prevalence (50 v 14%, p < 0.05), and average E/e (11.5 v 9.5, p < 0.05) were elevated within the HFpEF cohort. Peak VO2 (14.1 v 19.1 mL/Kg/min, p < 0.001) was also diminished among those with HFpEF. Resting (17.1 v 11.4mmHg, p < 0.001) and exercise wedge pressures (29.3 v 16.7mmHg, p < 0.001) were elevated whereas stroke volume (93.3 v 110.4 mL, p < 0.05) and cardiac output (Direct Fick; 8.0 v 9.8, p < 0.05) during exercise were diminished in HFpEF patients. FVC, FVC%, FEV1 and FEV1% were also significantly diminished in the HFpEF cohort. ConclusionsCardiorespiratory limitations exist as a feature of the HFpEF syndrome, independent of age and BMI. BSA remained associated with HFpEF in keeping with adiposity as a feature of pathophysiology.

title: Charted times of bedside pain assessments are slot labels: prevalence across hospitals, consequences for estimating analgesic onset, and when hourly charting is an adequate approximation
text: ObjectiveTemporal and causal analyses of electronic health records (EHRs) treat the charted time of an observation as the time it was made. We quantified how often bedside pain and sedation assessments are charted to a time slot, how this affects estimates of analgesic onset, and when hourly charting is an adequate approximation. MethodsWe used intensive care unit (ICU) data from one academic center (MIMIC-IV) and 78 hospitals (eICU-CRD). Slot labeling was identified from charted minutes and from the delay between charted and entry times. In MIMIC-IV, opioid administration times served as anchors, and faster onset of intravenous (IV) than oral opioids as a pharmacologic benchmark. We compared onset estimated from charted times with onset from exactly timed records, bounded true assessment times under alternative charting mechanisms, and used simulation to relate bias to the ratio of slot width to response time constant ({Delta}/k). ResultsIn MIMIC-IV, 68% of pain and 76% of sedation scores were charted on the hour and entered a median of 41-44 minutes later. Of the first reassessments after a dose, 32-34% of on-hour records carried a time before the dose, against 12-14% of off-hour records. Across eICU hospitals, the on-hour share ranged from 15% to 92% (10th-90th percentile). By charted time, oral opioids appeared nearly as fast as IV (pain change at 15-30 minutes, -1.76 vs -2.11 points); exactly timed records showed -0.80 vs -2.00. Slower oral onset held under every charting mechanism compatible with the data, but its magnitude was not identified (ratio of time constants 1.2-11.6). In simulation, analysis by charted time was adequate up to {Delta}/k {approx} 2 when rounding was to the nearest slot, but only up to {Delta}/k {approx} 0.1 when rounding had a direction. ConclusionCharted times of bedside assessments are often slot labels, and charting practice is hospital-specific. For ICU analgesic onset, neither condition for an adequate approximation can be assumed, and EHR data alone cannot recover the size of the effect.

title: Beyond the 24-Hour Rhythm: Functional Principal Components of Daily Activity Residuals and Mortality in NHANES
text: BackgroundAccelerometer-derived 24-hour activity profiles are usually summarised by cosinor rhythm parameters or by functional principal component analysis (FPCA). Applied to the raw profiles, however, the leading functional components largely re-express what the cosinor already captures: activity level, rhythm strength and timing. Whether the shape of the day carries health information beyond these parameters is unclear. MethodsWe analysed adults with seven valid days of accelerometry from two National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohorts: hip activity counts (2003-2006; n = 2,615) and wrist Monitor-Independent Movement Summary units (2011-2014; n = 3,208). Minute-level activity was transformed with the inverse hyperbolic sine, and a single 24-hour cosinor curve was fitted across each participants seven days. Each participants average residual curve was decomposed by FPCA and, to separate stable between-person patterns from day-to-day variation, by multilevel FPCA. The residual components were compared with standard FPCA of the average activity curves. In exploratory analyses, we related the three leading components to all-cause mortality and, secondarily, to cardiovascular and cancer mortality. We used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, ethnicity, income and the cosinor parameters, with the hip cohort for discovery and the wrist cohort for replication. ResultsThe three leading residual components explained 44% (hip) and 51% (wrist) of residual variance and consisted mainly of 12-hour and 8-hour patterns. The second component (FPC2) contrasts an early-starting, flat day with a day of distinct mid-morning and evening peaks. Its shape was nearly identical in the two cohorts (similarity 0.96), and multilevel FPCA recovered it as a stable between-person pattern. In unweighted models, FPC2 was the only component associated with all-cause mortality in the hip discovery cohort, which replicated in the wrist cohort. With survey weights that also accounted for selection into the analytic sample, the association was concentrated in cardiovascular deaths (hip 1.53, 1.12 to 2.09, p = 0.007; wrist 1.38, 1.10 to 1.72, p = 0.005). This association persisted after further adjustment for lifestyle factors, traditional activity metrics and self-reported diseases. In standard FPCA, the pattern was mixed with 24-hour rhythm variation, unstable in small samples, and showed no association unless the cosinor parameters were adjusted for. FPC2 was not associated with cancer mortality. Scores of the leading components did not form distinct clusters (average silhouette width[≤] 0.23), but FPC2 was selected as a continuous predictor of cardiovascular mortality in both cohorts by forward selection on 10-fold cross-validated, survey-weighted AUC. ConclusionsThe within-day structure of activity that a 24-hour cosinor cannot represent varies continuously between people. One replicated aspect of it, the loss of a two-peak daily pattern, was associated with mortality beyond rhythm strength and timing, most clearly cardiovascular mortality. The shape of daily activity therefore carries prognostic information beyond standard rhythm summaries. It can support mortality risk prediction that needs only a few personal details, and may help identify individuals at elevated risk and tailor interventions to their daily activity patterns.

title: Accurate Prediction of Hepatic Disease Severity in MASLD Using a Learned Phenotype
text: Background & AimsMost prognostic models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) target prespecified hepatic endpoints, potentially limiting attainable accuracy. We developed and externally validated a model that learns the future hepatic phenotype most reliably predictable from baseline clinical characteristics. MethodsWe analyzed 332 HALO-MASLD participants (456 follow-up observations). Sparse Canonical Outcome REgression (SCORE) learned a weighted phenotype from eight hepatic measures, coupled with broken adaptive ridge regression using 99 baseline predictor columns. Participant-level nested five-fold cross-validation compared prediction of the learned phenotype with future liver stiffness measurement (LSM), controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), and FIB-4 benchmarks. Models were externally validated without refitting in the independent NIDDK NAFLD Adult Database 2 cohort (520 participants, 732 follow-up observations). Biological validity and bootstrap stability were also assessed. ResultsThe learned phenotype emphasized lower platelet count and higher bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and LSM. In HALO, predictive correlation was r = 0.860 (95% CI [0.824, 0.896]) and predictive R2 = 0.671, versus r = 0.763 for LSM and r = 0.469 for CAP predicted from all baseline variables. All six prespecified comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (pHolm < 0.05). The phenotype correlated with MRE stiffness ({rho} = 0.694) and biopsy fibrosis stage ({rho} = 0.567), and was higher with imaging evidence of portal hypertension (p < 0.001). Bootstrap relearning yielded mean phenotype correlation 0.947. In NIDDK, predictive correlation was r = 0.836 (95% CI [0.805, 0.863]; predictive R2 = 0.680), and associations with fibrosis and portal hypertension replicated. ConclusionsLearning the prediction target produced a sparse, clinically interpretable hepatic phenotype more accurately predicted than conventional longitudinal MASLD endpoints in both cohorts. The resulting LIFT-MASLD model is available at https://liftmasld.github.io.

title: MorphoStain: Physics-Guided Latent Diffusion and Morphological Distillation for Multiplex Stain Decomposition in Alzheimer's Neuropathology
text: Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) enables simultaneous biomarker profiling, yet unmixing colocalized targets with identical spectra, such as dual-DAB marking Tau and Amyloid-{beta} in Alzheimers pathology, remains mathematically ill-posed. We propose MorphoStain, an unsupervised, physics-guided framework for morphological stain decomposition with epistemic uncertainty quantification. MorphoStain models stain separation via a conditional Latent Diffusion Teacher operating on a Beer- Lambert optical-density manifold, guided by pathology foundation models. To enable real-time clinical throughput, the teacher is distilled into a FastStudentU-Net (0.12M parameters, > 1,400 x compression), while a Symmetric Morphological Routing Module dynamically disentangles identical chromogen overlap. Evaluated on 9,908 held-out patches from the SEA-AD cohort, MorphoStain achieves 40.56 dB PSNR and 0.9961 SSIM at 140.1 FPS, showing statistically significant gains over InverseAE (Cohens d = 3.52) and NMF (Cohens d = 7.02), with p < 0.001 for both comparisons.

title: ZNF683-positive tissue-resident memory T cells organize treatment-refractory niches with targetable circuits in inclusion body myositis
text: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) is a progressive autoimmune myositis refractory to conventional immunosuppression, yet mechanisms sustaining chronic inflammation remain unresolved. Integrating comparative single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and orthogonal validation across autoimmune myositis, we identified ZNF683+IL7R+ cytotoxic tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells with natural killer cell-like features enriched in IBM. Trajectory analysis positioned an early-disease ZBTB16+ cytotoxic T cell state upstream of ZNF683+IL7R+TRM. ZNF683 overexpression induced memory and natural killer cell-like transcriptional programs while attenuating glucocorticoid-response signatures, linking this program to treatment refractoriness. Ligand-receptor modeling nominated candidate targetable circuits involving IL-15-IL15RA, XCL1-XCR1, and HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4. Spatial transcriptomics localized ZNF683+TRM to stress-associated IBM niches. These findings define a disease-specific TRM-centered circuit linked to treatment refractoriness and candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities in IBM. One-sentence summaryZNF683+IL7R+ TRM cells organize targetable treatment-refractory IBM niches involving IL-15-IL-15RA, XCL1-XCR1, and HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 axes.

title: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses
text: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR-related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non-FGFR-related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal-frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non-syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

title: Sex and Gender Reporting and Female Participation Relative to Disease Burden in ClinicalTrials.gov
text: ImportanceAssessing representation by sex assigned at birth and gender identity requires reporting of both in trials. If disclosure of full gender and sex participation from clinicaltrials.gov this is limited, it poses challenges in characterization and understanding of those participant experiences. ObjectiveTo determine how often ClinicalTrials.gov trials published trials report sex and gender, which characteristics are associated with reporting, and how participants female share compares with that of the general public. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsCross-sectional study of interventional trials registered to ClinicalTrials.gov, with or without US sites, with primary completion on or after September 27, 2008, and results first posted from January 1, 2009, through April 30, 2026. ExposuresFunder type, phase, US sites, enrollment, primary completion year, number of countries, and therapeutic area. Main Outcomes and MeasuresReporting of sex and gender, and the female participation-to-prevalence ratio (PPR; trial female share divided by the number of people with the condition). ResultsAmong 58,007 trials (median enrollment, 72 [IQR, 31 to 206]; 42,644 [74%] with US sites), 553 (0.95%) reported gender and 57,683 (99.44%) reported sex. Gender reporting was more common with National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding (odds ratio [OR], 9.05; 95% CI, 6.65 to 12.6), US sites (OR, 4.21; 95% CI, 2.96 to 6.22), and larger enrollment. Across 10 conditions (15,552 mixed-sex trials), median PPR ranged from 0.68 (95% CI, 0.64 to 0.71) for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease to 1.05 (95% CI, 1.01 to 1.09) for obesity and had a relatively lower female share in 8. Among the 10 conditions most prevalent in our cohort, 6,917 of 16,097 trial condition combinations (43.0%) reached a PPR of at least 0.90; odds of reaching it were higher for NIH-funded (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11 to 1.34) and lower for government-funded trials (OR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.33) as compared to industry-funded trials. Conclusions and RelevanceIn ClinicalTrials.gov, sex reporting is nearly universal, whereas gender reporting is concentrated among NIH-funded, US-based, and larger trials. Female trial enrollment fell below the female share of people with the condition for most conditions, emphasizing the benefit of condition-specific benchmarks in clinical trials.

title: Cell-free telomeric DNA and integrity indices in axial spondyloarthritis: associations with somatic and mental burden: a case-control study.
text: ObjectivesDepression and anxiety in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) are associated with higher disease activity. This study examined whether circulating cell-free nuclear DNA (cf-nDNA), mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA), relative telomere length (T/S ratio), and DNA integrity index (DII) are associated with mental burden and disease characteristics in axSpA. MethodsPlasma cf-nDNA, cf-mtDNA, T/S ratio, and ALU-247/ALU-115 ratio (DII) were analysed in 79 patients with axSpA and 88 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs). Mental burden was assessed using the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview (M.I.N.I.), Beck Depression Inventory-II, and Beck Anxiety Inventory. Clinical measures included the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score with C-reactive protein (ASDAS-CRP), and radiographic disease pattern. ResultsSex differences were observed in disease phenotype and hip involvement. Affective or anxiety disorders were more frequent in axSpA vs. HC (26.6% vs. 2.3%, p<0.001); depressive symptoms were also more frequent (20.2% vs. 2.27%, p<0.001) and higher in active vs. inactive disease (30.0% vs. 3.45%, p<0.001). Compared with HCs, patients had higher cf-mtDNA and lower DII (both p<0.01), with a trend towards lower T/S ratio. Females had higher T/S ratio and DII than males, and higher cf-mtDNA overall. Lower T/S ratio was associated with affective disorders, while only CRP independently predicted depressive symptom severity. ConclusionsAltered cfDNA profiles, particularly increased cf-mtDNA and reduced DII, are associated with axSpA, disease activity and mental burden, supporting their potential as biomarkers of disease-related processes.

title: Plasma Proteomic Identifies GDF15 as a Candidate Lithium Treatment Response Biomarker in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Secondary Analysis of the LATTICE Randomized Clinical Trial
text: Lithium (Li) demonstrates neuroprotective effects relevant to Alzheimers disease (AD); however, its molecular mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study analyzed plasma proteomic profiles from the Li as a Treatment to Prevent Impairment of Cognition in Elders (LATTICE) randomized clinical trial to identify markers associated with amyloid (A{beta}) pathology, disease progression, and response to Li treatment. In the LATTICE trial, 80 older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) were randomly assigned to receive either low-dose Li carbonate or placebo for two years. Longitudinal plasma samples were analyzed using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120 proteomic panel. Baseline protein levels were compared according to randomized treatment assignment, A{beta}-PET status, and MCI subtype. Analyses included longitudinal changes in protein levels associated with treatment and time, associations between baseline protein levels and subsequent cognitive, functional, and neuroimaging trajectories, and the influence of baseline protein levels on Li treatment effects. Among the 80 participants, 62 had amnestic MCI and 21 were A{beta}-PET positive. Baseline proteomic differences were more strongly associated with A{beta}-PET status than with randomized treatment assignment. Plasma p-tau217 concentrations were elevated in A{beta}-PET positive individuals and remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Over time, CALB2 and TREM2 exhibited nominal treatment-by-time interactions in the full cohort, while in the amnestic MCI subgroup, CALB2, TREM2, and A{beta}40 demonstrated nominal effects; none persisted after multiple-testing correction. GDF15 showed the most consistent associations with CDR Sum of Boxes trajectories and treatment-effect modification that remained significant after false discovery rate correction in the amnestic MCI subgroup, whereas p-tau217 was most consistently associated with hippocampal volume trajectories. Other protein-outcome associations were exploratory. Plasma proteomics identified distinct molecular patterns associated with A{beta} pathology and the MCI phenotype, along with exploratory evidence of Li-associated protein changes. Plasma GDF15 and p-tau217 emerged as potential markers of clinical progression and treatment-response heterogeneity, warranting validation in larger, adequately powered trials.

title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
text: Background and ObjectivesNormative modeling expresses an individuals brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. MethodsWe retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). ResultsWe included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. DiscussionUnivariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
text: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

title: Hidden Dependencies in Endometriosis Microarray Classifiers: Sample Reuse, Outcome-Informed Batch Correction, and Diagnostic Reassessment
text: Distinct Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) accessions do not necessarily represent independent transcriptomic samples. We investigated exact array reuse, access to test diagnoses during batch correction, and cohort and acquisition-date confounding in endometriosis classifiers. We compared decompressed CEL files using SHA-256, reconstructed a matrisome elastic-net workflow, changed test labels supplied to ComBat, and conducted 3,582 constrained training-label refits. We also evaluated the effect of removing matching training copies in a five-gene Huang-inspired random forest and performed a 324-probe nested internal benchmark within GSE51981. Of 37 test CEL files, 26 (70.3%) were identical to training arrays; all had been scanned in 2004-2005. Changing a test diagnosis supplied to ComBat moved the fixed classifier score toward the supplied label in all 37 interventions. In a deduplicated, batch-constrained comparison, median nominal balanced accuracy was 0.881 when ComBat received true test outcomes and 0.549 without them; the outcome-informed arm performed better in 1,193 of 1,194 matched refit comparisons. In the separate Huang-inspired reconstruction, removing each targets matching training copy lowered pooled AUC from 1.000 to 0.323 (conditional 95% interval 0.105-0.571). Exploratory nested AUC was 0.733 for endometriosis versus other gynecological conditions, and date-held-out AUC in 2009 was 0.698. For endometriosis versus healthy controls, a date-only out-of-fold model achieved AUC 0.935, compared with 0.893 for the molecular model. Together, these findings show how exact array reuse, outcome-informed preprocessing, and acquisition-date structure can compromise the interpretation of nominally independent validation. They describe reconstructions and exploratory internal analyses, not corrected performance estimates for the published classifiers.

title: Public Acceptability of Self-Payment for Community Pharmacists' Services: A National Online Survey
text: BackgroundThe traditional business model for sustaining United States (U.S.) community pharmacies has relied on income generated by product sales. A fee-for-service model could help alleviate insufficient profit by monetizing conventionally free pharmacy services if patients are willing to pay out-of-pocket. ObjectivesThis study evaluated public acceptability of out-of-pocket payment for community pharmacist-provided services, variation in payment acceptability across services, and assessed whether payment acceptability differed by respondent characteristics and trust constructs. MethodsThis study represents a cross-sectional online survey of U.S. adults conducted during spring 2026 using a non-probability sampling approach. Primary outcomes were binary stated payment-acceptability judgments for a variety of pharmacist and health services. The survey used a between-subjects randomized payment-framing design, where participants were assigned to either a stated-price condition or an any-payment condition. Secondary outcomes included trust designations and participant demographic characteristics. ResultsA total of 1069 respondents completed the survey. A $20 fee was viewed more favorably than a general "any amount of money" fee. In the $20 stated-price condition, agreement was highest for osteoporosis screening (75.8%) and travel-related vaccines (69.0%), and lowest for antibiotic use consultation (23.9%) and wound care (32.1%). Older respondents and Hispanic respondents were less likely to view payment as acceptable, whereas men and respondents with greater pharmacist trust were more likely to view payment as acceptable. ConclusionAlthough patients historically have received many community pharmacy services at no cost, this study demonstrates that the concept of self-payment ifor certain services is considered acceptable, especially for services not typically provided. Key pointsO_LIIn a quota-matched survey of 1,069 U.S. adults, this study evaluated public acceptability of direct out-of-pocket payment for 27 community pharmacist-provided clinical services. C_LIO_LIPublic acceptability of a $20 out-of-pocket payment varied substantially by service, ranging from 23.9% for antibiotic-use consultation to 75.8% for osteoporosis screening. Higher acceptability was observed for discrete or specialized services, including travel-related vaccines and pharmacogenomic result review. C_LIO_LIPayment acceptability was associated with respondent characteristics and trust in pharmacists. Older respondents and Hispanic respondents were less likely to view payment as acceptable, whereas men and respondents with greater pharmacist trust were more likely to view payment as acceptable. C_LI

title: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
text: BackgroundRisk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. MethodsThis secondary analysis included 9,289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-13). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 1-3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported no (low risk), yes (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. FindingsThe adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each womans three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). InterpretationFor fetal growth outcomes, how a womans predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a womans follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit. FundingNone. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed from database inception to Oct 28, 2026, for English-language studies in humans, combining terms for gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction or small for gestational age, and large for gestational age with terms for prediction models and for longitudinal or repeated assessment, risk trajectories, conformal prediction, or predictive uncertainty. We also searched for conformal prediction applied to longitudinal clinical data. Most models predicted a single complication at a fixed gestational age. Longitudinal models updated risk using repeated measurements of blood pressure, biomarkers or fetal biometry, and some showed that changes in these measurements, including fetal growth velocity, improved prediction. We found no study that tested whether a womans earlier predictions add information beyond her most recent prediction. Individual-level uncertainty was rarely quantified in antenatal prediction, and we found no application of conformal prediction in antenatal care. Conformal methods have been used for repeated prediction in other clinical settings, but we found no evaluation of how often prediction sets include the actual outcome across a patients successive predictions.

title: Microcirculation Mirror: A zero-install browser workstation for hand microvascular anatomy and nailfold capillaroscopy
text: BackgroundHand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 {micro}m lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange. MethodsWe present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module. The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app. ResultsIts 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z- Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer. The NVC module renders a 200x, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification. A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-{micro}m capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-{micro}m detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains {approx}0.016% effective contrast, about 60x below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is {approx}270x lower. The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6. ConclusionsThe camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled. No patient data are used. The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.

title: Requirements of a knowledge support tool for self-harm in general practice: a mixed-methods study with patients, carers, and clinicians
text: BackgroundGeneral practice has a central role in care following self-harm. However, clinicians frequently report uncertainty about best practice and patients describe poor care. A knowledge support tool is an add-on to electronic health systems that may improve services by providing personalised care information. AimTo understand what general practice clinicians, patients and carers need from a novel knowledge support tool for self-harm. Design and SettingMixed-methods, using quantitative ratings, focus groups and follow-on interviews with general practice clinicians and patients/carers with lived experience of self-harm. MethodClinicians were recruited through social media and professional networks, and patients/carers through a third-sector organisation. During four focus groups and follow-on interviews, we explored the utility of potential content and functionality of a knowledge support tool. Quantitative utility ratings were summarised descriptively and qualitative data were analysed thematically using the framework method. People with lived/living experience were involved throughout. Results13 clinicians and 14 patients/carers participated. Requirements of the knowledge support tool were captured across three qualitative themes: facilitating person-centred care, accessibility and usability, and balancing competing priorities of general practice. Across these themes, patients and carers needs were centred on promoting compassionate relationships and patient agency. Clinicians shared these needs but balanced them with a need to manage patient expectations and practice defensively under limited resources. ConclusionOur findings inform the core design of a knowledge support tool and suggest that such a tool could support the assessment and management of self-harm in general practice. How this fits inGeneral practice plays a key role in providing care for people who have self-harmed, yet clinicians report feeling underconfident in managing patients, who themselves frequently describe poor experiences of care. Research suggests that reducing knowledge gaps amongst clinicians, patients and carers may improve patient safety and experiences of help-seeking in this setting, where practical guidance for clinicians is currently limited. A knowledge support tool is a novel intervention that can be used during consultations to provide timely and personalised information that supports high-quality caregiving; however, less is known about how such a tool should be designed for general practice self-harm care. We outline what general practice clinicians and people with lived experience of self-harm need from a knowledge support tool for self-harm.

title: Eye-to-Eye: Gaze detection as a proxy for medical doctor behaviour during virtual and in-person appointments
text: The gaze direction of the physician during consultations plays an important role in patient satisfaction, with several studies pointing to the positive correlation between the amount of time the physician spends looking at the patient and patient satisfaction. Additionally, the effects of the virtual consultation environment on the gaze behaviour of the doctor have yet to be studied. Therefore, this study aims to assess the impact of the virtual consultation environment by comparing the amount of total time the doctor spends looking at the patient between face-to-face and virtual consultations, as well as the average duration during the consultation and the gaze frequency. The study population consisted of 14 doctors divided between 4 medical specialties: Gynaecology/Obstetrics (4), Neurology (3), Endocrinology (3) and General and Familiar Medicine (4). A low-cost desktop that runs an appearance-based gaze estimation pipeline was implemented in the clinical setup. Each doctor recorded 20 face-to-face consultations and 20 virtual consultations, which were then processed by the pipeline to obtain the percentage of time the doctor spent looking at the patient during the consultation. Overall, we found that doctors look more at the patient in virtual consultations compared to face-to-face consultations, both in total time and average duration during the consultation. Within medical specialties, three out the four specialties involved presented clear tendencies to look more at the patient in virtual consultations when compared to face-to-face consultations.

title: Evaluation of improvement training for cancer MDT members
text: BackgroundMultidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings are central to cancer care. National policy, including the 2026 National Cancer Plan for England, expects MDTs to improve how they work. Although validated tools assess MDT performance, little is known about training in their use. We evaluated structured MDT improvement training delivered across two UK Cancer Alliances. MethodsThree one-day courses, delivered in 2019, combined teaching and simulation using MDT assessment tools, including the Metric for the Observation of Decision-making (MDT-MODe). Participants completed a 14-item Likert-scale survey (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) and open-ended questions. Responses were summarised descriptively; subgroup comparisons used chi-squared tests with Bonferroni correction. Free-text responses were analysed thematically by two coders. ResultsForty-eight MDT members responded (26 doctors, 10 nurses, 10 administrative staff). Twelve of 14 items scored a median of 4 (agree); understanding the information scored a 4.5. Support for mandatory training was more modest (median 3.5). After Bonferroni correction, significant differences by grade remained for knowledge of the MDT-metric (adjusted p = 0.001) and MDT-MODe instrument (adjusted p < 0.001). Strengths included teaching (n = 14), utility of MDT-MODe (n = 10) and networking (n = 9). Weaknesses included poor audio-visual quality (n = 18) and difficulty identifying speakers (n = 8). ConclusionsExpert-led, simulation-based MDT improvement training was well received across professional groups. Although delivered in 2019, it addresses skills central to national MDT reform. Future courses should improve audio-visual quality and offer implementation support. Pre-post evaluation and longer-term follow-up are needed.

title: Uptake and outcomes of earlier viral load testing and longer visit intervals in the early HIV treatment period: retrospective cohort analysis of South Africas 2023 ART guidelines revision
text: South Africas 2023 revised ART Guidelines moved the first scheduled viral load (VL) test from 6 to 3 months after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and accelerated differentiated care eligibility from 7 to 4 months among virally suppressed clients. We assessed uptake of these changes and their association with virologic outcomes. We analysed routine electronic medical record data from 18 primary healthcare clinics in three South African districts among all adults initiating or re-initiating ART (N=16,338; January 2022-March 2025). Interrupted time series analyses were used to assess uptake of 3-month VL testing and assignment to [≥]6-month visit intervals following guideline implementation in April 2023. Modified Poisson regression was used to compare relative risks (RRs) for viral suppression at the first and second routine VL tests among clients tested at 3 months (test window=56-111 days) and 6 months (112-<252 days). At the first VL assessment, 27% of participants had VL tests at 3 months and 30% at 6 months; the rest had tests outside either window (19%) or no test documented (25%). Three-month VL testing rose immediately after guideline implementation, reaching 72-85% coverage by the end of the study period. Assignment to [≥]6-month visit intervals among clients with 3-month viral suppression increased after implementation, reaching 48-71% across districts. A second VL result was documented for 62% of clients tested in the 3- or 6-month window. Viral suppression did not differ meaningfully between clients initially tested at 3 months (72%) and those initially tested at 6 months (72%). Among clients with a second scheduled VL result, 82% were virally suppressed. Assignment to [≥]6-month visit intervals was not associated with subsequent viral suppression (aRR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99-1.06). Results should be interpreted with caution due to missing VL data. South Africas 2023 guideline revision was associated with rapid increases in 3-month VL testing and assignment to longer visit intervals. Viral suppression at the first VL test was similar among clients tested at 3 and 6 months, and longer visit intervals were not associated with poorer outcomes. These findings support earlier differentiation of HIV care within routine service delivery. Incomplete uptake of recommended testing and visit intervals offers opportunities to strengthen implementation and warrants continued evaluation of longer-term outcomes.

title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
text: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
text: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.

title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
text: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
text: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
text: Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.

title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
text: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
text: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

title: CAST: A Deployed Speech-to-Text Cascade for Closed Captioning of Entertainment Television
text: Despite rapid progress in automatic speech recognition (ASR), caption generation for long-form entertainment video remains challenging for content dense in music and effects, rich in accents, crosstalk, and noise. The transcript quality depends on segmentation and surrounding modules as much as the acoustic model. A single pass voice activity detection (VAD) can miss faint, low-energy voice while forwarding near-silent segments that induce hallucination and repetition in an autoregressive decoder. These competing errors motivate a hierarchical VAD that revisits rejected segments under semantic and acoustic retention checks. We present Captioning ASR Stack for Television (CAST), an integrated speech-to-text pipeline for closed captioning (CC) combining frozen Whisper large-v3 with segmentation, language identification, lyrics routing, and targeted hallucination detection and repair on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. On 100 in-house assets spanning 60.46 hours, CAST reduces normalized WER from 6.99% to 5.36% and subtitle edit rate from 254.2 to 221.9 min/hour against the WhisperX pipeline, and improves deletion rate by 11% on public datasets. We also present the behavior of each stage in the pipeline. CAST entered the production speech-to-text (STT) stage of our CC pipeline in late August 2026; we report the evaluation evidence and path to full-scale operation.

title: Distill the Correction, Not the Rewrite: Hindsight Twins for Self-Improving Text-to-Image Models
text: Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so a useful revision must go beyond the failed span, often rewriting the entire scene and adding details that overshadow the fix; (2) although the critic localizes the error to a single span, self-teachers condition on the rewrite, entangling the intended fix with unintended additions. Motivated by these insights, we propose Hindsight Twins (HinT), which fills the critic's revision template once with the intended fix and once with the observed error and distills only their velocity difference, anchored at the user's prompt. Because text encoders spread the edit of a single slot to all other tokens, HinT further aligns the twins' token states outside the slot. Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT keeps the rate of critic-induced bias at the base-model level while matching or exceeding the alignment gains of prior self-distillation, and it keeps improving over twelve rounds of self-training where contrastive baselines decay.

title: LeCellModel: Interpretable Density Estimation over the Gene Expression Manifold
text: Representation learning for single-cell RNA-seq has been evaluated by the identities representations capture -- cell types, lineages, perturbations -- rather than how faithfully they model the distribution of cell states on the gene expression manifold. As a result, density estimation, rare-state detection, perturbation scoring, and gene-level attribution are bolted onto frozen embeddings as separate models, disconnected from the geometry of the data. We argue that modeling the distribution of cell states should be the primary objective, and that representation quality follows from it. Building on LeJEPA, whose SIGReg objective enforces a provably optimal isotropic Gaussian latent, we introduce LeCellModel, which reads the encoder's Jacobian log-volume (JEPA-SCORE) under this Gaussian latent as a relative typicality score. Across several datasets, LeCellModel outperforms established methods on the scIB benchmark for representation quality. Furthermore, we show that LeCellModel enables detection of rare expression states using JEPA-SCORE as a typicality measure, applying it to a controlled cytokine panel, where it identifies stimulated cells across minority fractions and tracks pathway-response magnitude. We introduce gene-level interpretability of the typicality score -- to our knowledge, the first method for analyzing JEPA-SCORE in feature space. Leveraging this framework, LeCellModel recapitulates the known association of a profibrotic macrophage program with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, and discovers a CD177+ activated regulatory T cell subpopulation previously described only in tumor contexts. Both findings emerge directly from the geometry of the learned embedding, without relying on supervised annotations.

title: Modern Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Are Pareidolic
text: In human perception, pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a meaningful pattern, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous stimulus.We find a similar phenomenon in modern self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs): on white noise, which contains neither objects nor spatial structure, a few directions of their features still form spatially coherent patterns across the patches, imposed by the features themselves.We call this behavior pareidolia, and the span of these directions the pareidolic subspace.On natural images, it holds most of the feature variance in DINOv2 and DINOv3 but little in DINO.This excess explains why DINOv2 and DINOv3, despite stronger dense features, fall far behind DINO in object emergence, the hallmark ability of self-supervised ViTs to identify the patches of an object on their own.Our experiments further show that scaling down their pareidolic subspaces steadily restores their ability to discover objects, so their object emergence is hindered rather than lost.These findings naturally lead to a training-free calibration: Pareidolia Subspace Calibration(PSC) measures the pareidolic subspace only on a noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions.Across diverse object emergence tasks, PSC improves DINOv2 and DINOv3 by up to 31.7 CorLoc on object discovery, 30.2 maxF on saliency detection and 59.9~$\mathcal{J}$ on video object segmentation.To identify the cause of pareidolia, we trace it block by block and find that it forms in the middle blocks of every self-supervised model we examine but stays strong to the last block only in models trained with a patch-level loss; controlled training confirms that an image-level loss alone lets it fade.

title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
text: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
text: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.
