title: Depression and the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults: An integrative review
text: Objective: To analyze scientific evidence regarding the association between depression or depressive symptoms and the subsequent risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults without a previous diagnosis of dementia. Methods: An integrative literature review with a descriptive and analytical approach was conducted using PubMed, employing search terms related to aging, depression, and cognitive outcomes. A total of 416 records were identified, of which 27 underwent full-text assessment, resulting in the inclusion of 11 studies published between 2025 and 2026. Results: The studies demonstrated an association between depression and an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia, with variations related to the onset, persistence, and trajectory of depressive symptoms. The coexistence of insomnia, physical frailty, and loneliness was also associated with greater cognitive vulnerability. However, methodological heterogeneity, the predominance of observational studies, and the possibility of reverse causation limited causal inferences. Conclusions: Depression represents an important marker of cognitive vulnerability in aging, highlighting the need for integrated assessment of mental health, cognitive function, and functional status, alongside longitudinal follow-up. Further studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationship and underlying mechanisms involved in this association.

title: Home-Based Intelligent Integrated Healthcare for Elderly Well-Being
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: RECRUITING] This implementation study evaluates the effectiveness of the Home-based intelligent and integrated healthcare (HIIH) model in improving health outcomes and well-being among community-dwelling older adults. The HIIH system integrates AI, IoT, Digital Twin, and Health technologies to support proactive, personalized and continuous home-based care. The study examines physical , oral, psychological and social health outcomes as well as healthcare utilization and digital engagement.

title: Stereophotogrammetry of the Torso in Healthy Individuals and Patients With Scoliosis, Chest Wall Deformations, or Obesity
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] Background: \- Stereophotogrammetry (SP) uses four sets of digital cameras to generate a three-dimensional computer image. Unlike other types of evaluations which require radiation, SP only uses computer images to learn more about physical deformities such as scoliosis or about the placement of fat on the body. To refine the SP process, researchers are interested in collecting images and body data from individuals with skeletal structural problems such as scoliosis or chest wall deformities, individuals who are overweight or obese, and healthy volunteers. Objectives: \- To use stereophotogrammetry to study different individual body types and refine existing imaging techniques. Eligibility: \- Individuals at least 2 years of age who have spine, rib, or chest wall deformities; are overweight or obese (body mass index greater than 25); or are healthy volunteers. Design: * Participants will be screened with a physical examination and medical history. The physical examination will include measurements of range of motion and joint mobility, torso width and length, and other observational data. * Healthy volunteers and participants in the obesity group will also have bioelectric spectroscopy (bioimpedance), which uses an additional machine to measure how fat is spread in different parts of the body. * After the physical examination has been completed, participants will have SP photographs taken. Participants will be asked to remove all clothing from the torso, stand with arms raised at the center of four cameras, and remain still while several images are taken. A complete image takes less than 1 second. * Participants with spine or rib deformities, or who are in the obesity group, may also volunteer to return for followup SP imaging, once a year for 5 years, to study progress over time.

title: Effect of Acupuncture on Mild to Moderate Active Crohn's Disease
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: RECRUITING] To observe the clinical effect of acupuncture on Crohn's disease (CD) and its influence on brain function activity and the TRY-KYN metabolism level, and to screen the brain image markers of acupuncture on CD

title: Natural History of Coronavirus Disease (COVID-19) in Systemic Autoimmune Diseases
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] Background: Viral infections such as COVID-19 may lead to flare-ups in people with systemic autoimmune diseases (SAD). These infections may also change the function of their immune system and/or cause problems with their blood vessels. Researchers want to learn how people with SAD respond to treatments or vaccines for COVID-19. Objective: To understand how COVID-19 affects inflammation, the immune system, and blood vessels in adults and children with autoimmune diseases. Eligibility: People ages 15 and older who have been diagnosed with an autoimmune disease or are a healthy volunteer Design: Participants will have a screening visit. This will include: Medical history and physical exam EKG Chest x-ray COVID-19 test. A swab will be put in the participant s nose or the back of their mouth. Blood and urine tests Participants will be placed into 1 of 4 groups: 1. Those with previously documented COVID-19 infection or COVID vaccination 2. Those with a recently known COVID-19 exposure or vaccination 3. Those with no known COVID-19 exposure or vaccination 4. Those who developed an acute COVID-19 infection Depending on their group, participants will have 1 to 5 more visits. These will occur over 12 to 18 months. Visits may include: FDG PET/CT scan. Participants will lie in a doughnut-shaped machine. The machine creates pictures of the body. For the scan, they will have a radioactive substance injected into their arm through an IV. Kidney function tests Non-invasive vascular studies test. These tests are similar to what it feels like to have blood pressure checked....

title: Predicting Extubation Failure Using Machine Learning
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] The goal of this observational study is to predict who will have problems after the breathing tube is removed. Taking out the tube is called extubation, and having these problems is called extubation failure. Participants are adults in the intensive care unit (ICU) who use a breathing machine (ventilator). The main questions it aims to answer are: * How well can computer tools predict problems in the 7 days after the tube is removed? * Which information, such as age or blood tests, matters most for the prediction? Extubation failure means the participant needs the tube put back in, needs a surgical opening in the neck to help breathing, or dies. Researchers will use machine learning to build the computer tools. Machine learning is a type of artificial intelligence that finds patterns in data. Researchers will compare five types of machine learning to see which works best. They will build the tools with participants from Dr. Cipto Mangunkusumo National General Hospital in Jakarta. They will test the tools with participants from Universitas Indonesia Hospital in Depok. Participants get their usual care. Doctors do not use the tools to make treatment decisions. Researchers will: * Record health information about participants before the tube is removed * Follow participants for 7 days after the tube is removed

title: Endothelial Cell Dysfunction in Pulmonary Hypertension
text: [Fase: PHASE1; Estado: COMPLETED] This study will examine and test healthy volunteers and patients with pulmonary hypertension to try to learn more about the disease and find better ways to detect, treat, and, if possible, slow progression. Pulmonary hypertension is a rare blood vessel disorder of the lung in which the pressure in the pulmonary artery (the blood vessel that leads from the heart to the lungs) rises above normal levels and may become life-threatening. Normal volunteers and patients with pulmonary hypertension 18 years of age and older may be eligible for this study. All candidates are screened with a review of their medical records. Normal volunteers also have a medical history, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram (heart ultrasound), and pulmonary function test, in which the subject breathes in and out of a tube that measures lung volume, mechanics and function. All participants undergo the following tests and procedures: * Echocardiogram to measure heart function and blood pressure in the lungs. A small probe held against the chest uses sound waves to obtain pictures of the heart. * Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to evaluate the heart's pumping action. Subjects lie on a stretcher that slides into a long, tube-shaped scanner. The machine uses a magnetic field and radio waves to obtain images of the heart. * 6-minute walk to measure how far the subject can walk in 6 minutes. Subjects walk around the hospital for 6 minutes at a comfortable pace. * Exercise testing to measure the ability to exercise and the subject's oxygen levels during exercise. Subjects exercise on a bike or treadmill while the oxygen and carbon dioxide they breathe are measured using a small device placed in the mouth. * Right heart catheterization to measure pressure in the heart and lungs. A small catheter (plastic tube) is placed in an arm vein. A longer catheter called a central line is placed in a deeper vein in the neck or just below the neck, or in the leg or arm. A long, thin catheter that measures blood pressure directly is then inserted into the vein and advanced through the chambers of the heart into the lung artery to measure all the pressures in the heart and obtain blood samples. * Genetic and protein studies. DNA, RNA, and proteins from blood samples are studied for genes and proteins that might predict the development or progression of pulmonary hypertension. In addition to the above, patients whose pulmonary hypertension was caused by a blood vessel injury undergo the tests described below. The right heart catheter inserted for the catheterization procedure remains in place to obtain measurements of the effects of nitric oxide and nitrite in the following procedures: * Inhalation of nitric oxide (a gas naturally produced by cells lining arteries) at 30-minute intervals to examine its effect on lung and heart pressures. * Inhalation of aerosolized nitrite at 5-minute intervals to measure its effects on lung and heart pressures. * Inhalation of nitric oxide for up to 24 hours to obtain multiple measurements of its effect on lung and heart pressures. * Blood draws for laboratory tests. In patients whose pulmonary hypertension was caused by a blood vessel injury, we also plan to follow response to standard therapy. After the initiation of standard therapy, we will restudy the same parameters (excluding NO and sodium nitrite studies) in these patients at approximately 4 months, and yearly for 5 years ...

title: Machine Learning to Analyze Facial Imaging, Voice and Spoken Language for the Capture and Classification of Cancer/Tumor Pain
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] Background: Cancer pain can have a very negative effect on people s daily lives. Researchers want to use machine learning to detect facial expressions and voice signals. They want to help people with cancer by creating a model to measure pain. They want the model to reflect diverse faces and facial expressions. Objective: To find out whether facial recognition technology can be used to classify pain in a diverse set of people with cancer. Also, to find out whether voice recognition technology can be used to assess pain. Eligibility: People ages 12 and older who are undergoing treatment for cancer Design: Participants will be screened with: Cancer history Information about their sex and skin type Information about their access to a smart phone and wireless internet Questions about their cancer pain Participants will have check-ins at the clinic and at home. These will occur over about 3 months. They will have 2-4 check-ins at the clinic. They will check in at home about 3 times per week. During check-ins, participants will answer questions and talk about their cancer pain. They will use a mobile phone or a computer with a camera and microphone to complete a questionnaire. They will record a video of themselves reading a 15-second passage of text and responding to a question. During the clinic check-ins, professional lighting, video equipment, and cameras will be used for the recordings. During remote check-ins, participants will be asked to complete the questionnaire and recordings alone. They should be in a quiet and bright room. The room should have a white wall or background.

title: Physiological Investigations of Movement Disorders
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: COMPLETED] Background: * Previous studies have given researchers information on how the brain controls movement, how people learn to make fine, skilled movements, and why some people have movement disorders. However, further research is needed to learn more about the causes of most movement disorders, such as Parkinson's disease. * By using small, specialized studies to evaluate people with movement disorders and compare them with healthy volunteers, researchers hope to learn more about the changes in the brain and possible causes of movement disorders. Objectives: * To better understand how the brain controls movement. * To learn more about movement disorders. * To train movement disorder specialists. Eligibility: * Individuals 18 years of age or older who have had a movement disorder diagnosed by a neurologist and are able to participate based on the specific requirements of the small study. * Healthy volunteers 18 years of age or older. Design: * Participants will have a screening visit with medical history, physical examination, and questionnaire to determine eligibility. Eligible participants will give consent to participate in up to seven additional outpatient visits for study procedures. The number of sessions and the procedures needed for participation depend on specific symptoms. * Participants must avoid drinking alcohol or caffeinated drinks (sodas, coffee, and tea) for at least 2 days (48 hours) before each session. * Potential studies may include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, functional MRI scans, electroencephalography, magnetoencephalography, transcranial magnetic stimulation, nerve and sensory stimulation, or movement and mental tasks during any of the above procedures. * This study does not provide treatment for movement disorders. Participants will not have to stop any treatment in order to participate.

title: Youth-Onset Type 2 Diabetes and Heart Disease: The Young at Heart Prospective Cohort Study
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Background: Type 2 diabetes is a disease that affects blood sugar levels. Complications can include heart and blood vessel (vascular) diseases. Rates of type 2 diabetes have tripled in children and young adults over the last 40 years. Vascular diseases are also increasing in young people. Objective: To learn more about factors, including type 2 diabetes, that may cause vascular disease in young people. Eligibility: People aged 12 to 25 years who (1) have type 2 diabetes; (2) are overweight but not diabetic; (3) or are lean and healthy. Biological parents are also needed. Design: Young participants will visit the NIH clinic once a year for up to 25 years. Each visit will take 4 days. Before each visit, participants will wear devices to track their sleep, activity, and blood sugar levels for 7 to 10 days. At each visit, participants will have tests including: Samples: They will provide blood, urine, and stool samples. Heart: They will ride a stationary bike for 6 minutes with stickers applied to their chest. Scans: They will lie on a bed that slides into a tube; the machine will take pictures of the inside of their body. Energy: They will wear a hood over their head to measure the air they breathe. Social stress: They will give a speech for 10 minutes to show their body s response to stress. Glucose: They will drink a sweet drink to see how their blood sugar changes. Biological parents will have 1 study visit. They will have blood tests. They will fill in questionnaires about their lifestyle and stress. ...

title: Interactive vs. Standard Video Education for Improving Outcomes in Hemodialysis Patients
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: COMPLETED] The goal of this clinical trial is to find out if educational videos-especially interactive ones-can help people on dialysis better manage their treatment. Researchers want to answer the following main questions: Can interactive or conventional video-based education help patients better understand and follow their treatment plan? Does this type of education improve patients' ability to control their weight changes between dialysis sessions? Does this type of education improve patients' activation? Is interactive video education more effective than regular (non-interactive) video education? What Will Happen in the Study: Adults on hemodialysis will take part in the study. They will be randomly assigned to one of three groups: Group A: Will receive 10 interactive educational video sessions (30 minutes each). Group B: Will receive the same videos but in a non-interactive format. Group C (Control Group): Will receive routine education normally given at the dialysis center. Videos will be watched on a web platform. Interactive videos include pop-up questions and scenario-based feedback. All participants will be followed up immediately, 1 month, and 3 months after the program ends. What Participants Will Do: Watch educational videos over several days (totaling 5 hours). Answer questions and engage in follow-up group discussions. Complete surveys about their knowledge, treatment adherence, and health behaviors. Get weighed before and after dialysis sessions to monitor fluid retention. This study aims to improve how dialysis patients manage their condition and to help healthcare providers design better educational tools.

title: Natural History of Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 7 (SCA7)
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] Background: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7) is a disease in which people have problems with coordination, balance, speech and vision. It is caused by a change in the ATXN7 gene. A mutation in this ATXN7 gene causes changes in eye cells, which can lead to vision loss. There is no cure for SCA7 but researchers are looking for possible treatments. Researchers need more information about SCA7. They want to collect vision and neurology related data from people with SCA7. They want to learn how and what changes in the eye and brain when the ATXN7 gene isn t working properly. Objective: To learn more about SCA7 and its progression. Eligibility: People ages 12 and older with SCA7. Design: Participants will be screened with medical history and genetic testing from a previous National Eye Institute study or their personal physician. Participants will have at least 7 visits over 5 years. They will have 2 visits during the first week of the study. Then they will be asked to come back every year for the next 5 years. Each visit will last several days and will include: * Medical and eye history * Several eye tests: some will include dilating the pupil with eye drops and taking photos or scans of the eyes. * Electroretinography (ERG): Participants will sit in the dark with their eyes patched for 30 minutes. After this, the patches will be removed and contact lenses put into the eyes. They will watch flashing lights and information will be recorded. * Neurological exams: Sensation, strength, coordination, reflexes, attention, memory, language, and other cognitive functions will be tested. * Brain MRI: They will lie in a machine that takes pictures of the brain. * Blood and urine tests * Optional skin biopsy: About 3 millimeters of skin will be removed for more research testing; this is half the size of a pencil eraser.

title: Photothermal programming of CRISPR-Cas12a enables NIR-II imaging-guided LRRC15 editing for cancer and arthritis therapy.
text: Overexpression of leucine-rich repeat-containing protein 15 (LRRC15) is closely linked to cancer progression and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), making it a promising therapeutic target. Conventional single-target approaches suffer from limited efficacy and off-target effects. Here, we develop a dual-targeting nanoplatform based on Ag2S@ZIF-8 nanoparticles (NPs) and modified with hyaluronic acid (HA) for imaging-guided photothermal-gene editing synergistic therapy against LRRC15-related diseases. The resulting Ag2S-crRNA/Cas12a@ZIF-8@HA (ACZH) NPs deliver CRISPR RNA (crRNA) for sequence-specific LRRC15 recognition, together with HSP70 promoter-driven Cas12a plasmids. Ag2S NPs enable real-time NIR-II fluorescence imaging and generate localized hyperthermia (>42°C) that activates the HSP70 promoter to induce Cas12a expression and subsequent LRRC15 editing. In breast and lung cancer xenograft models, ACZH NPs achieve tumor inhibition rates of 81.37% and 82.5%, respectively; in an RA model, they reduce joint inflammation, prevent cartilage erosion, and promote bone repair. These findings offer a safe and effective strategy for LRRC15-related diseases.

title: [Modern treatments for hemoglobinopathies in adults].
text: Hemoglobinopathies are associated with lifelong multimorbidity. In addition to optimized supportive care, disease-modifying and potentially (functionally) curative therapies are available. To review modern treatment options for thalassemias and sickle cell disease in adults. In beta-thalassemia, luspatercept targets ineffective erythropoiesis, while mitapivat, an oral pyruvate kinase activator, improves erythrocyte energy metabolism. Both therapies improve anemia and may reduce transfusion burden but are not curative. Through clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9)-mediated gene editing, exagamglogene autotemcel reactivates fetal hemoglobin production, enabling transfusion independence in beta-thalassemia and preventing recurrent severe vaso-occlusive crises in sickle cell disease. Hydroxyurea remains the cornerstone of pharmacological therapy for sickle cell disease. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and gene editing offer the possibility of a (functional) cure but require careful assessment of organ function, fertility, and treatment-related risks. Key advances include the optimization of established supportive therapies and the establishment of specialized centers providing access to potentially (functionally) curative treatments. In adults, the anticipated benefits, pre-existing irreversible organ damage, conditioning-related risks, potential long-term complications, and access to treatment must be carefully considered at an early stage. HINTERGRUND: Hämoglobinopathien verursachen eine lebenslange Multimorbidität. Neben optimierten Supportivtherapien stehen krankheitsmodifizierende und (funktionell) kurative Verfahren zur Verfügung. ZIEL DER ÜBERSICHT: Darstellung der modernen Therapieoptionen bei Thalassämien und Sichelzellkrankheiten bei Erwachsenen. Luspatercept greift bei der β‑Thalassämie an der ineffektiven Erythropoese an; Mitapivat verbessert als oraler Pyruvatkinaseaktivator den Energiestoffwechsel der Erythrozyten. Beide führen zu einer Verbesserung der Anämie und potenziell der Transfusionslast, sind aber nicht kurativ. Exagamglogen-Autotemcel reaktiviert durch CRISPR/Cas9-Editierung fetales Hämoglobin und erreicht eine Transfusionsfreiheit und/oder verhindert erneute schwere vasookklusive Krisen (CRISPR/Cas9 „clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9“). Bei der Sichelzellkrankheit bleibt Hydroxycarbamid die medikamentöse Basis. Eine allogene Stammzelltransplantation bzw. Geneditierung bietet die Option auf eine (funktionelle) Heilung, erfordert jedoch eine sorgfältige Organ‑, Fertilitäts- und Risikoevaluation. Die wesentlichen Neuerungen liegen in der Optimierung von (etablierten) Supportivtherapien unter Schaffung spezialisierter Kliniken mit Zugang zu (funktionell) kurativen Verfahren. Bei Erwachsenen müssen Nutzen, irreversible Organschäden, Konditionierungsrisiko, potenzielle Langzeitrisiken und Zugang rechtzeitig evaluiert werden.

title: Emerging CRISPR Technologies for Environmental Protection: From Genetic Engineering and Biosensing to Environmental Deployment.
text: Since its discovery, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) has revolutionized biomedical science and engineering with its ability to recognize and edit gene sequences with high specificity and precision. Despite the growing interest in using these capabilities to address environmental and sustainability challenges, the broader potential of CRISPR in environmental systems remains unexplored relative to its biomedical applications. Here, we provide a critical perspective on the emerging use of CRISPR for pollution management, ecological conservation, and environmental monitoring. Rather than viewing CRISPR solely as a gene-editing or biosensing technology, we consider both capabilities together to examine how advances in CRISPR engineering can translate into practical environmental solutions. We highlight the fundamental principles behind CRISPR-based editing and sensing and evaluate the challenges that constrain their transition from proof-of-concept experiments to field deployment, including off-target effects, delivery methods, ecological risks, and low sensitivity. Addressing these hurdles requires a multifaceted approach that integrates emerging technologies such as reversible CRISPR technology, amplification and cascade reactions, and machine learning, with strict regulatory oversight and rigorous risk assessments. This perspective identifies critical strengths, weaknesses, and research priorities for advancing CRISPR from laboratory technology toward robust tools for environmental applications.

title: Exosome-Based Nanocarriers for CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery Targeting katGMediated Drug Resistance in Tuberculosis.
text: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, remains a major global public health challenge, particularly because of the emergence and spread of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains. Mutations in the katG gene, which encodes the catalase- peroxidase enzyme responsible for isoniazid activation, are among the major molecular mechanisms associated with isoniazid resistance in M. tuberculosis. CRISPR-Cas9 technology has emerged as a potential approach for targeting bacterial genetic determinants of antimicrobial resistance. However, its therapeutic application against intracellular M. tuberculosis remains challenging because effective delivery must overcome both host-cell and bacterial barriers. Exosomes, a subclass of extracellular vesicles, have attracted considerable attention as potential biological nanocarriers because of their biocompatibility and capacity to transport nucleic acids and proteins between cells. This review examines the molecular mechanisms underlying isoniazid resistance, recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 technology, the potential applications of exosome-based delivery systems, and the major challenges associated with their development for tuberculosis treatment. Unlike reviews that discuss CRISPR-based antimicrobial strategies and extracellular vesicle-mediated delivery separately, this review integrates these approaches to examine their potential application in targeting katG-associated isoniazid resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The review further evaluates the theoretical potential of extracellular vesicle-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 delivery for mutation- specific targeting of katG-associated isoniazid resistance, while considering the biological barriers that may limit its therapeutic application. Particular emphasis is placed on the need for mutation- specific correction rather than complete disruption of the katG gene, because loss of functional KatG activity can itself contribute to isoniazid resistance. However, the proposed exosomemediated CRISPR-Cas9 strategy has not yet been experimentally validated for targeting intracellular *M. tuberculosis*. Further in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo investigations are required to establish its delivery efficiency, mutation-specific editing feasibility, safety, and potential therapeutic effectiveness.

title: Neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease: from glial heterogeneity and gut-brain immune crosstalk to precision therapeutic strategies.
text: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, α-synuclein pathology, and a broad spectrum of motor and non-motor manifestations. Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as an important component of PD pathobiology; however, traditional frameworks have largely focused on canonical inflammatory pathways and simplified classifications of glial activation, which do not fully capture the spatial, temporal, and functional heterogeneity of immune responses in PD. Emerging evidence from single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, together with studies of peripheral immunity and the microbiota-gut-brain axis, indicates that PD-associated inflammation is dynamic, context dependent, and systemically integrated. In this review, we critically synthesize current evidence on microglial and astrocytic activation, bidirectional glial crosstalk, α-synuclein-inflammation feedback loops, and the selective vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons. We further discuss region- and disease-stage-dependent glial states, systemic immune and gut-brain interactions, and inflammation-associated microRNAs as potential links between peripheral and central inflammatory responses. Therapeutically, we evaluate conventional anti-inflammatory strategies alongside emerging RNA-based interventions and targeted delivery approaches. Particular attention is given to the persistent translational gap between robust preclinical efficacy and limited disease-modifying benefit in patients, including limitations related to disease models, therapeutic timing, biomarker availability, patient heterogeneity, and blood-brain barrier penetration. Collectively, current evidence supports a shift from broad suppression of inflammation toward biomarker-guided, disease-stage-specific, and cell- or pathway-selective immunomodulation in PD.

title: A Spatial and Single-Cell Atlas of Early Human Alveolar Bone Healing.
text: To construct an integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlas of early human alveolar bone healing to delineate cellular heterogeneity and intercellular communication during the proliferative phase. Granulation tissue was harvested from the extraction sockets of seven healthy patients 4 weeks post extraction. Six patients provided samples for single-cell RNA sequencing and one for spatial transcriptomics. Bioinformatic analyses characterised cellular subpopulations, pseudotemporal relationships and predicted communication networks. Immunofluorescence assessed spatial proximity between fibroblast and endothelial cell populations. Fifteen major cell populations and two transcriptionally distinct fibroblast subsets were identified: WNT5A+ fibroblasts were associated with inflammatory responses and immune cell recruitment, whereas OGN+ fibroblasts were linked to extracellular matrix organisation, tissue remodelling and ossification. Macrophage, T-cell and endothelial subsets were also identified. OGN+ fibroblasts showed extensive interactions with immune and endothelial subsets, including CXCL12-CXCR4. Spatial transcriptomics revealed heterogeneous distributions of major cell populations and their subsets. Immunofluorescence further indicated spatial proximity between CXCL12-expressing fibroblasts and CXCR4+ endothelial cells. This atlas characterises cellular and spatial heterogeneity during early human alveolar bone healing and highlights fibroblast-associated interactions for future functional investigation.

title: An SPP1-Associated Macrophage State Marks Lesion-Centred Inflammatory Persistence During Subacute Spinal Cord Injury.
text: Persistent subacute neuroinflammation limits tissue repair after spinal cord injury (SCI), yet how macrophage state heterogeneity is organized within lesion-centered inflammatory niches remains unclear. We integrated time-resolved mouse single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics with trajectory analysis, regulatory network inference, ligand activity analysis, exploratory in silico Spp1 perturbation, and interpretable machine learning, followed by tissue-level and donor-recipient validation. Time-resolved profiling revealed early neutrophil and monocyte recruitment, subsequent macrophage accumulation, and delayed microglial activation. Macrophage subclustering resolved seven injury-responsive states comprising inflammatory, transitional, tissue-associated, lipid-associated, SPP1-associated, repair-associated, and homeostatic programs. Among these states, SPP1_Mac expanded prominently, peaked at 7 days post-injury, and retained marked inflammatory activity. Spatial mapping localized the SPP1_Mac signature and focal Spp1 expression to lesion-centered regions within a broader Cd44-enriched cellular territory. Regulatory network, ligand activity, communication, and machine learning analyses prioritized SPP1-associated signaling within this state-niche organization. Injured spinal cords showed increased lesion-associated SPP1 and CD44 expression and enrichment of SPP1 within IBA1-positive myeloid regions. In a BV2-to-RAW264.7 donor-recipient system, donor cell Spp1 silencing attenuated recipient cell CD44 and CD86 expression, the proportion of F4/80⁺CD86⁺ cells, and IL-1β and TNF-α secretion following conditioned medium transfer. Together, these findings support a state-niche-communication framework in which SPP1_Mac represents a prominent cellular feature associated with lesion-centered inflammatory persistence during subacute SCI, providing a biological foundation for further stage-informed investigation of the post-SCI inflammatory microenvironment.

title: Selective suppression and biasing of chemokine receptors CCR9 and ACKR4 through targeting CCL25 with de novo miniproteins.
text: Chemokines and their receptors mediate cell migration and coordinate immune responses, while dysregulation can lead to inflammation. Therapeutic modulation of the chemokine signaling axis has proven difficult. Most drug discovery efforts target the receptors, whereas natural regulatory mechanisms modulate immune responses by directly binding to or modifying the chemokine ligands. Despite this insight, development of effective chemokine-directed modulators has remained elusive. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer an unprecedented opportunity to produce high-affinity binders that efficiently block protein-protein interactions. We implemented a computational workflow leveraging the BindCraft platform to generate miniprotein binders against CCL25, the chemokine ligand for the receptors CCR9 and ACKR4, and implicated in inflammatory bowel diseases. The unbiased development results in several miniproteins designed to block the receptor N-terminus from wrapping the chemokine and preventing productive engagement. Thus, these proteins suppress CCL25-mediated effector coupling and halt MOLT-4 lymphoblast migration. Another class of miniprotein, represented by VUP25111, is predicted to bind CCL25 along the chemokine β1 strand and retained receptor binding. This complex inhibited arrestin recruitment to CCR9, but not to ACKR4, indicating receptor specificity. Additionally, G protein recruitment to CCR9 was unimpeded by VUP25111, suggesting that the miniprotein biased the native agonist towards G proteins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of differentially targeting CCL25 to suppress CCR9 signaling and new tools to resolve the structural basis of chemokine receptor activation and bias.

title: Dynamic Commercial Silicones Toward Sustainable, Task-Reconfigurable Suction Gripping.
text: Silicone suction cups are widely used in industrial automation for scalable, high-throughput handling, yet conventional designs are restricted to limited geometries. Advancing toward gripping is essential to transition robotics from single-task execution to versatile handling across dynamic environments but presents a fundamental materials challenge: balancing the properties of on-demand geometric reconfigurability with operational strength and elasticity. Existing universal grippers typically utilize composite materials that couple shape adaptation and gripping operation within a single cycle, introducing critical performance trade-offs in force, speed, and preload requirements while adding structural complexity that together hinder broad industrial adoption. To address this, we establish a versatile post-fabrication strategy that transforms commercial silicone thermosets into dynamic silicone materials via catalyst-mediated exchange of intrinsic siloxane bonds. This enables scalable transformation of industrial suction cups to reconfigurable grippers that reconfigure shapes at elevated temperatures while preserving high gripping performance via thermosetting properties at ambient temperatures. We demonstrate an all-silicone, hierarchically structured suction gripper combining a reconfigurable load-bearing body with a compliant sealing interface towards sustainable, task-reconfigurable gripping, ensuring infrastructure compatibility while delivering rapid suction actuation (50 ms) following thermal reconfiguration (e.g., ∼30 min at 140°C), efficient load capacity (27 kPa), and zero-preload attachment across diverse environments.

title: Laboratory medicine 2050: from testing to health intelligence network, a vision from the IFCC Emerging Technologies Division.
text: Laboratory medicine is undergoing a profound transformation driven by advances in artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and data interoperability. By 2050, laboratories may evolve from analytical testing facilities into an interconnected health intelligence capable of translating biological, digital, and environmental data into more personalized, preventive, and sustainable healthcare solutions. Building on previous foresight analysis conducted by the IFCC Emerging Technologies Division (ETD), global healthcare outlook reports, and expert-informed horizon scanning, this paper explores ten megatrends that may shape laboratory medicine by mid-century. These include precision multi-omics, AI-supported diagnostics, distributed healthcare models, patient-owned data ecosystems, digital twins, convergence of imaging and laboratory medicine, population-wide prevention strategies, regenerative therapies, sustainability imperatives, and workforce transformation. Collectively, these developments represent a paradigm shift from data generation to data interpretation, positioning laboratories as trusted nodes within the health intelligence network connecting patients, clinicians, and healthcare systems. The integration of automation with advanced multi-omics technologies, including robotic liquid handling, autonomous LC-MS/MS platforms, spatial proteomics, and real-time metabolomics, will accelerate the transition toward precision and planetary health. Four exploratory scenarios illustrate plausible trajectories for laboratory medicine in 2050. The Hyper-Intelligent Laboratory explores the implications of self-learning systems and advanced analytics capable of supporting earlier disease prediction and intervention. The Sustainable and Regenerative Laboratory illustrates how environmental stewardship and diagnostic excellence may converge within circular healthcare ecosystems. The Patient-in-the-Loop Revolution examines a future in which citizens become active stewards of their health data and participants in healthcare decision-making. The Spacefaring Laboratory extends this reflection beyond Earth, illustrating how extreme environments may accelerate innovation in autonomous diagnostics, sustainability, and human health monitoring. By 2050, laboratory medicine could serve as a central intelligence layer within healthcare systems, transforming biological signals into actionable knowledge. Achieving this vision will require scientific innovation, regulatory adaptability, equitable access, ethical governance, sustainability, and a future-ready workforce.

title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
text: Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

By 2050, laboratory medicine could serve as a central intelligence layer within healthcare systems, transforming biological signals into actionable knowledge. Achieving this vision will require scientific innovation, regulatory adaptability, equitable access, ethical governance, sustainability, and a future-ready workforce.

title: Vitamin E-Engineered Anti-Inflammatory Lipid Nanoparticles for Safer mRNA Delivery.
text: Great strides have been achieved in lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mediated mRNA delivery. However, traditional LNPs can induce undesirable side effects such as inflammatory reactions. Oxidative stress damage arising from ionizable lipids within LNPs is regarded as a major underlying cause of these adverse effects. Herein, we propose incorporating endogenous vitamin E (VE) into the tail moiety of commercial ionizable lipids to improve biosafety. Proof-of-concept investigations using SM-102-derived W3 confirm that this endogenous antioxidant modification substantially mitigates the inflammatory toxicity of mRNA-loaded LNPs. Following intravenous administration, W3 LNPs markedly decrease the levels of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, demonstrating an improved safety profile compared to SM-102 LNPs. Further analysis reveals that W3 LNPs significantly reduce intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, alleviate oxidative stress damage, thereby inhibiting the activation of key inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB. Of note, the optimized formulation, sW3 LNPs enable efficient mRNA delivery to the spleen, with stronger antitumor efficacy and higher safety than SM-102 LNPs. In summary, W3 lipid confers minimal inflammatory adverse effects while preserving excellent delivery capability, which indicates that the VE-engineered LNPs possess great potential to serve as powerful and multifunctional platforms for next-generation mRNA therapeutics.

title: Efficient Delivery of PIKFYVE mRNA-LNPs Rescues Lysosomal Dysfunction in PIKFYVE Knockout Lens Epithelial Cells.
text: PIKFYVE deficiency has been implicated in congenital cataract, and gene therapy based on PIKFYVE mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) represents a potential therapeutic strategy. We developed an SM-102-based LNP delivery system encapsulating human PIKFYVE mRNA with a long coding sequence, thereby overcoming the payload capacity limitations of conventional viral vectors. To evaluate this LNP system, we identified differentially expressed lysosomal genes via RNA sequencing and investigated its biocompatibility, transfection efficiency, and capacity to rescue lysosomal defects in PIKFYVE knockout lens epithelial cells (PIKFYVE-/-SRA01/04). Additionally, in vivo localized expression was assessed using firefly luciferase (FLuc) mRNA-LNPs administered via subconjunctival, intracameral, intravitreal, and subretinal injections in female C57BL/6J mice. The mRNA-LNP system exhibited high cytocompatibility and over 99% transfection efficiency in vitro. Treatment dose-dependently increased expression of PIKFYVE, partially rescuing lysosome-related transcripts and attenuating vacuolization in PIKFYVE-/-SRA01/04 cells. This functional restoration enabled the deficient cells to regain a nearly normal morphology, with the intracellular vacuolar area reduced from 14.29% to 7.98%. Furthermore, in vivo imaging demonstrated localized FLuc expression upon mRNA-LNP delivery across four ocular administration routes. This study demonstrates that the PIKFYVE mRNA SM-102-LNP delivery system effectively restores protein expression and rescues lysosomal dysfunction in PIKFYVE-/-SRA01/04 cells. LNP-mediated mRNA replacement represents a practicable, translatable strategy for PIKFYVE-associated cataracts. We constructed a PIKFYVE mRNA-LNP platform that restored protein expression, ameliorated lysosomal dysregulation, and significantly improved cellular morphology. These findings provide a proof-of-concept for an mRNA-LNP therapeutic approach to ophthalmic disorders.

title: Advancing Digital Nursing and Midwifery Leadership: Policy Implementation Across the World Health Organisation European Region.
text: To examine how national nursing and midwifery leaders implement the International Council of Nursing position statement on digital transformation and the World Health Organisation Digital health action plan for the European Region (2023-2030), and factors influencing digital health policy implementation. Sequential mixed methods. Phase one comprised an online survey of national nursing and midwifery leaders responsible for digital health policy implementation across all 53 WHO European Region member states. Survey items examined awareness and use of international digital health policies, leadership structures, and workforce readiness (see supplementary file). Phase two involved three online focus groups with survey participants to explore findings in greater depth. Survey data were analysed descriptively; qualitative data from focus groups and free-text survey were analysed using thematic analysis, and the findings integrated during interpretation. We identified four integrated themes (from 24 survey responses, 19 countries and 6 focus group participants): (1) Awareness and integration of digital health policy, (2) The nature of nursing and midwifery leadership in digital health, (3) Workforce capability and capacity, and (4) Infrastructure and systems readiness. A cross-cutting theme of person-centred care in a digital environment underpinned all findings. Participants reported variable awareness of WHO/ICN policies, limited visibility and legitimacy of nursing and midwifery leadership roles in digital governance, gaps in digital competencies and leadership pathways, and ongoing challenges with system interoperability and infrastructure maturity. Other concerns were digital exclusion and risks to relational care when digital systems are implemented without nursing and midwifery involvement. Structural, educational, and governance barriers limit national nursing and midwifery leaders' influence on digital health policy implementation across the WHO European Region. Strengthening leadership roles, digital policy literacy, and nursing and midwifery involvement in digital governance is essential to enable effective, equitable, and person-centred digital health transformation. What problem did the study address? The study addressed the limited understanding of how national nursing and midwifery leaders engage with and implement international digital health policies across the WHO European Region. Despite global policy recognising nurses and midwives as central to digital transformation, little empirical evidence exists on their role, influence, and capacity within national digital health governance, leadership, and implementation. What were the main findings? The study found variable awareness and inconsistent integration of WHO and ICN digital health policies across countries. Nursing and midwifery leaders reported limited visibility, legitimacy, and representation within digital governance and procurement structures, alongside gaps in formal digital leadership roles and career pathways. Persistent challenges related to workforce digital capability, system interoperability, and infrastructure maturity were identified. Participants consistently emphasised the importance of person-centred, relational care and highlighted risks of digital exclusion when digital systems are implemented without nursing and midwifery input. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The findings are relevant to national nursing and midwifery leaders, policymakers, educators, regulators, and health system planners across the WHO European Region. The research will inform digital health policy development, leadership role design, education and workforce planning, and governance structures. It also has wider relevance for international health systems seeking to embed nursing and midwifery leadership in digital transformation to support equitable, safe, and person-centred care. This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design,

title: Wearable Digital Health Technologies for Enhancing Patient Safety in Hospitals: A Scoping Review.
text: Wearable digital health technologies (WDHTs) have emerged as promising tools to advance patient safety. Existing studies prioritize technical verification and single-scenario application, while comprehensive synthesis of inpatient safety deployment remains insufficient. To clarify the application of WDHTs for inpatient safety and identify implementation enablers and barriers within the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework. A scoping review. Evidence was systematically retrieved and thematically integrated following SEIPS. Six electronic databases were searched from database inception to August 31, 2026. Forty-four studies involving 51,609 participants from 20 countries were included. WDHTs support continuous realtime monitoring across six patient safety scenarios, with evidence of earlier detection of physiological decline and risk-stratified prevention than intermittent assessment. Improvements in clinical outcomes were observed mainly in targeted high-risk populations. Implementation outcomes are jointly determined by work-system factors covering personnel, tasks, technology, organization and environment, while human-centred design, standardized training, interdisciplinary collaboration and complete digital infrastructure facilitate stable clinical adoption. WDHTs provide opportunities for the construction of proactive inpatient safety systems. Heterogeneity in clinical effectiveness does not simply stem from hardware limitations, but arises from complex interactions within the entire healthcare socio-technical ecosystem. Future translation should shift from isolated device optimization to the coordinated integration of digital equipment, clinical workflows and institutional safety policies, as well as the development of unified assessment criteria, the realization of hospital information system interoperability and the explicit clarification of the requirements for nursing roles, workflow integration and digital competence. This review constructs a socio-technical analytical framework to support holistic implementation and provides actionable references for clinical nurses, hospital managers, technology developers and patients. PRISMA-ScR guidelines. No Patient or Public Involvement.

title: Laboratory medicine 2050: from testing to health intelligence network, a vision from the IFCC Emerging Technologies Division.
text: Laboratory medicine is undergoing a profound transformation driven by advances in artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and data interoperability. By 2050, laboratories may evolve from analytical testing facilities into an interconnected health intelligence capable of translating biological, digital, and environmental data into more personalized, preventive, and sustainable healthcare solutions. Building on previous foresight analysis conducted by the IFCC Emerging Technologies Division (ETD), global healthcare outlook reports, and expert-informed horizon scanning, this paper explores ten megatrends that may shape laboratory medicine by mid-century. These include precision multi-omics, AI-supported diagnostics, distributed healthcare models, patient-owned data ecosystems, digital twins, convergence of imaging and laboratory medicine, population-wide prevention strategies, regenerative therapies, sustainability imperatives, and workforce transformation. Collectively, these developments represent a paradigm shift from data generation to data interpretation, positioning laboratories as trusted nodes within the health intelligence network connecting patients, clinicians, and healthcare systems. The integration of automation with advanced multi-omics technologies, including robotic liquid handling, autonomous LC-MS/MS platforms, spatial proteomics, and real-time metabolomics, will accelerate the transition toward precision and planetary health. Four exploratory scenarios illustrate plausible trajectories for laboratory medicine in 2050. The Hyper-Intelligent Laboratory explores the implications of self-learning systems and advanced analytics capable of supporting earlier disease prediction and intervention. The Sustainable and Regenerative Laboratory illustrates how environmental stewardship and diagnostic excellence may converge within circular healthcare ecosystems. The Patient-in-the-Loop Revolution examines a future in which citizens become active stewards of their health data and participants in healthcare decision-making. The Spacefaring Laboratory extends this reflection beyond Earth, illustrating how extreme environments may accelerate innovation in autonomous diagnostics, sustainability, and human health monitoring. By 2050, laboratory medicine could serve as a central intelligence layer within healthcare systems, transforming biological signals into actionable knowledge. Achieving this vision will require scientific innovation, regulatory adaptability, equitable access, ethical governance, sustainability, and a future-ready workforce.

title: Cysteinyl leukotriene profiles in obstructive and non-obstructive feline lower urinary tract disease.
text: Feline lower urinary tract disease is a complex syndrome characterized by high recurrence rates, and standard treatments targeting the cyclooxygenase pathway often lack efficacy. This suggests that alternative inflammatory mechanisms are involved in the pathology. This study aimed to investigate the role of the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and its byproducts, cysteinyl leukotrienes, along with the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-18, in the pathophysiology of obstructive and non-obstructive feline lower urinary tract disease phenotypes. Serum and urine samples from 60 male cats (20 obstructive, 20 non-obstructive, and 20 healthy controls) were analyzed. Both disease phenotypes showed significantly elevated serum and urinary concentrations of leukotrienes and interleukin-18 compared to the healthy controls. The obstructive group exhibited a massive localized inflammatory burden, characterized by significantly higher urinary leukotriene and interleukin-18 levels. In contrast, the non-obstructive group presented a more prominent systemic inflammatory load, highlighted by elevated serum leukotriene B4 concentrations. An explainable artificial intelligence classification model achieved an 85 percent overall accuracy in differentiating the clinical phenotypes. The model identified elevated urinary interleukin-18 as the primary predictor for obstructive cases, and increased serum leukotriene B4 as the key indicator for non-obstructive cases. The 5-lipoxygenase pathway is concurrently activated and serves as a critical driver within the inflammatory cascade of feline lower urinary tract disease. While these robust findings pave the way for future interventional trials, comprehensive longitudinal research remains essential to definitively isolate their exact cellular origins and fully establish their clinical translation.

title: Preoperative Prediction of Lymphovascular Invasion in Breast Cancer Using MRI-Based Radiomics: a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis.
text: Lymphovascular invasion (LVI) is a major adverse prognostic factor in breast cancer, associated with increased risk of nodal and distant metastasis. It is typically confirmed on histopathological examination of surgical specimens, while reliable preoperative assessment remains limited due to the constraints of core needle biopsy. This meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic value of MRI radiomics in detecting LVI in breast cancer patients. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted. Eligible studies were studies developing radiomics-based predictive models using machine learning techniques, and studies using clinical-only models were excluded. SROC model curves were implemented using Reitsma's bivariate model. The pooled effect size was analyzed using the inverse-variance method. Publication bias was assessed using Deeks' funnel plot. The methodological quality was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool, the Radiomics Quality Score (RQS) and the METhodological RadiomICs Score (METRICS). This study was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251186235). 23 studies published from 2019 to 2025 were included in the review. Seventeen studies (n=1,668) were included in the SROC analysis, yielding an AUC of 0.83 (95% CI 0.80-0.85), with pooled sensitivity of 0.73 and specificity of 0.80. The pooled AUC analysis including all 23 studies (n=1,902), was 0.78 (95% CI 0.75-0.81), with moderate heterogeneity (I²=33.6%). Externally validated models showed higher sensitivity than internally validated models (0.83 vs. 0.62, p=0.02), while performance did not differ significantly by feature extraction software, MRI field strength or segmentation region. Deeks' funnel plot showed no statistically significant evidence of publication bias (p=0.49). MRI-based radiomics show promising diagnostic performance for preoperative prediction of LVI. This is relevant in the neoadjuvant era, where treatment response may obscure histopathologic evidence of LVI and mask an important adverse prognostic factor. Prospective studies with robust external validation are needed.

title: Evolution of Research Topics in Arthroplasty: A Machine Learning Analysis of Over 10,000 Journal of Arthroplasty Publications (2005 to 2026).
text: The Journal of Arthroplasty (JOA) is the leading peer-reviewed outlet for arthroplasty research. As volume expands, narrative review cannot efficiently characterize this literature. We applied a transformer-based topic modeling framework to all English-language JOA abstracts indexed in PubMed (2005 through May 2026). In total, 10,597 abstracts were encoded. Temporal trends across complete calendar years (2005 to 2025) were assessed by ordinary least-squares regression with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, classifying topics as Emerging, Hot, Stable, or Cold; partial-year 2026 was descriptive only. Slopes carry 95% confidence intervals (CI), were re-estimated by negative binomial regressions, and clustering was repeated across eight parameter and seed configurations. We identified 83 research topics; 41.0% of documents were unclustered, so topic-level findings describe the clustered 59.0% of the corpus. We classified 36 topics as Emerging, 31 as Stable, and 16 as Cold. There was no topic that met Hot's criteria, because every topic with a significant positive slope also concentrated at least 60% of publications in the most recent decade. Fastest-growing were knee-specific patient-reported outcome measures (+0.199% per year, 95% CI 0.158 to 0.241) and periprosthetic joint infection (+0.166%); an observational-study reporting-language cluster also grew (+0.189%), reflecting reporting style, not clinical content. Steepest declines were primary total hip arthroplasty technique (-0.497% per year, 95% CI -0.574 to -0.419), case reports, cup orientation, and bearing surfaces. Trend direction was concordant in every configuration in which a theme was recovered. Over two decades, published emphasis in the JOA shifted from implant-centered biomechanical investigation toward outcomes-driven, technology-enabled, and value-based science, tracking payment reform, registry infrastructure, and new technology. These findings map where investigation is published rather than where clinical importance resides; declining topics reflect advances in implant design and technique, not resolved questions.

title: Choosing the Right AI Model for Uveal Melanoma From Detection to Prognosis.
text: Ocular oncology sits in an unusual position for medical artificial intelligence (AI), imaging heavy and multimodal by nature, but constrained by the rarity of the tumours it treats. Uveal melanoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, accounts for approximately 7095 new cases worldwide each year. Choroidal naevi are present in approximately 5% of the white population aged 40 and over, of which roughly 1 in 8845 transforms into melanoma each year, leaving a large benign population within which a small number of melanomas must not be missed. This narrative review follows the uveal melanoma clinical pathway through detection, diagnosis and prognosis, asking at each stage which class of AI model the evidence supports. A structured PubMed search returned 176 unique records, from which 29 primary studies were included, 17 (59%) published in 2025 or 2026. At detection, heavy self-supervised foundation models generalise well across imaging hardware but lack calibration to a clinical decision, while lightweight purpose-built classifiers show the opposite trade-off, and only one tool has been tested in a real referral workflow, quadrupling the odds of correct referral and cutting false positives 10-fold. At diagnosis, purpose-built convolutional classifiers calibrated to a referral threshold remain most mature, reaching 0.88 AUC on two cohorts, while multimodal fusion claims rest on a single 0.01 AUC gain. At prognosis, biomarker prediction from routine pathology reaches 0.93 to 0.99 AUC, survival prediction lags, only 7 of 29 studies (24%) had external validation and none of the tools has regulatory clearance.

title: Multimodal neuroimaging fusion with interpretable deep learning for speech motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.
text: Speech motor dysfunction affects approximately 90% of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), but multimodal neuroimaging models for prediction of this impairment remain limited. We developed MCTA-FusNet, an interpretable deep learning framework that integrates structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion MRI to predict speech motor dysfunction in PD. The model incorporates modality-specific encoders and a hierarchical triple-attention fusion mechanism to capture channel-, spatial-, and modality-level interactions. Using cross-domain transfer learning, MCTA-FusNet was first pretrained on the PPMI dataset (n = 400) to predict motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) and then fine-tuned on the FAH-SYSU dataset (n = 81) to predict speech motor dysfunction, indexed by vocal response magnitude (VRMag) to pitch perturbations. MCTA-FusNet outperformed all unimodal and multimodal models with transfer learning, achieving the lowest mean absolute error (1.388 ± 0.62) and highest correlation between predicted and observed VRMag (r = 0.731, p < 0.001). Interpretability analyses identified the superior temporal gyrus, primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, and supplementary motor area as key predictors, with greater coherence and phase synchrony between auditory and premotor regions significantly correlated with exaggerated VRMag. These findings establish a multimodal neuroimaging deep learning model for predicting and explaining speech motor dysfunction in PD, offering a novel framework with potential for symptom-specific monitoring and therapeutic intervention.

title: Bias in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency testing: observations from a real-world evidence study.
text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) affects an estimated 80,000-100,000 individuals in the US, yet fewer than 10% of those with severe genotypes are identified. Despite guidelines recommending testing all COPD patients, real-world testing rates remain low, and the clinical features driving testing decisions-and whether they validly identify AATD-are poorly characterized. We aimed to characterize who undergoes AATD testing in COPD and whether the features driving testing align with AATD-specific risk. Using de-identified EHR data from the EVERSANA database (2015-2023) covering >2.8 million COPD patients, using a combination of diagnosis codes, treatments and laboratory results patients were identified as AATD-positive (n = 5962), AATD-negative (n = 36,837), or AATD-unknown/untested (n = 2,223,048). After entropy balancing, demographic, clinical, and medication characteristics were compared across groups to identify features associated with testing and assess whether those features corresponded to positive identification. Only 1.7% of eligible COPD patients were tested. AATD-negative patients showed the highest prevalence of symptom-related diagnoses and COPD medication use, including shortness of breath (66% vs. 59% in positives) and albuterol use (73% vs. 64%). Emphysema-the feature most specific to AATD-was more prevalent among AATD-positive than AATD-negative patients (40% vs. 34%) and lowest among the untested (20%). Untested patients were older (53% ≥65), less symptomatic, and less intensively treated. Testing decisions appear driven by general symptom burden and severity rather than AATD-specific features like emphysema, systematically overlooking older, less symptomatic patients most likely to be missed. Machine learning-assisted candidate identification, reflex testing, and clinical decision support offer promising strategies to close this gap.

title: SurvStudio for browser-based survival analysis and model comparison in cancer genomics.
text: Molecular prognostic studies need to test whether markers improve prediction beyond clinical variables. This requires survival analysis, model comparison and checks of data coding and model assumptions, steps that existing tools often provide separately. We developed SurvStudio to combine survival analysis, marker assessment and machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) model comparison in one browser workspace. SurvStudio analyzes prepared clinical and molecular tables and compares models in the same test patients. Users install SurvStudio locally and run it through a web browser. We evaluated it using synthetic data and public cancer cohorts and compared its outputs with existing tools. Browser controls provided survival curves, clinically adjusted marker estimates, selection-stability summaries and comparison of nine prediction models. Fixed marker models could also be applied to external cohorts. Adding established isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation/1p/19q codeletion groups to age, sex and grade increased the concordance index (C) of the primary gradient-boosting model in two external glioma cohorts (ΔC = 0.118 and 0.084, 95% confidence intervals 0.067-0.171 and 0.035-0.136). The nine models had similar C values (0.632-0.646) in 381 breast cancer test patients. Input checks blocked specified invalid inputs and asked users to review predictors that may contain outcome information. In a public gastric cancer cohort, correct event coding changed estimated five-year survival from 89.3% to 52.2%. With SurvStudio, researchers can test whether molecular markers improve survival prediction beyond clinical variables and compare survival models in one browser workspace, while input checks and model diagnostics show whether the data and models support each result.

title: Physiologically Anchored Deep Learning Using Paired Sinus Rhythm and Premature Ventricular Contraction Electrocardiograms for Ventricular Ectopic Origin Localization.
text: Accurate non-invasive localization of premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) is important for preprocedural planning before catheter ablation. Most artificial intelligence-based electrocardiography (ECG) models evaluate ectopic beats without incorporating patient-specific baseline ventricular conduction patterns. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a patient-referenced, QRS-centered deep learning framework integrating paired sinus rhythm and PVC 12-lead ECG recordings for binary localization of ventricular ectopic origin and to assess the incremental value of sinus rhythm information compared with PVC-only input. This retrospective, single-center diagnostic accuracy study included 270 patients with paired sinus rhythm and PVC ECG recordings and procedurally confirmed ventricular ectopic origin. Raw ECG signals were segmented using annotated QRS boundaries and aligned using a QRS-centered strategy. Three input strategies were evaluated: paired PVC + sinus rhythm, PVC-only, and sinus rhythm-only. A 1-dimensional residual convolutional neural network (CNN) (1D ResNet) and a 2-dimensional time-domain CNN (2D time-domain CNN) were trained directly on raw ECG waveforms, with late-fusion probability averaging used for ensemble predictions. Performance was assessed using 5-fold patient-level cross-validation. The primary endpoint was the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). For paired PVC + sinus rhythm input, pooled AUROC values were 0.753 for the 1D ResNet, 0.743 for the 2D time-domain CNN, and 0.762 for the late-fusion ensemble, with no statistically significant differences among architectures. In the cross-input comparison, ensemble AUROC was 0.762 for paired PVC + sinus rhythm, 0.731 for PVC-only, and 0.551 for sinus rhythm-only input. Paired PVC + sinus rhythm significantly outperformed PVC-only input (DeLong P = .0313), whereas sinus rhythm alone showed limited discrimination. Patient-specific sinus rhythm information provided incremental discriminatory value when combined with PVC morphology for binary left ventricular-right ventricular (LV-RV) localization, while sinus rhythm alone had limited discriminatory value. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence supporting paired sinus rhythm-PVC modeling as a physiologically informed approach to ventricular ectopic localization. External validation and comparison with established ECG-based localization criteria are required before clinical implementation.

title: Beyond Human Helpers: Young People's Help-Seeking in the Era of Chatbots.
text: BackgroundChildren and young people are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health support, particularly when barriers limit access to traditional services. Although these systems are often perceived as accessible, immediate and non-judgemental, there is limited understanding of how they function within the complex developmental context of adolescence. Chatbots may simulate empathy and validation without possessing clinical judgement or contextual awareness, raising questions about safety, reliability and their influence on help-seeking behaviours.MethodThis commentary adopts an interdisciplinary perspective, integrating insights from clinical psychology, philosophy and machine learning. It draws on emerging evidence, conceptual analysis and approaches to AI safety evaluation.ResultsChatbot failures are most likely to occur in ambiguous or high-risk situations, where systems may provide misplaced reassurance, inappropriate validation or fail to recognise the need for escalation. Current evaluations often prioritise engagement and acceptability, overlooking clinically important risks. Young people need support to recognise the limitations of AI-generated advice and respond critically when systems operate beyond their competence.ConclusionsRigorous interdisciplinary frameworks are required to evaluate chatbot safety and effectiveness. Researchers should prioritise clinically meaningful outcomes, transparency and accountability, while ensuring responsibility for safe use is addressed as a collective ethical and public health concern. Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are becoming a common source of mental health support for young people. Many offer immediate, anonymous and non-judgemental conversations, which can be appealing when accessing professional help is difficult or delayed. Some young people use chatbots to learn about mental health, explore coping strategies, or seek emotional support during difficult times. However, there are important questions about how safe and reliable these systems are. Unlike trained professionals, chatbots do not truly understand a young person’s circumstances, relationships or wider life context. They generate responses based on patterns in data and may sometimes provide misleading reassurance, inappropriate advice or fail to recognise when a young person needs urgent human support. Because these systems often communicate in a confident and caring way, it can be difficult for users to recognise their limitations. This commentary brings together perspectives from clinical psychology, philosophy and artificial intelligence to explore the benefits and risks of AI-assisted help-seeking. We argue that research should focus not only on whether young people like using chatbots, but also on when and how they may fail, particularly in complex or high-risk situations. We also highlight the importance of helping young people develop the skills to engage critically with AI systems. Responsibility for safe use should not rest solely with young people and families but should be shared across researchers, technology developers, services, educators and policymakers.

title: DEPI-MS: Density-Equalized Pseudo-Image Learning for Drift-Tolerant LC-MS Metabolomics Classification.
text: Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)-based metabolomics captures system-level biochemical variation, but classification remains difficult under realistic acquisition variability. Conventional peak-table workflows reduce the continuous retention time (RT)-m/z intensity field to discrete features, thereby losing structural information such as peak morphology, co-elution patterns, and local background. Pseudo-image learning provides a way to preserve this signal field, yet current approaches often allocate image resolution inefficiently, rely on generic image backbones, and remain sensitive to chromatographic drift. Here, we present DEPI-MS, a Density-Equalized Pseudo-Image learning for LC-MS-based metabolomics. DEPI-MS combines three practical design choices tailored to LC-MS data. First, it preserves uniform RT binning while using QC-derived nonuniform m/z binning, assigning more pixels to signal-dense mass regions without disrupting chromatographic interpretation. Second, a compact multi-scale classifier aggregates local peak-like responses and broader RT-m/z context through channel-wise global feature reweighting. Third, differentiable RT-axis warping is applied during training to reduce sensitivity to smooth chromatographic displacement without regenerating pseudo-images from raw files. In a nasopharyngeal carcinoma serum cohort, DEPI-MS achieved an AUC of 0.984 on an independent external validation set and remained stable under a 60 s RT-drift stress test, outperforming representative peak-table and pseudo-image baselines. Cohort-level attribution further localized recurrent model evidence to RT-m/z regions, providing candidate signal loci for biochemical follow-up. These results support DEPI-MS as a practical route toward transferable LC-MS metabolomics classification under acquisition variability.

title: Preoperative anastomotic response microbial subtypes (ARMS) are associated with anastomotic leakage after colorectal cancer surgery.
text: Anastomotic leakage (AL) is a severe complication following colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery, associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Identifying predictive factors for AL may improve risk stratification and facilitate early diagnosis. In this post hoc exploratory analysis of 421 CRC patients undergoing elective resection with primary anastomosis across two international, multicentre clinical studies, we profiled their preoperative fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. AL occurred in 28 patients (6.7%). Fecal profiling revealed a bimodal distribution of Segatella copri, which served as the foundation for our two-step stratification pipeline. In Step 1, high relative abundance of S. copri was associated with successful anastomotic healing, defining candidate anastomotic response microbial subtype 1 (ARMS-1, low risk). In Step 2, among patients with low S. copri abundance, analysis of microbial metabolic potential identified 165 KEGG orthology (KO) terms enriched in AL patients. Machine learning models trained on these KOs predicted AL with high accuracy, significantly outperforming an externally validated anastomotic leak risk calculator, and differentiating candidate ARMS-2 (medium risk) from ARMS-3 (high risk). In mice, colonization with Palleniella intestinalis, the murine homolog of S. copri, enhanced the expression of transcripts key to barrier integrity, while reducing postoperative circulating markers associated with AL in our human cohort. Overall, this study demonstrates that preoperative fecal microbiome profiling enables accurate AL risk stratification through a functional two-step pipeline and offers mechanistically plausible insights into microbial contributions to anastomotic healing.

title: Response to "Inconsistent D-Dimer Units, Cutpoints, and Interaction Estimates in a Machine-Learning Model for Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage".
An Interpretable Machine Learning Model to Predict Skip Lymph Node Metastasis in Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma.
text: Skip lymph node metastasis (SLNM) poses major diagnostic challenges for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), and existing prediction models rely merely on clinicopathological data and have limited predictive efficacy. This research constructed an interpretable machine learning prediction model integrating clinicopathological features and peripheral blood immune-inflammatory markers, aiming to realize personalized SLNM risk assessment and guide clinical treatment decision-making for patients with PTC.
