Retrospective data from 1004 patients with PTC from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang were collected. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression filtered predictive variables, and seven supervised machine learning models were built to predict SLNM. Model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were evaluated via area under the curve (AUC), decision-curve analysis, and multiple auxiliary metrics, and the optimal algorithm was screened out. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis interpreted feature contribution. Among all 1004 enrolled subjects, 193 (19.2%) presented with SLNM. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator analysis retained two immune-inflammatory markers-platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio and systemic immune-inflammation index-alongside five ultrasound-based clinical predictors: age, maximum tumor diameter, lesion site, multifocality and extrathyroidal extension. Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) outperformed all other tested algorithms, with an AUC of 0.970 in the training cohort and an AUC of 0.897 in the internal validation cohort. SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis further assigned quantified importance weights to each predictor variable. This study first integrated systemic immune-inflammatory biomarkers and clinicopathological indicators into an interpretable machine learning system then developed an open-access online prediction calculator. The model significantly improves SLNM predictive accuracy, providing quantitative evidence for individualized risk stratification and therapeutic management of PTC.

title: Predicting coronary artery aneurysm regression in Kawasaki disease using CST3 mRNA and explainable machine learning.
text: To develop a prognostic model for long-term regression of coronary artery aneurysm (CAA) in Kawasaki disease (KD). Five hundred KD patients with CAAs were retrospectively analyzed in a derivation cohort and 159 patients in a temporal validation cohort. Ten clinically relevant variables, including age, fever duration, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) response, CAA classification, white blood cell count (WBC), haemoglobin, platelet count (PLT), C-reactive protein (CRP), prealbumin and CST3 mRNA expression, were included for model development. Eight machine learning (ML) algorithms underwent performance assessment using 10-fold cross-validation. Model explainability was explored through SHAP analysis, and final algorithm was implemented as a Streamlit-based online prediction tool. The random forest model demonstrated the best overall performance in both cohorts (derivation cohort: AUC = 0.9305; temporal validation cohort: AUC = 0.9338) and was selected for further SHAP-based interpretation. Lower CST3 mRNA expression, smaller aneurysm size, younger age at diagnosis, lower inflammatory burden (WBC, CRP and PLT), lower prealbumin, higher haemoglobin levels, shorter fever duration and responsiveness to IVIG were associated with a higher probability of CAA regression. We developed an interpretable ML model incorporating CST3 mRNA to predict long-term CAA regression in KD. Its web-based implementation may facilitate individualised risk stratification and clinical decision-making. An explainable machine learning model accurately predicts long-term coronary artery aneurysm regression in Kawasaki disease. CST3 mRNA emerged as an exploratory molecular predictor and ranked second only to aneurysm size in SHAP-based feature importance. Integration of molecular and clinical variables improved individualized risk prediction beyond conventional clinical models. The web-based prediction tool may support precision follow-up and clinical decision-making in children with Kawasaki disease.

title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
text: Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

title: An Interactive Trustworthy AI Pathology Copilot to Improve Biomarker-Driven Prognostic Stratification and Therapeutic Response Prediction
text: Predictive assays for precision oncology increasingly rely on multi-scale biomarkers that manifest as morphological signatures in routine whole-slide images (WSIs). However, most computational pathology models treat biomarker profiling and outcome prediction (i.e., prognostic stratification and therapeutic response) as independent tasks, and lack the interactive and trustworthy capabilities required for clinical translation. Here, we present TEAM, an interactive trustworthy AI pathology copilot that improves biomarker-driven outcome prediction. Pretrained on 55,648 pan-cancer WSIs and 1,750,648 regions of interest (ROIs), comprising 360 million patches, TEAM learns risk-aware embeddings by conditioning on clinical metadata and aligning with the relative risk prior. Patch-level data (aleatoric) and model (epistemic) uncertainty are quantified for trustworthy assessment and then propagated to slide-level predictions. In outcome prediction, TEAM uses profiled biomarkers as intermediate features to contextualize prognostic and therapeutic estimates. Beyond passive prediction, we integrate vision-language models with agentic orchestration for clinical reasoning, and provide a web-based clinician-in-the-loop interface for interactive prediction refinement. TEAM outperforms existing methods on 88 benchmarks spanning 51 multi-institutional cohorts across biomarker profiling, prognostic stratification, and therapeutic response prediction, supporting trustworthy AI-assisted decision-making in computational pathology.

title: External Validation of a Brain Imaging Model for Predicting Psychosis in Clinical High-Risk Cohorts
text: ImportanceStructural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) models for predicting psychosis in people at clinical high risk (CHR-P) are rarely tested in new cohorts, so whether and why they lose accuracy is unknown. ObjectiveTo test whether a structural MRI model predicts psychosis in external cohorts and adds to symptom ratings, whether its accuracy varies with participant characteristics, and what explains differences between cohorts. DesignThis prognostic study applied the PRONIA structural MRI model, re-estimated in its training sample (329 participants; 26 transitions), without refitting to 4 external cohorts. Data were analyzed from July 2025 to October 2026. SettingEarly-recognition services in North America and Europe. ParticipantsPeople at CHR-P in 4 external cohorts. ExposureBaseline MRI risk score. Main Outcomes and MeasuresTransition to psychosis by study-specific criteria (symptom duration, 1 week to 1 month); discrimination (area under the curve [AUC]), calibration, net benefit, added value beyond symptoms, and discrimination by participant characteristics, site, and outcome group. ResultsAmong 685 external participants (mean [SD] age, 20.0 [5.1] years; 319 [46.6%] female; 106 transitions), the AUC was 0.53 in NAPLS-3, 0.56 in MUC-FRUE, 0.65 in ZInEP, and 0.69 in FePsy (pooled, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.51-0.62), compared with 0.74 in PRONIA. The calibration slope was 0.17 (95% CI, 0.01-0.34), no probabilities gave clear net benefit, and adding the MRI score to symptom ratings changed AUC by 0.01 (95% CI, -0.02 to 0.05). Only negative symptoms hinted at better discrimination, and not robustly (q = .15). Participants without transition scored like those in PRONIA, whereas those with transition scored lower, so sensitivity fell from 0.92 to 0.57 with similar specificity (0.52 vs 0.55). Within-site comparisons, reweighting for age, sex, and symptoms, and alternative classifiers did not restore discrimination. Conclusions and RelevanceOutside its training cohort, this MRI model predicted psychosis poorly, a loss confined to people who developed psychosis and unexplained by scanners or participant characteristics. People may reach psychosis by routes that differ between cohorts, only some of them visible in brain structure. Identifying those for whom an MRI risk score works, if any, requires far more transitions, counted by shared criteria. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDoes a structural brain imaging model predicting psychosis keep its accuracy in other clinical high-risk cohorts, and if not, why? FindingsIn this prognostic study of 685 participants across 4 external cohorts, discrimination ranged from chance to moderate (area under the curve, 0.53-0.69 vs 0.74 in the training cohort), and the score added little to symptom ratings. Participants without transition scored as in the training cohort despite different scanners, whereas those with transition scored lower. MeaningBrain imaging may predict psychosis in only some people at risk, so it could help only if symptoms or other tests first identify these people.

title: Efficacy of Personalized Connectivity-Guided Accelerated Brain Stimulation in a Naturalistic Treatment-Resistant Depression Population
text: Personalized connectivity-guided accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) has shown promising efficacy for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in carefully selected trial populations. Evidence remains limited in naturalistic TRD patients with complex psychiatric comorbidities often excluded from such trials. Here, we report an open-label, single-arm proof-of-concept study of a personalized connectivity-guided targeting approach, TAO-TMS (Tree-based Algorithm for Optimized Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation), in a naturalistic Asian TRD sample. Participants averaged 1.7 psychiatric comorbidities, including personality disorders, autism and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Of 21 enrolled participants, 20 completed 50 iTBS sessions over 5 days. The primary outcome was response rate ([≥]50% reduction in Montgomery-[A]sberg Depression Rating Scale score) immediately after treatment. Among participants with available data, response rates were 65% immediately after treatment, 50% at 1 month and 31% at 3 months. In exploratory analyses, 70% responded within 4 weeks post-treatment; the corresponding rate was 83% in a subgroup of participants meeting typical randomized-trial eligibility criteria (N = 12). For descriptive local context, we note that a retrospective cohort at the same hospital receiving non-accelerated TMS with scalp-based BeamF3 targeting had an immediate response rate of 22%. Post hoc electric-field modeling confirmed that TAO-TMS achieved the intended targeting of attention networks. Statistically significant functional connectivity changes were observed in each participant, but varied widely across participants. Exploratory economic modeling suggested lower one-year costs for TAO-TMS than electroconvulsive therapy, with similar quality-adjusted life-years. TAO-TMS was feasible and well tolerated. Its preliminary clinical signal warrants evaluation in randomized controlled trials.

title: Prospective multi-omic profiling identifies predictive and genetically supported molecular determinants of incident epilepsy
text: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, yet biomarkers capable of identifying individuals at risk before clinical onset are lacking, and the molecular mechanisms preceding disease onset remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated plasma proteomic, metabolomic, and genomic data from the UK Biobank to characterize molecular changes preceding epilepsy and evaluate their predictive and causal relevance. We quantified 2,923 plasma proteins in [~]53,000 participants and followed incident epilepsy for up to 15 years before epilepsy diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards analyses identified 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy, led by neurofilament light chain (NEFL; HR=2.03) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15; HR=1.73). These proteins were enriched for extracellular signaling, immune regulation, and cell-death pathways and displayed distinct subtype-and age-specific signatures. A proteomic risk score comprising 32 proteins stratified epilepsy risk, with individuals in the highest quintile exhibiting a 3.5-fold greater risk than those in the lowest quintile (AUC=0.70). In parallel, 154 of 249 circulating metabolites were associated with incident epilepsy, with the strongest inverse association observed for citrate (HR=0.72) and positive associations across HDL-related metabolites (HR=1.16-1.21), implicating dysregulated energy and lipoprotein metabolism. A metabolomic risk score showed more modest discrimination (AUC=0.63). Integrating proteomic, metabolomic, polygenic, and demographic information yielded an overall AUC of 0.71 for incident epilepsy; in a separate cross-sectional analysis of individuals with early-onset epilepsy discrimination reached an AUC of 0.79. Proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomization identified 12 proteins associated with epilepsy after false discovery rate correction, predominantly for genetic generalized epilepsy. O-GlcNAcase (OGA), a regulator of protein O-GlcNAcylation with established roles in neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, showed the strongest protective association (OR=0.71, FDR=2.7x10-). Serine protease 53 (PRSS53), a poorly characterized serine protease, showed strong evidence for a potential shared causal variant with epilepsy (colocalization PP.H4=0.95). Together, these findings demonstrate that circulating molecular alterations precede epilepsy diagnosis by years and reveal complementary proteomic, metabolic, and genetic determinants of disease susceptibility, providing a framework for biologically informed risk stratification and therapeutic target prioritization.

title: Active Health Problems in Real-World Consultations on a Purpose-Built Medical AI Platform
text: ImportancesConsumers use conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for health at scale, but whether purpose-built medical AI is used primarily for information seeking or as an entry point into care remains unclear. ObjectiveTo characterize the clinical concepts users present, their visit intentions, and progression to physician telehealth care in real-world consultations on a purpose-built medical AI platform. DesignExploratory retrospective cohort study of consultations sampled in equal monthly numbers between June 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. SettingA free, publicly available, consumer-facing, anonymous-by-default medical AI platform. ParticipantsRandom sample of 26,000 English-language consultations by users aged 18 years or older, each with at least 5 chat interaction rounds. ExposureA chat consultation with the medical AI. Main Outcomes and MeasuresClinical concepts linked approximately to SNOMED CT; visit intentions classified with a prespecified 11-category schema and reclassified with a published 12-category consumer-health taxonomy; completion of the AI consult with a structured SOAP note; and progression to a completed physician telehealth visit. Automated extraction pipelines were validated against physician annotation in a random subsample. ResultsOf 26,000 sampled consultations, 56.7% were by users recorded as female and 50.9% by users aged 18 to 34 years. Among 25,975 consultations with successful extraction, 77,597 clinical concepts were identified; headache, abdominal pain, fatigue, and fever were the most common presenting concepts. Of 55,257 classified intentions, 60.1% (95% CI, 59.7%-60.5%) concerned a new or worsening condition. When consultations were reclassified with the published consumer-health taxonomy, 74.3% (95% CI, 73.8%-74.8%) included symptom questions or health concerns, whereas 5.0% (95% CI, 4.7%-5.2%) included health information or education, reversing the rank order published for a general-purpose assistant. Overall, 53.9% of sampled consultations ended with a structured SOAP note, and 15.1% of those progressed to a completed physician telehealth review. Conclusions and RelevanceUsers of this purpose-built medical AI platform predominantly presented active personal health problems rather than general information requests. Symptom-driven use, generation of structured clinical documentation, and progression to physician care suggest that purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to clinical care for some users. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDo people use a purpose-built medical AI platform primarily to seek health information or to present active personal health problems? FindingsIn this retrospective cohort study of 26,000 randomly sampled consultations on a medical AI platform, 74.3% included symptom questions or health concerns and 5.0% included health information or education, reversing the rank order published for a general-purpose assistant. MeaningUsers predominantly presented active personal health problems rather than general information requests, and purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to clinical care for some users.

title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
text: PurposeTo develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. MethodsThis retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. ResultsOf 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. ConclusionManifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

title: WITHDRAWN: A Modality-Invariant Measure of Neural Health
text: Withdrawal StatementThe authors have withdrawn this manuscript after identifying a computational error in the analysis code that affected the results presented in the Main Figures, associated Extended Data figures, Supplementary Materials, and the corresponding statistical analyses. We have identified and corrected the error. Preliminary reanalysis indicates that the theoretical framework and principal scientific conclusions remain supported. However, the numerical results, figures, and associated statistical findings in the current preprint should not be relied upon. The authors are conducting a comprehensive reanalysis and independent verification of the corrected findings as part of the ongoing journal review process. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as a reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.

title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury
text: ImportanceTraumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. ObjectiveDetermine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) DesignThe prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health-National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH-NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants929 GCS 13-15 patients [≥]17 years old (38.5 {+/-} 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT [≤]24 hours and brain MRI at 2 weeks post-injury and had at least one GOSE-TBI outcome score during 1 year follow-up. Exposure(s)Acute non-penetrating head trauma Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s)Frequency and co-occurrence of CT and MR features; incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8) and unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. [≥]5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months ResultsGeneralized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. [≥]5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8). For prediction of GOSE-TBI <5 vs. [≥]5, TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and RelevanceTraumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of [≥]4 TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning. KEY POINTSO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDo traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)? FindingsIn this cohort study of 929 mTBI patients, traumatic microbleeds were common; [≥]4 TMBs in at least 2 distinct regions of the brain were observed in 11.3% of participants on brain MRI performed 2 weeks post-injury. TMBs were associated more strongly with intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) than with other neuroimaging findings including brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural and epidural hematomas. The presence of [≥]4 TMBs on brain MRI, or any TMB or IVH on head CT, were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) out to 12 months after mTBI. Specifically, these neuroimaging findings had odds ratios (OR) of 8.3 [2.4-29.2], 7.5 [1.8-30.8], and 5.4 [1.6-18.0] for GOSE-TBI <5 vs. [≥]5 at post-injury months 3, 6, and 12, respectively. These far exceeded the ORs for other predictors including other CT and MRI findings, admission GCS score (13 vs15), age, sex, years of education, history of neuropsychiatric disorder, history of prior TBI, and contemporaneous major extracranial injury. MeaningTMBs and IVH are associated with each other, and with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) out to at least 12 months after mild TBI. The association persists after controlling for other CT and MRI findings, socio-demographic factors, and clinical characteristics.

title: Deep learning grading of Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis from ultrasound images: a weighted soft-voting ensemble of convolutional and transformer networks
text: BackgroundDespite progress towards schistosomiasis elimination in China, Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis remains a source of morbidity. Ultrasound grading is subjective, and experienced sonographers are scarce in endemic counties. MethodsWe developed a deep learning ensemble to grade fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image without manual region-of-interest delineation. We analysed 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18-88 years; median age 54; 46.4% female) at a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China (2019-2023). Grades 0, 1, 2 and 3 accounted for 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% of images, respectively. Reference grades were derived from clinical ultrasound records and radiologist reassessment using the Chinese Handbook of Schistosomiasis Control, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Predictions from ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T were combined by validation-weighted soft voting. Performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of 440 images. ResultsThe ensemble achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184-0.8856), accuracy of 0.8500 (95% CI 0.8136-0.8818) and quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (95% CI 0.8983-0.9373) for four-grade classification, outperforming each individual network in macro-F1. All ensemble misclassifications involved adjacent grades. For detecting significant fibrosis (grades 2-3; test-set prevalence 53.0%), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity 0.9179, positive predictive value 0.9300, negative predictive value 0.9645 and AUROC 0.9817. ConclusionsThis single-image approach may assist automated grading of S. japonicum-associated liver fibrosis in endemic settings. External validation is needed before clinical implementation.

title: Early-life hallmarks of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity
text: BackgroundInternalizing disorders and cardiometabolic disease are common conditions that frequently co-occur in later life and may be attributed to shared genetic influences. While phenotypic effects of polygenic liability of adult disorders may emerge early in life, studies have not investigated this in the context of multimorbidity. This study set out to investigate early manifestations of polygenic liability to adult internalizing-cardiometabolic multimorbidity (ICM-MM) in a UK population birth cohort. MethodsWe used data from 5,934 individuals in the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC). We modelled trajectories of 12 mental and cardiometabolic health outcomes using mixed effects models, and investigated effects of adult ICM-MM polygenic liability on these trajectories. We also investigated associations of adult ICM-MM polygenic liability with circulating inflammatory proteins (Olink Target 96 Inflammation panel) at ages 9 and 24. ResultsAdult ICM-MM polygenic liability is associated with cardiometabolic traits and inflammation, and with changes in depressive symptoms and cardiometabolic traits over time in childhood through to early adulthood. A notable early life biological footprint is inflammation. We found that higher ICM-MM polygenic liability is consistently associated with higher interleukin-6 (IL6), tumor necrosis family superfamily member 14 (TNFSF14) and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) levels in both childhood and early adulthood. ConclusionsAdult ICM-MM polygenic liability manifests early in life through changes in mental and cardiometabolic health and blood biomarkers, especially in increases of circulating inflammatory proteins related to obesity, immune cell chemotaxis and migration that may contribute to disease pathogenesis by seeding inflammation in relevant tissues.

title: 2D anomaly detection of fatal cerebral hemorrhage on postmortem CT
text: Postmortem computed tomography (PMCT) is increasingly used in forensic medicine, yet image interpretation remains largely manual and time-consuming, and supervised deep learning is constrained by the scarcity of annotated forensic datasets. This study investigated whether diffusion-based generative models can detect fatal cerebral haemorrhage on PMCT through reconstruction-based anomaly detection, using solely image-level labels derived from the documented cause of death. Postmortem brain CT examinations acquired at a single forensic institute between 2011 and 2025 were retrospectively analyzed, comprising 265 healthy subjects and 33 cases of fatal intracranial haemorrhage. After automated brain extraction, slice selection and intensity normalization, two diffusion frameworks were trained: an unsupervised denoising diffusion probabilistic model (AnoDDPM) trained on healthy anatomy alone, and a weakly supervised classifier-guided diffusion model exploiting image-level labels. Anomaly scores were derived from the reconstruction error between each slice and its pseudo-healthy reconstruction, and detection was assessed at the image level using 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. AnoDDPM achieved an AUROC of 0.928 (95% CI 0.812-0.989) and an AUPRC of 0.794 (95% CI 0.429-0.946), whereas the classifier-guided model reached an AUROC of 0.991 (95% CI 0.984-0.997) with an AUPRC of 0.960 (95% CI 0.855-0.994). These results demonstrate excellent feasibility of diffusion-based anomaly detection for forensic PMCT and indicate that weak, image-level supervision substantially improves detection, thereby supporting the future development of automated triage tools for postmortem brain imaging.

title: Intracranial pressure waveform estimation using extracranial signals with deep learning
text: Continuous intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring requires invasive instrumentation and reaches only a subset of the critically ill patients who may need it. We tested whether deep learning models trained on routinely acquired extracranial signals can estimate ICP waveforms with clinically motivated point-estimate accuracy. Five architectures were trained on arterial blood pressure (ABP), photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiography (ECG) waveforms, using invasive intraparenchymal ICP as ground truth, and compared across two fusion strategies and three training objectives. Models were externally validated on the independent MIMIC-III (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III) Waveform Database. Performance was assessed by mean absolute error (MAE) and Pearson correlation (r). Across 158 critically ill adults ([~]5,322 hours) from two institutions, external MAE of configurations selected using internal validation data only ranged from 4.266 to 5.899 mmHg and r from 0.585 to 0.719; three of five architectures (multiscale encoder-decoder, long-memory recurrent, temporal convolutional) fell below a clinically motivated 5 mmHg benchmark. Unlike prior work validated within single-site cohorts, these models generalized across institutions at the level of mean pressure and pulsatile trend, but did not reproduce beat-level peak morphology. This work extends prior research through large-cohort, cross-institutional validation and motivates evaluation across broader populations and ICP ranges.

title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
text: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
text: BackgroundMisdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. MethodsRetrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by a previously developed agentic AI system, Dr. CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). FindingsThe median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two physician reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, Dr. CaBot and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. InterpretationDr. CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance can be translated into improvements in care requires prospective evaluation. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed using the query ((Pediatric[Title/Abstract]) AND (Emergency medicine[Title/Abstract]) AND ((Artificial Intelligence[Title/Abstract]) OR (Diagnostic reasoning[Title/Abstract]))), for articles published from 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2025, yielding 28 results, of which 16 were deemed not relevant based on title, 6 were reviews not presenting novel data, and 3 were surveys of physician perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI). There were 3 remaining studies of AI applications to pediatric emergency populations. One assessed AI management decisions of critically ill patients. One attempted to automate triage categorization using machine learning. One assessed the diagnostic reasoning of various general large language models (LLMs; e.g. ChatGPT-4o) on adapted cases from a pediatric emergency department in Italy. Overall, there is limited data on the use of specialized AI agents on diagnostic reasoning on real-world pediatric emergency cases. Added value of this studyThe diagnostic accuracy of an LLM-based agentic process was similar to that of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians across 100 cases of children evaluated in a pediatric emergency department. Using real world data from electronic health records and a masked multi-physician evaluation of open-ended agentic responses, we demonstrated physician-level accuracy of artificial intelligence in generating differential diagnoses for children. Implications of all the available evidenceThe agent shows promise as a diagnostic aid among children presenting to the emergency department.

title: Evaluation of a Study Advisory Group on the Facilitators and Barriers to Patient Engagement
text: The facilitators and barriers to patient engagement in an advisory group (AG) were evaluated. The AG was formed to provide the "patient" voice in the development of a pragmatic trial to study multinutrient treatment in children with ADHD. The AG consisted of patient partners (those with lived experience and caregivers) and healthcare professionals (those working with children with ADHD). Eleven AG members completed the Patient Engagement in Research Scale, and five members participated in semi-structured interviews. Qualitative data were analyzed thematically, and five themes were identified. Together with the quantitative findings, key facilitators of engagement included flexible engagement, a sense of trust among AG members and the research team, and meaningful opportunities to contribute. Barriers included irregular communication from the research team, ambiguity regarding members roles, and underutilization of members competencies. Findings highlight the importance of interpersonal relationships and team dynamics and informed improvements such as more regular communication, improved onboarding processes to strengthen role clarity, and better leveraging of members expertise to support full engagement. This evaluation provides insights into the use of research evaluation to strengthen patient engagement in applied research settings.

title: Blood acceleration metric: A potential surrogate for fractional flow reserve to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenosis
text: Purely morphological assessment of an arterial stenosis is not sufficient to adequately evaluate its functional significance. The metric of fractional flow reserve (FFR) is the gold standard for assessing coronary artery stenoses. However, the risks associated with catheterization and induction of hyperemia needed to measure FFR impede its application to cerebral vessels. Approaches based on a combination of computed tomography (CT) with computer simulations have been proposed to address this issue, yielding an estimate of fractional flow reserved (FFRCT). While promising, they are time-consuming and difficult to integrate into established clinical workflows. Here, we propose a new, easily derivable parameter termed the blood acceleration metric (BAM). It incorporates readily measurable morphological and hemodynamic features, such as minimum stenosis diameter and peak systolic velocity, to assess the functional severity of carotid artery stenoses. Preliminary assessment on 27 mild to moderate stenoses indicates a strong negative correlation (R=-0.85) between BAM and FFRCT. BAM should be further evaluated as a potential surrogate for FFR and, thereby, as a possible predictor of stroke risk.

title: Central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation at 5 Hz or 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation for ataxia in multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type: a retrospective cohort study of efficacy and predictors of response
text: ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficacy of central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) at different frequencies (5 Hz and 10 Hz) combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation on the core domains of ataxia in patients with multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C), and to explore the independent predictors of the response. MethodsIn this retrospective study, 48 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of MSA-C were included. All patients received bilateral cerebellar hemispheric 1 Hz rTMS as background therapy and were divided according to the frequency of central cortical stimulation into a control group (cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation only, n=15), a 5 Hz combination group (n=16) and a 10 Hz combination group (n=17). Ataxia severity before and after treatment was assessed with the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS); absolute improvements and improvement rates were calculated for each subscore and for the total score. Continuous variables were described as mean {+/-} standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) according to normality; within-group pre-post comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and between-group comparisons used one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction. Clinical response was defined by an absolute improvement threshold ({Delta}ICARS total score [≥]8 points), and independent influencing factors were analysed by Firth-penalised logistic regression; sensitivity analyses were performed with a total-score improvement rate [≥]20% (and with [≥]15% and [≥]30% as alternative thresholds), and robustness results are reported for the {Delta}ICARS [≥]10-point criterion. Missing cognitive and mood scale scores were imputed by multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; m=5; the mean of the five imputations constituted the analysis dataset) and then included in the analysis. Subgroup and interaction analyses were performed according to the median disease duration (2 years) and median age (57 years). ResultsAfter treatment, the ICARS total score in the overall cohort was significantly lower than at baseline (median difference 7.0 points, P<0.001), and posture and gait (ICARS1), limb kinetic function (ICARS2) and speech function (ICARS3) all improved significantly (P<0.001 for all), whereas oculomotor disorders (ICARS4) did not improve significantly (P=0.799). Efficacy differed significantly among the three groups: median total-score improvement rates were 10.7%, 20.3% and 21.9%, respectively (P=0.004); when a total-score improvement rate [≥]20% was used to define clinically significant efficacy, the response rates of the three groups were 6.7%, 50.0% and 58.8% (P=0.006), and both the 10 Hz and 5 Hz groups were significantly better than the control group (Bonferroni-corrected P=0.006 and P=0.040), with no statistically significant difference between the two frequencies. Domain-specific comparison showed statistically significant between-group differences in both the absolute improvement and the improvement rate of limb kinetic function (P=0.013 and P=0.005), with the 10 Hz group significantly better than the control group. When clinical response was defined as {Delta}ICARS [≥]8 points, the response rates of the three groups were 20.0%, 56.2% and 64.7% (P=0.029); Firth-penalised multivariable regression showed that baseline ICARS total score was an independent predictor of clinical response (OR=1.076, 95% CI 1.013-1.143, P=0.017), whereas 5 Hz (OR=4.298, 95% CI 0.757-24.412, P=0.100) and 10 Hz (OR=5.847, 95% CI 0.885-38.640, P=0.067) stimulation did not reach independent statistical significance after adjustment. When response was defined as {Delta}ICARS [≥]10 points, the response rates were 0%, 43.8% and 47.1% (P=0.007), and there were no responders in the control group. Subgroup analysis showed a significant groupxage interaction (P=0.020); the clinical response rate of patients aged

title: Adverse Events and Baseline Psychological Distress Among Dementia Family Care Partners in the Tele-STELLA Study
text: BACKGROUNDAdverse event (AE) narratives may reveal physical and psychological challenges experienced by family care partners of people living with Alzheimers disease and related dementias. OBJECTIVETo characterize care partner AEs during the national Tele-STELLA study and explore differences in baseline psychological characteristics by AE category and subcategory. METHODSThis descriptive, exploratory analysis included 43 AEs reported by 36 care partners. Narratives were classified as Physical, Psychological, or Random/Other. Baseline depressive symptoms, grief, and behavioral reactivity were compared between care partners with and without each AE type within this sample. RESULTSPhysical events accounted for 48.8% of AEs, Psychological events for 39.5%, and Random/Other events for 11.6%. Infections predominated among Physical events; stress/distress accounted for half of the Psychological events and care-recipient aggression accounted for the other half of the Psychological events. Psychological AEs were associated with higher baseline grief and behavioral reactivity. Stress/distress-related AEs were associated with higher depressive symptoms and reactivity, whereas aggression-related AEs were associated with greater grief. CONCLUSIONSCare partner AE narratives captured heterogeneous physical and psychological experiences. Classification may complement conventional assessments of care partner health and distress. These exploratory findings do not establish causality or predictive validity and warrant prospective study. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRY NAME, URL, AND REGISTRATION NUMBERClinicalTrials.gov, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04627662, NCT04627662

title: Evaluating the Clinical Utility of a Brief Remote Speech Assessment for Screening and Triage of Speech Disorders
text: PurposeSpeech abnormalities can often be early or clinically important manifestations of neurologic disease, yet access to clinicians with specialized expertise required for comprehensive motor speech evaluation may limit timely assessment. Brief remote speech assessment could provide a scalable approach for identifying patients who warrant more comprehensive evaluation, but its utility across heterogeneous speech presentations remains unclear. This study evaluated the validity and clinical utility of the Mayo Speech Test (MST), a brief ([~]5-minute) audio-recorded remote speech assessment, relative to a comprehensive in-person motor speech examination ([~]1-hour). Specifically, we examined whether MST could support clinically meaningful screening and triage decisions by distinguishing normal from abnormal speech and identifying the presence of a speech disorder. MethodOne hundred participants completed a comprehensive in-person speech evaluation and a remote MST. Participants were excluded when the interval between assessments exceeded 90 days (n = 13) or either rater judged audio quality insufficient for diagnostic interpretation (n = 6), with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final analytic sample of 82 participants. Remote recordings were independently evaluated by two speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who were blinded to participant identity. In-person evaluation classifications served as the clinical reference standard and were grouped as normal (n = 33), dysphonia only (n = 5), or speech disorder (n = 43). One participant could not be classified. Performance was evaluated for two clinically motivated binary decisions: distinguishing normal from abnormal (such as dysphonia or speech disorder; Tier 0) and identifying normal speech or dysphonia only versus speech disorder (Tier 1). Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, agreement, and error patterns were examined. ResultsBoth remote raters demonstrated similar overall performance despite differing error profiles. For Tier 0 screening, Rater 1 demonstrated 93.6% sensitivity and 71.9% specificity for identifying abnormal voice/speech, whereas Rater 2 demonstrated 78.7% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity. For Tier 1 identification of speech disorder, sensitivity and specificity were 83.3% and 86.5%, respectively, for Rater 1 and 71.4% and 97.4% for Rater 2. Interrater agreement was 79.7% for Tier 0 ({kappa} = 0.60) and 86.1% for Tier 1 ({kappa} = 0.72). Missed speech disorders represented an important source of error, with differences between raters indicating distinct thresholds for assigning abnormality and speech-disorder classifications. ConclusionsA brief remote speech assessment showed promising performance for broad clinical classification, particularly when used to address screening and triage questions rather than reproduce the diagnostic granularity of a comprehensive examination. Similar overall performance across raters masked meaningful sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs, highlighting the importance of examining error profiles in addition to aggregate accuracy. MST may therefore have clinical utility for identifying patients who warrant comprehensive motor speech evaluation, but should not be considered a substitute for a full diagnostic assessment.

title: Genetic Risk and LDL-C Response to Low-Carbohydrate and Low-Fat Diets: A Secondary Analysis of the DIETFITS Trial
text: BackgroundVariability in low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) response to popular diets is well documented, but the factors contributing to this variability remain unclear. We examined whether genetic predisposition to high LDL-C impacts the effects of healthy low-carbohydrate (HLC) and healthy low-fat (HLF) diets on LDL-C. MethodsThe Diet Intervention Examining the Factors Interacting with Treatment Success (DIETFITS) trial randomized 609 adults (ages 18-50 years; body mass index 28-40 kg/m2; not on lipid-lowering therapy) to a HLC or HLF diet for 12 months. This secondary analysis included 431 genotyped participants (HLC, n=223; HLF, n=208) with 24-hour recall and LDL-C data at baseline and 6 months. The primary exposure was a genome-wide polygenic score for LDL-C (PGSLDL). The outcomes were 6-month change in LDL-C, LDL-C increase versus decrease, and new-onset hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C [≥]130 mg/dL). Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic and linear regression adjusted for baseline LDL-C, weight change, and other factors. ResultsMean baseline LDL-C was 116 mg/dL (SD, 26.1) in the HLC group and 111 mg/dL (SD, 30.6) in the HLF group. On average, LDL-C increased on the HLC diet (+4.7% [SD, 19]) and decreased on the HLF diet (-2.3% [SD, 22]), with substantial variability for both. In the HLC group, higher PGSLDL was associated with risk for LDL-C increase (OR per 1-SD, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.02-2.05) and new hypercholesterolemia (OR per 1-SD, 2.27; 95% CI, 1.18-4.81). Similar effects on LDL-C lowering were not seen for HLF. In both, change in saturated fat intake was associated with change in LDL-C, independent of PGSLDL, but this association was modified by PGSLDL only in the HLC arm (P for interaction <0.0001). ConclusionsRisk for elevated LDL-C on a HLC diet is greater for individuals with genetic propensity to high LDL-C. This effect may be partly attributed to heightened sensitivity to saturated fat within a low-carbohydrate diet. Trial Registrationclinicaltrials.gov ID: NCT01826591.

title: Earlier confirmation of glaucoma progression with risk-weighted visual field and OCT scheduling
text: Glaucoma is monitored with visual field (VF) tests of function and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of structure, but models that predict progression do not determine when each test should be repeated. Here we present GEAR (gated expected-delay allocation rule), a policy that pairs a longitudinal risk predictor with a decision layer and gives each eye separate VF and OCT intervals. In the decision layer, clinical gates define the admissible test intervals, and an explicit objective selects the intervals that minimize risk-weighted detection delay plus a penalty on expected testing, with penalties fixed to a routine-testing budget. In retrospective replay of held-out records (5,935 visits from 1,681 patients), GEAR with risk-based confirmation timing confirmed simulated progression 3.4 months earlier than annual VF and OCT testing (95% confidence interval, 2.7-4.1) at a comparable testing rate. The reduction persisted against a guideline-informed comparator and a reconstructed Kalman comparator, under an alternative onset assumption and with a VF-only adaptation in an external dataset.

title: The vertical velocity step test and vertical sinusoidal harmonic acceleration test
text: OBJECTIVECurrent rotational chair testing assesses only horizontal semicircular canal (SCC) function. This study characterizes vertical SCC responses and provides preliminary descriptive reference ranges using sinusoidal harmonic acceleration (vSHA) and velocity step (vVST) paradigms. METHODSForty-one healthy adults were tested with an adapted rotational chair to position the left anterior-right posterior (LARP) and right anterior-left posterior (RALP) SCCs in the Earth-horizontal plane. vSHA (at 0.08, 0.16, and 0.64 Hz) and vVST (at 100/s) were performed. Gain, phase, asymmetry, time constants (TC), and maximum slow-phase eye velocity (MSPEV) were compared across planes. Correlations with video head impulse test (vHIT) gain were also examined. RESULTSvSHA gain (LARP: 0.37-0.43; RALP: 0.38-0.42) was lower than horizontal gain (0.59-0.63), consistent with previously reported vertical canal measurements. Cross-plane Friedman tests confirmed significantly lower vertical than horizontal gain at all three frequencies (all p < .001). Vertical phase lead exceeded horizontal at 0.08 and 0.16 Hz (all p-adjusted [≤] .021). Vertical TC were significantly shorter than horizontal for both per- and post-rotation (all p-adjusted < .001), and per- and post-rotation TC did not differ significantly in any plane. No significant LARP-RALP differences or vHIT-vVST correlations were found. CONCLUSIONSvSHA and vVST characterize vertical SCC function non-redundantly with horizontal testing and vHIT. In the vertical planes, gain values and TCs were reduced, which represents a pattern consistent with reduced velocity storage. Validation in larger and clinical samples is required before clinical adoption.

title: Transparent Implementation and Benchmarking of ACMG/AMP Variant Classification in fastVEP
text: BackgroundThe ACMG/AMP framework is the standard for germline sequence variant interpretation, but applying it in scalable automated software requires operational choices that the original framework and later ClinGen guidance do not always specify. We implemented an ACMG/AMP classification engine within fastVEP and evaluated which implementation choices improved agreement with expert-curated classifications without increasing concerning opposite-direction calls. MethodsThe classifier implements all 28 ACMG/AMP criteria and can evaluate 15 from a sites-only VCF using nine public evidence sources. For selecting the optimal classifier, we compared symmetric and hybrid evidence-combining schemes, pathogenic class cutoffs, population-frequency thresholds, and benign-evidence thresholds against 673,660 ClinVar variants with review status of two stars or higher from April 2026. Clinical geneticists reviewed opposite-direction calls. We then applied the selected final classifier unchanged to 116,078 variants that newly reached the two-star threshold in the October 2026 ClinVar release. ResultsThe final fastVEP ACMG/AMP classifier uses the Tavtigian point scale on the pathogenic side and the 2015 ACMG/AMP combining table on the benign side. Using the 2015 table on both sides reduced pathogenic-side recall from 62.5 to 57.1 percent and lost 4,900 same-direction calls while avoiding 10 opposite-direction pathogenic calls. Using points on both sides increased benign-side recall from 66.4 to 77.0 percent, but increased opposite-direction benign calls from 27 to 399 and reduced recall of ClinVar uncertain variants from 97.1 to 69.5 percent. The 6-point Likely pathogenic cutoff was retained because lowering it to 5 points increased pathogenic-side recall to 73.9 percent but also classified 6,003 additional ClinVar uncertain variants and 17 additional ClinVar benign-side variants as pathogenic-side. The final classifier reproduced ClinVars exact five-tier class for 431,727 variants or 64.1 percent and its pathogenic, benign, or uncertain direction for 534,335 variants or 79.3 percent. Only 51 calls or 0.0076 percent were opposite in direction to ClinVar. On the later variants, same-direction agreement was 72.6 percent and 20 calls were opposite in direction. ConclusionsThe rules used to combine evidence affected classification more than several individual numeric thresholds. The hybrid scheme increased pathogenic-side recall while preventing a single Supporting benign criterion from producing a directional call. This conservative operating profile is suited to large-scale variant triage because it makes high-confidence calls while leaving variants uncertain when the available evidence does not support expert-level resolution. fastVEP is a research and decision-support tool and does not replace case-specific expert review.

title: PointX: Multi-View Consistent Intrinsics by Querying Surface Points
text: The appearance of a scene is determined by the albedo, roughness, metallicity and normal of every point on its surface, and by the light that reaches it, its irradiance. Recovering these intrinsics from images is ambiguous, and methods that predict them per pixel give the same surface point a different decomposition in every view. We introduce PointX, a simple feed-forward model that predicts intrinsics per 3D surface point instead. A multi-view transformer encodes a set of unposed images, and for any queried surface point, PointX pools the point's tokens across the views in which it appears and decodes the point's intrinsics once. Each point of a 3D reconstruction of the scene, such as a point cloud or a mesh, thus receives a single prediction, which is exactly consistent across views by construction and enables view-consistent relighting and editing. The same model also predicts per-view maps, from one image or many, by querying the point seen at every pixel. These maps agree across views up to the precision of the estimated geometry and correspondences. PointX is significantly more consistent than existing methods, while remaining competitive in accuracy from a single image and improving as views are added. Project page: https://pointx-paper.github.io/

title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
text: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.

title: Bayesian Learning of Spatially Heterogeneous Causal Structure in Spatial Transcriptomics
text: Spatial transcriptomics preserves the location of each expression profile, making it possible to study how gene regulatory networks differ within a tissue. Across regions of a tissue, regulatory relationships may vary and even reverse direction, so identifying the causal relationships in a specific pathological region can provide insight into therapeutic targets. We propose SpaDAG, a Bayesian method for learning spatially varying causal directed acyclic graphs. By defining the graphs on a triangulation of the tissue, SpaDAG allows each edge to have its own spatial pattern and even to reverse direction across regions. We show that the graphs nonetheless remain fully identifiable, and develop an MCMC sampler that explores them efficiently by reversing an edge over an entire connected region in a single move. SpaDAG outperforms competing methods in simulations with and without direction reversals. In a section spanning a renal cell carcinoma and the adjacent kidney, SpaDAG finds largely different relationships in the two tissues, with those in the tumor concentrated on genes associated with therapeutic targets. Between two of these genes, it identifies a relationship whose direction reverses across the tumor boundary, generating hypotheses about their region-specific coupling. Supplementary materials and code for this article are available online.

title: One, No One and One Hundred Thousand CTs: Testing Anatomical Control in Text-to-CT Generation
text: Recent advances in deep learning and the public availability of computed tomography (CT) datasets with paired reports have enabled many Text-to-CT generators. However, their evaluations almost always differ in preprocessing and metrics, which hinders comparison. Moreover, their protocols almost never test how editing the report changes the CT, not even at the same seed, so the report is often assumed to control the anatomy without evidence of how much and how consistently it does. We therefore propose CtrlCT, a toolkit that tests two properties of a generator, Credibility and Control. Credibility tests compare generated CTs, as a population, with real CTs and reports; Control tests are metamorphic and need no reference CT: at a fixed seed, editing one finding should change it as requested, keep negated findings absent and shift distant anatomy no more than a new seed, and the change should hold across seeds. A Report Card summarises all measures and insights for each generator. We benchmark five public generators on 940 chest CTs and 687 edits of pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, holding out a sixth to test the toolkit. Among them, the most credible generators barely respond to an added effusion, while the most responsive produce less realistic and less diverse CTs. The analyses proposed in the literature do not reveal this. We release CtrlCT, its edits, seeds and 30,525 synthetic CTs after acceptance.

title: Increasing the Precision of IR Mapping for Incremental Data Analysis
text: Static analysis tools operate on an Intermediate Representation (IR) --- an internal model of the program on which dataflow analysis computes and stores facts against IR object identifiers. Incremental dataflow analysis reuses these cached facts across consecutive program versions, but requires an accurate mapping between IR objects in the old and new versions. When this mapping is imprecise, the consequence is not merely a missed optimization: unmapped IR objects inflate the change set, increasing the number of program points that the analyzer must recompute and forcing it to redo work that a more precise mapping would have avoided. This cost is not specific to any one kind of IR object; it arises wherever IR-level identity is unstable across versions. Any IR that decomposes nested source expressions generates temporary variables which are assigned names by a method-local counter that shifts whenever a statement is inserted or deleted earlier in the method, breaking any name- or attribute-based mapping. We present a systematic algorithm that establishes a sound, oneto-one mapping of these temporary variables across consecutive versions, and formalize and prove the soundness of the mapping, guaranteeing that every produced mapping is semantically correct. The resulting precise mapping shrinks the change set, reducing the number of program points the incremental analysis must recompute. Implemented within the Soot framework for Jimple IR and evaluated on 8 real-world Java projects with genuine edits from the BUGSWARM dataset, our approach reduces the IR change set by over 82% on average compared to Reviser's graph-differencing algorithm, while completing the full pipeline within 250 ms per project---directly countering the common assumption that a more precise change set necessarily costs more time to compute.

title: Aqua2CAD : Observation-Guided Point Cloud Correction and Completion for CAD Reconstruction from Underwater Stereo Images
text: Recovering editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from underwater stereo images requires accurate and complete geometry, yet stereo reconstruction produces displaced points and missing regions. The original views retain cross-view disagreement and ray evidence lost during point-cloud fusion. Aqua2CAD exploits this evidence in two stages: view-conditioned correction and quality filtering establish reliable geometric support, while multi-view observations condition a learned shape prior to infer missing surfaces in the original metric frame. The recovered points support surface fitting and solid assembly with manually revised face groups. On an OceanSim-based synthetic benchmark, Aqua2CAD reduces point-cloud Chamfer distance by 60% relative to the stereo reconstruction. Compared with a matched point-only completion backbone, it improves missing-region recovery at 5,mm from 16.27% to 24.16%. With a shared CAD backend, exterior acceptance increases from 6/19 to 14/19. Qualitative results on selected real underwater captures demonstrate recovery of the main structures of six 3D-printed objects.

title: PhysMend: Verification-Guided Program Refinement for Physics-Aware Video Generation
text: Video generative models synthesize realistic scenes, yet their interactions often violate physics. A ball dropped onto sand should displace grains and settle into a crater, whereas a generated video may show it passing through the surface or leaving the sand flat. Post-hoc methods typically score generated videos with a vision-language model (VLM), but such scores offer limited guidance on which object or parameter to modify, and each correction costs another synthesis. Simulation-based pipelines instead run fixed stages before synthesis, so simulation errors reach the video. To address these limitations, we present PhysMend, a training-free framework for verification-guided program refinement. PhysMend describes the target event as an editable physical program of grounded objects, events, and required relations, paired with tunable execution parameters. Our key insight is to verify and repair the event on its simulated rollout and on the depth video that conditions the generator (depth control) rather than on generated videos, enabling quantitative violation measurement, targeted editing, and fast re-verification before synthesis. A hybrid verifier evaluates semantic event consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and visibility in the depth control. VLM judgments are confined to event semantics and cannot override failed physical measurements, which limits the impact of VLM hallucinations. Each failed check localizes the program fields eligible for repair, and its measured violation scales a bounded update of their parameters. Only accepted depth control reaches the generator, which runs once per input. Experiments on the commonly used benchmarks Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0 demonstrate substantial gains across different generator backbones; for example, PhysMend raises the overall Physics-IQ score of Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40.

title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
text: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.

title: Beyond Fixed-Context Likelihood: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Context Perturbation Discrepancy
text: The same increase in token log probability from earlier context can be typical at one position and unusually large at another. We introduce Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot detector that measures this gain relative to what a single pretrained language model expects. Keeping the passage fixed, CPD scores each observed token under its full prefix and under a short window of recent tokens. Under the full-prefix distribution, the expected gain equals the KL divergence from that distribution to the restricted-prefix distribution. CPD subtracts this expectation from each observed gain and scales the sum of the signed deviations by its analytical reference standard deviation. On unedited human and AI texts from GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART, subtracting the expected gain raises AUROC by 32.78-35.81 percentage points at the same variance scale. CPD outperforms seven zero-shot baselines, averaging 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate. On original and edited HART passages, the same scores separate texts more clearly by draft origin than by the benchmark's final-expression labels (89.15% versus 65.50% AUROC). Code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-tyf/CPD.

title: GeoSurge: Geometry-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning for Auditable Liver Resection Planning
text: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.

title: Topological insulators on site-eliminated, projected, and patterned fractal lattices
text: Identifying fractal lattices of fractional (Hausdorff) dimension as geometric descendants of parent crystals, we showcase the successful realization of canonical topological insulators in one-, two-, and three-dimensional crystals on their self-similar descents using three complementary approaches, starting from lattice-regularized models in integer dimensions. (a) In the first approach, we construct the fractal Hamiltonian by removing all parent-lattice sites that do not belong to such a network (method of site elimination). (b) In the second one, we integrate or project out the same set of sites to obtain an effective Hamiltonian for the fractal lattice (method of projection or renormalization). (c) In the third approach, we retain the parent-crystal lattice intact but spatially pattern the on-site mass parameter, which controls the topology of the parent insulating system, such that it assumes two topologically distinct values on the fractal network and its complement (patterned fractal lattices). By numerically diagonalizing the resulting Hamiltonians and computing appropriate topological invariants or local markers, corroborating the bulk-boundary correspondence through gapless modes at outer or inner boundaries, we establish Su-Schrieffer-Heeger topology on the Cantor set using all three approaches, Haldane topology on the hexaflake [using (a) and (b)] and Qi-Wu-Zhang topology on the Sierpiński carpet [using (c)], and strong $Z_2$ topological insulating phases on the tiled Menger sponge from methods (a), (b), and (c). These findings complement and substantially extend the previously reported realization of Qi-Wu-Zhang topology on the Sierpiński carpet using methods (a) and (b) [Phys. Rev. B 110, L241302 (2024)].

title: Lost on Campus: Evaluating Embodied Spatial Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in the Wild
text: Embodied Spatial Reasoning (ESR) is central to deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world embodied tasks, yet remains inadequately evaluated. Existing benchmarks primarily assess spatial reasoning in static images or synthetic indoor environments, where semantic shortcuts often suffice, making it difficult to faithfully evaluate spatial reasoning capabilities in the wild. In light of this, we present Lost on Campus, a benchmark for evaluating ESR in large-scale real-world outdoor 3D environments reconstructed by 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our benchmark introduces a unified reasoning-action evaluation framework that seamlessly integrates diagnostic QA for isolated reasoning with closed-loop interactive navigation for active reasoning under multimodal instructions. To enable fine-grained diagnosis, we evaluate six capability aspects of ESR: action grounding, spatial foresight, metric awareness, goal-directed planning, ego-allocentric localization, and spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments reveal that: (i) Compared to indoor settings, real-world outdoor environments impose substantially higher demands on spatial reasoning, where existing models exhibit poor performance; (ii) VLMs still struggle with fine-grained visual alignment, with failures in spatial foresight and ego-allocentric localization emerging as primary bottlenecks; (iii) Improving multimodal interaction capabilities and long-term spatial reasoning is crucial for advancing embodied intelligence. These findings highlight that faithful evaluation of ESR demands benchmarks tightly coupling perception, reasoning and action within realistic and continuous environments.

title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification
text: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.

title: Neural Implicit Representation for Bathymetry Estimation using Sidescan Sonar Imagery
text: Bathymetry measurement and estimation is critical for understanding the structure of underwater environments.
