title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
text: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

title: PyRUA-Dex: Learning Programmatic Policies for Dexterous Bimanual Manipulation with Coding Agents
text: Learning for dexterous manipulation is limited by the scarcity of high-quality demonstrations: retargeting from human video is imprecise, teleoperation gives no force feedback to the operator, and exoskeleton-based collection is hard to scale up. We present PyRUA-Dex, a framework that enables coding agents to develop dexterous manipulation through programmatic policy, without the need of demonstrations. The programmatic policy is developed in two stages: during exploration, multiple agents explore in parallel for task skills and ways to compose them, and a distilling agent condenses the successful attempts into a task library and one program. During refinement, this program is improved through randomized layouts for enhanced robustness and execution efficiency. In simulated environments, PyRUA-Dex achieves SOTA on Bench2Dex with a score of 72.9 and reaches 81.0% success on DexJoCo under full randomization, ahead of every trained policy on both benchmarks. In real world experiments on a bimanual platform with two 22-DoF hands, PyRUA-Dex learns to play piano, write calligraphy, and other tasks efficiently: learning a new piece from sheet music takes as little as 30 minutes. These results suggest that PyRUA-Dex is an effective framework for developing dexterous manipulation policies with coding agents in the absence of high quality dexterous manipulation demonstrations.

title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
text: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.

title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
text: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
text: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.

title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
text: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $β$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.

title: A note on input-oblivious unambiguous hierarchies
text: Unambiguous hierarchies are defined similarly to the polynomial hierarchy; however, all witnesses must be unique. Their versions differ in the mode of using oracles. We consider input-oblivious unambiguous hierarchies built from the class OUP, in which all positive inputs of the same length have the same unique witness: the hierarchy OUH with language oracles and the hierarchy OUH$_\bullet$ with loose access to promise oracles, which is the input-oblivious version of the loose unambiguous hierarchy of Hirsch and Sokolov (IPL, 2015). We show that languages in OUH$_\bullet$ can be decided in deterministic polynomial time with an ONP oracle, and for languages in OUH oracle queries can be made nonadaptive. Moreover, languages in OUH can be decided in deterministic polynomial time with a tally NP oracle, and languages in OUH$_{\bullet}$ can be decided in P/OptP, that is, a subclass of P/poly where the advice is generated by a function that maximizes outputs of a nondeterministic machine on a unary input. We show that P/OptP can be characterized in terms of OGTD and OUGTD generator--tester--decoder classes recently considered by Hirsch and Volkovich (arXiv:cs.CC/2611.16096) and, in particular, is contained in their "ultimate" Karp--Lipton collapse class OUM. We also observe several other facts related to OUP: (1) the hierarchy defined by input-oblivious unambiguous dot-operators collapses, (2) in OUP computations, a single loose query to prOUP can be replaced by a query to OUP, (3) SOUP=OUP$\cap$coOUP, where SOUP is the same-witness class recently considered by Hirsch, Volkovich, and Williams (2026).

title: A prime-editing-based strategy for pooled protein tagging and subcellular localization mapping
text: The subcellular organization of proteins carries important information on cell state and gene function, yet there are limited technologies that enable routine measurements of protein localization at scale. Here we develop pooled endogenous protein tagging using prime editing to image subcellular localizations for many proteins in parallel within a heterogeneous cell pool. We constructed three prime editing libraries comprising 17,280 prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs) to exhaustively tag 60 endogenous proteins spanning diverse localization patterns and explore a broad space of genomic and pegRNA design parameters. We integrate pegRNA features into a predictive computational model for tagging efficiency to constrain the search space of effective pegRNAs for large-scale peptide knock-in. Last, we show that combining in situ pegRNA sequencing with deep learning image analysis enables scalable exploration of subcellular organization, setting the stage for systematic studies of proteome dynamics across cell types and perturbations.

title: Iso-Seq enables discovery of novel isoform variants in human retina at single-cell resolution
text: Recent single cell transcriptomic profiling of the human retina provided important insights into the genetic signals in heterogeneous retinal cell populations that enable vision. However, conventional single cell RNAseq with 3’ short-read sequencing is not suitable to identify isoform variants. Here we utilized Iso-Seq with full-length sequencing to profile the human retina at single cell resolution for isoform discovery. We generated a retina transcriptome dataset consisting of 25,302 nuclei from three donor retina, and detected 49,710 known transcripts and 241,949 novel transcripts across major retinal cell types. We surveyed the use of alternative promoters to drive transcript variant expression, and showed that 1-8% of genes utilized multiple promoters across major retinal cell types. Also, our results enabled gene expression profiling of novel transcript variants for inherited retinal disease (IRD) genes, and identified differential usage of exon splicing in major retinal cell types. Altogether, we generated a human retina transcriptome dataset at single cell resolution with full-length sequencing. Our study highlighted the potential of Iso-Seq to map the isoform diversity in the human retina, providing an expanded view of the complex transcriptomic landscape in the retina.

title: Protocol for developing a gel-free 3D culture system to generate spheroids from axolotl blastema cells
text: The axolotl ( Ambystoma mexicanum ) is a well-established model for studying limb regeneration. Here, we present a gel-free 3D culture protocol to generate spheroids from axolotl blastema cells under fully defined, serum-free conditions. We describe blastema collection, mechanical dissociation, spheroid formation, and culture for up to 10 days. We then assess Prrx1 expression, cell viability, and mitochondrial membrane potential using RT-qPCR, calcein-AM/propidium iodide (PI) staining, and JC-1 staining, respectively. These spheroids provide an accessible three-dimensional platform for molecular, cellular, viability, and regenerative studies.

title: Translons upstream of protein-coding regions rather than their products are crucial for proliferation of human cells of distinct origin
text: Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are a widespread class of translated regions (translons) occurring in 5' leaders of messenger RNAs. They serve critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation and some are known to encode small proteins and peptideins. Yet it is not known which of these modes of function is more critical for human cells. We conducted a CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis screening targeting 969 translated human uORFs across three cell lines of distinct origin. Disruption of 155 uORFs impaired cell proliferation, although these effects were highly cell-type specific, with only six shared across all cell lines. Neither evolutionary conservation, comparative protein-coding potential, nor population mutational constraint distinguished uORF hits. Instead, high-throughput analysis of CRISPR-induced mutations combined with reporter assays demonstrated that proliferation phenotypes arise from altered cis-regulation of coding sequence (CDS) translation. In particular, uORFs located within short 5' leaders were disproportionately sensitive to indels, which frequently changed the uORF-CDS configuration, resulting in altered gene expression. We further identified naturally occurring human variants that are predicted to perturb these uORFs-CDS configurations, potentially contributing to disease phenotypes. Together, these findings identify uORF translation as a pervasive layer of gene-expression control. This study demonstrates that for most uORFs, it is their native translation rather than the activity of their products that is critical for the proliferation of human cells. It also provides a systematic resource for investigating uORF functions.

title: Helical repeat protein mRSiC is required for rRNA fragment accumulation in T. gondii mitochondria
text: Myzozoans, including apicomplexan parasites Plasmodium falciparum and Toxoplasma gondii , possess unusual mitochondrial genomes that only encode two to three respiratory chain subunits and extensively fragmented rRNAs forming a divergent mitoribosome. Heptatricopeptide repeat (HPR) proteins are expanded in myzozoans, with some functioning as mitoribosomal constituents. Additional HPR proteins have been proposed to function in post-transcriptional mitochondrial gene expression, though their specific roles remain unexplored. We present a phylogenetic analysis of HPR proteins that reveals extensive lineage-specific expansions, consistent with diversifications of mitochondrial gene expression systems within myzozoans. We further characterize mRSiC, a HPR found in T. gondii and its closest relatives. Using sRNA sequencing and RNA gel blot analyses, we show that mRSiC is required for the stabilization of two lineage-specific mitochondrial sRNAs, RNA33 and RNA42. Loss of mRSiC causes rapid depletion of these RNAs, followed by secondary reductions of rRNA fragments, defects in the respiratory chain, and impaired parasite proliferation. Together, these findings highlight the importance of HPRs in apicomplexan mitochondrial gene expression and illustrate how lineage-specific RNA-binding factors support highly derived mitochondrial expression systems.

title: ATP8B1–TMEM30B flippase activity maintains stereocilia lipid asymmetry required for hearing
text: Sensory hair cells convert sound-induced vibrations into electrical signals through a process called mechano-electrical transduction (MET). While the protein components of the MET complex are well studied, increasing evidence indicates that MET channel properties are significantly modulated by the surrounding lipid bilayer. The asymmetric distribution of membrane lipids between the inner and outer membrane leaflets is well established to shape membrane mechanics. The recent discovery that the core MET components TMC1 and TMC2 also act as lipid scramblases suggests a direct role for membrane lipid asymmetry in the dynamic shaping of auditory transduction. Because scramblase activity of TMC1/2 disrupts lipid asymmetry, we hypothesized that an opposing flippase may be required to restore and maintain lipid asymmetry. Here, we identify the P4-ATPase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B as selectively expressed in mouse outer hair cells (OHCs), enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated following the onset of MET and hearing. Loss of either protein results in elevated auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization, and rapid hair-cell degeneration, demonstrating that lipid homeostasis is crucial for OHC survival. Together, these findings establish ATP8B1 and TMEM30B as key regulators of membrane lipid asymmetry in sensory hair cells and establish TMEM30B as a novel deafness gene.

title: Diurnal rhythmicity in metabolism and salivary effector expression shapes aphid performance on host plants
text: Diurnal rhythms influence insect behavior, physiology, and metabolism, optimizing their performance by adapting to daily changes in the environment. While their impact on agricultural pests has been briefly explored, our understanding of how these rhythms drive adaptive responses in pest biology and influence host colonization remains elusive. Here, we show that a notorious global aphid pest, Rhopalosiphum padi , exhibits distinct diurnal patterns in feeding behavior, with elevated honeydew excretion at night and extended phloem salivation during early nighttime. Temporal aphid transcriptome profiling reveals four diurnally rhythmic clusters, two of which peak at night, exhibiting enrichment in carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. Beyond the established role in manipulating host responses and allowing sustained feeding, our study reveals novel evidence of cyclical fluctuations in salivary effector expression in an insect species. Silencing key effector genes, peaking in expression during the increased nighttime salivation, results in a more pronounced reduction in aphid excretion activity on host plants during the night compared to the day, a phenomenon not observed on artificial diets. A better understanding of aphid diurnal rhythms and their roles in shaping aphid performance provides a promising avenue to refine and optimize pest management, granting a strategic advantage for minimizing crop damage.

title: Iso-Seq enables discovery of novel isoform variants in human retina at single-cell resolution
text: Recent single cell transcriptomic profiling of the human retina provided important insights into the genetic signals in heterogeneous retinal cell populations that enable vision. However, conventional single cell RNAseq with 3’ short-read sequencing is not suitable to identify isoform variants. Here we utilized Iso-Seq with full-length sequencing to profile the human retina at single cell resolution for isoform discovery. We generated a retina transcriptome dataset consisting of 25,302 nuclei from three donor retina, and detected 49,710 known transcripts and 241,949 novel transcripts across major retinal cell types. We surveyed the use of alternative promoters to drive transcript variant expression, and showed that 1-8% of genes utilized multiple promoters across major retinal cell types. Also, our results enabled gene expression profiling of novel transcript variants for inherited retinal disease (IRD) genes, and identified differential usage of exon splicing in major retinal cell types. Altogether, we generated a human retina transcriptome dataset at single cell resolution with full-length sequencing. Our study highlighted the potential of Iso-Seq to map the isoform diversity in the human retina, providing an expanded view of the complex transcriptomic landscape in the retina.

title: Conservation of the transition of breast stroma into CAFs
text: To understand the development of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), we performed scRNA sequencing on normal and tumor breast tissue from mice and humans. We identified three conserved CAF subtypes: Matrix, Chemokine, and Contractile. These were reproducible across breast cancer molecular subtypes (Luminal, HER2+, and TNBC), in METABRIC and TCGA cohorts, and a published GEO dataset. Matrix and Chemokine CAFs originated from resident fibroblasts, while Contractile CAFs exhibited transcriptional features consistent with a pericyte origin. Human and mouse CAFs displayed upregulation of matrix organization, oxidative phosphorylation, antioxidant responses, and cell migration programs. Trajectory inference revealed that the fibroblast-to-CAF transition is regulated by AP-1 transcription factors. Computational ligand-receptor analyses suggested a common mechanism for CAF education involving overexpression of TGF-β, PDGF, TNF, and NOTCH ligands in tumor microenvironment cells with reciprocal receptor expression in CAFs. These findings broaden current models of CAF development by integrating cross-species conservation, metabolic reprogramming, and multi-cohort robustness.

title: MatriSpace: Identification and visualization of spatially resolved ECM gene expression patterns in health and disease
text: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a highly dynamic network of proteins forming the structural organizer of all tissues. Different cell populations contribute to the assembly of the 150+ proteins of a functional ECM. In addition, different ECM subtypes, supporting distinct cellular functions, are found in every organ. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides a unique, yet untapped, opportunity to identify which cell populations contribute to ECM production with spatial context. Applied to healthy and diseased samples, this method can identify ECM changes that could be exploited for therapeutic purposes. Here, we introduce MatriSpace, a computational framework to mine ST datasets with a focus on ECM genes. MatriSpace offers two operating modes: researchers can either upload their own ST datasets or explore a large collection of public datasets. Upon analysis, MatriSpace returns spatially resolved maps of matrisome gene expression in relation to cell populations, at multiple levels: from single-gene analysis to tissue niches and functional ECM units. MatriSpace is available as an R package and an online Shiny App (https://izzilab-matrispace.share.connect.posit.cloud), making it accessible to all users regardless of their level of expertise.

title: Genetic architectures of floral pigment and patterning in hybrid monkeyflowers
text: Coloration in living organisms varies in hue, saturation, and pattern. Here we use genetic mapping to investigate all three elements in monkeyflowers Mimulus luteus var. variegatus and M. cupreus, whose flower petals differ in both yellow carotenoid and magenta cyanidin (anthocyanin) pigmentation and whose hybrids exhibit anthocyanin pattern variation not seen in either parent. We report two QTLs associated with carotenoid intensity, and show that lighter yellow petals accumulate relatively high proportions of beta-carotene at the expense of downstream carotenoids. We propose that the derived loss of carotenoid saturation in M. l. variegatus is due to a function-reducing mutation in a Beta-Carotene Hydroxylase candidate gene, possibly coupled with a reduction in the availability of carotenoid-storing chromoplasts influenced by the ORANGE candidate gene. We next identify five QTLs associated with the spatial patterning of anthocyanin pigment. Two QTLs, 9b and 23, each contain genes in the anthocyanin-activating subgroup of the MYB family. We hypothesize that MYB5a/NEGAN, at QTL-9b, activates spot formation in hybrids as part of a Turing-type reaction-diffusion system, while a MYB at QTL-23 activates solid, non-Turing-type anthocyanin pigmentation and may also be able to activate the variegatus allele of MYB5a/NEGAN. In addition to the apparently stochastic placement of most spots (consistent with a Turing mechanism), some pattern aspects – such as spots at the petal tips – appear to conform to a positional specification model in which spot location is predetermined. Collectively, this work begins to identify how combinations of yellow and red hues, shifts in carotenoid intensity, and two cryptic patterning systems all contribute to the complexity of color divergence between two close relatives.

title: Tissue‐Distinct Features of Follicular Cytotoxic CD8 + T Cells in Trypanosoma cruzi Infection
text: T lymphocytes that combine helper and cytotoxic functions. While their phenotypic and functional properties have been described in several infectious and inflammatory settings, little is known whether Tfc cells exhibit distinct characteristics across secondary lymphoid organs. Using acute Trypanosoma cruzi infection as a model of systemic immune activation, we performed a comparative phenotypic, transcriptomic, metabolic, and functional characterization of Tfc cells arising in the spleen and inguinal lymph nodes. Tfc cells emerged transiently in both organs with similar kinetics and antigen specificity yet segregated primarily according to tissue of analysis at the transcriptional level. Splenic Tfc cells exhibited enhanced glycolytic and mTORC1-associated signatures, increased mitochondrial mass, and stronger cytotoxic and B cell helper functions, promoting immunoglobulin production and plasmablast death. In contrast, Tfc cells from lymph nodes preferentially displayed memory-associated features, including higher CD127 and CD122 expression, increased IL-2 production, and preferential persistence during chronic infection. Together, these findings demonstrate that Tfc cells are not a homogeneous population but can adopt organ-associated transcriptional, metabolic, and functional states during T. cruzi infection.

title: G2PT: a genotype–phenotype transformer to assess and explain polygenic risk
text: Genome-wide association studies have linked millions of genetic variants to biomedical phenotypes, but their utility has been limited by lack of mechanistic understanding and widespread epistatic interactions. Here, we introduce the Genotype-to-Phenotype Transformer (G2PT), a framework for modeling hierarchical information flow among variants, genes, multigenic systems, and phenotypes. We train G2PT to model the genetics of metabolic traits including insulin resistance, LDL and type 2 diabetes. G2PT predicts these traits with accuracy comparable to best-in-class methods, demonstrates transferability across cohorts, and captures epistatic effects. This work positions hierarchical graph transformers as a next-generation approach to polygenic risk interpretation.

title: AlphaFold models of host-pathogen interactions elucidate the prevalence and structural modes of molecular mimicry
text: Pathogens exploit host cellular machinery through protein-protein interactions (PPIs), often using molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular processes. While there have been thousands of host-pathogen PPIs determined to date, the lack of structural information for these impedes the study of the prevalence of molecular mimicry and convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. To address this, we benchmarked AlphaFold2 and 3 for prediction of structures of host-pathogen interactions observing that accurate models can be retrieved when ranking by modelling confidence, despite an overall low performance. We predicted structures for 6,782 pathogen-human PPIs yielding 803 models of higher confidence. Most pathogen proteins interacting with a common human protein are predicted to do so via the same interface, suggesting a high degree of convergent evolution of protein interaction interfaces. When comparing structural models from host-pathogen and host-host interactions, we observe that a majority of pathogen proteins are predicted to target existing human PPI interfaces. We categorized instances of mimicry into different modes, occurring at different frequencies: 1) via the same domain family (least common); 2) via a similar structural motif; and 3) via a similar linear peptide (most common). We selected examples of linear peptide interactions for binding assay testing, confirming 8 out of 12 predicted interfaces, including 3 viral linear peptide interactions. This validates AlphaFold’s ability to model some host-pathogen interactions and the mechanisms underlying molecular mimicry. This work showcases the value of large-scale structural modelling to study convergent evolution of host-pathogen interactions and how molecular mimicry may contribute to infection or host defense.

title: Rhodopsin 7 is an ancestral non-canonical photoreceptor that shapes light-responsive behavior
text: Animals rely on light not only for vision but also to adapt behavior to their environment through non-image-forming pathways. In Drosophila , most rhodopsins mediate retinal image formation, but Rhodopsin 7 (RH7) is widely expressed in the brain and optic lobe, acting as a non-canonical light sensor reminiscent of mammalian melanopsin. We combined expression mapping, behavioral assays, and phylogenetic comparisons to investigate its function. RH7 detects temporal changes in luminance, guiding rapid behavioral responses, and regulating daily activity patterns. Flies lacking RH7 are less active during the dark phase, while strains with constitutively active RH7 show increased activity. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that RH7 is an ancient rhodopsin present across panarthropods, representing an intermediate between G protein–coupled receptors and specialized rhodopsins, highlighting a key step in the evolution of non-visual light perception. These findings show that RH7 functions as a melanopsin-like sensor, shaping behavior, and illuminating the origins of light detection.

title: Extraordinary Evidence: Synthesis of High Purity Peptides Using Substoichiometric Amino Acids on a Variable Bed Flow Reactor
text: Sixty years ago, solid‐phase peptide chemistry revolutionized peptide science. Innovation has occurred, but the fundamental basis of the technology, the ability to easily wash away the required excess of amino acids needed to obtain quantitative conversion, remains unchanged. This also highlights its limitation: we use super‐stoichiometric amounts of amino acids, designing‐in waste as part of our process. When using commercial amino acids this is acceptable. When using a custom‐made residue, “wasting” 60%–90% of your valuable material becomes a scientific tragedy. This is no longer inevitable; we report that variable bed flow reactors allow for the high‐purity synthesis of peptides using less than one equivalent of amino acid per coupling. By avoiding wasting amino acid building blocks, this technology likely represents the most significant effort to date in both reducing the environmental footprint and reducing the economic cost of peptide synthesis since Merrifield’s innovation in 1963.

title: Computational components and assurance reporting in digital patient reviews
text: Introduction Digital Patient reviews describe heterogeneous data, models, software, and intended outputs; however, naming these components does not establish an operational or credible system. Methods Herein, we descriptively mapped computational components and assurance reporting in a shared cohort of 61 reviews searched in October 2025, without incorporating an updated search. Results Categories were counted non-exclusively at the review level. Imaging appeared in 49 reviews, sensors or wearables in 43, electronic health records in 29, and omics in 24. AI or machine learning appeared in 50, mechanistic modeling in 38, and hybrid modeling in 33. DICOM, HL7, FHIR, and OMOP were named in 15, 14, 13, and 11 reviews, respectively. These marginal counts establish neither integration nor capabilities of individual systems. Validation, reproducibility, prospective evidence, and maturity totals remain withheld because semantic classification rules produced false-positive assignments; therefore, readiness prevalence cannot be estimated. Eleven source reviews reported a named appraisal of the evidence they included. Selected review findings illustrated assurance-reporting gaps without estimating their frequency. An eight-claim framework organized established credibility and life-cycle principles, accompanied by two published-study illustrations. Discussion This framework is neither a readiness score nor an empirically validated standard, and the illustrations do not validate it. The contribution is a component inventory and an account of the limits of review-level assurance evidence, rather than a new implementation study. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261458411 , identifier CRD420261458411.

title: Griffiths Electromagnetic Bowl Cutter (GEMBC): Field-Governed Comminution and Emulsification Architecture for High-Integrity Industrial Food Processing
text: Industrial bowl cutters impose three structurally unresolved limitations on fine-emulsion meat processing: shear CV 12–18%, frictional temperature rise 2–5°C per cycle, and absence of real-time comminution state feedback. This paper presents the Griffiths Electromagnetic Bowl Cutter (GEMBC), a retrofit architecture governing comminution through shaped EM fields: an inductive bulk stage at the 6.78 MHz (lean phase) and 13.56 MHz (fat phase) ISM bands, and a nanosecond pulsed field across the knife-to-bowl gap for fat-globule fragmentation; 2.45 GHz is not used. Eight coil elements are embedded in alumina ceramic window inserts (Al₂O₃ 99.5%, εr = 9.8, tan δ < 0.0003) machined into the 316L stainless shell, preserving structural integrity, IP69K rating, and food-contact compliance. L-network impedance matching at each coil achieves VSWR < 1.5:1; reflected power < 4%. Coil thermal model predicts steady-state coil operating temperature 35–45°C with forced air cooling at rated power. Dielectric CI probe (coaxial open-ended stub, 50 MHz, flush-mount 316L) provides first real-time comminution index feedback available during bowl cutter operation. DIGSP two-layer control with stability margins of 1.67–17× across all five subsystems governs shear field, thermal envelope, and blade torque. Parametric uncertainty analysis (Monte Carlo, n=1,000; ±15% εr″ and Δεr, gap field 2.0–2.6 MV/m) gives a critical globule radius 95% CI of [4.7, 8.7] μm and pulse heating of 0.16–0.31 K per pulse. Mechanical load analysis: blade torque −35–50%, motor current −28–42%, bearing L10 life +430%. Retrofitting requires machining 8× aperture windows to ±0.05 mm tolerance with minimum 6 mm wall land retained. EMC compliance: CISPR 11 Group 2 Class A; conducted emissions suppressed >40 dB by an EMI line filter at the PMU supply input; radiated emissions < 30 dB(μV/m) at 30 m. Eight-test validation protocol with defined instrumentation and acceptance criteria. TRL-3 → TRL-7 deployment roadmap: 27 months. Practical Applications GEMBC targets fine-emulsion cooked sausage and frankfurter production (thermal governance and shear uniformity), pâté and coarse-emulsion products (inductive-stage-only operation with the pulse module off preserves chunk structure), and high-value charcuterie (batch-to-batch CI consistency via dielectric feedback). The same architecture, coil array, PMU with pulse module, DIGSP, CI probe, applies to dairy emulsion homogenisation, pharmaceutical wet granulation, and cosmetic emulsion manufacturing without hardware modification. The retrofit pathway (12–16 weeks, six steps, commercial components throughout) enables adoption by existing K-series operators without capital investment in new machines.

title: Advancing FAIR data management through AI-assisted curation of morphological data matrices
text: Curation of biological and paleontological datasets is a labor-intensive process that requires standardization and validation to ensure data integrity. In particular, manual curation of datasets is prone to human errors such as typographical errors, inconsistent formatting, and incomplete metadata, which hinder reproducibility and compliance with Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability (FAIR) principles. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers a transformative solution for enhancing research efficiency by automating data validation, improving accuracy, and streamlining curation workflows. This study presents a proof-of-concept implementation of an AI-assisted curation tool developed for MorphoBank, an open access repository established to enhance standardization and usability of morphological character datasets. Specifically, this work presents an AI tool designed to extract, structure, and standardize morphological character data from published literature into the NEXUS file format, a widely used format for phylogenetic analyses. This tool leverages machine learning techniques, including Large Language Models (LLMs) orchestrated via LangGraph and dynamically optimized using Declarative Self-improving Language Programs (DSPy), to automate the extraction of character names and states from text in various formats, reducing manual data entry errors and improving data completeness. The system enables efficient conversion of matrix-only files into complete, machine- and human-readable datasets that include key character metadata. By assisting with these tasks, the tool reduces the manual effort required for curation while improving consistency and standardization. This approach increases the FAIRness of morphological character data and provides a framework for extending AI-assisted curation to other types of biological data. These results illustrate the potential of AI-assisted workflows to support scalable data curation and reuse in paleontology, systematics, and evolutionary biology.

title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale
text: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eight-fold to >16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes, single-amplified genomes, and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms, and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.ziemertlab.com/.

title: From benchmarking to application: a scalable mitochondrial DNA analysis and variant identification framework for whole-genome sequencing
text: Purpose: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants are implicated in a wide range of diseases. The increasing availability of whole-genome sequencing enables mtDNA analysis in large-scale clinical and population studies. However, optimal tools for accurate variant detection from short-read data remain unclear. Methods: We systematically benchmarked four scalable mtDNA variant calling tools: MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity, and mtDNA-Server 2. Using 1000 Genomes Project (1KG) data and simulations across diverse haplogroups, we evaluated performance in detecting homoplasmic and heteroplasmic variants. Using the optimal tool, we built MARVel (https://github.com/bahlolab/MARVel), an integrated workflow combining variant calling, automated quality-control reporting, and interactive variant curation, including an mtDNA principal component reference from 1KG that captures haplogroup structure and enables projection of external cohorts. We then applied MARVel to an independent ataxia cohort to assess research utility. Results: MitoHPC and mtSwirl showed the strongest overall performance, particularly in non-European populations, with MitoHPC preferred for its ease of implementation. mity excelled in detecting low variant allele frequency single nucleotide variants (SNVs) but underperformed for insertions/deletions and showed inconsistent multi-nucleotide polymorphism normalisation. mtDNA-Server 2 maximised SNV sensitivity but had a higher false-positive rate and missed variants in the MT-RNR2 region. Applying MARVel (MitoHPC) to the ataxia cohort recovered known pathogenic mtDNA variants and identified additional candidates for investigation. Conclusion: We provide guidance for mtDNA tool selection in large-scale sequencing studies, along with a reproducible benchmarking framework for future evaluation as methods evolve. We also developed MARVel to facilitate disease-associated mtDNA variant discovery and reporting, supporting robust and scalable mtDNA analysis.

title: Linking microbial and geochemical processes in a deep volcanic lake (Lake Albano, Central Italy)
text: Volcanic lakes have been extensively studied for their physical-chemical mechanisms governing greenhouse gas dynamics and potential limnic eruptions. However, the role of microbial communities in these processes remains underexplored. Here, we integrate geochemical, isotopic, and microbial data from Lake Albano (Central Italy), a temperate volcanic lake (167m deep), to elucidate how biological processes influence carbon cycling and water column stability. A marked stratification characterized the water column, with oxygenated surface waters and progressively anoxic deeper layers where CO₂ and CH₄ accumulated. Microbial community composition changed accordingly, shifting from predominantly aerobic and phototrophic taxa in the upper water column to anaerobic, sulfur-cycling, methanotrophic, and methanogenic groups in the hypolimnion. Functional profiles mirrored this vertical organization, indicating a transition from oxygen-dependent and phototrophic processes to anaerobic carbon- and sulfur-related metabolisms with depth. The coupling between dissolved gas distributions, isotopic signatures, and microbial functional patterns suggests that microbial processes contribute to the transformation of CO₂ and CH₄ within the water column, potentially modulating their vertical accumulation and transfer toward the surface. Overall, this study underscores the crucial role of microbial-geochemical interactions in shaping greenhouse gas dynamics and stratification stability in temperate volcanic lakes, providing novel insights into carbon cycling and ecosystem resilience.

title: A prime-editing-based strategy for pooled protein tagging and subcellular localization mapping
text: The subcellular organization of proteins carries important information on cell state and gene function, yet there are limited technologies that enable routine measurements of protein localization at scale. Here we develop pooled endogenous protein tagging using prime editing to image subcellular localizations for many proteins in parallel within a heterogeneous cell pool. We constructed three prime editing libraries comprising 17,280 prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs) to exhaustively tag 60 endogenous proteins spanning diverse localization patterns and explore a broad space of genomic and pegRNA design parameters. We integrate pegRNA features into a predictive computational model for tagging efficiency to constrain the search space of effective pegRNAs for large-scale peptide knock-in. Last, we show that combining in situ pegRNA sequencing with deep learning image analysis enables scalable exploration of subcellular organization, setting the stage for systematic studies of proteome dynamics across cell types and perturbations.

title: Targeting PI3K signalling for broad inhibition of β-Coronavirus infection
text: The phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) signalling pathway plays a central role in regulating key cellular processes such as survival, metabolism, and immune responses. Aberrant activation of this pathway is associated with tumorigenesis, and several PI3K inhibitors have been developed as anticancer agents. Emerging evidence suggests that viruses, including β-coronaviruses, have evolved mechanisms to exploit host PI3K signalling for their replication and immune evasion. In this study, we evaluated the antiviral efficacy of a panel of PI3K inhibitors against β-coronaviruses, including murine hepatitis virus (MHV), human OC43 (HuCoV-OC43) and four major SARS-CoV-2 variants using both cell line and organoid models. Our findings reveal that these compounds exhibit low micromolar potency in inhibiting viral replication. Notably, the PI3K/mTOR inhibitor C20 (PWT33597) demonstrated broad-spectrum activity against multiple β-coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, MHV, and HuCoV-OC43, in conventional cell lines and in air-liquid interface (ALI)-cultured, differentiated primary human bronchial epithelial cells. Given that cytokine storm is a major contributor to SARS-CoV-2-related multi-organ failure and mortality, we further explored the impact of PI3K inhibition on host inflammatory responses. We found that MHV infection markedly increased cytokine expression in RAW264.7 macrophages. Interestingly, treatment with C20 further amplified cytokine production, suggesting complex immunomodulatory effects that may not be universally beneficial. Together, our findings indicate that PI3K inhibitors such as C20 exhibit promising broad-spectrum antiviral activity. Although their immunomodulatory effects, such as enhanced cytokine production, warrant further investigation, these compounds may offer a dual opportunity to fine-tune both antiviral and host immune responses with appropriate therapeutic strategies.

title: Next-generation multispecific antibodies for oncology: mechanisms and clinical translation
text: Monoclonal antibodies are central to modern targeted cancer therapy and immunotherapy. However, clonal heterogeneity and dynamic changes in the tumor microenvironment can enable solid tumors to evade single-target therapies. Multispecific antibodies offer a strategy to address these limitations by integrating distinct binding specificities within a single molecule. Yet neither increasing the number of targets nor increasing binding affinity alone guarantees clinical benefit. A central challenge is to coordinate immune-cell redirection, conditional activation, and Boolean logic gating with precise spatial and temporal control. These capabilities must be achieved while ensuring molecular developability, meeting chemistry, manufacturing, and controls requirements, and maintaining an adequate therapeutic window. Using intended biological function as the organizing principle, this Review examines how molecular architecture, affinity engineering, Fc-region engineering, and logic-gated design shape pharmacological profiles and clinical safety. We also discuss the implications of internalization kinetics for bispecific antibody-drug conjugates. We then examine mechanisms of therapeutic resistance and immune-niche remodeling within the tumor microenvironment and assess progress in clinical translation. Particular attention is given to the fidelity of preclinical models, biomarker limitations, strategies to widen the therapeutic window, and combination and sequential treatment regimens. Finally, we discuss emerging directions, including logic-gated activation, in situ immune priming with oncolytic viruses or vaccines, and artificial intelligence-guided antibody design. Together, these perspectives provide a framework for aligning molecular design with biological context and translational requirements to guide the development of next-generation multispecific cancer therapeutics.

title: A multi-faceted benchmark for electronic health record retrieval with semantic match assessment
text: Electronic Health Record (EHR) retrieval plays a pivotal role in various clinical tasks, but its development has been severely impeded by the lack of publicly available benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce a public EHR retrieval benchmark, CliniQ, to address this gap. We consider two retrieval settings: Single-Patient Retrieval and Multi-Patient Retrieval, reflecting various real-world scenarios. Single-Patient Retrieval focuses on finding relevant parts within a patient note, while Multi-Patient Retrieval involves retrieving EHRs from multiple patients. We build our benchmark upon 1,000 discharge summary notes along with the ICD-9 codes and prescription labels from MIMIC-III, and collect 1,246 unique queries with 77,206 relevance judgments by further leveraging powerful LLMs as annotators. Additionally, we include a novel assessment of the semantic gap issue in EHR retrieval by categorizing matching types into string match and four types of semantic matches. On our proposed benchmark, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various retrieval methods, ranging from conventional exact match to popular dense retrievers. In-depth analyses on various matching types reveal the strengths and drawbacks of different methods, enlightening the potential for targeted improvement.

title: Computational components and assurance reporting in digital patient reviews
text: Introduction Digital Patient reviews describe heterogeneous data, models, software, and intended outputs; however, naming these components does not establish an operational or credible system. Methods Herein, we descriptively mapped computational components and assurance reporting in a shared cohort of 61 reviews searched in October 2025, without incorporating an updated search. Results Categories were counted non-exclusively at the review level. Imaging appeared in 49 reviews, sensors or wearables in 43, electronic health records in 29, and omics in 24. AI or machine learning appeared in 50, mechanistic modeling in 38, and hybrid modeling in 33. DICOM, HL7, FHIR, and OMOP were named in 15, 14, 13, and 11 reviews, respectively. These marginal counts establish neither integration nor capabilities of individual systems. Validation, reproducibility, prospective evidence, and maturity totals remain withheld because semantic classification rules produced false-positive assignments; therefore, readiness prevalence cannot be estimated. Eleven source reviews reported a named appraisal of the evidence they included. Selected review findings illustrated assurance-reporting gaps without estimating their frequency. An eight-claim framework organized established credibility and life-cycle principles, accompanied by two published-study illustrations. Discussion This framework is neither a readiness score nor an empirically validated standard, and the illustrations do not validate it. The contribution is a component inventory and an account of the limits of review-level assurance evidence, rather than a new implementation study. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261458411 , identifier CRD420261458411.

title: WWUPS: A Systems Framework for Global Payment Interoperability
text: WWUPS: A Systems Framework for Global Payment Interoperability – Architecture, Modeling, and Policy Design for Cross-Border Payment Systems explores the architecture and systemic foundations of interoperable global payment networks. It focuses on the challenges and opportunities associated with connecting payment infrastructures across national borders, financial institutions and regulatory environments. The book presents a systems-oriented perspective on global payment interoperability, bringing together architectural considerations, modeling approaches and policy design. It addresses the need for coordinated frameworks that can support efficient, reliable and interoperable cross-border payment arrangements in an increasingly interconnected financial ecosystem. By considering the relationship between technological architecture, institutional coordination and regulatory policy, this work offers a framework for examining the design and development of cross-border payment systems. It is intended to contribute to discussions on financial infrastructure, payment innovation and international financial connectivity. The book may be of interest to researchers, academics, financial technology professionals, policymakers, banking and payment-system practitioners, and students working in banking, finance, digital payments and international financial systems.

title: Real-Time Water Quality Forecasting Using a Simulation-Driven IoT and Machine Learning Framework for Resource-Constrained Smart Cities
text: This study proposes and evaluates a simulation-driven Internet of Things (IoT) and machine-learning framework for real-time water-quality monitoring and forecasting in resource-constrained smart cities. Ensuring timely and reliable water-quality data remains a critical challenge, as conventional monitoring approaches are often delayed, infrastructure-intensive, and difficult to scale. While IoT-based systems support continuous environmental monitoring, many existing implementations emphasise data acquisition rather than predictive analytics and deployment-oriented design. To address this gap, the study develops a unified simulation-based modelling framework in which virtual sensors generate key water-quality parameters, including pH, turbidity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen. The generated data are processed using a machine learning pipeline and used to train supervised models, namely XGBoost, Random Forest, and K-Nearest Neighbours. Model performance is evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score to ensure balanced assessment across water-quality conditions. The results show that XGBoost achieves the highest predictive performance (91% accuracy), demonstrating strong capability in modelling non-linear environmental patterns and detecting unsafe water conditions. In addition to predictive performance, the framework supports real-time forecasting and visualisation through an integrated dashboard, enabling continuous monitoring and data-driven decision-making. The study contributes a reproducible and scalable framework that integrates simulation-based modelling, IoT-enabled monitoring, and machine learning for predictive analytics. The proposed approach provides a cost-effective pathway for advancing sustainable water management and environmental monitoring in resource-constrained smart-city environments.

title: Evaluating Digital Technologies’ Economic and Environmental Effects on Compliance, Governance, and Privacy in Sustainable Environmental Management
text: The purpose of the study was to analyze new technologies impact on environment. The prospective benefits and challenges of new technologies on the use of technologies within environmental governance and compliance were uncovered in this study. Utilizing a convergence approach of qualitative and quantitative studies, the researchers sent out a survey to 9407 stakeholders within the environment, which included civil society, the private sector, and government. The study found out that the enforcement and reporting of compliance with environmental legislation would be greatly assisted by the streamlining of governance and compliance in the adoption of new technologies such as blockchain, artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things (IoT), The study also acknowledged the presence of other challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, expensive technologies, and poor technical capacity. The gaps and challenges on the governance of the environment, compliance, and sustainability would be solved by the introduced new technologies, which in turn would create a sustainable environment. This would lead to the development of Nigeria in an economically sustainable manner, while also providing overall environmental sustainability. The paper recommend that Nigeria's should increase her investment in the construction of training facilities within the administrative regulatory systems of new technological systems in environmental sustainability, collaborative Joint ventures should be encouraged so as to achieve economies and environmental sustainability.

title: G2PT: a genotype–phenotype transformer to assess and explain polygenic risk
text: Genome-wide association studies have linked millions of genetic variants to biomedical phenotypes, but their utility has been limited by lack of mechanistic understanding and widespread epistatic interactions. Here, we introduce the Genotype-to-Phenotype Transformer (G2PT), a framework for modeling hierarchical information flow among variants, genes, multigenic systems, and phenotypes. We train G2PT to model the genetics of metabolic traits including insulin resistance, LDL and type 2 diabetes. G2PT predicts these traits with accuracy comparable to best-in-class methods, demonstrates transferability across cohorts, and captures epistatic effects. This work positions hierarchical graph transformers as a next-generation approach to polygenic risk interpretation.

title: A Bayesian Model-Selection Approach for Determining the Number of Spectral Peaks in Neural Power Spectra
text: Neurophysiological brain activity comprises rhythmic (periodic) and arrhythmic (aperiodic) signal elements, which are increasingly studied in relation to behavioral traits and clinical symptoms. Current methods for spectral parameterization of neural recordings rely on user-dependent parameter selection, which includes selecting the correct maximum number of spectral peaks to fit to the spectrum. This challenges the replicability and robustness of findings. Here, we introduce a data‑driven model‑selection procedure for determining the appropriate number of oscillatory peaks to fit to neural power spectra, based on the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). We present extensive tests of the approach with ground-truth and empirical magnetoencephalography recordings. Data-driven model selection substantially improves positive predictive value while preserving broadly comparable sensitivity under the tested conditions. Overall, the proposed spectral decomposition with data-driven model selection reduces reliance on user‑defined ‘maximum number of peaks’ settings, enabling more robust, reproducible, and interpretable spectral parameterizations.

title: Alzheimer’s disease brain phenotypes are age-dependent
text: A widespread view of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), frames their effects as accelerated aging, with the brain-age gap (BAG, the deviation of predicted ‘brain age’ from chronological age) as a staple biomarker. However, BAG relies on a fundamental, untested assumption: that AD can be identified via age-invariant brain phenotypes. Using invariant representation learning on brain MRI from 44,482 individuals, we created neural representations that optimally convey age information (age-aware) or conversely remove it (age-invariant) while minimizing reconstruction distortion. We provide the first causal evidence that age information is necessary in brain biomarkers for AD detection: age-aware representations achieve competitive state-of-the-art performance and significantly outperform age-invariant ones (0.84 vs. 0.77 AUC, p < 0.001, with external validation). This necessity reveals a conceptual flaw in BAG: by subtracting chronological age, it discards the very information essential for accurate detection. Using conditional decoders to simulate aging trajectories, we found that healthy aging and AD operate along multiple independent anatomical dimensions (deep gray matter, frontoparietal, temporal). AD patients diverge from rather than accelerate healthy aging, showing pathological temporal shifts alongside, remarkably, relative frontoparietal preservation. Furthermore, representational similarity analysis suggests that even models pretrained on non-age tasks (e.g., sex or BMI) implicitly converge toward age-related features when optimized for AD. Given that the AD phenotype cannot be decoupled from age, our results establish a hard limit for age-independent biomarkers and favor multidimensional models that preserve aging structure over unidimensional summaries like BAG.

title: Firefighter's Longitudinal Airway and Respiratory Exposome/Multiome Study (FLARES)
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] Background: Exposure to smoke increases the risk of many diseases. People can be exposed to dangerous levels of smoke during wildfires. Also, smoke from fires that burn manmade materials may contain toxic chemicals. Researchers want to know more about how breathing smoke affects a person s airways (nose, sinuses, lungs) and immune system. Objective: To learn how exposure to smoke over time affects the health of people who work as firefighters. Eligibility: Healthy, nonsmoking people aged 18 to 65 years who work as firefighters. Some people older than 65 may also be included. Design: Participants will have study visits about every 6 months for up to 10 years. They will also have visits after a smoke exposure event. Some visits may be by telehealth. Each visit will include some or all of the following: Imaging scans of the sinuses or chest. Sample collection. These will include blood, nasal fluids, a skin swab, urine, and fluid coughed up from the lungs. Lung function test. Participants will blow air into a machine that measures the volume moving in and out of their lungs. Particles in exhaled air (PExA) may be performed. Participants will breathe into a device that collects particles. Heart function test. Smell test. Participants will identify odors on scratch-and-sniff cards. Wearable air monitors. Participants may be asked to wear a device that measures particles and chemicals in the air around them for 1 to 20 days. International Public Safety Data Institute (IPSDI) reports. Participants will provide copies of these fire suppression event reports, if they are available. Participants who have exams of the airways as part of their routine health care may have extra tissue samples collected for research.

title: Daily Amino Acid Supplementation for People With Parkinson's Disease
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if a tailored amino acid supplement works to help adults living with Parkinson's disease to improve nutrition, metabolic function, body composition, and physical and mental function. The main questions it aims to answer are: Does the tailored amino acid supplement increase essential amino acids (nutritional status)? Does the tailored amino acid supplement increase an antioxidant (complex amino acid) and decrease an amino acid associated with oxidative stress? Does the tailored amino acid supplement improve physical and mental health compared to a placebo supplement? Researchers will compare the tailored amino acid supplement to a placebo (a look-alike substance that contains no active ingredients) to see if the tailored amino acid supplements work to support health for people with Parkinson's disease. Participants will: Take the tailored amino acid supplement or a placebo every day for 6 months, visit the lab at baseline, after 3 months, and after 6 months for fasting blood draws, body composition assessment, and physical and mental health testing and keep a diary of their food intake and supplement intake.

title: Natural History, Pathogenesis and Outcome of Melorheostosis A Rare Osteosclerotic Disease
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Background: \- The rare disease melorheostosis causes bones to thicken. This may lead to pain, and can affect bones, joints, and muscles. Researchers want to learn more about the disease and how it progresses. Objective: -To see what happens to people with melorheostosis over time and understand the causes of the disease. Eligibility: * People 18 and over with melorheostosis. * Their unaffected relatives. Design: * All participants will have a medical history and physical exam. * Participants who are relatives will give samples of blood or cheek cells. * Other participants will be in the study for about 1 week. * They will have blood and urine collected. * Strength, walking, and range of motion will be measured. * Participants may also have * X-rays and scans. * A pain and neurological evaluation. * Their skin evaluated by a dermatologist. * A small sample of bone taken. * Nerve conduction studies. Small electrodes with to wires will be put on the skin. A metal probe will give a small electrical shock. * Electromyography. A thin needle will be placed into the muscles. * An ultrasound, which uses sound waves to examine the muscles and nerves. An ultrasound probe will be placed over the skin. * A bone scan. They will get a small amount of radioactive fluid through a needle in an arm vein. This fluid travels to the bones. The bones will be photographed in a machine. * Bone Densitometry, a low-level x-ray. * Photographs taken. * A small circle of skin removed with a surgical instrument. * Questionnaires about their quality of life. * Participants will be asked to return about every 2 years. At these visits, participants may have blood and urine tests and x-rays.

title: This Study Evaluates the Use of a Data-driven Lower Limb Exoskeleton Controller for Stroke Rehabilitation.
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: RECRUITING] The goal of this clinical trial is to test a new, impairment-aware robotic control software framework to see if its smart adaptation can improve walking recovery in healthy adults and chronic stroke survivors. . The main questions it aims to answer are: Can the new control software safely use sensors and machine learning to predict and instantly adapt to a user's specific walking needs? Does training with a robotic device driven by this new adaptive control framework improve walking speed and overall mobility in stroke survivors? Researchers will compare a lower-limb orthosis operating under the new "smart" control software (which adapts to the user's impairment) to the same device operating under a standard, non-adaptive controller (which uses rigid or fixed assistance) to see if the new control approach leads to greater improvements in walking ability. Participants will: Walk on treadmills, flat walkways, or stairs while wearing a robotic leg orthosis driven by the different control software systems being tested. Wear small tracking tools (like reflective motion-capture markers and muscle activity sensors) so researchers can precisely measure how their movements interact with each control program. Complete standard walking tests to measure their walking speed and overall mobility under each software condition.

title: Adaptive Optics Scanning Light Ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) and Microperimetry (MP) Sub-study
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION] This research sub-study is to evaluate if combining images from Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans with Adaptive Optics Scanning Light Ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) and Microperimetry (MP) could show a link between structural changes in the back of the eye and vision. 10 participants that were enrolled in the COmparison of Clarus and Optos Ultrawide Field Imaging Systems for Geographic Atrophy study \[NCT05961332\] will be approached to enroll. Participants may complete OCT imaging and initial assessments during an initial visit and may return for additional procedures, including microperimetry and AOSLO imaging, within a window of up to 4 weeks.

title: Reproductive Axis Maturation in the Early Post-Menarchal Years
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Background: Most adult women with irregular periods of unknown cause report symptoms dating back to early adolescence. This study aims to learn how girls' periods change in the 2 years after their first period. We are also looking at girls who may have a condition called PCOS. This will help researchers learn what healthy puberty looks like and how they can spot signs of hormone problems early on. Objective: To learn how long it takes girls to develop regular menstrual cycles after their first period. Eligibility: Healthy girls ages 8-14 who either (1) haven't had their first period but show signs of puberty, such as breast development and hair in the genital area; or (2) had their first period in the past 6 months Girls at risk for PCOS age 8-14 who have a mom or sister with PCOS Girls with irregular menstrual cycles age 11-17.5 To compare with the girls, we are looking at women \>=18-34 years old with PCOS, Healthy women \>= 18-34 years old without PCOS, and Mothers of pediatric participants age 18-65 Design: Both parents or guardians must allow their daughter to participate. They must attend all study visits with her. Participants will first be screened by phone. Those who qualify will be screened in person. They will have a physical exam. They will give blood and urine samples. They will have an ultrasound of their abdomen. They will fill out questionnaires. They will sit in a BOD POD for 6 minutes: This is an egg- shaped machine that takes body measurements. They have the option to provide DNA samples. Participants will have sets of visits at home or at the clinic about every 6 months. The number of visits in each set will depend on their menstrual cycle. Then they will have a final visit. Visits will include repeats of the screening tests. There are additional parts that participants may choose to be involved in depending on how involved they want to be. At home, participants will collect their urine daily to measure hormones. They will keep a diary of their periods. Adults: Women with known PCOS will complete the same Screening Visit as the girls and will collect dried urine specimens at home for 8 weeks; The Healthy control women group will complete the same Screening Visit as the girls and collect dried urine specimens at home for 2 menstrual cycles; The Mothers of pediatric participants group will complete a Screening Visit (informed consent, urine pregnancy test) and collect vaginal swab specimens at home for 2 menstrual cycles (approx. 8 weeks)....

title: A Prospective Natural History and Outcome Measure Validation Study of Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] Background: Congenital myasthenic syndromes (CMSs) are a group of inherited disorders that affect how the nerves communicate with muscles. These can cause many problems that affect how people can move and use their bodies. Objective: This is a natural history study to learn more about how CMSs affect the body and cause changes over time. Eligibility: People aged 6 months or older with a CMS. The study will focus on DOK7- and COLQ-related CMSs, as well as other forms. Design: Participants will have up to 7 visits in 5 years. At each visit, participants will undergo many tests, including: Physical exam with blood and urine tests. Tests of their heart and lung function. Exams of the eyes, lungs, muscles, and nerves. These will be done with different specialists. Exams of the arms and hands and of body use and movements. These will also be done with specialists. Photos and videos may be taken. Muscle ultrasound. Participants will lie still as a wand is rubbed over their skin. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. Participants will lie still on a bed that slides partway into a large tube. A parent or other person may remain in the room, too. The scan will take 60 minutes. Electromyography (EMG). Participants will lie still or may be asked to move around. A machine will measure the electrical activity in their muscles. An activity monitor may be placed on the participant s wrist, ankle, or hip for up to 2 weeks. The monitor is about the size of a wristwatch. A sample of skin may be removed....

title: Tailoring a CRISPR-Cas-based epi-editor for decreased cytotoxicity and enzymatic specificity.
text: CRISPR-based epi-editors can robustly modulate cellular transcription and chromatin structure, but off-target activity and cytotoxicity limit their utility. Here, we engineer the acyl-CoA binding pocket of the human p300 histone acyltransferase to reduce its cytotoxicity and tune its acylation profile when fused to dCas9. We discover a single amino acid substitution (I1417N) that decreases cytotoxicity related to exogenous p300 overexpression yet preserves dCas9-p300 mediated histone acetylation and gene activation. We find that dCas9-p300 I1417N is less perturbative to the transcriptome and proteome of human cells, and that this behavior is driven by favorable stability kinetics. We also develop a crotonylation-biased dCas9-p300 variant (I1395G) that selectively deposits histone crotonylation and activates transcription from endogenous promoters at levels comparable to wild-type p300. The p300 variants generated here enhance epi-editing capabilities and demonstrate that engineering of catalytic domains can be a powerful strategy for tailoring enzymatic activities and mitigating effector-driven toxicity in epi-editing.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 editing of myeloid lectins reveals target-dependent transcriptional remodeling in tumor-associated macrophages.
text: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) integrate multiple microenvironmental signals, including lectin-mediated recognition of tumor-associated glycans. Although several myeloid lectins have been implicated in tumor-macrophage interactions, their contributions to immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes remain poorly defined. We implemented a CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) workflow in primary human monocytes to enable comparative loss-of-function interrogation of five potentially immunosuppressive lectins we previously reported. CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery conditions were benchmarked in freshly isolated monocytes using CD14 as a technical target, followed by sgRNA editing efficiency screening for CLEC4E, CLEC6A, CD209, SELL, and SIGLEC9 in HeLa S3 cells. Selected guides were applied to primary monocytes before co-culture in a 3D model with BT474 breast cancer cells. Editing was quantified by Sanger-sequencing deconvolution, while co-culture-derived CD45+ macrophages were isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting and characterized by bulk RNA sequencing. All five lectins were successfully perturbed, although gene editing efficiency remained target- and donor-dependent. Transcriptomic analysis revealed target-specific reprogramming and recurrent immunometabolic responses. mTORC1 signaling was consistently enriched, together with the remodeling of cholesterol homeostasis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation. CLEC6A deletion achieved attenuation of hypoxia-, angiogenesis-, and TNF/NF-κB-associated programs. CD209 and SIGLEC9 deletion similarly reduced hypoxia- and angiogenesis-associated signatures while promoting lipid and oxidative metabolism. CLEC4E perturbation induced broad remodeling of lipid and oxidative metabolism and stress-response, despite comparatively limited editing efficiency. Comparative lectin perturbation thus identified CLEC6A as the strongest candidate for further mechanistic investigation, while CLEC4E showed broad transcriptional remodeling despite lower editing efficiency, supporting its prioritization for improved genetic interrogation. Responses to CD209 and SIGLEC9 targeting further support tumor glycan-myeloid signaling as a regulator of TAM state. Overall, lectin perturbation redirected TAM transcriptional states through distinct immunometabolic programs rather than a uniform pro-inflammatory polarization, highlighting lectin-dependent immunometabolic regulation as a promising axis for further investigation.

title: Complement-associated injury readouts following CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of C3 in primary mouse renal epithelial cells: an exploratory in vitro study.
text: Complement contributes to antibody-mediated kidney allograft injury, while locally synthesized C3 may influence renal inflammatory responses. We examined the association between CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of C3 and complement-associated injury readouts in primary mouse renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (RPTECs). C3-targeting ribonucleoprotein complexes were delivered by electroporation. Editing was assessed using T7 endonuclease I, Sanger sequencing with Inference of CRISPR Edits (ICE), and immunoblotting. Wild-type, non-targeting scrambled-guide and C3-targeted cultures underwent an anti-mouse major histocompatibility complex antibody challenge with normal mouse serum. Complement deposition, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release and inflammatory mediator measurements were evaluated descriptively. Analyses were limited to existing aggregate summaries; no replicate-level reanalysis was performed. The aggregate editing estimate was 78.4% ± 4.2%. C3-targeted cultures showed reduced C3 immunoblot signal and lower C3d and C5b-9 fluorescence, with reported reductions of 65.2% ± 3.1% and 72.4% ± 4.5%, respectively. Lower LDH release was observed qualitatively. IL-6 concentrations were 1850 ± 120 pg/mL in wild-type cultures and 578 ± 45 pg/mL in C3-targeted cultures; MCP-1 secretion was reported as 2.5-fold lower. These are existing aggregate summaries rather than a new replicate-level analysis.
