title: Resolving cell states in spatial transcriptomics with SCATTER
text: A capture spot can contain transcripts from multiple cell types. Differences between spots may reflect changes in cell-type proportions, expression within a cell type, or both, making local cell-type expression difficult to infer from mixed counts. We developed SCATTER to estimate cell-type proportions and relative expression profiles for each cell type at each spot from spatial transcriptomic counts, coordinates, and annotated single-cell reference data. SCATTER weights reference cell profiles using local spatial context, then jointly fits the resulting profiles and cell-type proportions to reconstruct spot counts. Cell2location estimates regularize the proportions. After fitting, SCATTER uses learned gene-specific calibration factors and fitted proportions to allocate observed counts among cell types. In five pseudo-spot benchmarks constructed from imaging data, SCATTER achieved higher cross-spot correlations with measured expression for 82.8-99.8% of evaluated gene-cell type pairs in pairwise comparisons with DestVI, PANDA, and STged. In breast cancer Xenium data, it recovered gene expression associated with the tumor neighborhood and regulon scores. In breast cancer Visium data, inferred stromal and macrophage expression showed distinct associations with neighborhood malignant cell proportions. In multiple sclerosis brain tissue, SCATTER recovered lesion-associated glial expression programs. In colorectal cancer Visium HD data, it mapped cell-type-specific programs at the invasive front and ranked candidate ligand-receptor pairs. SCATTER enables analysis of spatial expression variation within cell types from mixed tissue measurements.

title: A multi-patch model for sylvatic hematophagous vector dynamics: the impact of landscape anthropization
text: We develop a multi-patch model for sylvatic hematophagous vector--(wild) animal interactions with nonlinear migration terms that depend on landscape anthropization. Every patch is a suitable habitat for both animals and vectors, but anthropization reduces the animal carrying capacity and induces animal and vector displacement. We considered three dispersal types. Under unconstrained global dispersal, displaced individuals can move to any other patch. Under the more realistic random and constrained neighbor dispersal, displaced animals move to a neighboring patch chosen either at random or preferentially among less anthropized ones. We parameterized our model for tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) in the districts of Campo, Nyé'été, and Ma'an, Ocean division, Cameroon. We characterized the equilibria and their local stability analytically for unconstrained global dispersal, and found numerically that, under both neighbor dispersal regimes, populations progressively expand before settling into a stable equilibrium. Under random neighbor dispersal, the effect of anthropization on migration had a much larger impact on steady state densities than its effect on animal carrying capacity. Under constrained neighbor dispersal, populations spread noticeably more slowly, and numerous patches maintained extremely sparse populations. We further investigated invasion speed under different anthropization scenarios. For random neighbor dispersal, invasion times decreased upon introduction of newly anthropized regions, while for constrained neighbor dispersal, anthropized regions either increased or did not affect invasion times. Approximating invasions by pulled traveling waves, we found that anthropized regions act as ``invasion highways'' or ``invasion barriers'' depending on the dispersal type. We conclude that more empirical data on animal dispersal are needed to understand these dynamics.

title: First Order Real Resonant Digital Filters and A Novel Orthogonal State Generator
text: We describe FOREST, a real, first order digital resonant filter and orthogonal state generator. We show that in spite of the imaginary nature of the roots of the transfer function of a resonator, appropriate interpretation of this transfer function nonetheless leads to a practical first order filter with real coefficients. We use a discrete state space model of FOREST to predict the resonator properties, and implement the filter in digital signal processing slices on a digital signal processing platform. Applications are in real time digital signal processing, engineering fields such as mains electricity monitoring and motor control, any application requiring a phase locked loop, and physics applications utilising high-quality-factor resonators.

title: An Embedded Ergonomic Posture Monitoring and AI-Assisted Home Learning System on a Raspberry Pi 3B Edge Platform
text: During independent home study sessions, students frequently sustain improper sitting postures, accumulate excessive sedentary hours, and experience productivity loss from off-task digital distractions. Furthermore, learners often lack real-time pedagogical scaffolding for demanding self-study curricula. To mitigate these ergonomic and instructional challenges, this paper presents an affordable, privacy-preserving cyber-physical embedded system for domestic study spaces. Engineered on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B (1 GB RAM) paired with a UVC optical camera and a USB condenser microphone, the system executes on-device computer vision utilizing MediaPipe Pose and OpenCV to monitor upper-body alignment, sagittal head inclination, and coronal shoulder asymmetry in real time without persisting raw video streams. A deterministic finite state machine (FSM) quantifies active study durations, enforces health-compliant rest periods, and detects illicit smartphone usage. Simultaneously, an integrated multimodal AI tutoring agent parses voice and text queries via an encrypted API gateway, synthesizing Socratic conceptual hints rather than direct solutions. A lightweight parental web dashboard delivers encrypted session analytics and scheduling configurations. Empirical benchmarks on the physical prototype confirm an end-to-end inference latency of 244-250 ms at a 352x288 resolution (4.0-4.1 FPS), a trunk-angle estimation error of 4.39 degrees MAE over 5,760 synthetic ground-truth poses, a resident set size of 320 MB, a peak SoC temperature of 58.0 degrees Celsius under sustained load, and a 1.58 s total latency for the offline TTS feedback path, proving high practicality for resource-constrained edge deployment.

title: Atunda: Building an Afrogenic Dance Movement Dataset for AI-Driven Classification
text: This paper introduces Atunda, the first systematically collected video dataset of Afrogenic dance moves, designed for training and evaluating deep learning models for movement classification. The first phase of the dataset includes nearly 400 videos covering 13 distinct dance moves from African and African Diaspora performative culture, making it the first AI-ready resource of its kind. Using this dataset, we train and evaluate various configurations of temporal convolutional neural networks, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 95%. The baseline results provide a benchmark for future studies in movement classification, especially in the understudied area of Afrogenic performative culture and tradition. This work lays the foundation for developing in the future digital metrics of similarity, automated attribution systems, and tools that preserve and promote the cultural heritage of Afrogenic dances.

title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
text: Camera-controlled video generation re-renders a video along a target camera trajectory, yet moving the camera around an object, the most natural way to change the viewpoint of an object-centric scene, remains difficult. Existing methods condition either on camera parameters, which are scale-ambiguous in monocular video, or on explicit geometry such as warped point clouds or depth, which breaks down under large viewpoint changes. We present AnyCam, a method that represents the camera with an anchor object in the scene: we reconstruct it in 3D and render it along the target trajectory, a camera signal that is scale-aware, view-complete and easy to specify relative to the object. A video diffusion model transfers the content and dynamics of the source video to the new viewpoint. Its H-Concat layout aligns source and target frames in time, so the model can be distilled into AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control. Both models are trained on paired videos with pixel-aligned anchor renderings from multi-camera videos and static-scene captures. Experiments on diverse datasets and trajectories show that AnyCam performs favorably against camera-controlled video generation and 3D reconstruction methods in camera control and visual quality.

title: LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
text: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.

title: DynMF2: Rigid Motion Factorization by Expectation-Maximization for Monocular 4D Reconstruction and Motion Segmentation
text: A single casual video leaves a moving scene under-determined: a point seen once from each place can slide toward or away from the camera and still match every frame. We constrain the reconstruction with the structure of the motion itself. Building on DynMF, we model a scene's motion as a handful of SE(3) trajectories, each rigid, and let every point follow one of them alone, never a blend. DynMF2 computes this factorization directly from 3D point trajectories, with no rendering, by Expectation-Maximization (EM). Its M-step fits, in closed form, every rigid motion to the points assigned to it, and its E-step reassigns every point to the motion that explains it with the least error. The background is simply one more motion, the camera's, so no masks are needed. Three tools then revise the factorization: requery adds trajectories where the rendering shows parts the tracker missed, merge joins motions that move together, and split separates those that do not. Thus the number of motions follows the scene. Without masks, DynMF2 clearly outperforms the mask-based baselines in view synthesis on iPhone and NVIDIA and in 3D tracking on iPhone. It recovers what masks leave out, from thin parts and details to small movers far in the background. Its motions segment the moving parts of MOVi-F and iTACO scenes competitively, although DynMF2 is never trained to segment. What moves in a scene is not decided in advance: it emerges from the rigid motions themselves.

title: Magnons in solids with correlated atomic and nanoscale disorder
text: Atomic defects and disorder affect both the microscopic magnon excitations and the macroscopic physical properties of real-world magnetic materials. The rationalization of this relation has hitherto remained elusive, because of the intertwined challenges of simulating with quantum accuracy atomic- and nanoscale inhomogeneities and correlations, and their effect on the magnon spectral function determining observables such as spin stiffness. Here, we introduce a theoretical and computational framework to address these challenges. First, we develop the Coupled Optimization of SpIN Environment (COSINE) algorithm for efficiently relaxing the atomic structure and magnetic configuration of a solid with defects or disorder to a local energy minimum. Then, we discuss how to efficiently obtain exchange interactions accounting for local compositional, structural, and magnetic-moment inhomogeneities. Finally, we develop a paraunitary unfolding approach for Bogoliubov bosons, which allows us to predict the magnon spectral function in materials with any magnetic order, including systems with canting and full, partial, or no magnetic-moment compensation. We showcase our approach in a representative defective ferrimagnet for generality, and then combine it with state-of-the-art spin-informed machine-learning potentials to quantitatively predict how nonuniformities in the spatial distribution of vacancy defects control blurring of effective magnon bandstructures.

title: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
text: We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite $G_N$. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in $G_N$ and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in $G_N$ yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

title: Vacuum correlation measures as CFT partition functions
text: We show that in any $d$-dimensional CFT, the vacuum sandwiched Rényi mutual information (SRMI) of integer order $n$ between two disjoint balls maps to a CFT partition function on a manifold of topology $\#^{n-1}(S^1 \times S^{d-1})$, with moduli fixed by the ball configuration and single-ball modular flow. At $n=2$, it is given by the thermal partition function on $S^{d-1}$, upper-bounding the von Neumann mutual information. For $n>2$, SRMI diverges at finite separation due to a hot-spot limit of the partition function. Explicit CFT evaluations agree well with density matrix computations.

title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
text: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen π0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a π0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID π0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.

title: LiveVAE: Causal Window Attention Makes Efficient Streaming Video VAE
text: While video diffusion models have grown faster and increasingly streamable, the video VAE remains a primary latency bottleneck across interactive generation and editing pipelines. Existing VAEs and their acceleration methods rely mainly on heavy convolutions or full frame attention, and most focus only on decoding, leaving encoding costly for streaming conditional generation and editing. This raises a natural question: Do video VAE encoding and decoding actually require such global spatiotemporal modeling? By analyzing the effective receptive fields of pretrained video VAEs, we find that both encoding and decoding a patch rely almost entirely on its spatial and temporal neighbors. To exploit this strong locality, we introduce LiveVAE, a streaming encoder and decoder built on causal window attention, which cuts per frame compute while keeping the temporal KV cache bounded for streaming. Decoupled encoder/decoder distillation followed by joint finetuning preserves the pretrained latent space, making LiveVAE a drop-in replacement for the original VAE. On MiniMax-H3, LiveVAE achieves 5.2-6.2x faster encoding and 3.0-3.3x faster decoding than the official VAE with higher PSNR. Paired with our dedicated inference infrastructure, LiveVAE pushes the speedup to 13.4x with almost no quality loss. Code and models will be released.

title: A comparison of two- and one-fluid dust solvers for dusty, supersonic turbulence
text: We model 3 and 10 $μ$m dust grains in supersonic, turbulent molecular cloud conditions to compare two different numerical methods solving dust coupled to gas through a drag term. One method models dust and gas as two separate species (two fluid) and the other the combination of dust and gas as a single mixture (one fluid) using the diffusion approximation. Simulations are performed in a 3D periodic box using the Phantom code. The gas probability distributions are consistent with a lognormal distribution for both methods and grain sizes. The dust distributions are different in the two methods, showing discrepancies particularly in regions of low density. The most significant difference between the two methods is in the dust-to-gas ratio distributions. Both methods peak at the mean dust-to-gas ratio of 0.01, but the two-fluid method has wider distributions than the one-fluid method suggesting excess dust concentration in dense filaments. Filaments are where the one-fluid method results are most accurate. The narrowing of the one-fluid distribution is also caused by the stopping time limiter used to maintain the terminal velocity approximation. This artificially makes the mixture more coupled in low-density regions. Our overall conclusion is that both methods are viable for the study of dust in molecular clouds, but that the correct method should be chosen based on the numerical Stokes number regime of the calculation to avoid numerical artifacts.

title: The thermodynamic budget of objectivity
text: An event becomes a fact when enough independent records of it exist such that no operation is possible that leaves all observers ignorant of it again. Records are physical, and creating, keeping, and destroying them have thermodynamic costs. We compute these costs exactly in a minimal broadcast model with a driven central qubit writing records into $N$ initially thermal registers, with work sources and baths at temperature $T$. The basic arguments for the operations are outlined here, with full treatment in the text. Creation of one event record at redundancy $R$ and information deficit $δ$ requires work $W \ge R\, k_\mathrm{B}T \ln 2\, (1-δ) H(\varepsilon)$, linear in redundancy at the Landauer coefficient. Recording in a basis misaligned by $θ$ with the einselecting interaction fails at a critical angle, $θ_c = 2\arcsin\sqrt{H_2^{-1}(δ)}$, beyond which objectivity is unreachable at any work, and below $θ_c$ the optimal work is a closed form in the pointer basis that minimizes the work of objectivity. Reducing objectivity is impossible at any work with access to fewer than $R - R_{\min} + 1$ records, while work protects nothing if given access. Inter-record redundancy is extractable free energy and erasing the accessed records yields a net gain of work beyond the first copy. The second law constrains the destruction of the correlation: erasing a fact from a sector an adversary controls dissipates at least the mutual information erased, but a consolidation dissipates nothing. Records in re-thermalizing media are nonequilibrium steady states, and the minimal power to maintain a record at $(R,δ)$ is the known two-state driving bound evaluated at the record-quality boundary.

title: A microscopic continuum model for moiré transition metal dichalcogenides
text: Twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (tTMDs) have emerged as a fascinating platform for many-body phases --- displaying fractional Chern insulators and superconductivity as a function of doping. Here, we give a microscopic derivation of a continuum model which accurately describes their bandstructure across a range of twist angles with angle-independent parameters. This angle-independent description rests on retaining both the monolayer valence and conduction bands, which introduce tunnelling paths through AB-stacked regions; upon downfolding to the valence band, these paths supply a substantial twist-tunable contribution to the interlayer coupling. We show that the model is a perturbation of a chiral model with a magic angle, explaining the near-ideal quantum geometry of the moiré bands. The model further produces a strongly different orbital magnetic moment to the single-orbital theory --- predicting an anomalous Landau level slope --- and a redistribution of charge between the layers, modifying the moiré ferroelectric potential.

title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
text: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.

title: Neural Network Decoders For Qubit Loss
text: Qubit loss is a significant source of error in many quantum hardware platforms, requiring circuits that periodically replace or reset qubits to maintain fault-tolerance. When the reset process includes loss-resolving measurements, this information can improve decoding and substantially reduce overhead compared to the case where this information is not available. Prior work has demonstrated loss-tolerant circuits for the surface code that show significantly improved thresholds and subthreshold scaling by incorporating loss information. However, the computational complexity of loss simulation and decoding, which falls outside of the usual stabilizer framework, has limited extending these studies to high-rate qLDPC codes, which are already challenging to decode in the absence of loss. In this work, we present a loss-aware convolutional neural-network (CNN) decoder framework that circumvents this challenge. Training is enabled by a novel sampler, \texttt{slim}, which achieves a throughput for circuits with Pauli noise and loss that is comparable to the state-of-the-art for pure Pauli noise. On the surface code with loss, the decoder matches the accuracy of computationally expensive most-likely error (MLE) decoders at much lower latency. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ bivariate bicycle (Gross) code, we study a walking syndrome extraction circuit with Pauli and loss errors. For physical error rates $p<1\%$, we observe a more than $10^3$-fold lower logical error rate for a pure loss model, relative to a pure Pauli error model at the same physical error rate, along with significantly enhanced sub-threshold error rate scaling. This demonstrates that loss-dominated error models can also significantly improve performance in a high-rate qLDPC code, and provides a simulation and decoder training platform that can be extended to other codes and algorithmic gadgets.

title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
text: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to $N \times M$ integrations when evaluating $N$ methods on $M$ benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.

title: A Reconfigurable Four-State Sensor Based on Orthogonal Thermal and Chemical Stimuli
text: This article presents a novel four-state refractive index (RI) sensor based on distinct phases of palladium (Pd) and vanadium dioxide (VO$_2$), controlled by orthogonal thermal and chemical stimuli. This is a numerical, simulation-only study: all results are obtained from two-dimensional finite-element method (FEM) simulations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported multi-state reconfigurable RI sensor tuned by external control. VO$_2$ serves as a phase change material (PCM) offering two thermally switchable phases with highly contrasting optical properties, while the hydrogen absorption property of Pd provides two additional phases. Combining these, four operational states are realized: (i) $α$-Pd/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (ii) $β$-PdH$_x$/low-$T$ VO$_2$; (iii) $α$-Pd/high-$T$ VO$_2$; and (iv) $β$-PdH$_x$/high-$T$ VO$_2$. Thermal crosstalk between Pd and VO$_2$ is mitigated through tungsten (W) doping of VO$_2$. This work further introduces conditional state sensitivity (CSS), a novel figure of merit quantifying the optical contrast between each state transition. The proposed sensor achieves a peak sensitivity of 2871 nm/RIU for the undoped reference configuration and 2798 nm/RIU for the practical W-doped device, together with a peak CSS of 16,872 nm/RIU, establishing it as a multi-state reconfigurable platform with reduced thermal crosstalk and potential applications in industrial safety monitoring and optical logic gates.

title: Decision and Support Mechanisms under Platform Information Overload: A Generative-Agent Experiment on College Application
text: People now make major personal decisions surrounded by far more online information than they can read, yet research says little about why information overload affects some people more than others. We study this question in Chinese college applications, a high-stakes decision made amid heavy online content where each list can be scored objectively once admission cutoffs are released. We simulated 90 applicants using language-model agents with family backgrounds from a national household survey. Each applicant wrote a list of eight programs alone and revised it four times: after parent and teacher advice, after reading a feed of twenty real online items, after a mentor gave advice based on the applicant's rank, and after a second mentor offered only emotional support. After each step, we scored the list and asked how anxious the applicant felt. When applicants decided alone, admission rates were similar across socioeconomic status (SES) groups. The gap appeared once family background entered through parents and teachers: low-SES parents asked for low tuition and schools near home, leaving fewer reachable programs, so admission was 100% for high-SES vs. 77% for low-SES applicants. The platform feed gave everyone the same amount of information but did not narrow this gap; applicants maintained their decisions while reporting higher anxiety. Personalized advice cut the gap to 3 points by raising low-SES admission from 80% to 97%, but led students to higher tuition and less preferred majors. Emotional support did not further lower anxiety, but helped applicants go back and use helpful items they had ignored. These simulation results suggest that when information is abundant, more of it neither improves decisions nor reduces inequality. Personalized information does both, while moving inequality from the outcome to its cost.

title: A Failure-Driven Data Flywheel for Post-Training Vision-Language-Action Models
text: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.

title: BridgeHammer: DNN Backdoor Attack via CPU-iGPU Shared-memory Rowhammer
text: Heterogeneous systems-on-chips (SoCs) share physical memory between CPUs and integrated GPUs (iGPUs), creating a path for CPU-side memory corruption to compromise the integrity of deep learning models used for iGPU inference. Implanting a backdoor that causes targeted misclassifications on trigger-bearing inputs while retaining accuracy on normal inputs requires carefully selected weight changes. However, realizing these changes presents two challenges: where to induce faults, since vulnerable DRAM locations may not contain the targeted weights, and when to intervene, since memory placement and fault injection must align with different stages of the model deployment lifecycle that involve two distinct computation domains. We present BridgeHammer, a Rowhammer-based backdoor attack that addresses these challenges by coordinating targeted weight placement before zero-copy binding for the iGPU and fault injection before inference. The iGPU then uses the corrupted model for subsequent inferences. We evaluate BridgeHammer on a heterogeneous Intel CPU-iGPU platform using OpenVINO, targeting ResNet-20, VGG-16, and ResNet-50 at both INT8 and FP32 precision. Across all six configurations, BridgeHammer achieves an 88.9% attack success rate (ASR) and 86.3% clean accuracy on average, with reliable target-page placement and bit-flip reproduction. These results demonstrate a new integrity vulnerability on heterogeneous CPU-iGPU SoCs, motivating cross-domain memory integrity protections.

title: First Order Real Resonant Digital Filters and A Novel Orthogonal State Generator
text: We describe FOREST, a real, first order digital resonant filter and orthogonal state generator. We show that in spite of the imaginary nature of the roots of the transfer function of a resonator, appropriate interpretation of this transfer function nonetheless leads to a practical first order filter with real coefficients. We use a discrete state space model of FOREST to predict the resonator properties, and implement the filter in digital signal processing slices on a digital signal processing platform. Applications are in real time digital signal processing, engineering fields such as mains electricity monitoring and motor control, any application requiring a phase locked loop, and physics applications utilising high-quality-factor resonators.

title: An Embedded Ergonomic Posture Monitoring and AI-Assisted Home Learning System on a Raspberry Pi 3B Edge Platform
text: During independent home study sessions, students frequently sustain improper sitting postures, accumulate excessive sedentary hours, and experience productivity loss from off-task digital distractions. Furthermore, learners often lack real-time pedagogical scaffolding for demanding self-study curricula. To mitigate these ergonomic and instructional challenges, this paper presents an affordable, privacy-preserving cyber-physical embedded system for domestic study spaces. Engineered on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B (1 GB RAM) paired with a UVC optical camera and a USB condenser microphone, the system executes on-device computer vision utilizing MediaPipe Pose and OpenCV to monitor upper-body alignment, sagittal head inclination, and coronal shoulder asymmetry in real time without persisting raw video streams. A deterministic finite state machine (FSM) quantifies active study durations, enforces health-compliant rest periods, and detects illicit smartphone usage. Simultaneously, an integrated multimodal AI tutoring agent parses voice and text queries via an encrypted API gateway, synthesizing Socratic conceptual hints rather than direct solutions. A lightweight parental web dashboard delivers encrypted session analytics and scheduling configurations. Empirical benchmarks on the physical prototype confirm an end-to-end inference latency of 244-250 ms at a 352x288 resolution (4.0-4.1 FPS), a trunk-angle estimation error of 4.39 degrees MAE over 5,760 synthetic ground-truth poses, a resident set size of 320 MB, a peak SoC temperature of 58.0 degrees Celsius under sustained load, and a 1.58 s total latency for the offline TTS feedback path, proving high practicality for resource-constrained edge deployment.

title: LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
text: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.

title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models
text: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.

title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
text: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.

title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
text: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios. Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
text: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.

title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
text: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.

title: Robust large-scale approximate solutions of the constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem
text: The Kemeny aggregation ranking problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the well-known Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy many fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall-tau distance which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. While having various applications in computational social choice, machine learning, operations research, and biology, the problem of computing the consensus rankings is NP-hard and encounters a severe bottleneck in practice. In this paper, we consider the more general Kemeny aggregation ranking problem under immutable input pairwise constraints and propose robust and scalable approximate methods with provable guarantees. We thus provide an algorithmic solution to the more general constrained problem of incorporating a posteriori immutable pairwise constraints into past rankings (e.g., historical voter ballots or legacy laboratory assays) without incurring the cost of generating new data. Our base algorithm $Γ$-XCC provides a source of rankings with a bounded constant approximation factor. $Γ$-XCC generalizes the Copeland ranking method and satisfies the constrained Condorcet consistency property, an extension of the Condorcet winner criterion for elections with immutable pairwise constraints. Thereby, our methods provide large-scale solutions that address the reliability and explainability issues. Our algorithms are also applicable to weighted tournaments with input pairwise constraints and satisfy similar properties in this larger context.

title: Shape-Aware Three-Way Merge for RDF Knowledge Graphs: The schema defines the conflict: an implementation and evaluation
text: Merging RDF serializations creates ordering conflicts and misses semantic ones. We describe and evaluate a three-way merge in which the schema defines a conflict: set algebra combines canonical triples, and a slot is contended only where a SHACL shape bounds its cardinality and both sides' changes cannot stand within that bound. Unbounded predicates union; contended slots go to a person. The same shapes graph validates the result. We do not claim the first three-way merge for RDF. Our contribution is an implementation in a production multi-agent store and an evaluation against a reimplementation of Quit Store's Context Merge overlap rule, which it extends rather than replaces, and six other strategies. Across five synthetic seeds, the shape-aware operator raised 33 conflicts, all true positives as judged by the same shapes that define them, with no triples lost or fabricated and no SHACL violations admitted. The context-overlap baseline, counted per slot, detected the same 33 conflicts but asked 845 questions. A replay built from recorded production incidents covers 105 human alias repairs (93 after excluding 12 chained pairs) and 939 duplicate-value incidents. It reproduces a triple-level limit: different names for one entity remain invisible (0 of 93 alias repairs detected, matching 0 of 21 synthetic cases). In a study of evolving shape contracts, merging shape declarations first handles the tested cardinality changes, while datatype evolution exposes a detector blind spot caught by post-merge validation. An oracle that reads no shapes agrees with the shipped operator on the facts and history of all 23 reachable single-slot cases. Under wrong shapes, a missing bound loses data silently and a spurious one only adds questions. The supported claim is fewer human decisions with nothing silently lost, for cardinality conflicts in one deployment, not general merge correctness.

title: Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Singularly Perturbed Systems
text: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have emerged as a flexible and efficient approach for enforcing dynamic safety constraints. In this paper, we consider a class of uncertain nonlinear systems with singular perturbations and develop an adaptive CBF framework for such systems to enforce safety constraints on both the slow and fast subsystems in the overall singularly perturbed nonlinear system with uncertain parameters. We first develop a robustness property showing that if an adaptive controller for the slow subsystem satisfies the slow CBF condition with an appropriate safety margin, then for sufficiently small values of the singular perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$, the slow subsystem remains within an $O(\varepsilon)$-neighborhood of its safe set. We then consider the more general case of safety constraints on both the fast and slow subsystems and provide conditions under which joint slow-fast safety is achieved despite the parametric uncertainties. The reduced-order slow model and the slow and fast CBF conditions are evaluated using an online parameter estimate and the parameter mismatch between the estimated and true reduced-order models is addressed via a state-dependent robustness margin in the CBF inequalities. To illustrate the proposed framework, we present simulation studies for two systems with parametric uncertainties: a synthetic two-time-scale fourth-order example system and a unicycle with a fast turn-rate actuator and an obstacle avoidance safety constraint.

title: Resolving cell states in spatial transcriptomics with SCATTER
text: A capture spot can contain transcripts from multiple cell types. Differences between spots may reflect changes in cell-type proportions, expression within a cell type, or both, making local cell-type expression difficult to infer from mixed counts. We developed SCATTER to estimate cell-type proportions and relative expression profiles for each cell type at each spot from spatial transcriptomic counts, coordinates, and annotated single-cell reference data. SCATTER weights reference cell profiles using local spatial context, then jointly fits the resulting profiles and cell-type proportions to reconstruct spot counts. Cell2location estimates regularize the proportions. After fitting, SCATTER uses learned gene-specific calibration factors and fitted proportions to allocate observed counts among cell types. In five pseudo-spot benchmarks constructed from imaging data, SCATTER achieved higher cross-spot correlations with measured expression for 82.8-99.8% of evaluated gene-cell type pairs in pairwise comparisons with DestVI, PANDA, and STged. In breast cancer Xenium data, it recovered gene expression associated with the tumor neighborhood and regulon scores. In breast cancer Visium data, inferred stromal and macrophage expression showed distinct associations with neighborhood malignant cell proportions. In multiple sclerosis brain tissue, SCATTER recovered lesion-associated glial expression programs. In colorectal cancer Visium HD data, it mapped cell-type-specific programs at the invasive front and ranked candidate ligand-receptor pairs. SCATTER enables analysis of spatial expression variation within cell types from mixed tissue measurements.

title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
text: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.

text: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
text: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
text: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.

title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
text: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen π0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a π0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID π0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.

title: Linear Single-Source Shortest Path, Almost
text: We give a comparison-addition algorithm for single-source shortest paths in undirected graphs with nonnegative real edge lengths. For each input with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, its expected running time is $O(m+n\log\log\log n)$. It terminates almost surely. Every terminating run returns exact distances and a shortest-path tree on the reachable vertices. The bound is independent of the ratio of edge lengths and is linear whenever $m=Ω(n\log\log\log n)$.

title: Sliding-Window Detection of Hidden Regimes under Stochastic Switching
text: A sliding-window average is a simple estimator of the current state of a hidden regime-switching process, such as a hidden Markov model. A longer window averages out more noise but is more likely to contain a switch, and the question is what such a switch costs. We analyse the decoder that assigns the average of the last $m$ observations to the nearest regime mean. For two regimes with conditionally independent, stochastically ordered observations, a switch inside the window, averaged uniformly over its positions and directions, causes an error with probability exactly $1/2$. Consequently, for every stationary switching law, the error is at most $\bar P(m)+\bar s(m-1)/2$, where $\bar P(m)$ is the stationary-weighted single-regime error and $\bar s$ the switch rate. Under Markov switching, time reversal shows that a window whose oldest and current regimes differ is misclassified with probability exactly $1/2$, however many switches it contains, and the bound is attained up to a factor $p_{\min}^{m-1}$. For Gaussian noise with common variance, minimizing the bound gives an explicit window length which, in units of $σ^2/Δ^2$, depends only on the expected number of switches in that time. As switching probabilities vanish proportionally, the optimal error is $\bar s\log(1/\bar s)/(2I)(1+o(1))$, with $I$ the single-regime Chernoff exponent. In the Gaussian case this is twice the Bayes error. For symmetric switching, exponentially weighted moving averages reduce this factor to at most $2\log2\approx1.39$, and two-block weights adapted to the switch rate attain the Bayes rate. For three or more regimes, long-window switch costs are set by the geometry of the regime means. For Markov-modulated random walks with $\pm1$ steps on a reflecting lattice, a position-aware decoder learns as fast as without walls under holding boundaries, while steps at bouncing boundaries carry none.

title: Floquet Decomposition: Floquet Multipliers and Time-Periodic Modes from Period-Sampled Snapshot Data
text: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) fits one constant linear operator to a sequence of snapshots. When the dynamics, or the view of them, vary periodically, as in a parametrically excited flow or a rotating structure seen in a fixed plane, no such operator exists, and stability is decided by the Floquet multipliers, the eigenvalues of the map over one period. In the paper that introduced DMD, Schmid observed that snapshots sampled at the period of an oscillatory flow would identify the Floquet matrix. We develop that observation into a method and analyze it. The Floquet decomposition (FD) applies DMD to fixed-rate data subsampled once per period; the ensemble Floquet decomposition (EFD) stacks the snapshots of each period into one column, giving one set of multipliers and phase-resolved modes. For linear time-periodic systems both are exact: FD when the measurement at one instant determines the state, EFD when the measurements over one period do---so EFD succeeds with partial measurements. EFD and Hankel (delay-embedded) DMD use the same data matrix with different shifts between columns. With $p$ samples per period, Hankel-DMD returns each Floquet mode as a carrier with sidebands, a comb of $p$-th roots of its multiplier, which the period shift collapses onto the multiplier. The methods are verified against known multipliers; outside their hypotheses, on nonlinear or noisy data, the estimated moduli are biased and are not decay rates. Measurements of velocity, scalars, and acoustic pressure in a swirl-stabilized combustor illustrate the choice of period, rank, and data scaling.

title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
text: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios. Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
text: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/ρ$, and its yield stress $σ_Y/ρ$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.

title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
text: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.

title: Tokenisation is not in APX
text: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

title: DexLink: Synthesizing Dexterous Behaviors from Chained Hand-object Poses
text: Synthesizing diverse dexterous manipulation policies is challenging: existing simulation-based approaches rely on human demonstrations which are difficult to scale, or use generic reward functions, which provide limited control over the hand-object interactions. We propose DexLink, which addresses these limitations by synthesizing diverse dexterous behaviors from sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates. Given key task waypoints, DexLink retargets static interaction templates to target objects using an optimization that preserves spatial hand-object relationships. It then links the retargeted poses into an approximate reference trajectory and uses residual reinforcement learning to refine this reference into a closed-loop policy in simulation. Experiments spanning single-hand, bimanual, articulated, and dynamic tasks demonstrate that DexLink provides fine-grained control over task timing, grasp types, and high-level execution. The modular interaction templates transfer reliably across object scales, instances, and categories; without object-specific human demonstrations, the framework also matches the performance of dense reference-tracking methods. Finally, zero-shot deployment of policies trained purely in simulation shows promise for the simulation-based framework.

title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
text: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
text: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
text: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.
