title: Magnons in solids with correlated atomic and nanoscale disorder
text: Atomic defects and disorder affect both the microscopic magnon excitations and the macroscopic physical properties of real-world magnetic materials. The rationalization of this relation has hitherto remained elusive, because of the intertwined challenges of simulating with quantum accuracy atomic- and nanoscale inhomogeneities and correlations, and their effect on the magnon spectral function determining observables such as spin stiffness. Here, we introduce a theoretical and computational framework to address these challenges. First, we develop the Coupled Optimization of SpIN Environment (COSINE) algorithm for efficiently relaxing the atomic structure and magnetic configuration of a solid with defects or disorder to a local energy minimum. Then, we discuss how to efficiently obtain exchange interactions accounting for local compositional, structural, and magnetic-moment inhomogeneities. Finally, we develop a paraunitary unfolding approach for Bogoliubov bosons, which allows us to predict the magnon spectral function in materials with any magnetic order, including systems with canting and full, partial, or no magnetic-moment compensation. We showcase our approach in a representative defective ferrimagnet for generality, and then combine it with state-of-the-art spin-informed machine-learning potentials to quantitatively predict how nonuniformities in the spatial distribution of vacancy defects control blurring of effective magnon bandstructures.

title: CARM1-mediated methylation controls interactions of ALIX with key partners important for cytokinesis
text: CARM1 is an arginine methyltransferase with a well-established role in regulating gene expression, but its cytoplasmic functions remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we identified ALIX, a cytoplasmic protein acting with the ESCRT-III machinery in numerous membrane remodeling events, as a partner and substrate of CARM1. We demonstrate that CARM1 methylates arginine residues within the proline-rich motif of ALIX. At the molecular level, ALIX methylation impairs SH3-dependent association with CD2AP, CIN85, and endophilin-A2 that are required for cytokinesis. Using a mutant of ALIX that is unable to bind these proteins, we further show that these interactions are essential for ALIX functions during cytokinesis. Mechanistically, ALIX methylation controls the levels of CD2AP at the cytokinetic midbody, which are known to be critical for successful cytokinesis. Altogether, this work highlights the significance of arginine methylation as a regulatory post-translational modification important for the final step of cell division, by modulating interactions between proline-rich domains and their SH3-containing partners.

title: Induced ubiquitination drives ER protein degradation through a VCP-dependent pathway
text: Heterobifunctional proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) enable degradation of disease-relevant proteins but have largely been limited to cytosolic targets. Using reporter cell lines and the dTAG system to recruit cytosolic E3 ligases, we found that luminal substrates are resistant to degradation, whereas ER membrane proteins are efficiently degraded across multiple topologies. CRISPR screens confirmed dependence on cullin–RING ligases but did not identify canonical ER-associated degradation (ERAD) components, except the AAA ATPase VCP. Combined loss of DERL1/2/3 and depletion of HRD1 did not impair degradation, further supporting independence from canonical ERAD machinery. Mechanistic studies showed that ubiquitination is required for VCP binding and that removal of ubiquitin chains releases VCP, suggesting direct extraction of ubiquitinated substrates. An atorvastatin–cereblon PROTAC induced VCP-dependent degradation of HMGCR, preventing its compensatory accumulation during statin treatment. Together, these findings support a model in which ubiquitination by a cytosolic E3 ligase is sufficient to engage VCP and drive extraction, potentially bypassing canonical ERAD machinery.

title: Addressing the biological and environmental dimensions of human reproductive decline
text: Global fertility rates have declined rapidly and universally in recent decades and most nations now have rates below replacement level. This striking reversal from previous concerns about population explosion raises the question: is falling fertility driven primarily by social and cultural change or is biological fecundity—the intrinsic capacity to reproduce—also deteriorating? This article posits that both processes are at work and that technical innovation alone is unlikely to reverse demographic decline. Socioeconomic and cultural factors remain central, particularly where education, career trajectories, housing costs, economic insecurity, and changing gender roles delay family formation. However, accumulating evidence suggests that biological reproductive capacity is also challenged by environmental toxicants, including endocrine-disrupting chemicals, air pollution, and climate-related stressors. These influences adversely affect ovarian and uterine function, spermatogenesis, embryo development, implantation, and pregnancy. Reproductive aging, driven in part by DNA damage response pathways and genetic susceptibility, further reduces both ovarian reserve and oocyte and sperm quality as parenthood is increasingly delayed. Technological innovation offers important but partial mitigation. Advances in fertility preservation, reproductive tissue engineering, in vitro gametogenesis, embryo modeling, genome editing, and automation of assisted reproductive technologies may improve diagnosis, treatment, scalability, and access for individuals. However, many approaches remain experimental, costly, ethically complex, or unlikely to reverse age-related, environmental, and socioeconomic drivers of fertility decline at the population level. The strongest long-term responses are therefore likely to combine treatment with prevention. This will require reducing reproductive toxicant exposures and climate-related harms, improving reproductive health surveillance and biomonitoring, and expanding cohort studies that link environmental exposures to reproductive outcomes. Equitable access to fertility care will also be needed, alongside social and political interventions that address healthcare affordability, childcare, housing, workplace flexibility, and parental support. Without such integrated action, declining fertility and fecundity are likely to reshape global population structures with profound societal consequences.

title: Endogenous variability in transcription factor concentrations shapes their genome-wide occupancy
text: The control of transcription factor (TF) concentrations is crucial for the precise regulation of gene expression and cell fate decisions during development. Yet, TF concentrations can display substantial temporal fluctuations and intercellular variations. How TF levels quantitatively shape genome-wide occupancy patterns remains largely unexplored. Here, we systematically investigate how physiological fluctuations in the concentrations of the pluripotency TFs OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG impact their genomic binding profiles in mouse embryonic stem cells. We uncover distinct concentration-dependent binding behaviors for each TF. NANOG occupancy increased monotonously with its concentration, even though a common set of regions made accessible by OCT4 and SOX2 are highly and uniformly bound at all NANOG concentrations. In contrast, SOX2 occupancy does not increase with its concentrations, while OCT4 displayed an intermediate behavior. Our results challenge the notion that TF binding follows simple mass-action dynamics and reveal a core set of pluripotency regions that are bound by all three TFs at all TF concentrations, revealing how pluripotency can be maintained despite marked fluctuations in core pluripotency TFs.

title: EcoVAE: a generative deep learning method for global species distribution prediction
text: Anthropogenic pressures on biodiversity necessitate efficient and scalable methods to predict global species distributions. Current species distribution models (SDMs) face challenges with large-scale datasets, complex species associations, and data quality. Here, we introduce EcoVAE, an autoencoder-based generative model that integrates bioclimatic variables with georeferenced occurrences. The model is trained separately for plants, butterflies, and mammals to predict global distributions at both genus and species levels. Through unsupervised learning, EcoVAE captures underlying distribution patterns from large-scale species occurrence data. It achieves high precision and speed, outperforming traditional SDMs in spatial block cross-validation. EcoVAE also reveals signatures of species associations that align with known prey-predator relationships. Taken together, these capacities enable the robust evaluation of global sampling efforts and interpolates distributions in data-limited regions, offering new applications for biodiversity exploration and monitoring.

title: Differential co-localization analysis of multi-sample and multi-condition experiments with spatialFDA
text: Advances in spatial omics data generation have led to an explosion in new datasets that record the spatial location of transcripts and proteins. However, challenges remain in the analysis of spatial omics data. One important analysis is differential cellular co-localization (CCoL): the quantification of the clustering, or spacing, of one or more cell types across multiple conditions. Our framework spatialFDA combines methodology from spatial statistics with functional data analysis to accurately quantify and test for differences between conditions in CCoL across spatial scales. Using two simulation studies, we show that spatialFDA performs well in controlled settings. Furthermore, spatialFDA recovers known biological processes in type-1 diabetes and adds insights about the CCoL strength in space. spatialFDA is readily available as an open-source Bioconductor R package.

title: Long-term neonatal mouse testis organ culture is associated with altered physiological polyunsaturated fatty acid remodeling
text: Spermatogenesis requires coordinated polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) remodeling to support membrane biogenesis and germ cell differentiation, yet its dynamics during long-term testis organ culture remain poorly defined. Here, neonatal mouse testes collected at postnatal day 6 were cultured at the gas-liquid interface for up to 44 days and compared with age-matched in vivo testes using histological and cytological analyses, lipid class profiling, fatty acid composition, transcriptomic reanalysis, and RT-qPCR. Cultured explants preserved seminiferous tubule organization sufficiently to support meiotic progression and the appearance of round, elongating and late spermatids, with rare spermatozoa detected by day 44, although progression was delayed and heterogeneous. Long-term culture induced a marked neutral lipid storage phenotype, characterized by accumulation of alkyl-diacylglycerols and cholesterol esters, increased lipid droplets and Plin2 upregulation. Fatty acid profiling revealed a major divergence from physiological development: explants failed to reproduce the in vivo enrichment of n-6 PUFA and very-long-chain PUFA, particularly within glycerophospholipids, and instead accumulated n-9 species, including 20:3n-9 and 22:4n-9. Consistently, genes involved in PUFA transport, desaturation and elongation were persistently upregulated. These findings identify altered PUFA remodeling as a metabolic feature associated with impaired and heterogeneous spermatogenic progression in long-term testis organ culture.

title: Optimized conformal selection: powerful selective inference after data-dependent score construction
text: We study data-driven score construction in conformal selection, which uses conformal p-values and multiple testing to select ‘interesting’ instances with large unobserved labels from a pool of unlabelled data, while controlling the FDR in finite sample. While existing solutions require the score function to be constructed independent of the calibration and test data, it is desirable to select or construct powerful conformity score in a data-driven manner and to leverage all labelled data for score training when presented with many score choices and limited labelled data. We propose Optimized Conformal Selection (OptCS), a general framework that allows valid multiple testing after flexible data-driven score construction. We introduce general conditions under which OptCS constructs valid conformal p-values despite substantial data reuse and handles complex p-value dependencies to maintain finite-sample FDR control. We instantiate this general recipe to propose three FDR-controlling procedures, each optimizing the models differently: (i) selecting a powerful score function among multiple candidates, (ii) training the score with all labelled data without sample splitting, and (iii) combining full-sample training and model selection. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methods via simulation studies and real applications in drug discovery and large language models.

title: De novo identification of protein domains in cryo-electron tomography maps from AlphaFold2 models
text: Sub-tomogram averaging of cryo-electron tomography maps often fails to reach the resolution required for atomic model building based on side-chain information, preventing accurate protein identification from the density alone. We develop DomainSeeker, which identifies protein domains by integrating AlphaFold2 models with experimental data. It partitions these models into domains by clique analysis of predicted aligned errors, fits them into segmented densities, and evaluates each fit globally and locally, deriving prior probabilities. Bayesian inference integrates the priors with cross-linking mass spectrometry, computing posterior probabilities. Applying prior probability analysis to mouse sperm microtubule doublet densities reveals higher recognition accuracy and resolution robustness than existing approaches. Incorporating cross-linking mass spectrometry for yeast nuclear pore complex densities further improves recognition performance and confidence. An interactive ChimeraX plugin facilitates user access. In this work, DomainSeeker addresses a bottleneck in in situ structural biology and supports visual proteomics in native cellular environments.

title: A Comparative approach to the effects of aqueous leaf and root extracts of Moringa oleifera on selected biochemical, haematological, and gut microbiota parameters of alloxan-induced diabetic Wistar rats
text: Background: Diabetes mellitus is one of the metabolic diseases known all over the world. This syndrome features symptoms like hyperglycaemia, oxidative stress, and associated organ dysfunctions. Moringa oleifera is a commonly known medicinal plant explored by many for its healing activities. This study seeks to find out the comparative effects of the aqueous root and leaf extracts of M. oleifera on some biochemical, haematological, and gut microbiota parameters in alloxan-induced diabetic Wistar rats. Methods: About thirty-six (36) adult Wistar rats were used in the study. These rats were randomly divided into six (6) groups, viz the normal control, diabetic control, diabetic treated with leaf extract, diabetic treated with root extract, diabetic treated with both leaf and root extracts, and diabetic treated with metformin, the standard drug. 150 mg/kg body weight of alloxan monohydrate was intraperitoneally given to the rats to induce diabetes. The experimental rats were exposed to treatments orally for 21 days. The study adopted standard methods for the estimation of the biochemical and haematological parameters, including fasting blood glucose, lipid profile, liver enzyme activities. Faecal sampling and culture-based methods were used to estimate the gut microbiota composition. Results: The results of the study show that both the extracts from the leaves and roots of M. oleifera lowered blood glucose levels and lipid profile status at p < 0.05 level of significance. Similarly, the haematological and antioxidant parameters were normalised compared with diabetic controls, with the leaf extract exhibiting moderately higher potency. The results of the gut microbiota analysis showed that both the leaf and root extracts of M. oleifera exerted the modulation of bacterial diversity, reduction of pathogenic taxa and enrichment of beneficial commensals, with the combined extract showing synergistic effects. Conclusion: The findings revealed that the leaf and root extracts of M. oleifera exert potent blood-sugar lowering and microbiota-modulating effects, hence support their use as a complementary therapeutic agent for the management of diabetes mellitus.

title: ZipAEr: A compressive convolutional autoencoder for high-dimensional spatial omics data at subcellular resolution
text: Background Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics, such as the CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager, enable the detection and quantification of thousands of RNA transcripts at subcellular resolution. While these data offer unprecedented insight, computational analysis remains a significant bottleneck. Current methods typically aggregate transcripts at the cell level, relying on precise cell segmentation—a notoriously difficult task in complex tissues like the brain. Deep learning autoencoders offer a segmentation-free, pixel-level alternative but face a major engineering hurdle: standard convolutional architectures expand channel depth while reducing spatial resolution. When applied to high-plex data, this “channel expansion” creates prohibitive memory requirements that exceed the limits of currently available hardware. Results To overcome this computational barrier, we introduce ZipAEr, a deep learning framework featuring a novel “dual-compression” architecture that simultaneously reduces dimensionality along both the spatial and channel axes. We validated ZipAEr on the CosMx human frontal cortex dataset—a publicly available resource that provides single-molecule subcellular resolution (20–50 nm) and ultra-high-plex coverage (more than 6,000 genes) in human brain tissue. ZipAEr effectively compressed these high-dimensional data, reducing memory requirements by factors of 195 × to 1,649 × (depending on model depth) while preserving essential biological information. In a downstream classification task identifying MAPT -positive neurons, a classifier trained on ZipAEr’s latent representations outperformed a baseline model with the same architecture but trained on raw data, with similar accuracy (69% vs. 68%) but substantially higher precision (75% vs. 68%) and specificity (69% vs. 48%). Conclusions ZipAEr establishes a scalable, segmentation-free framework for pixel-level analysis of high-plex spatial omics data. By resolving the channel-expansion problem, ZipAEr enables researchers to investigate subcellular mechanisms in complex tissues.

title: Obesity-associated changes in immune cell dynamics during alphavirus infection revealed by single-cell transcriptomic analysis
text: Obesity alters host immunity, resulting in worse disease outcomes following infection with various pathogens, including arthritogenic alphaviruses. However, the impact of obesity on the functional landscape of immune cells during acute arthritogenic alphavirus infection remains incompletely explored. Here, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to dissect the blood and tissue immune responses to Mayaro virus (MAYV) infection in lean and obese mice. Footpad injection of MAYV caused significant shifts in immune cell populations and induced robust expression of interferon response and proinflammatory cytokine genes and related pathways in both blood and tissue. In MAYV-infected lean mice, single-cell analysis of the footpad response revealed a unique macrophage subset (F4/80 lo MHCII +) with high expression of interferon-responsive genes that was replaced by an alternative, F4/80 int population in infected obese mice. Macrophages isolated from lean mice had higher levels of inflammatory gene expression. Furthermore, obese macrophages infected with MAYV and CHIKV ex vivo produce an immunoregulatory response (IL-10) compared to lean macrophages that produce a higher pro-inflammatory response (TNF). The stronger inflammatory response in lean macrophages was associated with less severe systemic disease in lean mice. These results provide evidence for the role of a unique population of macrophages that may contribute to the superior capacity of lean mice to control arthritogenic alphavirus infection. IMPORTANCE Arthritogenic alphaviruses—including chikungunya, Mayaro, and Ross River viruses—cause chronic, often disabling joint and muscle disease and are expanding into new regions, yet no approved therapies target the disease process itself. Obesity is a known risk factor for more severe outcomes after infection, but the underlying immune mechanisms have been unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that infection drives widespread interferon and inflammatory responses in blood and infected tissue and that obesity specifically alters the macrophage populations present at the infection site. Lean mice mount a highly activated, interferon-driven macrophage response linked to better control of local inflammation, while obese mice instead accumulate a related but less activated population enriched for necroptosis-associated genes and linked to greater tissue damage. These findings identify a specific macrophage subset as a likely contributor to the more severe alphavirus disease seen with obesity and a potential target for future therapies.

title: Subphenotyping and precision medicine approaches to ARDS
text: Sixty years after its initial description, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains defined by bilateral radiographic opacities and impaired oxygenation rather than by its underlying biology. This syndromic definition encompasses considerable clinical and biological heterogeneity, which may contribute to the ineffectiveness of pharmacotherapy trials to date. Subphenotyping aims to address this heterogeneity by identifying more homogeneous patient groups that differ in prognosis and/or treatment response. In this narrative review, framed by the research questions outlined in the 2023 European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines, we synthesize current approaches to ARDS subphenotyping across complementary domains: clinical (etiology, rapidly improving ARDS), physiological (gas exchange, recruitability, elastance, and ventilatory ratio), morphological (focal versus non-focal radiological patterns), and biological (individual injury biomarkers and the hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory subphenotypes). We examine their pathobiological basis, temporal dynamics, and retrospective evidence for heterogeneity of treatment effect, and consider how parsimonious biomarker panels, machine-learning classifiers, and adaptive basket trial designs may support clinical implementation. Prospective validation across diverse populations, including resource-limited settings, remains a key priority.

title: From reactive care to predictive wellness: AI-integrated preventive medicine and holistic health in the era of precision healthcare
text: As chronic disease, mental illness, metabolic disease, and aging populations rise in prevalence, there has been a shift from reactive healthcare to predictive and preventive medicine. The healthcare system has experienced radical changes in technology with the introduction of artificial intelligence (AI), precision medicine, wearable devices, digital biomarkers, genomics, and microbiome analysis, which can provide individualized risk assessments, continuous monitoring, and adaptive preventive measures. In addition, a holistic approach to health, including nutrition, exercise, sleep, mental wellness and lifestyle medicine, can help individuals sustainably optimize their health. This article will review how AI can be integrated into the field of preventive healthcare, including applications of digital therapeutics, personalized nutrition, remote monitoring, cancer prevention, cardiovascular prevention, and longevity medicine. While there are still many challenges surrounding bias, privacy and data security, equity, and ethical considerations, addressing these issues will be critical. Ultimately, combining AI-based predictive wellness with holistic healthcare will create new possibilities for future precision healthcare systems that emphasize personalized prevention and have a positive impact on the overall health of communities.

title: UAV-assisted GWAS identifies candidate loci associated with tuber yield and maximum canopy area in autotetraploid potato
text: Optimizing canopy architectural traits, which strongly influence light interception and stress tolerance, is a key strategy for enhancing crop performance. In this study, remote sensing-based canopy phenotyping was combined with SNP array genotyping to perform a genome-wide association study of yield and four canopy architecture traits in a diverse panel of 279 European autotetraploid potato cultivars. We identified eight significant SNP associations for yield and two for UAV-derived maximum canopy area, grouped within five candidate QTL regions. All significant associations were detected using non-additive allele-dosage threshold models, and six of the ten SNPs were identified by all population structure correction methods. Annotation of associated genomic regions highlighted several putative candidate genes with functions related to carbohydrate metabolism, chloroplast regulation, and cell wall pectin modification. Notably, candidate genes associated with yield and maximum canopy area included a pectin methylesterase (Soltu.DM.07G006430) and a pectin acetylesterase (Soltu.DM.01G041220), suggesting pectin-related processes may warrant further investigation in relation to these traits. Additional yield-associated candidate genes included a carbohydrate-binding-like fold protein (Soltu.DM.06G000220), an isoamylase (Soltu.DM.06G000420), a genomes uncoupled protein (Soltu.DM.06G000230), and a chloroplast translocon component (Soltu.DM.09G023310). These results demonstrate the value of UAV-derived phenotypes for GWAS in potato and provide candidate genomic regions and associated genes for future genetic and functional validation studies.

title: A unified framework for scalable differential testing for spatial omics
text: A key challenge in spatial omics is identifying features whose values vary depending on both cell type and the surrounding cellular niche. Existing methods designed for spatial transcriptomic data do not generalize well to modalities beyond count-based data and do not scale efficiently to current data volumes. Here we introduce spotGLM, a mixture-aware generalized linear modeling framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalities, and SPARROW, a power-preserving data distillation strategy for scalable inference. SpotGLM accommodates diverse data types including count-based gene expression, binomial isoform proportions and continuous chromatin accessibility scores within a unified statistical framework. We demonstrate the framework across spatial omics applications. On Visium HD data of colorectal cancer and mouse kidney, we recover cell-type-specific niche effects with serial-slice cross-platform validation. On long-read spatial RNA-seq data, we resolve cell-type-specific isoform switching in the mouse olfactory bulb. On spatial ATAC-seq data from mouse brain, we recover cell-type-specific spatial variation in regulatory motif accessibility.

title: Cross-cohort benchmarking and validation reveals task-dependent generalisability in tuberculosis blood transcriptomic classification
text: Whole-blood transcriptomic signatures are widely proposed for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, but reported performance often degrades when applied to new populations. We attempt to identify how much of this can be attributed to variables like model choice, panels, tasks and cohorts. We evaluated three trained classifiers (logistic regression, random forest and a multilayer perceptron) alongside two untrained scores (singscore and directional gene average). These were applied to four published panels: Kaforou (task-specific), Zak16, Sweeney3 and Berry86. Two panels were derived internally and benchmarked: Nat(mRMR), and Nat. They were compared with 50 size-matched random panels for control and significance testing. The analysis used 952 unique samples from 10 public GEO series across three diagnostic tasks, with rotating leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation. Two independent cohorts, GSE144127 active tuberculosis (ATB) vs other disease (OD) and GSE152218 (ATB vs latent tuberculosis (LTB)), served as external validation; in these, panels were compared with Holm-adjusted paired DeLong tests. Generalisability was strongly task-dependent: ATB vs LTB achieved excellent cross-cohort generalisation, consistent with previous reports. However, for ATB vs LTB random panels performed comparably, with performance only diverging when panel sizes shrank, indicating that the task itself is simpler than the others. ATB vs OD exhibited lower performance depending on the panel chosen (AUCs of 0.40-0.94; median 0.75), with the mRMR-derived panel accounting for the lower bound and failing to exceed random panels in any fold. LTB vs control (CON) showed no discernible signal across panels, models and random controls (AUC 0.39-0.78; median 0.57). Model architecture exerted minimal influence compared to the underlying biological signal, with an exception for the ATB vs OD task. Both of the final locked panels were then tested on fully independent cohorts (AUC 0.86 and 0.96). There was no significant difference between these and the published panels post Holm adjustment. An additional test on sarcoidosis had failure across all panels.

title: MGnify analyses in 2027: enhancing the depth and breadth of analyses across metabarcoding, unassembled metagenomes, and assembled datasets
text: Microbiome derived nucleic acid sequence analysis has become an increasingly important aspect of many scientific fields. MGnify (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics/) provides standardized, versioned analysis pipelines for the taxonomic and functional characterization of microbiome samples. The latest release of the MGnify pipelines (version 6) provides amplicon sequence variant analysis, expanded functional annotations including viral and mobilome for assembly analysis, and a streamlined minimal raw-reads analysis. We have improved the reusability of the pipelines through transition to Nextflow as a workflow language and have undertaken a substantial overhaul of our automation systems, using Prefect to orchestrate the pipeline execution. Finally, we have released a new version of our programmatic and bulk access services to better support large-scale computational access of data, as well as rationalizing our contig browser to improve in-browser performance. These improvements serve to support the use of MGnify pipelines and data products going forward, and improve the AI-readiness of our outputs.

title: DrugMAP 3.0: an enriched molecular atlas featuring ADMET endpoints, pharmacogenomic perturbations, and bioactivity atlas of drugs
text: The paradigm of targeted therapeutics has shifted from static drug-target interactions to systemic absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) endpoints, dynamic transcriptomic perturbation signatures, and quantitative binding affinities, thereby amplifying the demand for multidimensional pharmacological atlases. In other words, it is necessary to bridge systemic safety profiles, cellular responses, and molecular interactions. However, such integrative data were inadequately covered by existing databases. In this study, DrugMAP was therefore substantially updated, which accumulated (i) 112 470 fine-grained ADMET endpoint profiles covering 126 endpoints for over 7680 drugs; (ii) 406 360 pharmacogenomic signatures for 3484 chemical perturbations and 11 033 molecules; and (iii) a quantitative bioactivity atlas covering molecular affinities, cellular sensitivity, and cytotoxicity for over 15 812 drugs and 4155 drug-interacting molecules. With the growing demand for quantitative pharmacology and the rapidly growing interest in AI-assisted drug discovery, DrugMAP is expected to act as an indispensable supplement to existing databases to facilitate drug discovery. DrugMAP is freely accessible at https://idrblab.org/drugmap/.

title: Calibrated analysis framework for nanopore direct RNA sequencing uncovers cell-specific m⁶A proportions at conserved sites
text: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) coupled with Dorado modification-aware base calling enables mapping of epitranscriptomic modifications including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) at the level of individual RNAs. However, the sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility of this method remain unclear and have only recently begun to be addressed through systematic benchmarking studies. Here, we aimed to establish a best-practice workflow for DRS-based epitranscriptomic analyses. Specifically, we evaluated multiple Dorado versions and models using RNA isolated from primary cells and unmodified in vitro transcribed RNAs. We further utilized an m6A methyltransferase inhibitor as a specificity control. We established that stringent filtering is necessary to reduce the contribution of background and found that Dorado predictions captured an increasing proportion of GLORI sites detected at high m6A/A proportions. Further, by applying DRS to a human primary fibroblast and a HD10.6 neuron dataset, we detected differences in the predicted m6A/A proportions at conserved sites between these datasets. Our study thus presents the first systematic comparison of Dorado and GLORI from the same input RNA and expands characterization of the m6A epitranscriptome to fibroblasts and neurons.

title: Time-resolved single-cell phenotyping identifies two major classes of antimicrobial peptides with shared principles and key trade-offs
text: Cationic antimicrobial peptides are a broad family of host defence molecules that neutralize bacteria by permeabilizing one or more membranes and/or inhibiting intracellular targets. However, the relative timings of these effects and their impact at the population level remain poorly understood. Here we present a time-resolved single-cell pipeline for quantifying these effects in Escherichia coli. Applying this pipeline to 18 diverse peptides and peptidomimetics reveals shared activities, but with different kinetics, defining two classes with opposite trade-offs. Class I peptides cause abrupt growth arrest coupled with inner-membrane permeabilization and ribosome/DNA reorganization, conferring fast, multipronged action. However, rapid intracellular absorption by the first permeabilized cells depletes the extracellular pool, rendering these peptides ineffective against dense populations, including biofilms. Class II peptides act more gradually, with delayed or absent inner-membrane permeabilization, limiting their speed of action. However, this results in slower intracellular absorption and greater efficacy at high cell densities and against biofilms. These opposing trade-offs point to important immunological and therapeutic implications.

title: CARM1-mediated methylation controls interactions of ALIX with key partners important for cytokinesis
text: CARM1 is an arginine methyltransferase with a well-established role in regulating gene expression, but its cytoplasmic functions remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we identified ALIX, a cytoplasmic protein acting with the ESCRT-III machinery in numerous membrane remodeling events, as a partner and substrate of CARM1. We demonstrate that CARM1 methylates arginine residues within the proline-rich motif of ALIX. At the molecular level, ALIX methylation impairs SH3-dependent association with CD2AP, CIN85, and endophilin-A2 that are required for cytokinesis. Using a mutant of ALIX that is unable to bind these proteins, we further show that these interactions are essential for ALIX functions during cytokinesis. Mechanistically, ALIX methylation controls the levels of CD2AP at the cytokinetic midbody, which are known to be critical for successful cytokinesis. Altogether, this work highlights the significance of arginine methylation as a regulatory post-translational modification important for the final step of cell division, by modulating interactions between proline-rich domains and their SH3-containing partners.

title: Normalized Nucleic Acid Payload in Lipid Nanoparticles: A Perspective on the Harmonization of Published Data
text: Precise and consistent reporting of the nucleic acid payload per lipid nanoparticle (LNP) is important for advancing the understanding and development of nanomedicines. However, the reported number of RNA molecules ranges between ∼1–300 in recent investigations. To evaluate the RNA payload across investigations, we introduce and apply a normalized nucleic acid payload metric which accounts for differences in LNP size, nucleotides per RNA and N/P charge ratio. The normalized payload results in a similar value for siRNA- and mRNA-containing LNPs of different LNP sizes, where the average value of 73 ± 17 nucleotides/zeptoliter agrees well with the expected payload density based on molecular packing arguments. The use of normalized payload harmonizes the reported payload, complements existing payload metrics and enables comparison across samples and measurement techniques at both the single-particle and ensemble-average level.

title: Combinatorial synthesis of novel polycations for mRNA delivery via Ugi 4-component polymerisation
text: RNA therapeutics offer solutions to treat previously undruggable diseases, but successful RNA delivery requires efficient and safe vectors. Cationic polymers provide one technology platform for this delivery, however, despite many current materials in this class showing promise when tested in cells, none have yet progressed to the clinic. Existing commercially available polymers evaluated for RNA delivery have either limited structural variety or poorly addressable functionality, which means that tuning of pharmaceutical properties is difficult. In order to control better some parameters of key importance for RNA delivery, such as assembly with nucleic acids, internalisation into target cells and degradation after payload release, new chemistries and structures are needed. Multicomponent polymerisations provide a means to access easily highly functionalised materials, thus here we report the use of Ugi 4-component polymerisation to synthesise a range of cationic polyamides. We demonstrate a facile synthetic route to a diverse polymer library which, when screened for in vitro transfection with mRNA, showed several polymer structures with high potency in selected cell lines.

title: Genetic circuit design across species and contexts: progress and future directions
text: Synthetic biology enables programmable control of microbial behavior. This has diverse applications across many sectors of the economy. For nearly a quarter century, synthetic biologists have reported ever more powerful and complex genetic systems in the model bacterium Escherichia coli. This has been driven by composable parts that perform as expected in well-defined laboratory conditions, which creates a positive feedback loop of increasing design complexity. While impressive, composability within one host does not by itself enable portability–predictably moving functional designs between host organisms and conditions. Yet, portability is essential for real-world applications. The lack of portability limits current practice - essentially circuits are re-engineered to suit each new host and context. However, a growing body of recent work has hinted that there may be generalizable rules for transferring parts and designs from E. coli to other bacteria. Thus, this review describes recent advances in the design and implementation of genetic circuits in diverse bacterial hosts and environmental conditions, highlighting key considerations for a new era of engineering portable genetic designs.

title: Building without Cells: Integrating Biomolecules, Synthetic Materials, and Devices into Cell-Free Systems
text: Bottom-up synthetic biology thrives at the intersection of biotechnology, chemistry, physics, and engineering. Bringing together researchers from these diverse fields is essential not only for understanding how living systems work but also for building molecular systems with functions and capabilities that go beyond them. The Special Issue “Cell-free systems” aims to showcase advances in the design and construction of cell-free systems, constructed only from defined components, and to explore methodologies and strategies for integrating biomolecules, synthetic chemicals, polymers, and nano-/micro-scale devices that exhibit valuable functions for practical application. Most cell-free systems consist of a large number of components, and their functions depend on how those components are combined. Although most of the components are well defined, creating such multi-component molecular systems and optimizing them to express the desired function remains challenging.

title: AI and biofoundries in metabolic engineering: linking biological data, predictions, and experimental validation
text: Metabolic engineering enables the production of chemicals, proteins and biopolymers from renewable resources, but its broader applications remain constrained by inefficient pathways, suboptimal enzymes and slow design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycles. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to address these limitations, yet translating computational predictions into biological improvements requires appropriate input data and experimental evaluation of model outputs. In this review, we examine AI applications in pathway design, protein and enzyme engineering, and genome-scale metabolic modeling from an input-output perspective, focusing on the biological information required and the predictions or engineering designs generated. We compare their practical advantages and limitations and outline how these modules can be integrated with biofoundry workflows. However, compared to rapidly developing AI tools, actual experimental implementation remains limited. Biofoundries provide platforms to validate AI-based designs through automated workflows, generating standardized experimental datasets at high throughput for model training, validation and refinement.

title: The EHRNavigator multi-agent system for patient-level clinical question answering over heterogeneous electronic health records
text: Clinical workflows increasingly depend on timely, context-aware access to electronic health record (EHR) data, but heterogeneous institutional schemas limit the portability of information-retrieval tools. Large language model (LLM)-based question-answering systems show promise yet typically address a single modality and are evaluated on point-in-time benchmarks. We introduce EHRNavigator, a multi-agent system that adapts to new EHR schemas without supervised training and answers patient-level questions by reasoning across structured tables, unstructured clinical narratives, and temporal relationships. Specialized agents iteratively explore EHR structure and use tools to formulate cross-modal queries without manual schema mappings. We evaluated EHRNavigator on three public benchmarks spanning structured, unstructured, and multimodal questions, and on an institutional OMOP database at Yale New Haven Hospital. EHRNavigator outperformed chain-of-thought prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and dedicated text-to-SQL baselines. Without schema-specific retraining or manual table mapping, it achieved 85% accuracy on a physician-curated patient-trajectory benchmark with interactive latency. By returning answers with supporting structured and unstructured evidence and operating across MIMIC and OMOP schemas, EHRNavigator provides a reproducible cross-institution foundation for LLM-based clinical question answering.

title: Bridging a gap in meta-analytical practices: A superior approach for converting standardized beta weights to correlations.
text: Meta-analysis is crucial to coping with the contemporary landscape of exponential scientific output. Hindering this effort is effect size variety, with standardized beta coefficients, regression weights, elasticities, or partial correlations proven to be nonequivalent to zero-order correlations, despite that these parameters are often aggregated together. Addressing this challenge, we developed two novel approaches that convert standardized betas to correlations, uninformed and informed imputation, and compare their accuracy and bias against the traditional method of Peterson and Brown (2005). In our simulations, we tested matrices from three to 10 variables, finding that Peterson and Brown's technique is inherently biased and less accurate and misestimates error variance. Uninformed and informed imputation were, on average, more accurate and unbiased and, by merging sampling error with imputation error, correctly identify error variance. Due to imputation error, reporting beta weights alone typically destroys 95% to over 99% of the information originally held by a full correlation matrix. For fields that almost exclusively report betas, such as economics, it necessarily hampers them from becoming cumulative sciences. We recommend that all previous uses of Peterson and Brown be reevaluated, future aggregations of standardized beta weights use our provided imputation techniques, and correlation matrices be routinely reported. title: Toward Personalized Neurofeedback for Meditation
text: Objectives Neurotechnological tools that provide real-time feedback during meditation have generated growing interest as potential aids for accelerating contemplative learning and enhancing mental health outcomes. Currently, the empirical evidence for neurofeedback-assisted meditation is preliminary, and many systems rely on generalized neural targets that may overlook substantial individual variability. Methods This conceptual paper draws on a narrative (non-systematic) synthesis of the literature to propose a testable research agenda, address limitations of neurofeedback, and outline necessary community partnerships. Results Current evidence is limited in demonstrating durable or transferable improvements in meditative skill. In the realm of meditation, individual variability can markedly affect how users respond to protocols and acquire meditative skills. Personalized interventions, tailored to these individual differences, are thus identified as a potential research direction within the field. Conclusions We propose an embrace of individual differences to guide the development of personalized neurotechnological interventions (a “qualia compass” calibrated to each practitioner), on the premise that personalization may increase efficacy and reduce adverse effects. As interest in the cognitive and health benefits of meditation continues to grow, the philosophical and cultural challenges involved in translating these contemplative practices into neurotechnological frameworks also require consideration. Although these complexities emphasize the importance of individualized, multimodal approaches, a personalized approach alone is insufficient to ensure the effective and ethical integration of neurofeedback into the modern mindfulness movement. Preregistration This conceptual paper is not preregistered.

title: The autoPET3 challenge: Automated lesion segmentation in whole-body PET/CT — Multitracer multicenter generalization
text: We report the design and results of the third autoPET challenge (MICCAI 2024), which benchmarked automated lesion segmentation in whole-body PET/CT under a compositional generalization setting. Training data comprised 1014 [ 18 F]-FDG PET/CT studies from the University Hospital Tübingen and 597 [ 18 F]/[ 68 Ga]-PSMA PET/CT studies from the LMU University Hospital Munich, the largest publicly available annotated PSMA PET/CT dataset to date. The held-out test set of 200 studies covered four tracer–center combinations, two of which represented unseen compositional pairings. A complementary data-centric award category restricted participants to a fixed baseline model to isolate data handling strategies. Seventeen teams submitted 27 algorithms, predominantly nnU-Net-based 3D networks with PET/CT channel concatenation. The top-ranked algorithm achieved a mean DSC of 0.66, FNV of 3.18 mL, and FPV of 2.78 mL across all four test conditions, improving DSC by 8% and reducing the false-negative volume by 5 mL relative to the provided baseline. Ranking was stable across bootstrap resampling and alternative ranking schemes for the top tier. Beyond the benchmark, we provide an in-depth analysis of segmentation performance at the patient and lesion level. Three main conclusions can be drawn: (1) in-domain multitracer PET/CT segmentation is sufficient and likely approaching reader agreement; (2) compositional generalization to unseen tracer–center combinations remains an open problem mainly driven by systematic volume overestimation; (3) heterogeneity and case difficulty drive performance variation substantially more than the choice of algorithm among top-ranked teams.

title: CONORM: Context-Aware Entity Normalization for Adverse Drug Event Detection
text: Adverse Drug Events (ADEs) are a critical aspect of patient safety and pharmacovigilance, with significant implications for patient outcomes and public health monitoring. The increasing availability of electronic health records, social media, and patient forums provides valuable yet challenging unstructured data sources for ADE surveillance. To address these challenges, we introduce CONORM, a framework integrating Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Entity Normalization (EN) for ADEs across diverse textual domains. CONORM comprises CONORM-NER and CONORM-EN, featuring a dual-encoder with Dynamic Context Refining (DCR). DCR adaptively combines isolated entity embeddings with contextual representations. Our analyses demonstrate that CONORM adapts to text formality, enhances precision on out-of-distribution concepts, and reduces errors compared to context-agnostic baselines. CONORM was evaluated on tweets, forum posts, and structured product labels, covering 30,000 annotated ADE mentions across the SMM4H, CADEC, and TAC datasets. It achieved end-to-end F1-scores of 63.86%, 72.45%, and 84.99%, surpassing the strongest baseline by an average margin of 20%. These results highlight CONORM’s robust adaptability across domains. CONORM offers a scalable solution for pharmacovigilance, with pre-computed target embeddings enhancing inference efficiency. Its generalization establishes it as a robust tool for ADE surveillance. The source code is available at https://github.com/ds4dh/CONORM.

title: Contextual Bandits and Optimistically Universal Learning
text: We consider the contextual bandit problem in general action and context spaces. This generalizes the standard multiarmed bandit to the case where side information is available—for example, patients’ records or customers’ history—which allows for personalized treatment. We focus on consistency (vanishing regret compared with optimal policy) and show that for large classes of non-independent and identically distributed (non-i.i.d.) contexts, consistency can be achieved regardless of the reward mechanism, a property known as universal consistency. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work giving consistent algorithms for any contextual bandits instance with finite action spaces and i.i.d. contexts. Further, we first give necessary and sufficient conditions on the context-generating process for universal consistency to be possible. Second, we show that there always exists an algorithm that guarantees universal consistency whenever this is achievable, referred to as optimistically universal. Interestingly, for finite action spaces, the processes admitting universal learning are exactly the same as in the full-feedback supervised setting: learning can be performed with partial feedback without any generalization cost. The algorithms balance a trade-off between generalization (similar to structural risk minimization) and personalization (tailoring actions to specific contexts). Lastly, we investigate the benefit of continuity assumptions on rewards for universal learning. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.2024.0443 .

title: Subphenotyping and precision medicine approaches to ARDS
text: Sixty years after its initial description, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains defined by bilateral radiographic opacities and impaired oxygenation rather than by its underlying biology. This syndromic definition encompasses considerable clinical and biological heterogeneity, which may contribute to the ineffectiveness of pharmacotherapy trials to date. Subphenotyping aims to address this heterogeneity by identifying more homogeneous patient groups that differ in prognosis and/or treatment response. In this narrative review, framed by the research questions outlined in the 2023 European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines, we synthesize current approaches to ARDS subphenotyping across complementary domains: clinical (etiology, rapidly improving ARDS), physiological (gas exchange, recruitability, elastance, and ventilatory ratio), morphological (focal versus non-focal radiological patterns), and biological (individual injury biomarkers and the hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory subphenotypes). We examine their pathobiological basis, temporal dynamics, and retrospective evidence for heterogeneity of treatment effect, and consider how parsimonious biomarker panels, machine-learning classifiers, and adaptive basket trial designs may support clinical implementation. Prospective validation across diverse populations, including resource-limited settings, remains a key priority.

title: Determinants of the Response to BTK Degraders (BTKd) in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] The aim of the REBELLE cohort - bio-collection is to collect samples from patients with Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia candidates or those exposed to BTK degraders to evaluate the mechanisms of resistance to these new molecules. To do this, an additional blood or bone marrow sample to those planned in the context of patient care or a residual lymph node biopsy sample will be collected after signing consent.

title: Spatiotemporal Single-cell Atlas of Peri-implant Soft Tissue Healing
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: RECRUITING] This study aims to explore the dynamic changes in different cell types and their molecular regulatory mechanisms during the healing process of peri-implant soft tissues, using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST). The research will focus specifically on the healing of soft tissues around dental implants in human subjects with the use of a healing abutment. Participants in the healing abutment group will have a micro healing abutment placed immediately after implant placement. Tissue samples will be collected at various time points (Day 4, Day 14, and Day 70) to construct a detailed single-cell map of the healing process. Spatial transcriptomics will be integrated to preserve tissue architecture, enabling the identification of the spatial distribution of different cell types and their interactions within the peri-implant microenvironment. This combined approach will allow for a comprehensive characterization of cellular interactions, spatial gene expression patterns, and regulatory networks specific to healing abutments. The goal is to identify key regulatory factors that could improve peri-implant soft tissue healing and help prevent peri-implantitis.

title: Molecular Characterization of Response to Immunotherapy in Renal Cell Carcinoma
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING] The treatment paradigm of metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) includes immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based combinations, either dual ICIs (nivolumab plus ipilimumab) or combinations of an ICI targeting PD-1/PD-L1 plus a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (VEGFR-TKI). One of the main challenges in selecting first-line treatment for mRCC is the lack of predictive biomarkers of treatment response. The aim of the ReNAL study is to characterize the molecular profile of mRCC and identify specific genomic alterations associated with primary resistance to treatment, angiogenesis-dependent disease (patients benefiting from VEGFR-TKI-containing regimens), and immune-dependent disease (patients achieving complete or partial response to nivolumab plus ipilimumab or prolonged disease control with immunotherapy following VEGFR-TKI interruption or discontinuation).

title: Deep Learning Framework for Continuous Depth of Anesthesia Forecasting
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in anesthesiology offers the potential to shift patient monitoring from reactive to predictive. Deep learning architectures, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, excel at processing complex, time-series data to forecast future clinical states. While standard PK/PD models (such as the state of the art Eleveld model for Propofol and Remifentanil) estimate target-site drug concentrations (Ce), they do not account for real-time, patient-specific dynamic responses. This study aims to deploy an AI framework designed to predict future physiological states.

title: Adaptive Versus Fixed Mobile Exercise in Preservice Teachers
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] This four-center randomized trial compares two mobile exercise prescription policies in preservice teachers in Uzbekistan. Both groups use the same OptiForma application and exercise library for 16 weeks, with three nonconsecutive sessions per week. In the adaptive arm, prescribed active time is modified using rules based on completion, perceived exertion, symptoms and current fatigue. In the fixed arm, the initial prescription is retained, with the same safety reductions when required. The primary outcome is the number of fully completed 20-m shuttle-run segments at week 16. Physical fitness tests, practicum fatigue, adherence and harms are assessed separately. Follow-up continues through week 28.

title: Genome-Wide Assocation Study in Patients With Brain Injury Associated Fatigue and Altered Cognition (BIAFAC)
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: COMPLETED] The aim of this study is elucidate genetic susceptibility of patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and symptoms of Brain Injury Associated Fatigue and Altered Cognition (BIAFAC) using genome-wide association study (GWAS).

title: Multimodal Biomarkers and Precision TMS for Postpartum Depression
text: [Fase: NA; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The purpose of this study is to identify multimodal biological markers associated with postpartum depression (PPD) and to evaluate the effectiveness of precision brain stimulation treatment. PPD is a common mental health condition after childbirth that can affect maternal well-being and early child development. Current identification of PPD relies largely on clinical assessments and screening questionnaires, which may not fully capture underlying biological changes. This study uses brain activity, cardiac signals, blood-based biomarkers, interoceptive assessments, and clinical measures to characterize multimodal biological profiles associated with PPD and treatment response. The main questions it aims to answer are: * What multimodal biological differences exist between women with diagnosed PPD and healthy comparison groups, including postpartum and non-postpartum controls? * Which biological or psychological markers can predict whether a patient will respond well to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) treatment? * Can a clinical model be created to help doctors choose the best treatment based on these markers? The study focuses on characterizing multimodal biological differences in women with diagnosed PPD and examining clinical response profiles following rTMS treatment, rather than predicting the onset of PPD in the general population. Participants will: * Undergo electroencephalography (EEG) using a 128-channel cap to measure neural activity. * Have electrocardiography (ECG) recorded to analyze heart rate variability and autonomic function. * Provide blood samples to measure inflammatory cytokines, endocrine levels, and metabolic markers. * Complete Interoceptive Assessments (tasks to measure awareness of internal body signals) and clinical psychological surveys. * Complete follow-up assessments via online surveys and scheduled visits at 2 weeks, 1 month, and 3 months postpartum. Participants in the PPD group will: * Receive 4 weeks of high-precision, robot-guided rTMS treatment (20 sessions total). * Undergo pre-intervention multimodal assessments, including EEG, ECG, blood biomarkers, and interoceptive tasks, to identify potential predictors of clinical response to rTMS treatment.

title: Assessing of Behavioral Risk and Response to Electromagnetic and Psychedelic Therapies
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] PRE-EMPT will assemble a cohort of 150 participants from three populations (low risk, intermediate risk, and high risk for self-harm). We will obtain clinical assessments, structural and functional MRI utilizing tasks pioneered by our team to assess cognitive control (CC) and emotion regulation (ER), and peripheral circular RNA (circRNA) levels to characterize the molecular brain states associated with behavioral risk. The clinical, imaging, and transcriptomic data will be fused and jointly analyzed to increase the accuracy of our risk prediction models. PRE-EMPT in three separate Aims will then prospectively assess three promising and innovative interventions for their potential to reduce suicidal ideation and alter activity in key neural networks: 1) neurofeedback (NF) using real-time fMRI with simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG), 2) a form of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) called accelerated intermittent theta burst stimulation (aiTBS) with dose optimization through electric field modeling; and 3) psilocybin assisted therapy (PSI), with flexible dosing plan to maximize the depth of psychedelic experience. These therapies were chosen based on our team's prior work in all three interventions demonstrating rapid action and large effects.

title: Development of a Non-invasive Screening Tool to Predict Metabolic Dysfunction-associated Steatotic Liver Disease
text: [Fase: s/d; Estado: RECRUITING] A generic screening study to establish structural and/or functional baselines of specific organs.

title: ANIMATOR - RehUP BCI Controlled Robotic Therapy vs. an Attention-based Control
text: [Fase: PHASE2; Estado: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] ANIMATOR aims to examine how BCI therapy vs. attention based control therapy can be used to treat people in the chronic phase of stroke with moderate to severe upper extremity impairment. This interventional trial has two phases: Pilot (10 consecutive days of intervention) and a Randomized Phase (24 sessions over 8 weeks).

title: Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists
text: Cuts to Medicare physician payment rates for certain same-day services could impact some specialists more than others.

title: RFK Jr. weighs in on plan to detonate toxic material in Iowa
text: This morning, the Army plans to detonate a cache of “dangerously degraded” toxic material in Iowa, with experts warning of dangerous health consequences:
